## Context

The Open Source CMS (OSCMS) project is expected to be used by people who have little experience in developing software.
To make sure everyone is able to contribute to the project, the platform should be easy to test and maintain.

## Options
### [Selenium](http://selenium.dev/)
Selenium is a well established open source framework to test front-end code.
Due to the high usage and maturity of this framework, it will be easy to get help and use the community resources and documentation.

### [NightmareJS](http://nightmarejs.com/)
NightmareJS is a new and less known framework to test front-end code.
It focuses on simple, understandable tests.
However, due to its new status, resources such as documentation and community support might not be as mature as those available for Selenium.

### [No test framework](https://github.com/oscms/cms-starter-kit)
As stated in the README of the CMS-starter-kit, it is an app that's meant to be integrated into a CMS environment.
The "tests" are unit tests, run through the console.
It was also noted that, using PHPUnit in combination with it, one would not get a UI test framework either.

### Other frameworks

There exist other frameworks to test code.
The most well known are [PHPUnit](http://phpunit.de/) and [XUnit](http://xunit.org/).

## Decision

Use [NightmareJS](http://nightmarejs.com/)
Because of the maturity of Selenium, using it to test front-end code is well supported and easy.
NightmareJS follows a similar approach, as it focuses on simple and understandable tests.
NightmareJS gives newcomers to the testing world a lighter, more approachable framework.
It focuses on simple, understandable tests.

NightmareJS seems to be in its early years of development.
Because of that, it won't be as mature as Selenium, as its documentation is less elaborate and community support is less experienced.

## Consequences
Using NightmareJS should give new developers to the Open Source CMS platform more resources to learn the platform, and make them contribute more.
However, they might need extra support due to their lack of knowledge in establishing automated tests.

There are two options how to proceed when the platform will be integrated into a CMS environment.
In combination with [WebDriverIO](http://webdriver.io/), the platform will use [NightmareJS](http://nightmarejs.com/) as the framework to test the front-end code.
In other combination, the platform will use the [NightmareJS](http://nightmarejs.com/) framework alone.
Both frameworks have the option to use the [NightmareJS Web Test API](http://nightmarejs.com/web-api.html) as [Web UI Automation API](https://docs.google.com/angular/fire-update-9.x/web-ui-automation.html).
NightmareJS gives people the opportunity to write tests for UI/UX, to add new features, or other changes to the CMS.

Date: 2021-06-02

## Status

Accepted

## Context

Back-end APIs tend to be event-driven, as they're frequently consumed by clients that can't or don't want to be kept up to date about changes to their data. Also, APIs are typically event-driven for loose coupling of their components.

## Decision

We'll use [Event Sourcing](https://martinfowler.com/eaa/event-sourcing.html) in the back-end.

## Consequences

Event-sourcing is a set of architectural best practices, not just a pattern for building event-driven systems. It includes:

* **All writes are to events and projections.**
* **Event logs are stored for audit and by using historical events to reconstruct the state.**
* **The state is held by projections using the read model projection model.**
* **Events are stored in an event log.**

Event-sourcing keeps a history of changes to an entity in an event log, and a state held by read model projections.

Storing events in the event log is used to reconstruct the state of the entity using the read model projection model.

Reading the state requires only a read model projection to read either the current state or a historical state by replaying the events.

If multiple read models need to know about the same event, then the event needs to be broadcast to all read models listening on that event.

Event-sourcing ensures that all operations on an entity are captured as part of an event. This enables both read and write operations to be done in a safe manner using the read model projection model.

Since we use a projection model, any change to a projection's behaviour is done by updating the projection's implementation. This ensures that any change to the projection's behaviour will not affect historical events logged for the entity.

Event-sourcing enforces all writes to happen through the event-sourcing model, and all read operations to happen using read model projections. The read model projection model provides a level of guarantee that the read data will never change, which is vital for many client applications.

As we'll use a projection model for reading our state, this means that the projection that we use for reading the state will have all operations that affect the state moved into it. This makes our implementations of the read models simpler to work with, because we know that we only have to update the state via the projections.

The read model projection model is also used in DDD to separate read data from the state held by the projection. The read model projection model is used for read-only operations, whereas the use of a different projection model is done for all write operations.

Using the projection model enables us to distinguish between two ways of reading data. To distinguish these two ways of reading, we can use the following questions:

* **Read operation is written to the projection?**
  * If yes, we'll update the projection.
  * If no, we'll read from the projection.

It's important to note that there's no distinction between read and write operations in the projection. The read operations update the projection via the read model projection model. The projection has no read operations that are independent to the projection's implementation.

If the projection implements an API with a dependency injection system, and that system is the source of truth, we can distinguish between read and write operations by seeing that the read API has multiple implementations using the read model projection model. The write API implementation is unique to the projection, and is used for read and write operations using the read model projection model.

Our API only has one implementation, which is used for read and write operations using the read model projection model.

Due to this dual-use of the API, the read model API needs to be protected from being changed. The projection system allows us to distinguish between read and write operations by seeing the API has multiple implementations, the read model API is protected because if we used a single implementation for read and write operations, there's no way to distinguish between read and write operations.

By not using a read model projection model, we enable read operations to always read the current state held by the projection. The read model projection model would mean that there was a single read implementation, that was used for read and write operations. We can mitigate this issue by distinguishing between read and write operations by the fact that if we are writing to the projection, then we will be using the write implementation, and if we are reading from the projection, then we will be using the read implementation.

The use of projection models is covered in this [pattern](https://martinfowler.com/eaa/ProjectionModel.html).

See this article for more details: https://martinfowler.com/articles

## Context and Problem Statement

There are two components that require registration of handlers in the message bus:

* the broker
* the processor

Both components use the message bus to send or receive messages.

What is the proper way to register a handler for each component?

## Considered Options

### 1. Register handlers in the message bus and forget about the broker

A handler is created in the client and registered with the message bus. The processor is configured with the message bus and can now access the handler. This is the same as described in [ADR 0004](0004-message-bus-architecture.md).

* Good, because it is simple and clear
* Good, because it can be done at any time
* Bad, because it is not clear how the handler is accessed later on when the broker is not available

### 2. Don't register handlers in the message bus, just pass them around when building the processors

The message bus sends the registration info along with the message handlers to the processor.
This is not done in the broker, but rather in the message bus itself. We can pass around the registration info when configuring the processors.

This works as described in [ADR 0003](0003-processor-broker-coupling.md).

* Good, because it is simple and clear
* Good, because registration is independent from the broker
* Bad, because it is not clear how to get an access to the handler when the processor is not available (like in the broker)

### 3. Register handlers in the message bus and register them twice for every processor

The message bus sends the registration info along with the message handlers to the processor. The processor is configured with the message bus and can now access the handler.
The broker can access the processors, which access the handler.
The handler could be stored in the processor, then access it in the message bus from there.

* Good, because it is simple and clear
* Good, because registration is independent from the broker
* Bad, because it adds some logic to the processor which is not needed and could be implemented into the message bus
* Bad, because then it could become a dependency between the message bus and the processor.
  * Which would not be the case if we only had to register once and all processors would share the same registration
  * It becomes even more complicated to remove a handler
  * That would be possible only after an already handler is registered twice and there are more than a single processor using the handler

### 4. Use a second message bus to handle message registration

We use the message bus to handle the registration of handlers.
The message bus will register a handler in the second message bus, which handles the processors.
If the second message bus is integrated into the message bus, we will have to take into account that the second message bus can be unavailable too.

* Good, because it is simple and clear
* Good, because registration is independent from the broker
* Bad, because it is not clear how to get an access to the handler when the processor is not available (like in the broker)

## Decision Outcome

Chosen option: 3, because this would be a very complex system with a second message bus and we wanted to implement the second message bus. We wanted to keep the processing the same so we could have the full message flow processing, even if the message bus was not available.
The second message bus was only supposed to be used by the processor and that is why it could be used, but the solution would become even more complex in the future because then we could not only be assured that there is no message bus and message flow processing can be done. It only works when the processor doesn't have the second message bus, but that way the second message bus doesn't have to be available either.
The system should be simpler and easier to implement.

## Status

Accepted

## Context

Having determined that we want to use a feature driven approach to testing, the features need to be able to be easily recreated and managed in the test. This would be far easier if the tests were executable, either once or repeatedly. 

[Selenium](https://selenium.dev/) is a tool that has been used for many years to enable automated tests of a website. It has a large community where much of our knowledge of it can be gleaned, and we have quite a bit of experience using it already.

## Decision

We will use Selenium as the platform for our automated tests.

## Consequences

Selenium is capable of doing most if not all of what is needed to be done in the automated tests. We can use a testing framework on top, perhaps [NightmareJS](https://nightmarejs.com/) if it suits our needs. 

Having determined to use Selenium means that any code that uses a different browser to what is default for testing Selenium is left unable to be tested. That means that we'd need to ensure that the site is able to be viewed in the default browser (probably Firefox) when running Selenium tests. This also means that we can only use tools that have an API to interact with a web page, which means that we can't use tools that would be able to interact with a mobile browser.

## Context

The 2018 election cycle saw a massive growth in the number of data files generated by the data platform, and the amount of data was expected to grow even more in future elections. The large amount of data not only made long-running queries slow, but it also often caused the entire system to become unable to process data requests, bringing down services, and impacting end users.

The amount of data that was affected by the outage in March 2019 was recorded as about 40TB, and the rebuild took a long time - three months, and the build was heavily supervised by stakeholders, including the Deputy Prime Minister and Treasurer Josh Fry. A key point of the rebuild was that the whole system has to reindex everything - this means that we need to take a data backup before major changes to make sure we can restore it, and we don't need to worry about dropping data along the way.

The data that was affected by the March outage was part of the "data-in-production" system in use by federal government services. This system includes data-in-production (which is the term for the services themselves), as well as data-in-production data (the files that the services talk to - records, files, and data objects)

## Decision

Based on an investigation and discussion with all interested parties, it was concluded that there were three main reasons why the production data became unavailable in March:

(1) 2018 was a record-breaking year for the Data Platform in terms of performance metrics; our storage was so fast that it could write the data without errors. That is, no errors occurred when a message was posted on the data platform. A "bad" message was one where there was no storage available to save the data and the message needed to be written elsewhere. Since we write more data each year and the amount of data grows and grows, at some point this capacity will get used up, causing an outage. However, the March outage was specifically caused by a transient "bad" message, triggered by a rare type of transient write error.

(2) Our storage has been designed by AWS to use a local disk for storing files. At the end of each day the data platform will check every available disk for file validity and consistency. This "disk check" can throw up exceptions that cause data to be dropped if it is too old and its disk has filled up.

(3) The data platform will check files and message metadata on disk every day to ensure that it's consistent. When it detects consistency issues, it will "mark" the file for re-ingestion. There are events and processes that occur between ingest and the next check that can throw off data in different ways, leading to failure.

The conclusion of the investigation was that while we had prepared for a major outage (we tested our restore operations before the March outage), we didn't have a plan for dealing with outages in the short-term - the system couldn't cope with a transient but short-lived type of error, but it was unclear how long it would take to restore.

## Context

If we have global namespaces, and different service instances can declare
namespaces with the same name, how can we know which instance owns a
particular namespace?

Some of our namespaces have sub-namespaces: in the future, they may grow
out into independent namespaces, but can currently only be declared
completely within the same namespace.

If a global service instance needs to store data in a namespace owned by
a local service instance, is it possible to tell the local service
instance to use the correct namespace?

## Decision

We have decided to use the universal namespace API to make explicit
the notion of universally accessible namespace. All namespaces declared
for a global service instance should declare their owning service
instance by specifying
`service_instance_namespace_id: namespace_name` in their
`namespace_declaration.json`.

For other all local service instances, we have decided that using
`namespace_declarations.json` for all namespaces is best, in which
case any global service instances not included in `namespace_declarations.json`
should not be considered universal.

## Status

Accepted.

## Consequences

This means that all namespace declarations for non-global service instances
must be made in a `namespace_declaration.json` for the global service
instance. This means that this JSON file should be checked for correctness
of spelling and casing, especially for service instance names.

All the other service instances are either global or local, and either
of them can use `namespace_declarations.json`.

If some service instances have a need to store information as if it is
shared amongst a local group of service instances, then that local
group can use `namespace_declarations.json`, and share that space.

The universal namespace API is part of the current client-side code, but
it is not yet included in the server-side code. Once that decision
has been made, the API should be added to the server-side code as
a minimum supported version of the protocol.

## Trade-offs

If we use the universal namespace API for everything, we may not be
able to support non-global service instances using namespace
declarations for local services.

If we don't use the universal namespace API for everything, how to do we
maintain consistency?

Using non-universal namespaces is effectively treated as an additional
use-case, which may be challenging to implement and test well.

## Related Work

See the relevant section of the [API specification](https://apidock.com/openmrs/specification/#/concepts/namespaces/universal_namespace).

We decided not to take up the proposal to treat the entire API as
universal namespace, but instead only the client-side implementation
of the universal namespace API. This was done because this API is
only meant to be used when accessing a global service instance. Therefore,
when we specify that namespaces can be "universal," we mean exactly that
it can be accessed from anywhere, from any service instance, which
wouldn't be possible for the non-universal part of the client-side
code.

## Other Considerations

All other code must still follow this convention for namespace naming.

## Context

In the API we have described how a single instance of a class can be described by an agent.

However, in order to build an agent which can be used to describe an instance of a class which has multiple such instances, we have to make sure that the agent is able to differentiate these instances.

One approach to solving this problem is to add class property to agents when we create them. This way, agents can differentiate instances of classes and represent them accordingly. This would mean that any agent we create using an existing class would be able to differentiate instances. However, as we have many classes and each class will have it's own properties it would make a lot of sense to have a way of describing an instance of a class without having to use an agent. This would make it easier to maintain all agents. One other solution is to create a class builder which builds agents that use a template and set some properties. However, this feels like a solution that will get messy when a class has multiple instances.

Since we want to be able to use the agent to describe the instance of a class and have a nice experience for users of the API, we should describe the instance of a class with a 2-step agent. This agent is named `InstanceOf`. `InstanceOf` is a node type. It has `type` and `id` properties, where `type` describes the type of an instance and `id` is an id of a class from which this instance is a member. `InstanceOf` will know how to differentiate instances when multiple `InstanceOf` nodes exist, since they can be differentiated by their class ids. We can describe an instance as an agent that is an `InstanceOf` node.

## Decision

We will change how we describe the instances of the classes in our API.

Rather than describing single instances of a class, we will describe the instances of a class with the following structure:

```
node: InstanceOf, type: MyClass, id: 123
```

This way the instance can be represented as an agent by a `InstanceOf` node with its class and id properties set accordingly.

We will still have single instances of a class described by a single agent but instead of having the entire instance be described by the agent, just the class and id will be.

This decision will result in us having a single description per instance instead of a 2-step description, so it should be noted that API users can specify 2 descriptions when describing an instance.

## Consequences

Since our API uses a 2-step agent, we need to convert all existing instances to use 2-step agents. This means that all the instances we have added in API will be re-described using 2-step agents.

## Further thoughts

I have noticed that the 2-step agent is usually not required for users to interact. If this proves to become a pain for someone, we could introduce a 1-step agent.

## Decisions

## API Client

There's a few decisions that will impact how the API Client will be written:

### 1. Add `content-type` to query strings

We currently need to create the query strings in a way that can be parsed for the application
backend to retrieve the fields for the query.

For example, for a query for an author with the name "Shakespeare", that would be formatted
as:

```
/author/Shakespeare
```

This needs to be expanded as:

```
/author/Shakespeare/?content-type=plain-text-utf-8
```

This might expand to:

```
/author/Shakespeare/?content-type=plain-text-utf-8%3[&]fields=id&fields=name
```

We would like to ensure the query can be parsed cleanly without the `c-type` being part
of the field being passed.

We can use an encoded query string to ensure no parsing problems occur, as the encoding
makes a string that can be cleanly parsed. This can be then encoded again in a query
string to expand to the query string for the application backend.

This approach allows us to send plain text or query strings with complex requirements
via a simple `fields` query parameter.

### 2. Use a generic field naming convention

Fields for an API can be defined as a simple array of strings.

For example, for an author there might be a field for "name" and "id". These would be
stored as a list of strings, so that the server could expect some sort of structured
data, which could then be mapped to fields.

We feel this is a fairly generic approach that is applicable to many different types of
request and will be reviewed and updated if and when we implement App Callbacks.

We felt it important to use a generic approach so that the logic for parsing the request
and creating the query string (as detailed above) would be simple.

### 3. Use fields to create query parameters and attributes for requests

The fields approach was chosen to enable us to specify arbitrary query string requests.

These query string requests are then encoded to be sent back to the application, either
in plain text or query string form depending on the type of query.

An API field string would typically be in some encoding (like UTF-8) which the server
would then decode to retrieve the API value, to be used as a query parameter.

An API attribute string would typically be used as a field name.

Some fields might be composite fields, which will be made up of a prefix and a field name.

This approach allows us to use a simple query string format that allows for arbitrary queries,
but ensures that everything can be represented as a string with a prefix.

This approach can also be used to add metadata for an API, such as a description of the
type, in a simple query string, to be used as a field.

### 4. Represent query string or attribute name fields as strings

API fields and attributes will be represented as strings, rather than numbers.

This makes the query string easier to read.

A lot of clients do this and it feels like the right thing to do.

## 5. Use a generic format for query string values

Query string values are represented by an encoded query string, formed by encoding a string
which can be parsed for the database.

This makes the query string and query database more readable.

## 6. Store the version of the field encoding in a field attribute

API fields and attributes will be represented as strings, such as "version_25" for a
query string field.

This provides a simple version identifier and marker that can be used to look up the encoding
in a database for the version.

This will allow the API to be updated for older versions of a query or search string.

The value must be set to the specific version when encoding a field in a query.

## 7. Have a data type of query_string in query attributes

Query attributes should take a data type, to indicate the type of value the field contains.

The database stores the data type as a string to ensure the type is checked during querying.

## 8. Have a data type of query_fields in query attributes for a query string field

Query string fields need to store data types to ensure query string fields are queryable
in a database.

By storing the data type as query_fields we can identify these fields as string fields.

## Context

Currently we only have a single partition, which is used to store all the data (both active and archived). This means that each partition can only store one set of data, i.e., either all active records or all archived records, but not both. This would work if we had a record of which records are active and which are archived (which we do not), but the problem is that all storage is filled up very quickly and we have no way of knowing which records are active or archived. Furthermore, data can only be stored in one partition, so once a partition is full, we have no way of knowing which records are active.

This ADR aims to resolve the following issues:

- How should we store the records that are both active and archived?
- How should we distinguish between records that are active and archived?

## Decision

For the purposes of this ADR we can ignore archived records, since they are no longer available to the public. The following strategies can be used to determine which records are active and archived:

### 1. Store active/archived in meta-data

Since we store records by their `metadata` and `records` keys, we can use the record `metadata` to determine which records are active and which are archived. If the `metadata` contains both `active` and `archived`, then it means that the `records` can be interpreted as both active and archived (though in reality the `records` contains only the active records). In this case we would have the following:

    partitioned_records = records + metadata

    active_records = records | metadata

    inactive_records = records - metadata

### 2. Store active/archived in meta-data with storage level

Since we use [levels](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1L3d5RsvD1_04F7aE8594I/levels) to make it easy to distinguish records that are active and archived, the only requirement for levels is that `active` has a lower level number than `archived`. This would mean that the `active` is stored with the `record` and the `records` and `metadata` will contain only the active records.

In this case we would have the following:

    partitioned_records = records + metadata

    active_records = records

    inactive_records = metadata

### 3. Store active/archived in separate tables

Another approach is to use separate tables for active and archived records. Then each table can store records of a single status. This would make it easier to create a table for each of the statuses, but the query to retrieve active and archived records would be more complex.

In this case we would have the following:

    partitioned_records = records + metadata + active_table + archived_table

    active_records = active_table

    inactive_records = metadata
    
## Status

Accepted.

## Consequences

### 1. Store active/archived in meta-data

- Easier to retrieve active records, since they can be stored in the same table as the records.
- Harder to retrieve archived records, since they cannot be stored in the same table as the records.
- Harder to retrieve active records, if the `metadata` has been corrupted and contains both `active` and `archived`.

### 2. Store active/archived in meta-data with storage level

- Easier to retrieve archived records, since they can be stored in the same table as the records.
- Easier to retrieve active records, since they can be stored in the same table as the records.
- Harder to store active and archived records in the same table (however it is not a problem for the purposes of this ADR).
- Harder to store active and archived records in the same table for the purposes of this ADR, if the `metadata` has been corrupted and contains both `active` and `archived`.

### 3. Store active/archived in separate tables

- Harder to retrieve active records, since they cannot be stored in the same table as the records.
- Harder to retrieve archived records, since they cannot be stored in the same table as the records.
- Harder to retrieve active records, if the `metadata` contains both `active` and `archived`.

## Decision

Archivematica is an open source system, designed specifically for archiving digital objects. It is used by many universities and libraries around the world to provide long-term preservation services for their collections and provides an XML-based digital preservation "recipe" called PREMIS that makes it easy to deposit and archive digital objects in the system.

We will use Archivematica for archiving documents and data sets.

The access storage servers will need to be shared between Storage Services (SS) and the Operations team, but the archivematica user base will be separate and will need access to the archivematica instance in a server-isolated manner.

Due to its complexity, a long-term solution, Archivematica should not be used for ephemeral storage of documents and data sets. This should be reserved for active work at the center of operations and is not the long-term solution for retaining active records.

## Acknowledgement

Part of this architecture decision is set up to acknowledge that we need a long-term solution for maintaining our records. While the concept of long-term storage of records is widely understood within government circles, the means to achieve this long-term storage of records are seldom discussed. To this end, we must select a long-term digital storage solution that fits our needs before this decision is made.

## Status

accepted

## Context

In the Federated Properties MVP we store all Federation properties in data storage.
Data storage was originally designed for storing documents.
We want to have all Federation properties in data storage so that they can be accessed
by all clients of the API.
Federated properties is thus one of the data types stored in data storage.
There is a well-established pattern for storing data in data storage.
Federated Properties for a client were previously described as a list of IDs.
IDs were previously used to identify a unique Federation property on a client,
while the list of IDs was the list of all Federation properties owned by that client.
This list of IDs does not contain the source information required to fetch all
Federated Properties from data storage.

## Decision

There is no need to identify a particular ID of a Federated property or it's source
when fetching data storage records from the API.
Federated Properties are fetched from data storage using an ID of a Federation property
in the request parameters.
There is no need to add source information to Property IDs for the Federated Properties MVP.
The ID of a Federated property is used to retrieve the record from data storage and
do not contain source information necessary for that.

## Consequences

### Risks
Federated properties can be fetched using the ID of a Federation property and there is
no need to add source information to Property IDs for the Federated Properties MVP.
Federated Properties can be fetched using an ID of a Federation property only.
There is no other information needed to identify a Federated property.

### Benefits
Federated properties can be fetched using the ID of a Federation property and there is
no need to add source information to Property IDs for the Federated Properties MVP.
Federated Properties can be fetched using an ID of a Federation property only.
There is no other information needed to identify a Federated property.

## Status
Accepted

Proposed by: Paul Dubs (19-06-2021)

Discussed with: Alex Black, Alex Green

## Context
One Core SDK application can produce an artifact with a name used in another Core SDK application
is this [part of its journey](https://github.com/coreos/cf-pipeline/blob/7525d6edba0e4f5f7ae335157de14c94a1687722/docs/deployment.md#step-5-deploying-artifacts).
Although it is not technically duplicated in the code the same code is executed. This is leading
to increased build times because the cache is not shared across applications.

It has been noted that one of the benefits of multi application build setups is not being
able to detect and avoid duplicated tasks (i.e. `build`, `create-docs`). We can mitigate 
this by renaming all the targets with a `cf-` prefix to make sure each run is unique. This makes 
it unclear though that we're mitigating it and if we're being consistent is this a good idea?

## Decision
All `build`, `create-docs` and `test` targets will be renamed `cf-build`, `cf-create-docs` and 
`cf-test` respectively. All apps will have the `cf` prefix.

In the case of artifact duplication, the build process should be triggered from the
first application. By triggering the build in the first application we'll only have
to trigger the build once for each artifact which will result in an application cache
being shared among all of the applications.

## Consequences
The build process should be started inside of the first application and will be triggered 
for each artifact of each application based on that.

## Discussion
### Paul
In this proposal we have a simple way to solve for artifact duplication.

### Alex
What we should really have is our own artifact type: a **SourceArtifact**.
We can solve this by only creating a SourceArtifact in the first application, and
using the SourceArtifact as a reference (like the build number).

As long as we only produce a single SourceArtifact per application in the first 
application we'd be able to see the SourceArtifact as an output when executing a 
pipeline job in the other applications. Also this makes it easier to detect when an artifact
is already present and to prevent duplication.

If we need to do more than this then we'll need to find a way to publish and pull the 
artifacts. For instance we could use the same file storage system that we use for build artifacts
to store SourceArtifacts.

Once a SourceArtifact is created and deployed then a cached version is available for 
other applications to consume.

### Alex
The only application that runs pipelines in an isolated environment is the build
applications. Therefore if the build pipeline fails and it isn't retried then the
Artifact won't be built but will get duplicated somehow, e.g. in an application cache?

### Paul
One thing to keep in mind is that while some apps can retrigger the build with the current setup,
it's not possible for others. If an application that run all the builds fails then
it will prevent others. As long as we've implemented the source artifact strategy then
we can mitigate this.

### Paul
The issue with this approach is to make it unclear that we're mitigating duplication 
and that if we're being consistent this is a good idea.

### Alex
So if there is an application that can run all the builds in a separate environment 
then the only way we'll know it is by doing it.

### Paul
So to recap the issue is that we don't know what the source application is which 
runs the build. We want a method to detect that a build is complete and it is available
in the application repositories.

### Alex
Maybe it's the best to keep this as we currently have and use the artifacts. 
We would just have to ignore the build applications and the pipeline would be triggered from
the build application.

### Paul
We should revisit this when we address to find out about the workflow.

## Status

Accepted

## Context

The problem motivating this decision, and any context that influences or constrains the decision.

Using Docker as a runtime platform makes this application suitable for multiple deployment targets that support running Docker containers and is compatible with the project's deployment platform.

## Decision

Use Docker as a runtime platform.

## Consequences

Using Docker facilitates many benefits such as portability, automation, and reliability. A notable example of these benefits is Docker's ability to isolate applications from their environment. In order to fully benefit from these advantages, it's important that we make good use of Docker when developing and deploying this project.

There are several options when it comes to platforms for running Docker containers. These include Local-based testing (e.g. for Windows see [https://github.com/hhatto/docker-in-Windows10](https://github.com/hhatto/docker-in-Windows10)), Azure containers (e.g. [Azure Container Registry](https://azure.microsoft.com/en-us/services/container-registry)), and Google Kubernetes (e.g. [Google Kubernetes Engine](https://cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/)).

The decision to use Docker for this project has several consequences. First, it makes the project more portable, since it can be run on any platform that supports running Docker containers. For example, Azure container registry that has recently gone into [general availability](https://azure.microsoft.com/en-us/services/container-registry/#announcing-general-availability). Second, it makes it easier to automate deployment processes since we can rely on existing Docker automation tools. For example, the [https://www.automate.sh](https://www.automate.sh) website. Third, it increases the project's reliability. For instance, the [https://docs.docker.com/en/best-practices/deploying-applications/manage-reliability/](https://docs.docker.com/en/best-practices/deploying-applications/manage-reliability/) documentation page on Docker.

There are also some downsides to using Docker for this project. For instance, it makes it difficult to deploy container orchestration applications like Kubernetes because Docker does not provide a way for one container to configure another. A [proposal](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/42400) was made to add this capability to Kubernetes and it is referred to as [Docker state](https://kubernetes.io/issues/42400) and currently exists in the `kubernetes-incubator` repository. Additionally, the [https://docs.docker.com/en/best-practices/deploying-applications/manage-reliability/running-multiple-containers#running-multiple-containers-on-the-same-host](https://docs.docker.com/en/best-practices/deploying-applications/manage-reliability/running-multiple-containers#running-multiple-containers-on-the-same-host) documentation page on running multiple containers on the same host.

Despite some of these drawbacks, Docker is still the right platform for this project. The benefits of portability, automation, and reliability are too valuable to pass up. The lack of Kubernetes support is a minor issue, which will likely be addressed in the near future.

### Context and Problem Statement

We've historically relied upon the `Fetchable` protocol to make API calls to retrieve data about the selected network.
This has been largely superseded by the NetworkManager service which handles these tasks.

### Considered Options

* Do nothing and keep using Fetchable protocol
* Replace Fetchable protocol calls with NetworkManager calls

### Decision Outcome

Chosen option: "Replace Fetchable protocol calls with NetworkManager calls".

If we continue to use Fetchable protocol we'll have to work around the fact that all calls must go through the `kdbGet` call.
In particular this means that no calls can be made directly from the `kdbGet` call.
This means that all calls to the API must go through the `kdbGet`.
This means that:
* No calls can be made to `kdbSet`, which means that no setter methods can be called.
* The return value of `kdbGet` does not include setter methods, which means that the result does not return a full object.
* Callbacks have to be passed around between several API calls.
* The network settings don't contain a full object, but instead only data about the selected network.

With NetworkManager our API calls are either direct calls from the `kdbGet` call, or calls to an API implementation which is entirely separate.
For example, the `kdbGet` call directly calls `kdbGet`, which returns a full object, which then can be passed to setter methods.

As the result, we would no longer have to do all of the following:
* Convert a string to a list of byte to a string to a list of byte to a list of bytes to a list of bytes.
* Avoid calling setter methods to avoid having to convert a list of bytes to a string and then back to a list of bytes.
* Avoid calling setter methods to avoid having to convert a string to a list of bytes and then back to a string.
* We no longer need a list of bytes to define a setting.
* Use a custom callback to pass information across several API calls.
* Do a lookup up using a global singleton instance.

We would need to implement a global singleton instance of the `NetworkManager` class (probably using `kdbGet` and `kdbSet` to retrieve and set the instance).

For a list of other possible advantages see [ADR 016](./016-networkmanager-as-api-interface.md).

There may also be a way to make existing use cases simpler, perhaps by retrieving all the network settings at once and parsing the result instead of processing it incrementally.

Date: 2019-04-03

## Status

Accepted

## Context

As our project scope grows in size and number of dependencies, we might run into situations where we will have to build IoC containers that span across module boundaries.
For example, the scenario where Service A from Module A relies on the Service B provided by Module B and also utilizes the IoC Container of Module B.
This can lead to a whole range of problems like mixing concerns between modules and impacting the testability of the project.
This can also lead to accidental leakage of internals from Module B to Module A which can leak confidential implementation details to project competitors.

## Decision

In order to avoid these problems, we've decided to create an IoC Container per module which will only hold modules' internal dependencies.
All the services provided by the module will be exposed externally by means of IoC Containers created by the module itself.
As a result, dependencies of those IoC Containers become available to all modules utilizing them.
Furthermore, IoC Containers can be reused across different modules.
Furthermore, IoC Containers can be created during initialization and destroyed at de-initialization.
Therefore, we can provide multiple services to multiple consumers (modules).
At the same time, it provides the consumers with a more controlled approach to dependency injection.

## Consequences

While this approach will make our project simpler, it would make it impossible for us to share/reuse IoC Containers with each other.
Because all IoC Containers are initialized upon startup.
To avoid this, we will create multiple classes in each module, each having its own IoC Container and holding the private definition of it.
Furthermore, we will also provide public interfaces for users of the module to retrieve their own IoC Containers.
When the user consumes more than one module, we will provide a way to get the container of a dependency of the consumer.
For example, when our project has dependencies on a Service A from module A and a Service B from module B, we can provide an interface for Service A so that it can retrieve Service B.
If we want to share/reuse the IoC Containers with each other (which is generally a good idea), we will initialize our container during the test setup and utilize it in our tests.

## Further Reading

- https://stackoverflow.com/questions/31478019/why-i-use-di-container-in-c-in-my-own-modules-and-not-in-my-existing-modules-in-project/39474272#39474272
- https://stackoverflow.com/questions/21308418/using-custom-di-containers-with-dependencies-within-modules-with-no-i-d-forward-compatibility-with-a-new-di-contain

Date: 2020-04-03

## Status

Accepted

## Context

In the current design of zos parameterization in the identity client we have a hardcoded string that's used in
the zos protocol messages. This presents an issue when we want to offer multiple versions of the protocol and
have to make a decision on which version of the protocol should be used in the messages.

In order to overcome this issue we want to parameterize the zos sal, which is a unique sequence used in the
protocol to make it unique, so it can change the version of the protocol.

## Decision

The zos parameterization is a unique sequence used to make it unique. It's not a random number sequence and
isn't meant to be used to generate random numbers. Instead it's specifically designed to make protocol-specific 
messages look different.

This will allow the client to dynamically version the zos protocol based on its parameters without creating
another protocol version. This will also allow us to add more parameters in the future to make 
protocol-specific messages even more unique.

## Consequences

Zos messages will be able to support multiple protocol versions. This will allow multiple protocols to 
be supported and versioned on the same machine.

Zos messages will have the ability to dynamically change the version of protocol. This will help in 
protocol migrations and protocol upgrades.

Zos messages that are created will have an increased amount of "length" within them. This will make 
larger messages, but also will make the messages much easier to differentiate from each other.

Increased message length might impact network performance and latency. This should be assessed on 
a per-protocol basis when protocols are in production.

## Context and Problem Statement

One problem, multiple subjects.
- Subject A: Multiple scenes from the same set, eg. set [T.20] - T.20 - Image - Multiple frames are related to the same model, eg. T.20:00, T.20:01, T.20:02.
- Subject B: Multiple scenes from different sets, eg. set [T.20] - T.20 - Video - Multiple frames are related to the same model, eg. T.20:00, T.20:01, T.20:02 (from different sets).

Question: How should the "parent" scene be set and handled? How to keep the model's model version constant?

## Considered Options

### 1. Use a separate collection for each "parent"

- `T.20.multiple.collection` - All frames are related to the same model, eg. T.20:00, T.20:01, T.20:02.
- `T.20.video.multiple.collection` - All frames are related to the same model, eg. T.20:00, T.20:01, T.20:02.

### 2. Use the same collection

- `T.20 - video - multiple.collection` - All frames are related to the same model, eg. T.20:00, T.20:01, T.20:02.

## Decision Outcome

We choose option 1, because we are adding a collection with the video. This collection has another collection as it's "parent". This implies that the parent needs to be set for the video.

### Positive Consequences

- Multiple collections can be used in a `MultiFrameViewer`.
- Multiple collections can be used in an `ImageViewer`.
- Sets and subjects can have multiple collections.

### Negative Consequences

- No standard way of setting parent collection.

# CSS Tooling

**User Story:** [184371155](https://dp3.atlassian.net/browse/184371155)

In order to help developers write and maintain front-end code, the design system team desired to use a tool to automatically generate styles and normalize styles. The aim was to enforce consistency and reduce risk in making breaking style changes. The CSS Tooling team was consulted on how to achieve this goal.

## Considered Alternatives

* [React-CSS-Modules](https://github.com/react-css/react-css-modules)
* [Styletron](https://github.com/styletron/react-styletron)
* [CSS Modules](https://github.com/css-modules/css-modules)
* [CSSinJS](https://github.com/css-in-js/css-in-js)

## Decision Outcome

Chosen Alternative: [React-CSS-Modules](https://github.com/react-css/react-css-modules)

Although all considered alternatives were deemed capable of meeting the desired goal, there were many benefits to using [React-CSS-Modules](https://github.com/react-css/react-css-modules). This includes support for [ESM](https://github.com/react-css/react-css-modules#module-styling), and its use in the [CCS](https://github.com/react-css/ccs-project) initiative. Additionally, the tool is popular, widely adopted, and used across the organization.

## Pros and Cons of the Alternatives

### React-CSS-Modules

* `+` Complies with desired goal
* `+` ESM support
* `+` Well-known and adopted
* `-` Still relatively new

### Styletron

* `+` Allows for atomic styles
* `+` Good at normalizing styles
* `-` Relatively new
* `-` Not very well known or adopted

### CSS Modules

* `+` Well-known and adopted
* `+` Can be used across the organization
* `-` Can't make sense of time or scale
* `-` Requires webpack

### CSSinJS

* `+` Can make sense of time or scale
* `+` Can use as a source of truth for components
* `-` Doesn't really normalize styles
* `-` Not very well known or adopted

## Not NPM package based solution

### npm package for each component (proposed)

This proposal creates a new npm package for each component that gets published to a NPM like repository (like npm, or github).

For this proposal, we need to clarify a few things:

**What component we're talking about**

Components refer to the source code for a Javascript module. For example, the "Flex" component refers to the source code for the "Flex" javascript module. It's the definition and implementation of the Flex component, and the source code lives in a repository.

**What an npm package does**

An npm package is a collection of files in an npm repository which are grouped together for the purpose of publishing to an npm like repository (like npm, or github).

**What a npm package contains**

An npm package contains files like `package.json`, `README.md`, `LICENSE`, and source code in folders like `src`, `cjs`, `types`, `dist`. These files and folders can be used to rebuild the package into the npm package to be published to an npm like repository.

## Clarifying the proposal and the consequences

### Clarifying the proposal

Having clarified the definition of a component, a package, and the type of a package, we can now clarify the proposal.

We propose that all components defined in the project will be created as an npm package. For now, we have only one type of package, but if we need to create other types of packages in the future, it's feasible.

This is a high level overview of the process.
1. Run `npx init-package` to create an npm package.
2. Update all the scripts to use the package
3. Publish the package

### Positive consequences

Creating packages for the components provides many advantages over not creating packages:
- Easy to setup and maintain component library
- NPM package allows the possibility to add unit tests, documentation, examples
- Use scripts for all operations related to package

### Negative consequences

Creating packages for the components can be very beneficial to the project. However, it has some drawbacks that need to be addressed.
- More complex installation process for consumers of the component library
- Each component will have its own package which results in more repositories

## Other options considered

### Just run scripts

Another possibility would be not to use an npm package for the components, but instead run scripts for all the operation with the components. For example, running `npm start` could start a local test or dev build of the component library.

We also could not deploy the package to the npm repository.

This is a simple solution, and it's feasible to implement. However, it has a major drawback.
- Doesn't provide unit tests, documentation, examples.

We also considered publishing the components as the NPM packages without bundling the packages. For example, we could publish just the js-sdk-core package, and then for each component library we publish a seperate package. This would give us more clarity, but it's more work to implement.

## Status

Accepted

## Context

We use the Flyway database tool to manage database changes in our service.

Flyway requires a database to be created before changes can be made. This may result in an environment being unavailable to users during a migration.

In response to this problem some teams use a blue-green deployment strategy to handle database migrations. The core idea behind blue-green deployment is to run multiple production-like environments at the same time (i.e. blue and green). One environment (i.e. blue) is used for regular production user traffic, and the other environment (i.e. green) is used to perform any work that causes a disruption to the service, including database migrations.

## Decision

We will use blue-green deployments to handle database migrations in our service

## Consequences

Blue-green deployments can potentially be disruptive to the service as our production service will need to be split into two production services and any traffic that is routed to the production service will be routed to either the blue or green environment. Traffic redirection can be implemented with ease using AWS Load Balancer or CloudFront.

We can mitigate the potential disruption to the service by creating an additional environment dedicated to deployments to support the project. All deployment activity can take place in the development environment, ensuring the service remains unavailable to users during a migration.

Using this approach will mean that at least one environment will always be available for users to access.

## Status

Accepted

## Context

We feel the need to define what is considered to be a correct "shape" when it comes to object creation in our codebase. So far, the only limitation that we had was due to the restriction that all functions need to have at least one parameter, which is a weird and counter-intuitive behavior in most other languages.

We believe that defining all the objects and their properties through code comments is a very un-efficient way of defining these specifications.

## Decision

Making it easier to understand what is going on in the code, we will use TypeScript.

## Consequences

While we're using TypeScript we can make sure that the objects that are being created are following a certain "shape", based on the definition. And if we're already defining the properties of the object, then we can also use interfaces to make the "shape" more explicit, which will add more clarity to the code.

The problem with interfaces is that they are basically just a list of properties. So to solve this, we will use types, which can also contain interfaces, for everything that we need to describe the "shape" of the objects. Using this kind of behavior allows us to be more precise when we describe the objects, and at the same time allow for flexibility when we need to add more "shapes" later on.

When the ADR opens up Kibana to all service teams, we have to ensure that they do not make any decisions based on the content of this ADR that may negatively impact the availability of Kibana.

### Context

After last week's outage it has become apparent the need for better maintenance and deployment of our infrastructure. To achieve this, we have requested that all environment be setup on docker. To aid in our automation, it has been suggested we use a 3rd party container orchestration platform to help manage and scale our deployment across multiple environments. The goal is not to manage a service like Slack teams and instead focus on the deployment and scale of our infrastructure.

### Decision

In an effort to ensure service reliability we have requested three services be available for our users:

#### Production
#### Staging
#### Testing

We initially attempted to accomplish this by creating a private docker hub account to store all these containers but it would require a public/private split of our docker hub account which does not present a great deal of benefit to us. In addition, a local dockerhub account would require us to be able to identify our users to those in the docker hub account. Having to pass that information on to users and knowing that not everyone will be involved in these actions presents a number of concerns for our internal controls.

In an effort to meet the requirements of our production docker deployment we have decided to use three groups in our docker hub account:

1. the primary containers for production
2. the backup containers for production
3. the support containers for production

These containers will be able to be deployed to three separate accounts under the banner of `justice-gov` in the following manner:

1. the primary containers for production
    - 1 container will be used per environment, which will be deployed to [prod.beta.govuk.digital](https://github.com/alphagov/paas-prod)
2. the backup containers for production
    - 1 container will be used per environment, which will be deployed to [dev.beta.govuk.digital](https://github.com/alphagov/paas-dev)
3. the support containers for production
    - 1 container will be used per environment, which will be deployed to [test.beta.govuk.digital](https://github.com/alphagov/paas-test)

This will allow us to deploy a list of containers to our three production environments using the [ginkgo deployment tool](https://github.com/alphagov/paas-ginkgo) in the following manner:

```bash
./ginkgo deploy --environment=production \
paas-prod \
paas-staging \
paas-testing \
paas-main

./ginkgo deploy --environment=staging \
paas-staging

./ginkgo deploy --environment=testing \
paas-testing

./ginkgo deploy --environment=main \
paas-main
```

This is only a temporary structure until a proper deployment process and potentially a container orchestration platform can be integrated into our deployment process. At that point, we will re-visit the decision to deploy production containers in three different accounts. 

In the meantime, we can achieve the three services requirement using a [docker-compose.lock](https://github.com/alphagov/paas-main/tree/master/docker-compose.lock) and the following docker-compose.yaml in our [docker hub](https://hub.docker.com/u/alphagov/paas) which can be deployed with [ginkgo deployment tool](https://github.com/alphagov/paas-ginkgo) or manually using the [docker hub container build](https://docs.docker.com/container/deploy/devops/#create-dockerhub-container-record-to-define-an-image) tool.

```yaml
three-services.yaml
---
services:
  - id: prod-mysql
    name: mysql
    image: mysql:5.7
    container_id: mycloud-mysql
    environment_variable:
      - name: $GCR_PATH
        value: "/cloud"
    ports:
    - host: localhost
      port: 3306
    volumes:
    - host: /cloud
      volume: /cloud/mysql
    labels:
      labels:
      - production
  - id: prod-redis
    name: redis
    image: redis:3.2
    container_id: mycloud-redis
    environment_variable:
      - name: $GCR_PATH
        value: "/cloud"
    ports:
    - host: localhost
      port: 6379
    volumes:
    - host: /cloud

## Context

A pattern is more than just a simple list of recommendations. It often includes additional metadata that makes it suitable for specific use cases. The following topics are relevant in this context:
- what metadata should be included,
- what is the role of a pattern in the bigger picture,
- how should a pattern be structured when including metadata.

## Decision

We define a pattern's metadata as consisting of the following topics:
- pattern name,
- pattern description,
- subject matter expert (SME) who wrote the pattern,
- publication date (for versions with change logs, see [Versioning](https://www.enterpriseintegrationpatterns.com/patterns/versioning-log.html)),
- change logs (for versions with change logs, see [Versioning](https://www.enterpriseintegrationpatterns.com/patterns/versioning-log.html)),
- tags (e.g. "best practice", "technology"),
- links to additional information (e.g. in the form of an URL)

Pattern structure must follow the following rules when adding metadata to a pattern:
- The first section always contains the pattern name.
- The second section always contains the pattern description (in `dev` section, do not include markdown formatting in the text. The following example from the repository `dev` section shows how this section should be structured):

```
----
description: >-
  The problem statement to solve is: [state the problem].

  The proposed solution is the implementation of [explain the solution].

  Note that the project team initially considered these alternatives:
    - [alternative 1]
    - [alternative 2]

  This document represents the most preferable solution option. 
----
```

Note that the above example uses multiline format.
```
----
description: >-
  The problem statement to solve is: [state the problem].

  The proposed solution is the implementation of [explain the solution].

  Note that the project team initially considered these alternatives:
    - [alternative 1]
    - [alternative 2]

  This document represents the most preferable solution option. 
----
```

- Any subsequent section should start with the section title. The section name will be the section index (e.g. `2. Project Initialization`). It should be formed as `2. Project Initialization`. The section title should be in markdown formatting, so that the section is heading and only the first line will be rendered.
- Each section should use the multiline format.
- A pattern's metadata contains topics relevant to the domain that it is aimed at, and can contain topics of a cross-domain nature (e.g. “URL naming conventions”), as long as they are presented as topics and do not follow the following format (which applies to all topics in the metadata): `index.keyword-argument` (e.g. `3. Keyword Matching`).
- The order of topics is not defined, other than the “index” section.
- The number of pattern versions is not defined.

## Status

Accepted

## Consequences

The metadata of an enterprise integration pattern will contain rich information, which will make it fit specific use cases.

It is easy to distinguish between a pattern written by a subject matter expert and one that was written in a collaborative fashion and so on.

The way to structure a pattern's metadata and its topics allow for the possibility of further extensions (e.g. for more sophisticated versioning systems) and for new metadata to be added in future (e.g. for including links to the PR with the latest version of a pattern).

A pattern is an architecture decision that can be used to solve multiple problems, which makes it an ideal tool for the lean development method lean, which favors “start small, think big” and favors the [single responsibility principle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Single_responsibility_principle).

3. Testing philosophy
*******************

Date: 2019-05-11

Status
------

Accepted

Context
-------

There are a lot of accepted testing methodologies, e.g. unit tests, functional tests, end-to-end tests, etc. The purpose of unit tests is mainly to ensure that isolated parts of the codebase work as expected. Typically this means testing functions and their arguments, without any external dependencies. Functional tests are a broader scope and attempt to test a component’s behavior as a whole, which usually includes external dependencies and the communication between them, such as HTTP calls. End-to-end tests are usually the most comprehensive kind of tests and they test a system as a whole, usually mimicking a user journey.

While it may be tempting to use a more functional or end-to-end approach, we have decided to use a more unit-based approach, particularly because we intend to have a microservices architecture. The main reason behind this choice is that the unit tests are more understandable for the majority of developers and easier to write for the rest. Additionally, they are usually easier to debug when encountering errors, which is a vital part of our Agile workflow. Using a purely functional approach might be harder to debug, but it is also worth mentioning that unit tests are usually faster, which is a vital part of our cycle time.

While functionality is important and tests should at least confirm that the application works as a whole and that all communication between parts is correct, we have decided to prioritize the functionality of the whole over the functionality of the parts. This means that for instance, a server communication should be tested and validated in a functional test, but this does not mean that all internal methods and functions of the server should be tested in a unit test. For that reason, it’s likely that a server is tested in a functional test for just a single HTTP request.

However, this is not to say that the functionality of the parts isn't tested at all. Unit tests will make sure that each part of a server behaves as expected.

Decision
--------

We will use a mix of functional and unit tests, with a strong focus on unit tests and testing the behavior of the parts of the system.

Consequences
------------

Even though we use a unit-based approach, we make sure that the application is tested from start to end. This results in a mix of unit tests, functional tests, and end-to-end tests.

While end-to-end tests are usually the most reliable tests for the whole system, our tests with a high focus on unit tests contribute to a more understandable codebase, which is even more vital to a more sustainable and long-lasting project.

While functional tests are more reliable and accurate than unit tests, unit tests are faster and that is vital for our cycle time. That’s why there will be a mix of both approaches and that’s not seen as a problem.

Using only unit tests can lead to an incomplete picture of the system. Hence we make sure to run functional tests to validate our application at a higher level.

## Context

Flyway's DB migrations script was written in JavaScript and was hosted in a server's root directory under `/webapps/flyway/scripts/db_migrate`. While this script does not trigger any other files, it was a source of confusion, since this was typically reserved for UI files. The default PHP setup on Vagrant's VM can only support one directory as the root directory, which also `/webapps/flyway` has been created in.

Given the Flyway VM had only been created as the project's primary CI environment, it was likely that the Flyway scripts will be used by other teams, or the wider team's projects.

## Decision

We remove the root directory by refactoring the Flyway scripts to `/apps/flyway/scripts/db_migrate`. Additionally, we write PHP code to help the utility, since, the [documentation][flyway-documentation] itself recommends using PHP in the utility.

For Flyway scripts we create a composer package `flyway-cli` where the scripts are stored, and a [PSR 7 compliant CLI interface][psr-7-compliant-cli-interface][psr-7-compliant-db-migrator]. This interface is used by our `flyway` command.

## Consequences

- Scripts will be split into two directories, `db_migrate` and `flyway/cli`.
- Flyway scripts will be migrated to the `db_migrate` directory and renamed to `.php`.
- Flyway scripts will be run on the CI machine (if it has PHP enabled) with a local directory structure.
- Flyway CLI will be installed in each host and will execute Flyway scripts locally, but will also be run from the remote CI, where the scripts will execute on the host, which will make the script run locally (where the [PSR 7 compliant CLI interface][psr-7-compliant-db-migrator] is installed).
- Flyway scripts will be able to execute using local commands.
- Flyway scripts will be able to access environment variables.
- Flyway scripts will be able to import other Flyway scripts using `require_once` and store variables in `global` scope.

[flyway-documentation]: https://docs.flywaydb.org
[psr-7-compliant-cli-interface]: https://www.php-fig.org/psr/psr-7-standard.html#c-7.1
[psr-7-compliant-db-migrator]: https://medium.com/php-fig/psr-7-compliant-db-migrator-c4d7129e7e8e

## Alternatives

Other options include:
- Use PHP for the Flyway scripts entirely.
- Rename the Flyway script directory to `db_scripts`.
- Use `PSR-7 compliant CLI interface` to launch Flyway scripts from the CI.

The main reason for not choosing a PHP-based Flyway script was to keep the scripts mostly "database-independent." (There was no expectation that in the future there would be no way of doing that, but I wanted to see *at least* some level of "database independence," which is what we have now).

Choosing PSR-7 compliant CLI interface was preferred, since the main justification for it is to help the tool run locally as well as in a deployment environment.

I felt that other options were not as much of an option for the following reasons:
- If I would choose `PSR-7 compliant CLI interface`, Flyway scripts would be run locally. However, it would not be the PSR-7 compliant DB Migrator which has a standard API.
- Rename the Flyway script directory to `db_scripts` does not follow Flyway's convention, which is using `db_migrate` for storing Flyway scripts.
- I felt that it would be too risky to completely rewrite the Flyway scripts for a project that has only had their first set of scripts written for it in the past 24 hours. Also, it would be risky to rewrite them with a different file structure.

However, the main reason for not choosing a PHP-based Flyway script was that this is the convention for storing Flyway scripts on any Flyway VM. PHP scripts in this manner was the only way I knew of for them to execute, since the [PSR 7 compliant CLI interface][psr-7-compliant-db-migrator] only supports the running of executable files.

## Status

Accepted

## Context

Backend architecture is quite important for the final quality of the Farmacy Food application. 
When we decide on the backend architecture it affects every aspect of the project.

## Decision

We've decided to use serverless architecture for our Farmacy Food backend. 
Serverless architecture allows us to focus on building API layer without worrying about low-level infrastructure details. 
Its main advantages are:
- lower costs for building and deploying app,
- better for small and middle size projects,
- better for projects with high variation in load,
- faster time to develop.

Serverless architecture has quite a lot of benefits, but also there are some concerns related to it. 
Serverless architecture can be less efficient for long computations,
- it might require a lot of additional calls to get the same computation done,
- can have poor performance.

That's why we're planning to use it only for our API layer and use lambda functions only for high-priority use cases. 

## Consequences

### Positive
- We'll focus on building the business value,
- It's easier to be deployable on a wide range of platforms,
- It's easier to scale in a fast and flexible way.

### Negative
- We'll have to work with a quite new technology,
- The deployment can be more complicated,
- We'll have to accept that we'll have to migrate to lambda architecture in the future.

### Neutral
- We'll have to use cloud native services,
- We'll have to use async architecture,
- We'll have to use stateless services,
- We'll have to use event-driven architecture,
- We'll have to use local data storage.

## Status

Accepted

## Context

Audio formats contain duration and position information which must be represented as a number. The range of values will vary, but will generally not exceed a few seconds and hundreds of thousands of milliseconds.

## Decision

Positions and durations will be encoded as milliseconds from the start time of the audio.

## Consequences

Values will need to be converted from seconds to milliseconds and vice versa, but the range of possible values is small, reducing impact on day-to-day work.

Conversion can be performed using standard integer arithmetic.

Audio formats can have an offset, which can be handled by adding and subtracting milliseconds from the encoded values.

Audio formats can specify that values are relative to a specific point, which can be done by converting all values to relative from that point. For example, a duration of `100%` can be encoded as a single duration in milliseconds.

Some audio formats specify duration information directly (e.g. mp3 `ext_duration`), which will need to be converted to milliseconds.

Some audio formats do not have the concept of position or duration information, which will need to be encoded using another format.

## Status

Accepted

## Context

As part of our work to promote Compliant Kubernetes, we aim to:

* Help new users get an overview of the Compliant Kubernetes deployment lifecycle
* Help users identify specific clusters
* Help users understand the usage of Compliant Kubernetes in the enterprise

We have done the first two using the [Kubernetes Service Discovery and Load Balancer](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/services-networking/service-discovery/#solving-for-high-availability), but we need to add a method for measuring uptime in order to get a full view of a compliant deployment.

## Decision

We will add a probe, such as an HTTP probe, to each compliant Kubernetes Service that we create in Compliant Kubernetes. It will be the last Kubernetes Service node.

All K8s deployments will be set to be [available on both hostnames/hostnames and IP addresses](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/services-networking/service/#metadata-for-ip-address-and-hostname-selectors). This ensures that the hostnames/hostnames we create for new compliant services are accessible via IP addresses, making it easier to measure uptime.

We will also add the following to a compliant Kubernetes [Service](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/services-networking/service) [definition](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/services-networking/service-definition/):

```
apiVersion: networking/v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: xxxx
spec:
  selector:
  - hostnames:
      - foo.host
    - IPAddress:
      - bar.host
  ports:
  - protocol: HTTP
    number: 80
    name: http
    listeners:
    - hostnames:
        - foo.host
        - bar.host
  - protocol: HTTPS
    number: 443
    name: https
    listeners:
    - hostnames:
        - foo.host
        - bar.host
  type: NodePort
```

`NodePort` is the Service Type. It makes it easy to test uptime while still accessing the service via a local host/name. It does not introduce traffic routing.

## Consequences

For compliant Kubernetes clusters, all the service nodes must have a `hosts` field and a `netfilter` field.

If no probes are used, K8s Services will expose port 6443 with a `ELB` type that exposes all the ports for the cluster. We can get uptime information from this endpoint.

The ELB is the endpoint of the [kubernetes [ELB](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/services-networking/elbs-Istio/)](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/services-networking/elbs/) that exposes the Kubernetes API server.

All of the service nodes will add a list of hosts/names to the ELB and then add the IPs of all the instances of the K8s Service to the list of hosts. This allows the ELB to automatically redirect all traffic for the Service to available instances from the cluster.

If all the nodes can be accessed from the cluster, we can identify service availability.

## Alternatives

We could use an Ingress controller to expose an external URL. They can be run in the same cluster. For example, we could use Istio Ingress Gateway.

Istio Istio Ingress Gateway adds a layer to a K8s Service that is available only to the cluster. Istio Istio Ingress Gateway creates an Istio-managed Istio Ingress Gateway service that exposes your deployed service as a global load balancer. Istio Istio Ingress Gateway is a Istio-managed service that is configured on Istio Ingress Gateway in the service cluster.

We can use Istio Istio Ingress Gateway to redirect all the traffic to a compliant Kubernetes service.
