## Context

Currently, we have a complex, messy code base distributed in several repositories. Angular (version 4 and 5) is the main technology that runs the application.

Since we started to develop the app we went for Angular, but without a clear technical direction. The initial team members were mostly backend engineers, so in order to make things more simple they started implementing the front end side of the application. With time, more people joined the team, and the angular technical knowledge wasn't as common among front end engineers as we thought.

This caused several consequences:
* In the beginning, we had the "spa" angular application, but later decided to separate other applications which communicates with our API (this is an Angular application too). This made the "spa" app to be the one and only application that runs the entire front-end side of our application.
* Since we still didn't have a clear technical direction, it caused Angular to be an in-memory solution rather than a production one. This caused a lot of dependencies and other considerations to be added to that.
* We could see a lot of features requested by our users being added to Angular, but our application getting slower.

After some time, the technical knowledge on Angular started to grow among the front end engineers. Also, we decided to move the domain part of our application to our API (see ADR 0007). Angular became a platform that we decided to use to replace the entire front-end of our application. It allowed us to be able to provide a reactive, unit-testable (thanks to the dependency injection) interface.

The problem was still there, our application wasn't as performant as we wanted and we had a lot of code added to our Angular applications. To cope with this we use the "change detection mechanism", which, as the docs say, is an "engine that detects changes in your application and triggers your app's change detection cycle."

Angular has several change detection mechanisms:
* [Change detection](https://angular.io/guide/change-detection/change-detection)
* [Change detection mechanism](https://angular.io/guide/change-detection/change-detection-mechanism)
* [Change detection trigger](https://angular.io/guide/change-detection/change-detection-trigger)

The problem with our code base is the number of all those code. We have more than 700 million lines of code, it is a massive amount and it's difficult to understand and find things to understand and improve our code base. It is very easy to make mistakes in such a complicated code base and it is very easy to add unnecessary features or things to it.

There is an easy solution, but it's not free: migrate to Angular version 15 and rewrite all the application from scratch.

## Decision

After long thinking, we decided to do it. We decided to rewrite our frontend with Angular, starting from scratch.

We decided to do it, so we can have a clear technical direction, a "production" mindset, and start using better practices to avoid the previous mistakes.

It will add a lot of value to the application, since we can rewrite and refactor the code base to avoid mistakes we made in the past.

The application will become a lot more performant, and will be easier to maintain.

We'll be able to make better code tests, using tools like [Ng ZORRO Ant Design](https://ng.ant.design/docs/use/getting-started) which has built in Ant Design's standards to create a production ready application.

By doing a rewrite, we can ignore all the unnecessary features, and focus on what's important and necessary for our users and business.

To solve the technical complexity problem, we decided to make a [scope planning board](https://github.com/scope-planning-board/scope-planning-board), to keep the technical direction clear.

## Status

Accepted.

## Consequences

Writing code from scratch can take a lot of time. Some engineers, which have started Angular development, and have been working with Angular for more than a year, and even more, they are using Ant Design as a frontend framework, and are rewriting the entire application in Angular.

But we started planning the rewrite process. In the ADR 0010, we will describe the tasks that we will do each month to achieve this goal.

Our product manager is very excited with this decision and is eager to see our application with Ant Design standards

## Status

Accepted

## Context

The service operator is responsible for implementing the Verify self service
provider on behalf of BEIS, and is responsible for ensuring that any claims
that the service operator processes are legitimate and that the claimant is who
they say they are.

The service operator is procuring the software as a service and paying for
the number of claims processed by the service operator through the Verify
self service provider.

The service operator needs to reduce the number of claims being processed in
the longer term and it needs to do this as efficiently as possible.

The service operator is aware of a number of options for identity assurance:

### DfE's ID service provider

DfE's ID service provider is used for all other DfE digital services.

This would use the same identity assurance process.
This uses a proxy to make the service user accept a URL that should be routed
via the proxy to the actual URL, which means users will not be redirected
to the real URL in case of an outage.
This is a one way proxy to help the site handle DDoS attack which means the
service will be unavailable if the proxy server is unavailable.

### GOV.UK Verify

GOV.UK Verify has been designed to handle high volumes of user activity with
complex and very high security requirements such as user privacy.

GOV.UK Verify is more flexible than DfE's ID service provider.

GOV.UK Verify allows the service user to accept a URL and access the service
whilst accepting the site URL in the browser (i.e. use a local proxy for the site
URL).
The local proxy then handles the security responsibilities.

GOV.UK Verify has a service ID that is embedded in the site URL in the browser
historically, but this has been replaced.
This means that whenever the service user accesses the service, the service ID
is stored.
Once the user leaves the site the service ID is also removed.

This means that we don't have to store the user ID in the browser's
session.

The proxy server is accessible 24/7 and is in charge of the service ID in the
browser.
A failover proxy is built in that supports HTTP 2.0.
This helps to keep the connection secure using client-side
forwarded-for header multiplexing.

[Google document capturing the architecture](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1-VqCzF5b-B_U_s4UeYyv1M_uA-MvLmfZfVAvA/edit).

## Decision

Use GOV.UK Verify.

The service operator will need to request an account id from GOV.UK Verify and
use this to manage permissions for accessing the service via the proxy.

## Consequences

The service operator will have to manage the proxy relationship with GOV.UK
Verify and will need to understand how a proxy works.

## Context
  
  There is an input/output structure in the pipeline such that:
  - The webadmin user is responsible for generating the input that is sent to the webops deployment
  - The webops user is responsible for returning a data update that is sent to the webadmin

  A person who is a user of the Admin API can run multiple users in the pipeline. Such a person might 
  be asked questions such as 'what is the status of that service they manage, etc, etc'.

  Thus such a person needs a way to mirror back and forth to that administration's webadmin that 
  should be able to be done using the simplest means available.

## Decision

  Whenever you send a request to either the admin, deployer, or the deployer-admin interface to send a command 
  to the pipeline (i.e. create/update a service), and that command takes a parameter like 'create-deployment' or 
  'change-deployment-status' to 'service-name' and 'change-deployment-status' to 'service-id', 
  that value should be echoed back to the administering (such as Admin API) entity.

  A full example of this is the following:

  ```shell
  {
    method: 'change-deployment-status'
    param: '{service-id}'
  }
  ```

  In this case, '{service-id}' should be reflected in an output to the webadmin something like:

  ```json
  {
    "result": {
      "success": true
      "status": serviceId
    }
  }
  ```

  Which has two effects: 
  1. It returns back an ID of a service that needs to be referenced or identified later
  2. In the case where it returns a string, the ID could be used as a JSON key

## Consequences

  The implementation of this requirement adds complexity to the webops deployment and some of the
  existing and new services built and deployed. However it allows the pipeline to be more 'bi-directional', which
  allows us to more easily exchange data such as logs.

# Version the Project with CMake

**User Story:**  [MB-765](https://dp3.atlassian.net/browse/MB-765)

In order to package this project for a wider audience we would like to have the version of this project in both the command line and within the project itself.

## Considered Alternatives

* Version the project with CMake
* Version the project with the header's version
* Do not version the project

## Decision Outcome

* Chosen Alternative: *Version the project with CMake*

## Pros and Cons of the Alternatives

### Version the project with CMake

* `+` Allows us to specify a CMake-defined version that is embedded in the project.
* `+` Allows us to specify a cmake version that can be retrieved from the command line.
* `-` Version has to be manually updated on release.

### Version the project with the header's version

* `+` No version has to be manually updated on release.
* `-` We have to add a header versioning mechanism to the project and would have to merge branches for different versions.
* `-` If the header version changes the project version changes as well, which is confusing.
* `-` When the header version changes the compiler would have to be rebuilt in order to get the new project version.

### Do not version the project

* `-` Do not specify a version within the project.
* `-` Version has to be manually updated on release.
* `+` Less confusing for newcomers.
* `+` Easy to implement, do not have to manage different branch versions.

# App DB

## Context

A fully-featured CRM is not only a collection of leads, contacts, and deals, but it's also a system to generate reports for management teams and analysts.

At the heart of every CRM lies a database to record the data. Typically, this is a MySQL database, but it could also be a Microsoft SQL Server, MongoDB, or Cassandra database.

Whether a CRM runs on premises or in the cloud, it relies on a server to process, store, and read data from the database. This server may be hosted by a vendor (Salesforce, Dynamics 365, Sugar CRM) or deployed and maintained by an IT team in the organization.

## Decision

An application in this project will be designed to be a fully-featured CRM that can meet user requirements from a variety of sources for a number of users at different levels of a company.

Since the project will be hosted on the Salesforce platform, Salesforce DB will be used.

The API layer will be hosted on API Gateways by a PaaS company to be determined.

## Consequences

### Advantages

Using Salesforce provides a lot of flexibility to accommodate user requirements. Salesforce provides a good set of core modules. 

Using Salesforce provides an easy interface for non-technical users to interact with the CRM.

### Disadvantages

Users have to pay for Salesforce and Salesforce is an entirely new product. A lot of training has to be provided to enable users to interact with the CRM.

A lot of customization has to be done for Salesforce to meet requirements of an organization. It involves a lot of resources and time.

Using Salesforce provides little or no audit trail. It's not recommended for the CRM that has to track who did what and when.

### Context

For some time, there has been a debate around testing tools, specifically, using integration tests vs. command tests. 

Integration tests were designed to ensure that different parts of an application, or different applications together, work correctly together. Command tests were designed to verify that a function executed in one command, whether it be a unit test, a component test, or an e2e test, executes properly and ends as expected.

Currently we have a lot of both. We have historically used xunit integration tests (which were just our old xunit unit tests) which have been re-named to integration tests and have been enabled in the `Debug` and `Release` configurations. These have been enabled all along. Some of these tests were also marked with [Unity](https://www.unity-project.com/) runners, which means that they ran with Unity itself as opposed to Unity test runners which run in Visual Studio. We have also had `unity_assert` in place for some time, which can either be a Unity runner itself or a test runner that can be run with the `Unity` project.

As we have moved toward writing more unit tests, we have been able to reduce our integration tests to verify mostly integration with other code, particularly with the database and with web API clients.

### Decision

Rather than try to answer the debate between integration vs. command coverage, we should just focus on writing the tests in such a way that we capture all of the relevant requirements to cover both of those objectives and also our other test objectives such as code quality, catching bugs, etc.. We should:

1. Continue writing unit tests using `unity_assert`.
2. Continue writing integration tests using Unity runners.
3. Continue writing commands which can be tested like projects which are in `Debug` and `Release` configurations.

### Status

Accepted

### Consequences

Some integration tests with Unity runners continue to run under Unity. Unity does not have a good method of failing tests by `Assert.NotFail`. Since many of our integration tests fail and end the command at the end of the test, Unity only shows whether the test *passed* or *failed*. We should add tests to our integration tests that fail immediately as well.

Many of our tests are actually not tests at all. Our tests run a `dotnet CLI` process, which is the same as `dotnet new build` and can execute the tests with `dotnet test`. Some of these tests are new, but many of them are old and were added and run as if they were tests. The change should be able to happen with both.

All of our commands have `dotnet CLI` processes, which can be run as `dotnet CLI task_name`. The process output is captured and can be saved and read at a later time. We should implement this for each command.

There will be command tests that will be similar to integration tests. The command tests will run in the same `dotnet CLI` process as the command, whereas an integration test can be considered as a separate process, while the integration test and the command process will still be part of the same `dotnet CLI` instance. We can continue writing these.

## Status

Accepted

## Context

We've been processing claims in batches for some time, and the latency of loading those batches is the source of the error.
Our latency target is a batch of claims taking <20s to load, but we've seen this approach consistently fail to deliver
this target. We've tried re-shaping our latency profile to smooth the load out over 3 months, but with inconsistent results,
and have felt the increasing need to use the event sourcing approach described by Martin. This gives us a way to handle
asynchronous scenarios like batch loading and gives us a way to handle processing on a more granular basis, which in theory
should give us more predictable latency spikes.

There's no particular trigger for this change, it's just been recognised that this is an existing requirement in principle.
There's an existing backlog item [B1205][b1205] and a [spike][b1356] done earlier in the year investigating the feasibility of
using an out-of-hours batch load process.

## Decision

Change batch-loading from being the last step in processing a claim to being independent from the processing step.

## Consequences

The event sourcing system needs to be removed from the processing steps, so processing can be split into distinct steps
in line with our target latency requirements.

## TL;DR
We must allow for schema information to be attached to entities.

## Context
We must allow for schema information to be attached to entities. This might include things like:
- what fields an entity has, like a sample. This might be useful when a sample entity has multiple different columns, depending on what kind of analysis it is.
- what fields an entity has, and what type of analysis they apply to. This might be useful when an entity has multiple columns that might be useful for different analyses.

This information might be used to decide what data to query from the entity, what field to use from the list of entity columns, etc.

As an example: consider `sample`, `measurement`, and `observation`. We might have the following requirements for these entities:
- each of these have `id` and `name` fields
- `measurement` and `observation` have a field `entity_id`
- `measurement` and `observation` have a field `value` and a field `value_label`
- `sample` has a field `value` and a field `value_label`

## Decision
We will attach schema information to entities using a [json field](https://documentation.google.com/datastore/json/index.html). This field will be attached to an entity using an annotation:
```
    { "entity_id": "sample", "value": {"id": "sample", "name": "sample" }}
```

Here the value is the schema information for that entity. As shown in the example above, each object in the array has a schema for an entity, and each schema has an `entity_id` and a `value`, where the value is the schema of that entity.

## Status
Proposed

## Consequences
### Advantages
This method is flexible and can accommodate multiple different schemas for a single entity.

This method is simple to implement, since it just stores a json field, and all of the data is organized by entity.

### Disadvantages
The schema information must be stored as text in the database. This might become difficult if the schema of entities changes a lot.
Storing the entire schema for an entity at once can lead to very long response times. For example, a `sample` table with 10 million rows might take 100 seconds to return all of the samples, where a normal query takes 0.1 seconds.

## References
- http://docs.oracle.com/javase/tutorial/essential/java/json/introduction.html

## Status

Accepted

## Context

Given that this system will have user interactions that can result in the loss of keys or accidentally discarded keys, we should have a way for users to easily backup up their keys. To do so, we will create a way to backup keys in private note taking apps like Notion or Google Note. 

**However, since keys are long strings, and some keys can be hundreds of characters long, how can users be sure they didn't make a typo while backing up their keys? Or accidentally paste another key instead of the one they intended to?**

For the moment, it will be easy for users to paste an incorrect key and continue. However, if a user accidentally loses their private key and their wallet, and someone gets access to their recovery account (that has the backup keys), they could steal all the cryptocurrency.

There is a way to mitigate this, and we will implement it here. **All keys that are backed up MUST be used in a separate wallet or system entirely.** This way, even if a user's wallet account is compromised, the attacker would not have access to their private key that is used to backup their private wallet.

## Decision

We will implement a method for users to backup their keys and private keys are used exclusively in separate wallets or systems.

## Consequences

Users must now have a separate wallet for all the cryptocurrency they hold. This is an extra layer of security and mitigates the risk of a user losing their keys and having an attacker access their wallet.

If users lose their private key and their wallet, but someone gets access to their recovery account, they still won't be able to access the users private key which is used to backup the wallet. This removes a huge amount of risk, and provides the right to privacy and security for our users.

If a user makes a mistake while creating a backup of their private key, and accidentally sends an incorrect key and continue, then they won't realize it until the next transaction. If this is repeated, the user can use their recovery account to recover their private key and try again. If a user ever loses their private key, they can use their recovery account to recover their private key.

## Context and Problem Statement

To simplify the usage and maintenance of the Community Manager app, it is desirable to manage the users directly in Github and to leverage the authentication and authorisation that GitHub provides.

What authentication and authorisation solutions shall we use?

## Decision Drivers

* **Authentication should work for all user activities in the app** (e.g. sign up, sign in, changing roles etc.)
* **Authentication should be a little bit 3Bot/K8sy compliant and easily maintainable by the dev team** (e.g. avoid OAuth with Facebook/Google/etc. since we're the owners/maintainers of the project)
* **Authentication should allow to sign in with the Office 365 (O365) users.** (e.g. provide a "b2C" authentication to make migration from Pivotal Cloud Foundry simpler)

## Considered Options

* GitHub OAuth
* Key-Based Authentication
* Database-Backend Authentication

## Decision Outcome

Chosen option: "Key-Based Authentication", because it's the option which meets all of our criteria.

## Pros and Cons of the Options

### GitHub OAuth

* `+` easy to set up and to keep up

### Key-Based Authentication

* `+` no additional infrastructure to maintain (server, database etc.)
* `+` simple to implement
* `+` users are in control of their authentication (they have to remember their password and they can reset it)
* `-` if the user forgets their password, they're locked out of their account
* `+` we don't have to track down the user if they get locked out
* `-` the user has to trust the project maintainers that they won't publish their private keys
* `-` we have to generate and store the private keys ourselves

### Database-Backend Authentication

* `-` more work in the beginning (to set up the database + migration scripts)
* `-` more work in the long term (we have to keep the database running and it's contents encrypted)
* `+` no key management is required
* `+` no user is locked out and they can reset their passwords
* `+` we're sure that the user is who they say they are (authentication can be revoked)
* `-` difficult to implement
* `-` we have to track the users (we cannot use `github-backend` solution from Pivotal)

## Context

The data pipeline's processing logic is not complex, which means it can run on AWS Lambda and finish in a matter of seconds, but the number of Lambda invocations is pretty low.
In this context, a task-based approach, where each "job" run independently from the others, is preferred over a single, massive job execution, which would be inefficient.

A [task-based approach to Continuous Delivery](https://github.com/dehal/a-better-cd-pipeline/blob/master/docs/How-to-do-CD-better.md) might be worth to check out if we ever need to increase the number of lambda invocations.

This approach results in two options:

1. Use a *task runner* to execute the tasks
1. Use the existing AWS services to do this - in this case, *Airflow* and *AWS' SQS* (simple queue service) 

## Decision

Use Airflow and AWS' SQS service for task execution.

Reasons:
* AWS SQS service is fully managed and quite affordable
* Airflow is a mature OSS project
* Airflow provides a GUI for tracking tasks

## Consequences

Tasks can be run as independent jobs and managed through a web-based GUI.

Jobs can be scheduled (or triggered) at precise moments in time using Airflow's scheduler.
You can trigger a job (or a set of tasks) via AWS' API or via the UI, too.

All tasks that run are logged to Airflow's UI, so any error that happens during execution is reported as well.

## Status

Accepted

## Context

We need a way to test features in our software products. There are a lot of
options on the market, including Selenium, Cypress, Nightmare, Webkit.
There are also local testing frameworks like TestJS.

There are many factors to consider when selecting a testing framework. For
example, would it work on our current frontend stack? Would it be too time
consuming to learn? Could we use it to test more than just frontend features?
Are there a lot of plugins available for it?

## Decision

We've decided to use the WebDriverIO framework to test features in our software products.

We didn't use some other frameworks because it seemed like they were all
designed for testing a single layer (either the front end or the backend). We
want to be able to test a variety of features, including both front end and
backend features.

We also like the WebDriverIO framework because it allows us to test features using the
tools that we're already familiar with, such as Google Chrome and PhantomJS.

There's a lot of documentation for the framework, so it will be easy to get
started with it quickly. There's also a lot of other resources online, such
as StackOverflow questions and answers. It seems that a lot of people like this
framework.

The framework allows us to test for any number of features, not just features
that are visible to the user. For example, we could use it to test that a
form field is bound to the correct model property, or that a successful HTTP
request is being routed to the right endpoint.

It's an open source project, so it's really flexible. If there's a feature that
doesn't work for us, we can always fix it ourselves. If someone makes a
discovery about a feature that would be useful for us, they can contribute
it to the project.

There's a lot of plugins available for the framework. If there's a feature
that we need, there's a good chance that someone has already written a
plugin for it.

We don't know enough about our future stack to decide whether it will be
compatible with WebDriverIO. For example, if we switch to using Firefox instead of
Chrome, will the framework still work with Firefox?

## Consequences

Some of the features that we need to test may be difficult or impossible to test
with the framework. For example, it's possible to capture the contents of
the entire DOM using the framework, but it's not possible to capture all
events that happen on a web page.

There's a lot of documentation and resources online to help us learn about
the framework, but it's still a complex framework. We'll need to invest
a lot of time to learn it and start using it effectively.

## Status

Accepted

## Context

The first decision was made on how to structure reads and writes (see [4. Use 3 layer architecture style](0004-use-3-layer-architecture-style.md)).

The first read layer would have been directly on the datastore, and the second read layer would have been a cached view of the datastore. The datastore layer would have been solely responsible for holding the data.

We felt that this would be too restrictive for reads. Most reads would not go through the datastore, so we felt that this layer would have been unnecessary for some reads. This also meant that each read layer would not cache, meaning that reads that did not go through the datastore were not cached. This meant that we would not be able to rely on the cached read layer for reads that were not datastore bound. 

## Decision

The architecture for the read layer changed so that there was a read cache, which contained the data from the datastore. A datastore read layer was kept to provide a read strategy, but the read cache was the more logical approach to use for reads.

The data layer keeps the data itself, and is accessed through the datastore read layer. 

## Consequences

This was the biggest change to the architecture decision for reads. Most reads go through the cached read layer, which does not go through the datastore read layer.

This approach allows us to make a simple caching policy, based upon the last read of a piece of data, but caching is done in an opaque manner, so that there is no way for datastore read layer to be implemented as the caching mechanism. We can assume that the cache has a replication mechanism, to ensure high availability.

As of the this decision, there are no read writes. If the database load becomes so great that writes need to be added, a new read write layer will be added.

## Context

One of the ways to help package testing across projects is to use a shared project. This is not only beneficial to project teams as it gives them a constant project that they can check-in and view-out, but it's useful to software engineers by giving them a library to use in their implementations. At DXC, this is typically done with `CronoGraph`, which gives a way to use "testable" objects for clients to interact with.

The problem with this approach is that there's no constant definition of what "testable" objects are in the code as it can have a large number of different definitions. This means that if at least one definition has changed and something has been built using that definition, the only way to understand what's been broken is to use the code viewer to view that definition and understand what it's been changed to.

## Decision

In the current set of tests, the pattern is to use `CronoGraph.Testable.testable.service.function.function()`, which returns a `function` object that can be used in tests. Now, if we start to use this object in the test code, there's no clear standard of what the function should perform. This is the problem we need to solve.

By introducing an object, such as `CronoGraph.Testable.testable.service.function.function()`, we're going to solve the problem by having a constant definition of what the function performs, which allows for us to use the standard function when doing statements that are not based on functions like `describe`, `it` and `expect`.

To make this explicit, the testable object should be an `function` type variable and the testable instance of `CronoGraph.Testable.testable.service.function.function()`. So the testable instance can be used as the `function` object.

To ensure that the testable object is the correct type, we can check by using `instanceof` in a test, and pass the object into the test, by using a mock object, instead. If the instance is correct, then a success condition in the test.

## Consequences

By introducing the `function` type variable, the tests and testable objects change. The testable objects are changed by the inclusion of a `function` type variable in their signature. This means that now it's not only possible to perform "typical testable" actions on the testable objects, it's possible to use a mock object for them.

We're going to create two kinds of tests: those that test the functions we create; and those that test how well our testable objects perform their duties. This will make them easier to understand, more readable and more reusable.

## Context and Problem Statement

SQL is written in plain text and is easy to read and write, but has been found to contain a wide range of issues like syntax errors, best practices violations, deadlocks, etc. It can be implemented without much help from IDEs and is quite easy for inexperienced developers to make mistakes and have the program fail silently. In general, a library like ASP.NET provides a DAL layer that attempts to fix these issues, as it contains various classes that are used to describe database-specific operations.

In `menu-generation` application, we'll have frequent database access. Therefore, it would be a good idea to adopt the DAL pattern to avoid typical SQL mistakes, but also unnecessary overheads related to the DAL.

## Decision Drivers

* Ease of use
* Learning curve
* Performance

## Considered Options

* Write all SQL statements in plain SQL and do not use the DAL
* Use the DAL to write all SQL statements
* Use the DAL to write only the database-related parts of the application

## Decision Outcome

Chosen option: the DAL, as it provides database-specific classes that can be used to describe queries in a type-safe manner, and the application developers do not have to worry about SQL issues. Moreover, the DAL could be used to implement common database patterns that prevent a wide range of SQL errors. 

However, no strict rules should be set when using the DAL, as plain SQL statements can be used in cases that do not require SQL patterns. For instance, simple `SELECT` statements should be allowed when the developers know exactly what they are doing.

## Context

Given the need to manage individual tickets with different priorities and deadlines it was agreed to make a decision on how to store that information.

Since the content of tickets may change over time, it was agreed that the content of tickets would be stored as a series of document objects.

Since many aspects of a ticket may change over time, it was agreed that the ticket’s document content would be stored within a series of properties.

Since the ticket’s content can cover a great range of topics it was agreed that the ticket document content would be stored as a series of properties where keys represent topic types and values represent the content of that topic type.

## Decision

The solution for storing ticket content will be to maintain a series of documents where documents can contain arbitrary properties.

For example, the property `title` could be a string, while the property `priority` could be an integer.

This approach means that future changes to the structure of the ticket properties will not invalidate previous data as a new version of the ticket document type can be created.

This approach means that it is possible to add new properties to tickets and support for them can be included in future versions of the application.

This approach means that it is possible for some data to be added to tickets at a later date, for example, `status` or `date_created`.

In general this approach means that the data structure of tickets can change over time.

## Consequences

The data structure of tickets will not be set in stone and any changes can be supported in the future by adding properties to the ticket documents type.

Since the type of ticket document is defined as a series of properties which can have arbitrary key and value pairs it will be possible for the future to determine properties that were previously unknown and were required, such as `date_created`.

This approach means that data can be added to tickets at a later date, for example, `status`.

This approach means that there is some flexibility in the data structure of the tickets and some data may have to be added at a later date to support future features.

## Decision

We will use architecture decision reports, as described by Michael Nygard in
[this article](http://thinkrelevance.com/blog/2011/11/15/documenting-architecture-decisions).

The decision reports format has two parts:
- a decision is described in a textfile, where for each decision a new section
  is used, where for each section a decision is described using the following format:
  - `[section name]. [decision] [decision date].`
  - e.g. `Do not store timestamps in the decision report`
  - e.g. `Date: 2020-06-04`

- the other part consists of a Github issue and a linked PR, where at least some
  decision report is linked to the issue. This gives the possibility to add more
  information at the PR, when some decisions require it.

When creating a decision report, one should be sure to add relevant background
information and context in the form of a decision. The decision is only a sentence
or two long.

## Consequences

The result is a decision report, which document architectural decisions made in
this project in a structured way.

Using this format provides several benefits over other formats. A list of those
benefits can be found in the article linked to in Decision.

In addition to this format, this project also stores information about architectural
decisions in its release notes.

If a decision report is added to a PR, when needed, the decision can be added to
the PR in a more detailed way.

# Go Dependency Management

**User Story:** https://github.com/UST-API-151/API-Pipeline/stories/574#

Go depends on external dependencies for functionality. It is necessary to pick appropriate dependencies and to manage the version of these. 

## Considered Alternatives

* Use dep to install and pin dependencies.
* Use dep to install all dependencies. Pin them with version constraints.
* Use dep to install and pin dependencies and use dep-pin to make pinning reproducible.
* Use dep to install all dependencies and use dep-pin to make pinning reproducible.

## Decision Outcome

* Chosen Alternative: *Use dep to install all dependencies. Pin them with version constraints. Use dep-pin to make pinning reproducible.*

* Impacts/Consequences: Using dep-pin makes it possible to make reproducible, small, and predictable changes to dependency pins, and make it easier to make changes and revisions to dependencies that have widely-accepted, well-understood, and well-documented changes.

## Pros and Cons of the Alternatives <!-- optional -->

### dep

Pros: 

* Can find dependencies online and install them
* Can add and manage version constraints

Cons:

* Dependencies get installed and stored in private repo (not private in production)
* Not widely used by rest of team

### dep-pin

Pros: 

* Can add dependencies to projects.
* Can make pinning reproducible by using dep-pin.
* Version pinning is fully integrated with the pipeline.
* Version constraints can be managed in one spot (Go.mod)

Cons:

* Requires dep dependency
* Not widely used by rest of team


### Alternative 1

Pros: 

* No effort to implement

Cons:

* Cannot get latest version of dep
* No built in version constraint management
* Not widely used by rest of team

### Alternative 2

Pros: 

* Can get latest version of dep
* Can make pinning reproducible

Cons:

* Requires dep dependency
* Cannot add dependencies to projects.
* Version pinning is not integrated into the pipeline
* Not widely used by rest of team

### Use dep (no pin) for packages and use dep-pin for dependencies
*Pros:*

* Full access to latest version of dep
* Complete integration with Go.mod
* Version pinning is fully integrated with the pipeline
* Can add dependencies to projects
* Can make pinning reproducible by using dep-pin.
* Version constraints can be managed in one spot (Go.mod)

*Cons:*

* Requires dep-pin to implement pinning
* Not widely used by rest of team

# 3. Use Ports & Adapter Architecture

Date: 2020-03-27

## Status

Accepted

## Context

The aim is to have the application be [testable](../testing-in-a-nutshell.md).

The aim is to have the application be [maintainable](../maintainability-in-a-nutshell.md).

The aim is to have the application be [flexible](0002-use-a-modular-monolith-architecture.md).

So the aim is to treat this project as if it were a [series of interconnected services](https://www.martinfowler.com/bliki/Interservice.html).

### Ports & Adapter

Ports & Adapter is a way of modelling how we can talk about different clients of a particular service.

As well as [testability](../testing-in-a-nutshell.md) and [maintainability](../maintainability-in-a-nutshell.md), Ports & Adapter implies:

* the client can be changed without affecting the service
* the client can be changed as long as the service makes sense
* the service can be changed without needing to make another client in a different service
* you have an API
* you can have multiple clients

### Ports
A container, such as a web service, that has a client (or several) that consumes it for different purposes.

### Adapter
A container, such as a web service, that has multiple clients that use the same interface, but for different purposes (usually different clients consume it and make API calls to it).

### Ports & Adapter
A system for multiple clients that consume different containers. Ports are how consumers view the service, while adapters are how clients access the service.

As a result Ports & Adapter implies that a system can be consumed by multiple clients, and then by different consumers.

### Ports & Adapter Architecture
This architecture is based upon a client/consumer architecture, where the various consumers use a common interface to access the services in the system.

This means that many consumers can live in separate containers, e.g. client-side libraries, and then have their own ports.

The adapters act as clients for the service containers, and also as consumers of the service containers.

### Adapters
An adapter is a container which has an API for the services within it, and is used by some consumer to access them.

### Ports
A port is a container which is used by consumers to access the services within it.

## Decision

This project will use the [Ports & Adapter architecture](https://martinfowler.com/articles/martinfowler_portsadapters.html).

We will allow client side code, either as an NPM package or as a CDN based module, to use the server side system through a ports & adapter layer. This layer will be provided via the NPM package.

We will allow testing in ports & adapter style, either through in browser tests, or in tests using the NPM package.

## Consequences

It will be easier to set up and use the service as a CDN based npm package.

It will be easier to use the service in other applications and services, because the service can be provided as an npm package.

Testing can be done either in a test suite added to the NPM package, or in an application that consumes the service, using its own ports & adapter layer.

A change to the service can be done with a new container, without changing the existing client containers.

A change to the client can be done without changing the existing container.

A change to the client can be done using the NPM package, without changing the existing container.

The service can be provided as multiple clients in different containers.

This implies we have an API, with clients that abstract from the implementation, which is something the service container provides. The API is used by the adapters.

We need to define the interface between the client and the service container.

We need to define what is the common interface between the adapter and the service container.

We need to define how the adapter consumes and presents the service.

To determine the interface between the client and the service container we should use the DDD tactical design pattern [the boundary adapter](./0001-use-tactical-design-patterns.md#the-boundary-adapter) -- to define an interface between the service and its client -- using a standard API and a language for describing the interface. The language used should define the interface (e.g. type definitions).

To define how the adapter consumes and presents the service we should use the DDD tactical design pattern [the facade](./0001-use-tactical

## Context

The concept of an API client was also present in the design of the
light-clients for Bitcoin Core.

The first iteration came as `git-light-core` which was the light-client
of Bitcoin Core. This had `git-box`, `git-tree` and `git-repository`
interfaces which provided reading and writing access to a local
repository (which was the result of a `git init --bare` for which the
client was created). This approach was taken, because we want to enable
projects (clients) to use the light-client without having their own
repository. This is useful for projects which don't want to host their own
`git-repository` (eg. in the case of the storage service for which the
light-client is made).

This approach was not considered as the best approach for all the reasons it
had not worked out with the `git-light-core` client.

Another iteration was `git-light-backup`, which as it name suggests, was
mainly meant to be a backup tool of some kind. But it had a light-client
in it, which was meant to be the way you can mount a light-client and
create a backup archive on the local system (as the source of truth) of
the files that the light-client is storing (in the sense that is storing
the entire filesystem). This was also not considered as the best approach,
since the light-client API was a `git-repository` and a standard `git`
interface. But the way the user requested the data out of the API, and
the API in terms of this project did not accept data requests like for
example the `git-light-core` client did.

While the first two iterations considered as light-clients did not
manage all the data internally, but were mostly used to manage large
amounts of data from the client (like git repositories), the third iteration,
the Light Client, is the first iteration to manage all the data (the data
of the client) itself. That means the `LightClient` API has to manage the
entire data of the client. This is a considerable difference to the first
two iterations. It can be useful or not for the developer.

So, the main question for this iteration was: Should we build a special
client that only builds/manages the API, or should we build the
light-client as an API that manages its own data?

## Decision

Based on the assumption that the concept of a light-client is meant
to help the users to learn about Bitcoin and its working in the most
lightweight way and that the main API should be kept as a reference
to Bitcoin's concept (for learning purposes, and as a reference to the
full client), we build the Light Client as a simple API to manage the
light-client data. It is not going to be used as a full client.

## Status

Accepted.

## Consequences

- The API will be simpler
- We will not have the possibility of having a full
  integration test and a light-client as an API that can be
  integrated in the test-kit for testing integration, like in the case of
  the `git-light-core` client.

Date: 2019-06-27

## Status

Accepted

## Context

Versioned data services are used to enable the migration of data from a legacy data warehouse to the new platform.

As part of the service migration there are requirements around data structure and type changes. This increases the need for strict versioning to avoid data loss and corruption during the process of data warehouse to platform.

Since we use a data pipeline to support the platform there is also a need for the ability to support multiple environments, which would be very difficult to achieve without the capability to version database systems.

Our technical team has also used versioned database systems in the past. These services allow developers and operations to view a historical record of changes that have been made to the database. This functionality is also valuable to us as the platform evolves.

Our team have two years of experience building with versioned database services in our legacy platform services.

## Decision

We will use a versioned database service to support the platform

## Consequences

Since our services are supported by a database service there are a number of consequences of using a versioned database system

### Versioning is a key feature of any services that we build to support the platform

A consequence is that the team must make a decision around the appropriate service to meet our needs. It must be agreed by the team the appropriate database service and technology to be used.

While our team have experience in building using these technologies there are still a number of decisions that must be made around database setup (e.g. service hosting/setup) and database management.

Some decisions around database services such as storage and backup requirements are needed. 

### We will need to apply database principles to the services that we build to support the platform

A consequence is that all new services which will build upon the platform must adhere to good database engineering principles, which will ensure the scalability of the platform.

### Developers have visibility of past changes to the services

Although there will be a need for some access control around who can use the versioning functionality it will be easy to provide this functionality using database user privileges.

Developers will be able to view changes to the database and other data structures that are required to run the platform.

### Migrations can be supported by the services

All database changes will be stored as a log, which can be reviewed to understand what changes are required to support the platform migration.

### Data can be recovered

The storage of past data makes it possible to restore the platform using a versioned database service. This functionality can be useful to support debugging and testing.

### Database changes can be easily understood

Since there is a historical log of changes to the database it should be possible to quickly understand the nature and intent of any changes made to the database.

### Database changes can be propagated to all services using the platform

Any changes to the database will affect all services that use the versioned database service. 

### There are limitations around what can be versioned

Some database services have a limited memory set; for example, 64kb on MySQL. This might limit our ability to view log data across a long period of time.

Although we use a [version-based log](https://dev.mysql.com/docs/8.0/ref/period_version_to_string().html) function to provide a timestamped log of changes to the database there may be a need to update this functionality to provide additional information.

Some database services have a set of stored procedures that can be called to enable the view of past database state. If there is a need to query data in the past then an additional change to the database will be required.

# 6 - Use Jenkins for Continuous Integration

Date: 2020-Nov-12

## Status

Accepted

## Context

A build lifecycle is needed to describe the phases of building a project.
These build phases and processes are a requirement for the funding application.

There are several different CI services available, which are commonly used in the
software industry. These include:

* Travis CI
* CircleCI
* GitLab CI

There are many benefits of using a CI service, including:

* the ability to run builds across many machines;
* integration with version control systems;
* continuous integration;

As well as this, using a CI service will make the grant application easier to submit to
DIT's Digital Standards team, since we can submit it using a service that they use.

A particular issue motivating this decision:

[A] We have used the following services to run builds in our previous projects:

* Travis CI
* CircleCI
* GitLab CI

With the exception of Travis CI, all of our builds used different methods of running
builds.

In this project we want to have a build process which follows the standards set by
the Digital Standards team, so they will support it in the future.
We also want the build process to be repeatable across builds, so that future
members of the team (and DIT) will be able to run the same build process and get the
same build artifact on their machine.

## Decision

We will use the [Jenkins](https://www.jenkins.io/) build system.

The project documentation will include a [Jenkins file](https://plugins.jenkins.io/ansible/Jenkinsfile/)
so that anyone can run a build locally.

## Consequences

Using a build server will allow us to:

* run builds in different environments;
* have repeatable builds;
* automate builds, making them easier for future team members to run.

A build server will mean that we have to maintain a build system for the project.

Using a CI service instead would have been a simpler solution to achieve the
goals above but would have meant using a cloud service, which has the following
advantages:

* it would allow us to use the same build process to run future builds, without having
  to maintain a build server.

The disadvantages of the CI approach are:

* it will be more expensive to run builds in the future;
* it is not available in DIT's infrastructure currently.

Date: 2019-12-13

## Status

Accepted

## Context

In order to have confidence in the system, we should take steps to reduce risk as much
as possible. This includes taking steps to reduce risk associated with node packages, to avoid
delivering functionality reliant on those packages to production. In this context, this means
reducing the risk of node packages being [out of date](https://dependency-check.com/results/web/06-03-2019)
and introducing bugs as a result.

Yarn makes it easy to manage node dependencies, introducing a layer of abstraction that makes
it easier to be confident the node modules on which we rely are up-to-date and free from bugs.

## Decision

We will use yarn instead of npm to manage the project's node dependencies.

## Consequences

We will be able to be confident our code is using dependencies that are as bug-free as possible,
reducing the risk of introducing bugs into the system, and providing a standard way to manage
node dependencies that should reduce friction in the project.

We should also be conscious that this introduces a dependency on [yarn workspaces](https://classic.yarnpkg.com/en/docs/workspaces/). This is
essentially a type of mono-repository with some added benefits, like:

- The `--workspaces` flag to switch the workcontext to the desired workspace
- Implicit locking of yarn workspaces and their dependencies to avoid mixing versions of dependencies
- Support of `node_modules/other-project` for the isolation of shared code

We should also recognise that there are restrictions around yarn workspaces, for example
they require yarn workspaces to be installed using `yarn`.

By reducing the need to manually install each package, yarn workspaces also save time. In most scenarios
a project's `--root` directory, [node_modules/other-project](https://classic.yarnpkg.com/en/docs/workspaces/#_isolation-of-shared-code)
is a project's root directory (or a directory that is used as such by the team).

As a consequence, introducing yarn workspaces will make it a little bit more difficult to switch
to [npm](https://www.npmjs.com/).

We should recognise also that we can't easily get node_modules/other-project in to our CI,
since this means we can't easily cache it, which may be useful for performance. Instead,
we will need to cache it by using `node_modules/other-project` in a [lock file](./yarn.lock).

We should also recognise that, although we can easily switch to [npm](https://www.npmjs.com/),
we can't easily switch from yarn to npm. The way to switch is to install the package locally
at the point of change. We also need to use `--npm-shrinkwrap.json` instead of yarn.lock
at the point of change.

Finally, [testing with yarn workspaces](https://www.garbados.org/2019/07/16/testing-with-yarn-workspaces/)
can be a pain. One solution is to try using the `--cwd` flag in the CLI at the point of change.

## Status

Accepted

## Context

Code that we have been working with for a long time was originally developed
by the "Armadillo" team. It was stored in two places:

- source repository with code
- source repository with tests (that ran on source branch)

Both of these repositories were created by [git subtree split](https://help.github.com/articles/splitting-a-subfolder-out-into-a-new-repository/). They were used together for many years and became somewhat out of sync.

## Decision

Copy source and tests to a Docker container.

We wanted to make it easier to run the code locally in Docker.

There were several options:

- copy the source code
- copy the tests code
- copy both
- use containers for tests

## Consequences

We tested different options. The main options considered are:

- copy the source code
- copy the tests code
- copy both
- use containers for tests

It turns out that the best way of doing this depends on the size of the file set:

- when there are small files, it is best to copy the tests because the `git add` and `git commit` is easier. It turns out that `git add` is the only thing you need to commit to test code.

- when there are a lot of files and directories, it is best to copy both, because it is easier to commit `git add`, where `git add` can be used for the tests in addition to the source code. However, committing tests alone is easy.

Use containers for the tests. We tried this with a single container (`armadillo-test-all`), but we found that the Docker containers take up too much space for long running jobs.

A Docker file is required for the tests. For the purpose of writing the documentation, the `test.md` is used instead of the real test files. There will be a separate Docker file for the real tests.

If you run `git push --tags`, tags will be added.

Tags will be added for each version of the test containers.

## Other options considered

### Keep source code locally

Based on the fact that we have been using the source branch tests and versioning for years, we initially considered keeping the source code locally.

Keep source code locally because:

- it allows you to have test code and versioning, and it's easier to commit.

Keep source code locally because:

- It's easier to edit the tests, because it's in the source branch.

Keep source code locally because:

- We were using the source branch version, the `master` branch version, and the release branch version.

Keep source code locally because:

- We've been using the local source branch version.

Keep source code locally because:

- We were already committing the source branch and using the version in the release branch.

Keep source code locally because:

- The `git push --tags` pushes release tags to GitHub and push tags to the release branch.

We wanted to remove this option because it doesn't work with the GitHub workflow.

### Use containers for tests

We have tried this approach with other projects. There are several options:

- write a container that runs tests, e.g., `armadillo-test-all`, where you can execute tests from inside a container that doesn't change your own.

- use containers to execute tests. You could run a `bash` shell from the test container (e.g., `armadillo-test-all`) to execute tests. You could run a `bash` shell in the source container to execute tests (e.g., `master`) and execute tests on your own machine.

These options have the following advantages and disadvantages:

- copy source
- copy tests
- use containers to execute tests

- source is kept locally:
- version is used for release branches, and the release branches tag release tags
- version is used for release branches. It's easier to edit than the source branch code because there's no Docker container

- containers:
- is a more portable way to run the tests
- some additional tooling is required to make sure it's portable
- a very portable way to run the tests
- can be used to run all the tests
- source can be kept locally

proposed

## Context

As we keep defining more and more API endpoints, it is a good idea to centralize the specification of the incoming requests and outgoing responses in one place.
API specifications can be written in plain text but it is hard to find out about changes or updates.
The documentation for a plain text API specification can become quickly outdated.
More formal specifications can be written in a more structured way using JSON schemas.
JSON schema is also the specification format that data providers for the EAI exchange.

## Decision

We use JSON schema for specifying requests and responses in APIs.

## Consequences

The outgoing responses and incoming requests can be specified declaratively instead of codewire/json by hand.
The EAI client software is able to read the schema of the API and retrieve the schema (by default).
A change in the schema has to be propagated to both, the API provider and the EAI client software.

## Context

The main application for the HackIT project, frontend and backend, will be stored in Github as versioned source code. At the time, the project was supported by DIT’s Open Source Technical Standards team. At the time, a number of other projects were also managed using Github; the key user base for them all is the DIT digital services team, whose users are expected to be using public repositories.

## Decision

While maintaining the Github repositories, the following practices should be observed:

- When creating a repository, the options for default visibility should be chosen, the default should be `public`, and the code should be uploaded immediately upon creation, while the repository is in "create" state.
- It is expected that most Pull Requests (PRs) should originate from and be merged into the `main` branch, although it is acceptable to make PRs directly to `deploy-branch` if they are not related to changes in the `main` branch's code. To manage this, a "custom merge rules" must be added to the `main` branch's forks in Github settings.
- Branches should be given meaningful names, and clearly follow this format: `feature-{short-description}/#corresponding-branch-name`.
- Commits should follow this format: `branch-name: corresponding-commit-name`
- Release branches should be prefixed with `release/` in branch names.

## Status

Accepted

## Consequences

- The HackIT team should have visibility of code changes, and the public can view their changes.
- Code can be stored in versioned releases.
- The project can be used as a sample for future Open Source Technical Standards projects on Github.
- It is likely that the HackIT team may need to make changes to the existing `custom merge rules` setting used by other projects with the `main` branch as their source.

## Context

In general, web services have some components that are shared across many modules. One of them for instance is the way they store data. This is usually done with a database, and there are various ways a database can be set up and provided to the modules that need it. It is possible to assume that the way the data is stored has an impact on the architecture, as the user usually has a good view and feel for the way they interact with the data.

The approach to setting up the data storage in the modules needs to be considered. A way the data can be retrieved and changed is needed to allow people who care about data to use the module. Another possible way of thinking is that the modules require and supply data. In fact, this could be viewed as two different aspects of the same thing.

An important result of the way the data is stored and accessed is that it can be seen as part of the architecture when a module relies on it. This is reflected in a way the module should use the data it needs.

The architecture approach is that the modules can be changed by the user of these modules (user code). This user code provides the data of a module or uses the data already stored in it. The data that is stored is important and could be used to understand how to work with the module. When the module changes and data has to be stored, it could be assumed the data will be stored in the best way to do this, in order to access the data in the future.

The architectural approach is to have a module that is changed by a user. The data should be accessible to the module.

## Decision

To ensure data can be changed by user code, the modules have to be able to store data to have some user interaction.

The architecture approach is that the modules can be changed by a user. This is part of the architecture.

## Consequences

### Positive

* The data that is stored is not just for communication, it is part of the architecture.
* The data can be changed by a user.

### Negative

* The user has to be conscious of what is stored in the module.

### Neutral

* The module has data to store.

## Status

accepted

## Context

This project is a first version of an API designed to be consumed by front-end applications. The main questions that we want to solve is:

- Should the API respond to multiple front-end applications, or just one?
- Should the API respond to multiple server side applications, or just the front-end applications?
- Should the API be a collection of separate, discrete endpoints and have state? 

We considered the following options:

1. Single frontend application, single endpoint that responds to all clients
2. Single frontend application, many endpoints responding to separate clients
3. Many frontend applications, single endpoint responding to all clients
4. Many frontend applications, many endpoints responding to separate clients
5. Single application with API, single frontend application consuming the API
6. Single application with API, many frontend applications consuming the API

In general, we felt that option 5 was the best fit, because it allowed us to create a single API that could serve multiple front-end applications, and was the closest to a micro-services architecture. However, we also felt that it might be complex to implement. So for this version of the API, we decided to take the simplest approach, while still maintaining some level of separation between the server and the front-end applications.

There are many advantages to this approach, such as reduced coupling, increased flexibility, and easier local testing. By decoupling the front-end and API applications, we can change the front-end technology or implementation without needing to change our API code, and we can start, stop, or change the API implementation without needing to make changes to the front-end. By keeping the API implementation decoupled from the front-end application, we make it easier to develop, test, and deploy our API locally.  

However, there are some costs to this approach, such as an additional round trip when accessing the API, and potential performance impact of data being stored on the front-end side. Additionally, data needs to be sent to the front-end in a serialized format for transmission, and deserialized when received.

Because of these costs, there are some things that we need to take into account when designing our API. For instance, we need to keep data-to-data interaction to a minimum, and aim for operations that are read-heavy. We also need to avoid excessive data representation, and instead focus on the data that is absolutely necessary for our API to perform its job.

## Decision

We decided to take an option 5 approach, using an API application for managing our APIs and a front-end application for consuming the API. By decoupling the front-end application from our API, we create an API that can be consumed by multiple clients, while still being simple and easy to implement.

## Consequences

Choosing an API application as the API implementation allows us to separate concerns, enforce type safety, and implement the best practice of using type ORMs. Because the API application exists as a program separate to the front-end, there are advantages for local testing and development.

However, there are also some costs to this approach. Since the API application exists as a separate program, the front-end must send HTTP calls to the API for any data it requires. Additionally, any data that is sent to the API must be serialized and deserialized between the front-end and API. This requires a simple serialization and deserialization library, but adds another step to the data flow process.

### Context

In this project we have to send email messages to the users and support other email related actions (like creating temp accounts).

Since we have the email sending functionality built in, we can use the email client capabilities of the messenger.

The project uses other (non-email related) capabilities, too.

Some functionalities (like saving the state of the email client, i.e. the user, that was already addressed in the email conversation) will not be supported by the messenger.

### Decision

We use the Messenger to send email messages.

### Status

Accepted.

### Consequences

The Messenger can send email messages to users and support related email actions, but is not able to save the state of the email conversation for them.

## Status

Accepted

## Context

We want to support users accessing our API in a protected manner.  
At the moment we use JWT's as our only means of authorization.  
While a useful tool to prevent front running on the API this is not the only type of attack to counter.  
For example an attacker could use multiple API tokens to spam the API with requests.  
Additionally our current JWT implementation is self-contained.  
This means our API cannot be easily accessed and the JWT is the only way to get access to the API.  
While this works in some scenarios it fails when a client needs to reuse their own JWT to access the API and will cause rejection of the JWT at the API Gateway.  
This requires us to provide the JWT to the API Gateway beforehand, and creates security issues when that JWT is shared among multiple clients.  

## Decision

We want to allow clients of our API to use their JWT to get access.  

The reason why we want to use JWT to access our API is simply because it's the currently best authentication / authorization mechanism.
While technologies like OID and CORS are quite new and aren't as flexible as JWT to use the JWT could potentially be implemented by these technologies at some point in time.

We found that it's not possible to implement client authentication with JWT through the API Gateway using dropwizard feature `api-keys`.  
The reason behind this is because dropwizard features cannot read the JWT out of the requests headers.
An additional middleware like `jersey-jwt-filter-provider` which can read the JWT out of the request headers is unable to set header information in the response (a limitation by the Open ID 1.0 specification).
This is unfortunately related to the fact that we also implemented a middleware `spring-jwt-authentication-filter-provider` using OpenAPI as the API documentation to retrieve our token expiry in JSON format which was originally implemented to authenticate calls to the API using JWT.
This current JWT middleware can set JWT access tokens in the response only when the JWT expiration was known.

There are 2 options to workaround this limitation.  
One would be to provide another custom middleware so that the API Gateway is used by the client to sign and verify JWT access tokens.
This adds additional latency in the chain of calls to the API Gateway and the client.
A second would be to fetch the API token from the JWT via a custom middleware and then get the API access token information using this API token from our API and use it to set the JWT access tokens in the API response.
For this approach we need to store the API token and its access token information in memory and will result in a need for more frequent calls to the [healthcheck API](0001-use-healthcheck-api.md) to ensure our API token stays up to date.
The implementation of our current healthcheck API for the first JWT middleware would not work with this approach, because it doesn't return information in JSON format.

## Consequences

We will be able to allow client authentication for our API by using JWT and making our API access token information stored in a database available to clients.
We will fetch API tokens from our healthcheck API which needs to be updated at least as frequently as our JWT.  
This would be required either to verify the JWT access token or to be used as API key when the JWT doesn't exist.

## Status

Accepted

## Context

[ADR019][adr-019] allows access to a custom etcd cluster for several applications in the PaaS.

To make this work we need to enable direct API access on the etcd cluster for the application pods:

- A new etcd API server for the cluster
- An etcd Cluster authentication mechanism (currently V1 API server authentication)
- A way for the Application to retrieve credentials for the cluster

### Solution:

We could configure our custom etcd cluster directly through the applications that need access.

This will mean each application service will need its own API client configured as a sidecar into the deployment pods.

This means that the API credentials are managed by the application pods.

### Thinking Tree:

* What is the correct way to manage etcd authentication credentials between applications?

| **What we're seeking** | **What we have** | **What we need** |
| - | - | - |
| * This configuration is part of the core etcd configuration, so applications can come up without it and then the etcd credentials are given out through sidecar containers. This would allow more than one application to use the same credentials. | * An API endpoint per application cluster to retrieve access tokens based on credentials to retrieve from etcd. | * *The etcd credentials for our applications should be stored in applications and a way to retrieve them through the etcd API.* |

* What happens if we need to store the etcd credentials outside of the application? *  
  Etcd will provide an API that stores the etcd credentials, e.g. a credentials file, and an API Gateway can then store them on behalf of the application. It will need to authenticate the requests and validate that the token is a valid token representing access to the etcd server. It should store the token data in the credentials database and then validate each request with the token before passing on to the underlying API.

### Pros and Cons:

* Storing all of the credential data in applications | * Does not involve an external etcd server to manage credentials or access control*
* Credential data that is only relevant to the PaaS*
* Can only manage one etcd cluster per region*

[ADR-019]: https://github.com/alphagov/paas-architecture/blob/master/doc/decisions/019-custom-etcd-cluster.md

## Status

## Context

We need a mechanism to describe the validation errors at field level.
Currently, we are storing the validation errors in a global error list. For example, for the field `password`, the error message can be either
`must be at least 8 characters`, `must contain at least one uppercase character`, `must contain at least one special character`, etc.
There are a lot of issues with this approach:
1. It's impossible to debug the problem
2. In order to solve the problem, you need to know the field that it's related to, which is the reason behind the error message
3. For most cases, even developers don't know the reason behind the error message
4. Makes it impossible to create new validation rules

## Decision

We need to store the validation errors for each field.

It's easy to solve the problem, as you can read the field that the error is related to.

You can even mix multiple errors for one field, for example:
- `must be at least 8 characters`, `must contain at least one uppercase character`, `must contain at least one special character`, etc.

## Context and Problem Statement

We want to document architectural decisions made in this project. Which format and structure should these records follow?

Chosen option: "MADR 2.1.0", because it was the only option that met both the project's current and future needs. The MADR format is simple, but capable of capturing the detail necessary for documenting architectural decisions, such as the rationale behind a decision, as well as its consequences. This format was selected in order to maximize the MADR format's value to stakeholders, both current and future.

The MADR project was chosen in part because it was an open-source project that was receiving contributions from an increasing number of people from around the world. For these reasons, and for the reasons outlined below, the decision to use the MADR format and structure should be considered a long-term commitment.

* The MADR format is lightweight and portable.

## Status

Accepted

## Context

We wanted to be able to enforce the following policy:

> We only communicate from app to app. We don't communicate from app to backend, nor do we communicate from backend to front-end.

The frontend must not initiate communication with the backend, but the backend should be allowed to talk to the front-end.

## Decision

Managed domains are configured in applications (both front-end and backend) and get their own API key.

For the purposes of this ADR we are going to treat both front-end and back-end as different apps (which they are for some purposes). In this way we can have a single API key and account ID for each app, and they have different restrictions.

Managed domain verification and blocking is going to be supported in all apps, but the actual APIs will have the following restrictions:

### front-end

The front-end will be allowed to talk to the backend, and the backend will be allowed to talk to the front-end, only if both apps are both connected to the same managed domain.

This is the same API key for both apps, but the API key is not used for blocking by the front-end. Rather the frontend uses the API key for verifying that the request is coming from the right application.

### back-end

The back-end will be allowed to talk to the front-end, only if both apps are both connected to the same managed domain.

The back-end can be used as a router for the front-end, which means if the back-end is not connected to a managed domain, it can still talk to the front-end in some way. The domain verification and blocking mechanism described in this ADR is about distinguishing *app to app* communication, and so this situation is envisaged when 3rd party services are communicating with the front-end.

## Consequences

### Advantages

* We can have a single API key for each managed domain, which will simplify access control.
* The API key is able to differentiate between front-end and back-end.
* There is no need to generate multiple API keys for different domains.

### Disadvantages

* Front-end and back-end communicate from app to app, and this is sometimes difficult to distinguish from other types of communication, such as 3rd party services talking to the front-end. For example the data warehouse needs to communicate with the front-end because it is logging data for all the apps.

We do not view this as a major disadvantage as we already have a mechanism for verifying that the communication is app to app, via the API key.
The API key will be able to differentiate between app to app communication, and 3rd party services. The API key is not going to differentiate between the front-end and the backend.
