A widely-known framework that inspired us for this decision is [Michael Nygard's lightweight architectural decision record (LADR) approach](http://thinkrelevance.com/blog/2011/11/15/documenting-architecture-decisions).

## Decision

We've decided to start using Architecture Decision Records, as the solution for our initial
motivation.

We've decided to start using this format for new architecture decisions.

We've decided to start using this format for old architecture decisions that we want to
record.

We've decided to start using this format only when making a decision around a topic
that affects or is relevant to more than one team in the future.

## Status

Accepted.

## Consequences

Start using a standardized approach to recording architecture decisions.

Use one ADR per topic.

Write a new ADR for each decision we make about a topic that affects or is relevant
to more than one team in the future.

Use this approach for new architecture decisions and also for recording old
architecture decisions that we want to record.

Update our [decision backlog](https://github.com/status-im/status-react/pull/3117)
with links to ADRs.

```
# [Number] - [Title]

## Consequences

```

Use [github templates](https://github.com/joelparkerhenderson/adr-tools/tree/master/templates)

needs of other projects.

be used as part of a production codebase) and it's mainly an example, rather than a
recipe for building a production piece of software, there's little reason for introducing
any undue complexity at this point. I can re-use the code if I feel it's appropriate
later on. So I'll continue to work with Java 8.

In terms of aggregates and processes, the best way to approach this is to separate
the two concerns in code, to make it clear which class or interface is responsible
for aggregate concerns and which class or interface is responsible for process concerns.

In this way, we can also avoid having to introduce a process lifecycle to the
aggregate class, because every process will use the aggregate to perform its task, and
so aggregates implicitly have a process lifecycle anyway (via the process model).

By separating aggregates and processes, we also open ourselves up to the possibility
of using a container to both implement aggregates and run processes. In particular, we
could use an EC2 instance to both implement aggregates and run processes.

If we were to use the aggregate to implement processes, we would probably use the
aggregate's repository to hold a list of processes that are in flight. This list could
be used to execute the processes (e.g., by subscribing to the repository's events).

Note that the aggregate should never be directly executable.

## Consequences

If using a container to both implement aggregates and run processes (for example an EC2
instance), then we should also consider how we could ensure that the instance is stateless.
While using the Repository in the aggregate to manage process queues would provide some
sort of state for the processes, we also need to consider how the instance would be reset
when a process completes or is terminated. The best approach is probably to ensure
the instance is stateless by passing additional data that guarantees a "fresh start"
each time, such as the process ID in a header. The container would then be able to
resume the process on a request that contains the process ID in the header.

So, while this ADR doesn't introduce any new processes, it introduces the notion of
how aggregates and processes can be linked, so that any processes that are used can be
abstracted out into a separate class, which can be removed after publication.

## Context and Problem Statement

Fragments are a part of the page that can be rendered at any time. This leads to two kinds of missing fragments:

1. Fragments that have not yet been loaded when the user arrives.
2. Fragments that have been removed from the page but still appear in memory.

Fragments that have not yet been loaded are simply skipped by the engine. However, fragments that were removed from the page can lead to problems when re-rendering the page later, as the engine thinks they are still present in the DOM. This is usually solved by removing all traces of the removed fragments from the DOM, including styling and class names. However, some fragments might have subtle differences or special properties that won't be removed by cleaning up the DOM.

In some cases, users might want to display a fallback content when a fragment is missing, or conversely they might want a fragment to appear even when the user arrived before it was loaded.

## Considered Options

* Use a "getInitialState" function to prevent missing fragments from appearing
* Use a fallback function to render fallback content instead of missing fragments
* Use a "getInitialState" function and use a fallback function to render fallback content instead of missing fragments

## Decision Outcome

Chosen option: "Use a getInitialState function to prevent missing fragments from appearing", because it leads to the most user-friendly experience, when the user arrives and the required fragments are present.

## Pros and Cons of the Options

### Use a "getInitialState" function to prevent missing fragments from appearing

* Good, because the "getInitialState" function can always return something valid, even when the fragment is missing
* Good, because we always get the final state of the application
* Good, because using a fragment instead of just a plain object creates a more explicit API
* Good, because using a fragment with a "getInitialState" function and a fallback function makes it easier to develop specific features for specific fragments
* Good, because developers can use an alternative implementation and still get the same API
* Good, because code is less confusing when using multiple "getInitialState" functions
* Good, because code is more readable
* Good, because developers can use their "getInitialState" function as a source of truth for the current state of their application
* Bad, because we have a "getInitialState" function in every fragment
* Bad, because developers have to have insight into the workings of the fragment to have the correct knowledge for the part of the code they want to use
* Bad, because the "getInitialState" function must return at least one property, even though we are using it only to get the final state of the application
* Bad, because it is harder to know how to correctly implement a "getInitialState" function and how the fragment is being rendered by the engine

### Use a fallback function to render fallback content instead of missing fragments

* Good, because code is more readable
* Good, because developers have insight into the workings of the fragment and the fallback function can be used to provide additional logic
* Bad, because no fallback function can be present in every fragment
* Bad, because there must be at least one fallback function for every fragment, making it impossible to have a general fallback function for all fragments
* Bad, because the fallback function can only be called when the fragment has been loaded but is missing (e.g., because we changed the page content)

### Use a "getInitialState" function and use a fallback function to render fallback content instead of missing fragments

* Good, because the fallback function can always return something valid, even when the fragment is missing
* Good, because we always get the final state of the application
* Good, because using a fragment instead of just a plain object creates a more explicit API
* Good, because using a fragment with a "getInitialState" function and a fallback function makes it easier to develop specific features for specific fragments
* Good, because developers can use an alternative implementation and still get the same API
* Good, because code is less confusing when using multiple "getInitialState" functions
* Good, because code is more readable
* Good, because developers can use their "getInitialState" function as a source of truth for the current state of their application
* Bad, because we have a "getInitialState" function in every fragment
* Bad, because we have a fallback function in every fragment
* Bad, because it is harder to know how to correctly implement a "getInitialState" function and how the fragment is being rendered by the engine

## Context
Many of the components in the project will emit some kind of event.
Usually, these are business-oriented events, such as "order created" or "payment received".
When such an event occurs, the system should notify some downstream systems in a timely manner.
For example, the "order created" event should be notified to the "customer" system so that it can send
an email to the customer asking for a confirmation of the order.

However, this is not the only type of event. There can be more "synthesized" events, which are actually notifications
about other events. For example, the "order created" event may generate an email about the order, which can be
considered as a "notification" event.

Often, these are used to notify that the event is waiting to be consumed for some specific workflow.

All these events should be "public" (available) in some sense, though the exact definition of "public" might vary.
In some cases, the public might refer to a collection of consumers; in others, it might refer to a single consumer.
However, in either case, all the consumers have access to the same data with each other.

There are two possibilities regarding who the consumers of public events are:

* Consumers are "within the domain" - For example, the "order fulfillment" system, or the "email sending" system. In this case, it is sufficient to synchronize data
with the source of truth.

* Consumers are "outside the domain" - For example, the "CRM" system, or the "analytics" system. In this case, we need to think about how to maintain data integrity.

## Decisions
### Event signing
We decide that all the public events are signed using a JSON web token (JWT).
Tokens are signed using a secret (actually, a private key/certificate), which is used by the event producer to
create the tokens and include them into the payload of events.

This makes it easy for all the consumers to verify that tokens come from the same (source) domain.

Token expiration time should be long enough to cover the entire project's lifetime.
The security of the token itself can be further improved using HMAC + JWT.

### Event payload
Every event payload contains at least the following fields:

* **scope**: string, required. Used for authorization and authentication. If the "scope" has more than one field, the delimiter is "."
* **timestamp**: integer, Unix timestamp, required. Used for ordering and for historical querying.
* **source**: string, required. Used for tracking the origin of the event.
* **data**: JSON object. Used for carrying the payload.

### Event
An **event** is a list of **event types** and the associated event payloads, which is sent to some downstream system.
In some cases, the same event can be generated multiple times for the same event type, but with different data.
For example, the same "order created" event may occur multiple times for different orders (one for each order).

An **event type** is a type name used for classification of events.
Each type corresponds to a specific domain concept.

## Consequences
### Positive
* Access to same data by all consumers of public events.
* Events will have consistent structure.

### Negative
* When an event is consumed multiple times, data need to be processed more than once.
* When a type of an event changes, it could lead to downtime.

### Neutral
* When a type of an event changes, that should be considered as a breaking change to the consumer of the event.

## Considered options
* Do not sign events.
* Use UUIDs for event IDs.

## Status

Accepted

## Context

This project's goal is to be used as a central hub for a number of CLI and related code projects. This means that there will need to be a process that can be used to create and publish a new command (and its associated code) project. This would then need to be versioned and hosted (probably GitHub).

## Decision

The commands, and the code they contain, will be published in two places. The first is the `npm` package manager (probably GitHub). The second is the `git` repository.

## Consequences

One of the main advantages to writing CLI code in NodeJS is that it is easy to publish in `npm`. The primary consequence of this would be that any code in this repository must be tested to ensure it works with `npm` and the dependencies that come with it.

Using a [semver](https://semver.org/) scheme for the versioning system for the commands would help make it possible to keep track of changes to dependencies, and make sure that when the CLI is updated and the version of the command code is updated along with it.

The code will also need to be stored in a `git` repository for historical tracking of changes, and collaboration.

Storing the commands code in a [dependency repository](https://semver.org/spec-08#dependency-management), such as the GitHub project for npm and `git`, would enable the community to view the history of the CLI code, see code changes, and take part in the build and publishing process. The `git` repository would also make it possible to collaborate in code changes.

## Context

We've gone through a fair amount of iterations on player. We should have a time to review player, and decide which player to go forward with.

Video player should be able to handle the following:

- play/pause
- stop
- get playback position
- move between tabs

We can use the ffmpeg player as a starting point, since it supports a lot of features. However, I'm worried about the player being bloated, and also that it's a javascript project. I'd like to avoid using a javascript project if we can.

### Alternatives
* [mediapinch](https://github.com/bbc/mediapinch)
* [ffmpeg-remix](https://github.com/mozmeao/ffmpeg-remix)

### Iterators
* [VideoContext](https://github.com/guardian/VideoContext)
* [Dashjs](https://www.dashjs.org)
* [Panoptes-Front-end](https://github.com/zooniverse/panoptes-front-end)
* [Video-Context-II](https://github.com/guardian/VideoContext-II)
* [Video.js](https://videojs.com/)
* [Supervideo.js](https://supervideojs.com/)

## Decision

We will go forward with ffmpeg-remix.

It's a javascript project, so the option to use html5 video has been eliminated. I felt like, in order to get the media player working well on IE, it might be best to get rid of javascript altogether. With a player that doesn't use javascript, the code is a lot less complicated and I feel a lot more confident that it will work on all browsers. ffmpeg-remix is a really interesting project. I like how they've made it a polyfill - which means we can't use it if the player doesn't support ffmpeg-remix, which means we should make sure we always run IE in IE9+, and Edge in Edge12+.

Video-context is great, but it's been implemented before, in Video-context-II. I feel like the project hasn't been maintained in a long time.

MediaPinch uses media-api, which can't be tested by mocking the api, so we can't just stub the api calls for this player. It's complicated, but the documentation for it is good, and they have a blog, so we can keep up-to-date with the project.

## Status

## Context

We use DDD in our domain model. We can map all our domain entities and values into that model. We do not have any external, aggregate objects in the domain model, except aggregate root objects.

## Decision

We use the Clean Architecture, defined by Robert Martin, and adapt some parts of it to our domain model. We use DDD to find and map our domain entities and values into the model. We don't use any external aggregate root objects or other "big ball of mud" style patterns.

We adapt the Clean Architecture to our model in the following way:

* The app layer only contains aggregate root objects and their associated service layers. This means that, for every aggregate type we have a corresponding service layer which is part of the app layer.
* All interfaces defined by our domain model are part of the service layer. This means that all types defined by our domain model have a corresponding interface which is part of the service layer.
* Only the base interfaces for all our data types and value objects are defined in the domain model. This means that all our data types and value objects have a corresponding interface which is part of the domain model.

We use a domain DDD approach. This means that all entities are defined by their type and are immutable objects (their state is not changed on the object level). All the operations performed on the entity should be done by external services (these services should not know anything about the entity). We can only store state changes of entities in our persistence. Entity type definitions are immutable and can only be extended by other types of entities.

We use DDD to decompose all the concepts in our domain model into aggregates and entities and by using interfaces we can expose them to services.

We use DDD to map our concepts to our ports. This means that every port should be mapped to a concept in the domain model. This means that it should be possible to ask a port for the concept which mapped to this port, and the port can answer with the corresponding concept.

We use DDD to manage concepts in our business domain model. This means that we treat our concepts as singular and try to avoid pluralized concepts. We avoid using general terms like "some", "many", "a bunch" etc.

## Consequences

This makes it easier for developers to read and work with our code. It ensures that our domain model can be easily read, interpreted and persisted. It's the easiest way to achieve both correctness and readability in our code.

In turn, we're enforcing a structure on our domain model which is really not a requirement. This structure could be found incidentally. We'll need to make sure to break it when a concept is really beyond our ability to encapsulate it into one type in our domain model. For example, we can't just define "discount" on the entity level because then we could mix price and discount on the same level. For this reason we use concepts in our domain model which cannot be simplified to a data type or value object.

DDD seems like a good way to map our domain model to our ports, and to manage concepts and aggregates in our domain model.

We use DDD for ports and integration with the outside world. We use other, less structured methods for managing concepts in our domain model. This makes it difficult to get concepts from one interface to the other without forcing the decision to be made to make the change. For example, we can't define an entity type on one interface and use it on another interface if the other interface doesn't require using the entity type on both. This makes us have to re-introduce the structure of our domain model using interfaces on one of the interfaces (usually, we would allow use of the entity type only on the interface which requires it). We use "concrete classes" to implement on the ports and use interface class definitions on the domain model for port implementation.

We use DDD for ports and integration with the outside world. We use other, less structured methods for managing concepts in our domain model. This doesn't make it harder to define concepts in our domain model than other design patterns allow, but this design pattern has unique features which make it more complex.

It's useful for us to have a clearly defined methodology on the use of DDD.

## Status

Accepted.

## Context

Search capability will be added in a timely manner to satisfy customer requirement.

## Decision

We decided to use [Elasticsearch](https://www.elastic.co/products/elasticsearch) for implementation. It’s a configurable search engine written in Java.

Elasticsearch is already used internally for several projects at DXC.

## Consequences

Because Elasticsearch is in beta state we will use it in preview mode.

There are 2 types of searches available, full and cached. Full searches require a write operation to Elasticsearch and cached searches do not.

Full searches will be triggered mainly via GET requests to /search-cache-entry endpoint. They will be done within milliseconds, for faster searches, we need to implement caching on top of it.

Cached searches will be triggered via GET requests to /search-cache-entry endpoint with a long request ID (55 chars). They will be done within 20 minutes, if no search is active in the system, we cache the data using a TTL of 20 minutes. They are fast and do not require a write operation to Elasticsearch.

Querying will be done with a number of nested objects. It will be necessary to do a list of queries, and reduce the number of requests using a pool of connections. Querying by a single field will result in one query, which is fast. However, using more than one field results in multiple searches.

When a search is done by more than one field, they need to be indexed using their ID (not their field name). Only then will a list of searches be returned, and they will be ranked by the field in which it was done. 

There is no support for range searches. This will need to be implemented on top of it.

When caching, the list of search requests per search query ID is maintained using an internal cache, which is stored with the request ID. This should make querying by request ID faster.

When using a single cache per search query ID, the same search query ID will have to be used for all the cached searches.

The full API version was used for search. Versioning will need to be added for search.

Each search query ID will represent a unique search. For example, the query `service-and-technology` will only record a single search. This means if the user runs several searches including `service-and-technology`, the searches are considered in order as they are received.

The search implementation is a combination of a query builder and a search executor. Query builder is responsible for assembling the query and the search executor runs it and returns results.

As the executor is a plugin, it can be changed. Search implementations can be easily extended by adding a new search executor plugin. This helps to prevent search functionality from being difficult to maintain and evolve over time.

## Context and Problem Statement

When we start building applications and deploying our code to services, our users want to be able to represent numbers or timestamps in various ways, for instance 0.0, 0, 3.14 or 10 minutes ago.

The OpenAPI specification only accepts integer or string representations. When the OpenAPI spec explicitly uses integers, it is often meant as a numeric quantity representing count of something (e.g. number of deployments).

## Decision Drivers <!-- optional -->

* **Consistent data model**
* **Making it possible for users to express data in a natural way**
* **Easily representing timestamps or other non-numeric values**

## Considered Options

* Use strings
* Use timestamps
* Automatically convert from/to timestamps (and other data types)
* Use custom, domain specific data types

## Decision Outcome

Chosen option: "Use strings", because converting time values to strings and then to integers (like to numbers) is not so much work. Furthermore, strings support encoding timestamps. If converting timestamps and other data types to strings is too much effort, then try to add custom types for those timestamps.

### Positive Consequences <!-- optional -->

* data can be freely represented in a natural way
* data can be easily encoded (like in time)
* conversion from time to string is possible

### Negative Consequences <!-- optional -->

* custom data types need to be implemented if we ever want to use more custom types

## Links <!-- optional -->

* Related to [decision on type safety](../20211201-custom-data-types.md)

## Context

* The `service-stac` project will be used by many different people in many different environments to manage their STAC instances. Some of these people will not have an in-depth understanding of STAC or SAML, and/or will not be familiar with how SAML works or even with what tools (e.g. `saml-serialisers`) to use. In other environments, a person who is a STAC maintainer might also have very little knowledge or understanding of SAML.

So we anticipate that either we will have a large number of support requests for assistance in setting up `service-stac` to handle STAC, OR we will have very few requests for assistance with setting up `service-stac`.

Since the `service-stac` project is aimed to be used by many users in many different environments, it's useful to distinguish between the different scenarios so we can ensure the proper level of documentation is provided in either case.

Since this codebase is specifically for managing STAC instances, and also handles the actual transmission and storage of STAC data, we can safely assume that any errors that occur when communicating with STAC have a valid explanation which was caused by an unanticipated circumstance.

## Decision

* If `service-stac` is used to setup an STAC instance or other services involving STAC, then we should provide a well-written, detailed guide on how to achieve the set-up (deployment) and operating procedure for that service.

* If `service-stac` is used to manage or service a pre-existing STAC instance or similar service, and STAC appears to be working, then the error message returned to the user should be as succinct as possible, but verbose enough to be understood by anyone who is familiar with SAML. Ideally, it should be comprehensible by a person who is only mildly familiar with SAML. For example, instead of the cryptic error code "INVALID_ARGUMENT_TYPE", the error message should be "Argument type mismatch: expected <TYPE>, got <ACTUAL_TYPE>"

* If `service-stac` is used to manage or service an STAC instance or other services involving STAC, and STAC is not working (e.g. as reported by logs) then the error message should be as succinct as possible but also verbose enough to be understood by anyone who is familiar with SAML.

* If `service-stac` is used to manage or service a pre-existing STAC instance or similar service, and STAC is reporting errors and the user has no context about what those errors mean, then the error message should be as succinct as possible but verbose enough to be understood by anyone who is familiar with SAML. For example, instead of the cryptic error code "INVALID_ARGUMENT_TYPE", the error message should be "Argument type mismatch: expected <TYPE>, got <ACTUAL_TYPE>"

* If `service-stac` is used to manage or service a pre-existing STAC instance or similar service, and STAC has requested an XML dump for debugging, then the message should be verbose enough to be understood by anyone who is familiar with SAML.

## Thinking

There is the possibility that more than one group can use `service-stac`. For example, we could support either the upload of files or storage of files, but not both. We anticipate that these groups will have quite different technical capabilities and varying expectations around documentation. These expectations could clash.

In a scenario where `service-stac` is used to setup an STAC instance or other services involving STAC, the documentation we provide would probably be consumed by the person installing the STAC services. So there's a strong argument for keeping the documentation straightforward and concise.

In a scenario where `service-stac` is used to manage or service a pre-existing STAC instance or similar service, the documentation we provide would probably be consumed by the person who manages the existing STAC instance. So it's less compelling to try and keep the documentation succinct at the risk of it being too obscure.

So far, the assumption has been that all users of `service-stac` have a more or less equivalent level of understanding of SAML and STAC and so we can treat them equally. So there's less of a concern about different groups having different expectations around documentation. There's also less of a concern about how "confusing" or "unclear" the documentation might be.

### Dependency 1: Postcodes.io
This project relies heavily on the [postcodes.io](https://postcodes.io) service to look up
the latitude and longitude of addresses and other geolocation specific data. This service
offers both a free and a paid tier and we should determine which tier best fits our needs.

For most of the frontend application, we use the [nhs.uk address form library](https://github.com/alphagov/nhs.uk-address-form)

nhs.uk

### How this project fits into GOV.UK Frontend

In the future, we want our address forms to be used on GOV.UK Frontend, so should we re-factor the way our application
is set up to make it easier to make the change.

This ADR does not attempt to answer this question as, as of November 2019, we do not have an established
timeline or concrete plans to integrate the NHS.UK Frontend project with GOV.UK Frontend.

rendering.

## Context

## Decision

We will use the following sections in the SDK documentation files:

- Status: Indicates if the feature is functional, under active development, or in its final version.

- Name: This section names the feature being described.

- Description: This section describes the feature. If the feature comprises multiple steps describe these either in sub-sections, or using bullet points.

- Usage: This section provides usage examples (ideally short code snippets)

- API: This section describes the methods or functions available.

- Related: This section describes related data or features which have an impact on the feature.

- Further reading: Links to useful additional resources.

We will also endeavour to keep the documentation language simple, short, and easily understood by non-engineers.

## Context

This project seeks to create a set of components that can be assembled and made available to a range of clients. These clients might be organisations, other government departments, or other service providers.

The modular design system architecture aims to:

- minimise coupling and maximise cohesion.
- promote code re-use by removing the need for client-specific code.
- help maintainability by removing the need for client-specific code.
- provide flexibility in terms of component behaviour and interface.

## Decision

This project will use modular design system architecture to ensure our components can be used by a wide range of clients and remain adaptable in future.

## Consequences

A modular design system is likely to result in:

- higher amounts of code.
- better re-use of code.
- improved maintainability.
- more unit testable code.
- more reusable code.
- easier customisation of components.

We should be mindful, however, of the risk of coupling too much code together. By coupling too much code together, it can become difficult to understand and modify the system later on. There are ways to mitigate this risk, but they add extra complexity. It is likely that we will have to compromise at some point in this direction, in particular regarding the use of variables.

## Context

Having the ability to have the test application environment be as close to the production application environment as possible helps us catch integration issues earlier, and make deployments between environments less jarring. In order to facilitate this, we must be able to deploy the application with the same configuration as production.

### Production Configuration

The configuration of production and staging are almost identical; they share many of the same parameters. However, the most obvious difference is that production uses S3 buckets that are owned by AWS, while staging uses the AWS CloudFront distribution that we own.

|Parameter|Description|
|---|---|
|version-0-2-4|e93c62b63c7af6771c44ea9790628ea17007059a|
|domain|cloudfront14354594.static.ir.gov.uk|
|s3|s3.amazonaws.com|

### Infrastructure as a Service (IaAS)

Both AWS and GOV.UK's hosting platform GOVUK PaaS have different ways of deploying the application. However, both can deploy the application as long as we keep the frontend as stateless as possible; the application will serve HTTP requests to the application server and then proxy internal links, where the client accepts the application's request, to the frontend.

### Continuous Deployment (CD)

AWS CloudFront has a caching capability (TTL and expiry) that we can use to ensure that if the staging application changes, the caching expires.

GOV.UK PaaS have a deployability score that indicates if the service is suitable for their platform. We have a deployability score of 96, and we can deploy the application on GOV.UK PaaS.

Based on the above context, the decision was made to implement a staging deployment.

### Application Configuration

The frontend will be configured for staging (e.g. s3-bucket, domain).

### Infrastructure Configuration

Applications will be deployed as [Terraform](https://www.terraform.io) modules.

### Continuous Deployment

Terraform will be used to execute the deployment scripts locally in order to create the test application environment, called "test".

## Status

Accepted

## Consequences

### Positive

Deploying a staging environment to GOV.UK PaaS or AWS makes the deployment easier to manage locally.

Terraform modules are reusable, and we use a modular application approach.

Terraform is an open source tool that has been adopted by many GOV.UK teams.

### Negative

It is more complicated than deploying the application to GOV.UK PaaS (we use "the deployability score" metric), as it adds a new level of complexity - a staging environment.

## Context and Problem Statement

We've recently decided to open the data provided for each API service to third-party providers (TPPs). We've had great feedback so far and a lot of external interest. However, it is also a fact that APIs can be heavily utilized and abuse can happen (spam, DDoS). Such abuse would negatively impact other services from the same platform, like WebAPI.

As such, we need to limit the capacity of each API provider and set a limit to the amount of requests per minute per service, as well as a daily request limit and a monthly request limit.

## Considered Options

* Define an anti-affinity mode for every API
* Define an anti-affinity mode for gateway and translator services only

## Decision Outcome

Chosen option: "Define an anti-affinity mode for every API", because it will set a global anti-affinity mode for gateway and translator services that will affect all APIs.

### Positive Consequences

* Set a global anti-affinity mode is set in place for gateways and translators, which will make the platform more secure.
* Limit to the amount of requests per minute per service is a flexible measure to stop abuses but still allows for high usage of our APIs.
* There's no need to decide different limits for each of the API service

### Negative Consequences

* Setting anti-affinity mode on every API service is another layer of code for managing request limits.

## Pros and Cons of the Options

### Define an anti-affinity mode for every API

Define an anti-affinity mode for every API service. Each API will receive the following statistics on the average usage during the last 30 minutes: 10K requests/minute / 300K requests/month

* Good, because it is flexible and sets a global rule across all services
* Good, because it limits most abuse cases and allows high usage, which is fair for partners who've signed up for paid services
* Bad, because it adds an extra layer to the API management and adds to the amount of code to be managed

### Define an anti-affinity mode for gateway and translator services only

Define an anti-affinity mode for gateway and translator services only.

* Good, because it is flexible and sets a global rule across all services
* Good, because it limits most abuse cases and allows high usage, which is fair for partners who've signed up for paid services
* Bad, because there's no way to know whether we'd be limiting capacity on the translator or gateway services alone. Since gateway uses translator to execute the API, the translator could be limiting capacity to the gateway. The translator is already rate limited at a global level due to its usage on Google Translate and therefore we'd be indirectly limiting capacity.
* Bad, because the translator would still accept more requests than the maximum allowed in our paid services.

## Links

# 5. Response meta links

Date: 2020-Sep-30

## Status

Accepted

## Context

Response meta links can be added to the headers section for multiple reasons:

- Add a custom link which does not appear in the source code. Eg. a link to a file downloaded from elsewhere or an image hosted elsewhere.
- Specify the media-type the resource is (e.g. image/gif)

### Problems with `rel` for responses

Since this is a response, the `rel` attribute should have a value of `http`.
The value `http` is too generic, and does not differentiate the attribute's value to which they reference.
For example, it could be a link to "the source code" or "the HTML".
It should be possible to determine which `rel` value was intended.

### How to specify `rel` in the source code

We wanted to avoid having an unreferenced `rel` value, as this would be confusing to other users of the server.

#### `rel` attribute in the template and template-level

The two options are:

1. `<!-- optional -->`, add `rel="http"`, `rel="http";` or `rel="http";` to the template. This will appear in all responses, regardless of whether the `rel` value was intended to be the template's own or to the response.
2. Use meta links on the template level. A meta-link can be specified using `meta` for template-level data links, which can be differentiated from response-level data links with `link` tags.
    - `meta` indicates template-level data links
    - `link` indicates response-level data links

#### Use of `link` or `meta`

1. `meta` specifies the data and is not used on any response (responses contain only `link`.)
2. `link` specifies the response and appears on any response (responses may contain both `link` and `meta`).

#### Case 1

When this case is used, `rel="http"` appears in responses. The link is not added if the original request did not contain a meta-link, even though responses with `rel="http"` always appear, this is not a new `rel` value added by the server. It does not affect any server processes (such as caching). `rel="http"` is also used in template files, but does not appear in the generated HTML.

#### Case 2

When this case is used, `rel="http"` is used in the responses and the link is added to all responses, this is a new `rel` value added by the server. It does not affect any server processes (such as caching).

### Use of `meta` and `link` for responses

A number of other features use the `link` or `meta` attribute for response data. These are not considered in the following argument.

#### `meta` for response types

## Context and Problem Statement

For a long time, we have ignored the OpenAPI specification and therefore missed some best practices for designing API's.

We need to define a standard in order to provide an API that will be easily consumable through multiple clients.

We want to enforce some API rules so that API will be well designed and easier to consume.

We want to be able to automatically generate API documentation so that API will be easier to consume.

We need to make it easier to evolve the API.

We want to be able to implement API testing so that we can ensure API is well designed and the documentation is up-to-date.

## Decision Drivers

* We will add API documentation so that API will be easier to consume.
* We will enforce rules so that API will be easier to consume.
* We will generate API documentation using OpenAPI specifications so that API will be easier to consume.
* We will implement API testing so that we can ensure API is well designed and the documentation is up-to-date.

## Considered Options

* We will enforce the OpenAPI specifications.
* We will not enforce the OpenAPI specifications.

## Decision Outcome

Chosen option: We will enforce the OpenAPI specifications.

## Context

Each time a dependency for DCL UI is upgraded, a new version of DCL UI
is published.

Each time DCL UI is upgraded, an application using DCL UI should also
be upgraded.

How can we ensure that there are no regressions and is an easy upgrade to use
the new version of DCL UI?

## Options

### Option 1: Don't upgrade applications that use DCL UI

If DCL UI is upgraded, a new release is published, the application using
DCL UI is tested, and if the new DCL UI contains any regressions (broken
features, new bugs, etc), then an new version of DCL UI is published with the
fix.

It's a [Rollout/Canary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Release_management/Canary_release_pipeline)
model where only the DCL UI application is released.

If the DCL UI contains no regressions, then the application will use the
newest version of DCL UI.

## Drawbacks

* This approach will not ensure a regressionless release.
* Maintaining the various versions of applications using DCL UI will
  be cumbersome.

## Option 2: Upgrade applications that use DCL UI when DCL UI is upgraded

If DCL UI is upgraded, a new release is published, the application using
DCL UI is tested, and the application using DCL UI will be upgraded if any
regressions are found.

It's a [Rollout/Canary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Release_management/Canary_release_pipeline)
model where DCL UI is released with the applications that are using DCL UI.

If the DCL UI contains no regressions, then the application can keep the
same version of DCL UI used to build the application.

## Drawbacks

* Maintaining the various applications using DCL UI might not be simple.
* In some circumstances, applications might use versions of DCL UI that
  are not maintained any more. This will lead to applications using
  unmaintained versions of DCL UI.

## Option 3: Don't upgrade applications that use DCL UI and always upgrade DCL UI

If DCL UI is upgraded, a new release is published, the application using
DCL UI is tested, and if the new DCL UI contains any regressions, then an
new version of DCL UI is published with the fix and the application using DCL UI is upgraded.

So it's a combination of a Rollout/Canary model and a Regular release pipeline
where the DCL UI is always upgraded to the latest version by the application
using DCL UI.

If the DCL UI contains no regressions, then the application using DCL UI will
be upgraded to the new version of DCL UI (using the latest version of DCL UI)
whenever a release of DCL UI is published.

## Drawbacks

* Applications using DCL UI might need an upgrade of their deployment
  when using a new version of DCL UI. However, this also means that applications
  that are using the old versions of DCL UI.

## Option 4: Don't upgrade applications that use DCL UI and never upgrade DCL UI

It's the same as Option 3 but the only difference is that, it's the first time
an application will be upgraded to DCL UI.

## Drawbacks

* DCL UI application version will be out of sync with other applications's
  DCL UI version.

## Decision

Option 2 was chosen as the option that best balances the effort of maintaining
new applications that use DCL UI, and ensuring deployments with applications
that use DCL UI will be upgraded to the latest version of DCL UI.

With the application using DCL UI being upgraded whenever there is a release
of DCL UI, it will be easier to maintain applications that are using the
newest versions of DCL UI.

While this might lead to more applications having upgrades of their deployment
when using a new version of DCL UI, it would also come in handy when adding
new components to the DCL UI that would be needed by the future deployment of
the application.

## Context
We are going to have a number of message delivery systems:

* API (REST)
* API (gRPC)
* gRPC Client

These all need some kind of discovery to look up. The API client will discover the
REST server and the gRPC server.

We might want a different message delivery system in the future. These systems would need to be 
discoverable too. This would be more likely to be done through an API, since the gRPC Client doesn't 
understand the gRPC server. So we need the discovery process to understand the gRPC client.

This would need a bit more research to decide how it would work.

## Decisions
The two components will be discoverable using the following naming conventions:

1. REST API: "[component_name].[message_delivery_system].[component_name].[message_type].[message_id]"
2. gRPC API: "[component_name].[message_delivery_system].[component_name].[message_type].[message_id]"
3. gRPC Client: "[component_name].[message_delivery_system].[component_name].[message_type].[message_id]"

These rules are the same as our naming conventions currently. This also ensures that we get 
automatically generated healthchecks. These healthchecks will look for messages of a specific type. 

## Consequences
This means all three services will have a healthcheck that can be done to check if the API is 
working correctly.

This means that the discoverability of the two systems becomes easier and we can be 
certain that we are talking about the right thing.

The main thing that will be affected by this is the gRPC Client. This will be discoverable 
through the API.

## Context

The purpose of this project is to provide developers an application they can use to
record architectural decisions, both as documentation, and as source of inspiration
for new features. The hope is this will enable others to understand the application
to be more confident in contributing, or even just knowing it exists.

## Decision

To achieve this goal, the application will need to have a clear and simple
specification that can be read both by humans, and machines.

Traditionally, this would have been achieved through documentation, either in
the form of text, images, diagrams, or other media. However, over time, these
styles of documentation and presentation were seen to become cumbersome and hard to
maintain.

As a result, APIs, Application Programming Interfaces, were created. APIs provide
a way of describing an interface to application developers through a language agnostic
specification.

As a result, APIs became the preferred way of describing an interface, both by
engineers, and by outside developers.

As described by REST API [Playbook](https://blog.restfulAPI.org/playbook/),
REST API provides the following benefits:

1. API First: API design comes before implementation, and documentation comes
   before code.
1. API contracts: a contract defines the API interface and behavior specification
   of a system. The contract defines the interaction language between clients
   and servers.
1. API implementation: the implementation of the API contract provides a set of
   tools and processes to build the API and related infrastructure.
1. API documentation: API documentation contains enough information to enable
   engineers to understand the implemented API and how to use it effectively.

In addition to this, REST API provides a number of benefits to engineers,
including providing a standard and easy to understand specification, ease of
implementation, and performance.

In this project, the OpenAPI specification will be used for several key reasons:

1. Provide a specification that can be read both by humans, and machines
1. Allow automated testing of API behavior, both for APIs written in this project,
   and other projects that use this project as a base
1. Allow automated generation of API documentation
1. Allow for easy analysis of API usage

Because most RESTful APIs share many similarities, we can accept and use the
OAS specification as a baseline.

## Consequences

One of the consequences of API design comes at the design phase, and is the
increased cost of API design. The API must be designed with potential future
users in mind, and it is not possible to know all possible use cases at once.
This is also why APIs are always in evolution, and rarely ever "finished."

In addition, to the design phase, comes development, and implementation of the
API. This includes building the server side code, which handles communication
with the data store, and caching, or other resources. It also includes creating
and implementing the API documentation.

Finally, API documentation can include many facets, including text, images,
and videos. Some tools, such as Swagger, allow the API to be "self documented,"
through code comments in the implementation.

In this project, the API specification will be built from scratch, rather than
using an existing specification, such as REST API. However, the underlying
principles of REST API will still be used.

For most API implementations, the API specification is an artifact, created
after the code, and used to document and implement the API. However, in this
project, the API specification is an active part of the code, and both
implemented, and updated, in tandem. This results in a two-way communication
between the specification and the code.

This approach results in several benefits. For example, because of the API
specification's close relationship to the code, the API can be automatically
tested, and documentation can be automatically generated.

By using API First, the team ensures the API is designed with long-term
usability in mind, instead of designing the API based on current or immediate
needs. This results in the API being more flexible, and more future-oriented.

In addition, by using the OpenAPI specification, the API is standardized, which
makes it easier to understand for people who are not familiar with this
specification or project. This results in API implementations based on the
OpenAPI specification being more accessible to others.

### Use a template

Instead of starting from scratch, an existing template could be used to build
the API specification. This would reduce the amount of work necessary to
create a specification, and could be used to generate the initial draft of
the specification.

## Context

At the moment we track application metrics using `(application, metric, value)` tuples.
For example `(5.0, latency, 150)` indicates that the application responded to a request within 150 ms.
Latency is a time dimension property of a request/response pair.
So it makes sense to associate the value of latency with the time the request/response pair was recorded.

## Decision

We add an additional property to the metric that captures the time dimension.
For example, the above tuple can be more accurately represented as `(5.0, latency, 150, at_time: "2018-11-04T14:58:51")`.

Some use cases for this feature are as follows:

- To analyze performance changes in a time-series manner
- To analyze performance changes using a custom time unit, e.g. hour, day, etc.

## Status

Accepted

## Consequences

It will be more accurate to represent the application metrics.

It may be slightly harder to understand the metrics because now a time property has been added.

When unit testing our components, we need to be able to mock the HTTP calls
that they make to the API.

The API server responds to HTTP requests via the client libraries
(`libp2p`, `libp2p-rust`).

These libraries already generate an OpenAPI specification, which we can use
to test our integration with the server.

But this does not allow us to test the interactions with the API separately.
For instance, the `start` method call in `libp2p` and the `accept` method call
in `libp2p-rust` cannot be tested separately.

This ADR seeks to provide a way for us to:

- Mock the calls for use in unit tests so we can make them private to that test.
- Maintain a record of these.
- Be able to use them in future tests.

### Option 1: `n_http`

`n_http` seems to fit the bill, but it appears to be widely unused within the team.

Its documentation is far from comprehensive, and some things appear to be hard to
do with it.

The code is a mess.

This would have been a good choice if we had used it before, but none of the
existing tests do either.

`n_http` feels old and is long-lived.

But it is arguably the most flexible, and there is documentation somewhere about
a test that mocks several calls.

And it's the only one that is actively maintained.

It's been in use at MoJ since at least 2019 (see ADR002).

### Option 2: `async_http_testing`

`async_http_testing` is a relatively new tool.

Its documentation is decent, and the tests feel much less cluttered.

This seems to be a sensible choice that we should try first.

### Option 3: Mocks in Integration

There is a pattern used by a user of `n_http` which uses mocks during
integration tests.

This is a pattern I am familiar with from past deployments.

With this approach, the API responses are mocked in integration tests.

There is no support for this in our unit tests; this would be a post-mortem
approach.

It seems likely that it would be necessary to make changes to our tests to start
using this approach; it is a change to the unit test architecture.

With this approach, we do not generate a OpenAPI specification.

### Option 4: "In House" Test Setup

If we use a mock HTTP server, we need to be able to specify the responses
that it sends for requests that we make to it.

This can be done via fixture files, or by registering the mock HTTP server with
the test.

We already use fixture files for some of our tests, but are ignoring others for
the time being.

If we start using different mock servers in different tests, then we'll have
a lot of churn.

At the moment we are ignoring the fact that there is a mock HTTP server in
the background.

## Decision

Use Mocks in Integration tests

## Status

Accepted

## Consequences

We have already started to see the consequences of ignoring the fact that we
are using Mocks in integration tests.

We should mitigate that as soon as we can.

If the API changes and the existing test fixtures are no longer valid, then we
should migrate those tests to new fixtures or move forward as required.

## Context

In our system, we have many parts of it connected. We need to ensure that all connections work well.

The main connection is to the Kubernetes cluster, and there are many others:

* Prometheus to the Ingress controller
* Ingress to the Istio-Gateway
* Istio-Gateway to the API-Server
* Istio-Gateway to the Log-Aggregator
* Istio-Gateway to the Connector-Gateway
* Connector-Gateway to the AMQP

In this case, a lot of things can go wrong during a connection.

Istio does not have a native way to retry the failed calls. This can cause failures and retries for many times, or it can lead to the eventual failure of Istio.

Istio recommends using Mesh Mappings to failover some Istio-Gateway components to Ingress and/or Prometheus. However, Istio still cannot retry failed calls for many times.

We want to know about every error and retry.

In case Istio fails, users do not have to be informed immediately when it's started to fail. Istio will keep retrying the message until it succeeds. The user will be reported when the message fails to be delivered several times.

Istio has a rate limiter which controls the number of messages Istio forwards per second.

We want to be sure about each error and retry.

We want to know when Istio fails.

We want to retry failed messages for an hour.

## Decision

Istio cannot retry the failed calls. For that reason, we will use external retry and notify methods to retry failed calls. We will add the retry and notify methods to the Ingress-Gateway component. The notification will be posted in the Istio user-group, and it will contain additional data that could help us investigate Istio.

## Consequences

Istio is connected to Istio-Gateway, and Istio-Gateway to the Ingress-Controller. It is not possible to access the Istio user-group from the Istio-Gateway or Istio-Connector. The notification will contain Istio service address information that can be used to locate a connection to Istio.

We may have to make changes in the Istio-Gateway and Istio connector to retry failed calls and send notifications to Istio user-group. There is a risk that these changes will become incompatible with Istio service updates.

The Istio user-group is a group in the Istio service-directory. Istio user-group can receive notifications only when Istio service-directory is available and Istio daemon is working.

This table is updated via a database trigger whenever a new entry is created. If the user_id is present in the list of users for that entry, it is added to the table. This ensures that there is one row per user-entry association, and the relation is reflected in the database.

To query the users associated with a given entry, use a SQL query like this:

```sql
select u.* from users u
inner join observations o
  on u.id = o.user_id
where o.entry_id = 1;
```

## Problem

One of the primary goals of *klokwrk* is to provide a simple way to monitor
performance metrics and identify bottlenecks in applications.

To this end, a large number of performance tests are supported for an arbitrarily
large number of application services.

With such a diverse range of tests, each of which has its own configuration,
it is not feasible to implement all of them for every possible application
combination.

Instead, a number of performance tests are provided that can detect a large
variety of bottlenecks and performance issues in applications, such as excessive
memory, excessive disk I/O, excessive network I/O, poor CPU utilization, and so
forth.

If one of these tests detects a performance issue, that issue is communicated to
the user in a manner that can be used to diagnose and solve the issue, such as
via a message in the `system` module.

## Constraints

## Assumptions

## Considered Alternatives

## Decision

Since the tests can detect a wide variety of performance issues, they need to
be as lightweight and simple as possible in terms of memory, both when
initialized and when executing.

They also need to be as platform-independant as possible so that they can be
applied to a wide variety of applications and operating systems.

The tests are divided into three classes:

- `base`: these test classes form the foundation of the entire class hierarchy
- `core`: tests that are implemented for every application, regardless of
  what other tests might be enabled
- `advanced`: tests that can be optionally enabled on an as-needed basis,
  but can be enabled for all applications in at most one case

## Rationale

The decision to go with the above design was made in part due to the need to
ensure that the tests can be applied to the barest minimum of applications.
Specifically, we hope the design can be used for single-processor
applications running on microcontrollers.

Another important reason is that the tests can be loaded independently of other
tests and the set of applications. This makes it easy to implement a variety
of tests for different kinds of application services.

For example, we can implement the `cpu_load` test, which detects and reports
high CPU utilization, without needing to implement the `disk_io` test, which
detects and reports high disk I/O usage.

This design approach is not exclusive to applications that are constrained by
low resource limits. It is important for us to keep this option open for as
many applications as possible and as early in the project as possible.

## Implications

Since the set of performance tests that can be selected is not unbounded, and
since they are only applied to a single application, changes to the tests
will necessarily have very limited impact.

## Status

Accepted

## Context

The proposed data model can be broken down into a number of logical sub-units, these can either be within the same class as the `DataSet` or external to it. This proposal looks at both scenarios.

**Scenario 1: no external modules**

The sub-units of a `DataSet` can be broken out into independent classes (e.g. `Sample`, `Observation`, `Measurement`). This can achieve a number of goals:

* Maintainability - A modular design improves the maintainability of the `DataSet` object as it's split into smaller, more focused units. This makes modification and refactoring easier.
* Reusability - Modules can be reused in other `DataSet` objects.
* Change/flexibility - Modules can be replaced by new ones or not used at all in a `DataSet`. This improves the flexibility of the model and allows for new features to be more easily added.

This proposal considers this approach to be preferable as it increases the overall flexibility of the `DataSet`.

**Scenario 2: with external modules**

A `DataSet` is initially loaded into memory as a `List<DataSet>`. These datasets may contain sub-units and can be created as individual `DataSet` objects. This results in the entire `DataSet` being created as a `List<DataSet>`.

This approach has a number of disadvantages:

* When loading many datasets, the `Dataset` class may be cloned in excess of a hundred times. This can be a performance penalty that may be undesirable for some users.

**Proposal**

The use of external modules is not desirable and should be completely avoided.

The proposed data model is to split the `DataSet` into a number of classes and store them internally. This proposal should be followed.

## Consequences

The benefits of the data model will be significantly enhanced.

The cost of storing `Dataset` and `DataSet` instances can be effectively reduced by maintaining the module internally.

It will be far more difficult to reuse the `Dataset` data model as it is not explicitly defined and requires internal knowledge to be maintained.

Date: 2020-05-15

## Status

Accepted

## Context

Datasets published by the Government Digital Service (GDS) follow a standardised
format which supports both querying and indexing. This format is defined in
[ADR 0003](adr-0003-define-the-standard-for-gds-datasets.md). We need to
make sure we record schema information in our databases to support querying
and indexing of these datasets.

We need to make it possible for us to store both the data itself and the
information about the schema (its columns, data types, and other attributes) in
our databases.

### Options

We considered the following options:

* All data and schema information live in the same database tables
* All data and schema information live in separate databases
* Only data is stored in a separate database
* Only schema is stored in a separate database
* We store schema data in the same tables as data

### Decision

We will store schema data in the same tables as data.

This approach has a number of advantages:

* We can make changes to the schema without having to make changes to our database migrations.
* We can make changes to data without affecting our database migrations.
* We can use common schemas for columns.

This approach has a number of disadvantages:

* A given table may have data for multiple schemas
* Data for a given schema may appear in multiple tables

We chose this approach because making a change to the schema is more likely to
be less impactful than making a change to a data table. We felt that a change to
a data table had a higher chance of requiring a more complex database migration,
and/or having more consequential effects on the data that had been indexed.

## Consequences

We chose to adopt this approach at the start of the team. This decision
has been reviewed a number of times, and it is now considered a well-supported
and well-understood approach.

## Context and Problem Statement

Since we started to extract data for each date of each timepoint of the data we tried to include the daily and monthly frequency of the data. However the more frequent that data is (daily or monthly) the more time it takes to retrieve it. 

For example, in a case that for every hour of a year 20 records are retrieved from Google Sheets the frequency will be 20 times per hour per year. This means around 48,000 times (20 * 24) in a month, more than half of the total number of records of the whole year. However we need only 10 percent of the records on average so far.

As there are multiple fields for each time point like “Open_in_Google_Sheets”, the number of records grows exponentially as the search on Google Sheets returns more data. With the current approach, we search Google Sheets every three hours, and the number of searches does not grow significantly.

A change in search pattern will not affect the data that has been already extracted. However the number of records that is accumulated from the search will impact on the rate of data growth and the rate will decrease with the number of records accumulated. We can solve this by keeping the data growth rate the same without depending on the number of records, but in case that a change in the search pattern occurs, the rate will change.

What are the possible options for the search pattern for the data by time?

* If we use a search based on time pattern of 1 year of 48,000 records: we will have data about Google Sheets for the whole year in every date.
* If we use a search based on time pattern of 1 year of 4,800 records, we will have data about Google Sheets for the whole year in every date.
* If we use a search based on time pattern of 1 year of 12,000 records, we will have data about Google Sheets for every date for one month and one day.

We have two parameters related to a time interval that can be used to extract data. To reduce the amount of records we use these two parameters. 

```
{
  data_by_year: 20,
  data_by_year_interval: 1 
}
```

For the first year we need to retrieve the whole year of Google Sheets data. To reduce that data amount for that year we must extract data only for a month, which means if the month has fewer than 12,000 records for a year, we will retrieve data in every date for that month, and continue from the month to the end of the year. The amount of retrieved data for a month will always be 12,000 when we change the search pattern and start the extraction from that month, and the amount will increase until the amount has reached 12,000 for a whole year, which means for every year that is greater than one we will return the amount for year in the end of the month.

This means we have to collect multiple data for different month, and we can retrieve a total amount of data for the whole year at the end of the month.

## Decision Outcome

* Use a custom search pattern for data extraction based on time and interval
* Retrieve data based on time-interval instead of date 
* We retrieve data every 30 minute between 8:00 and 21:00, we will retrieve more records because we retrieve the additional data only at 9:00 because we do not change the search pattern on google sheets to select a different date for search (when we change the search pattern we clear the query)

## Status

Accepted

## Context

We want to build an API that is robust to faults in the message broker that can only support projections.
Using a projection we assume that there are at least two different entities involved:
The projection target
The projection operation
The user who is making the projection

The first entity is the operation target, which we are currently assuming that it is a value object. The second
entity is the operation itself, which may take a long time to return, and the last two entities are the message broker and
the operation's executor. 

The message broker does not check the message or update the database, the only database that the broker can update
is the message broker's own database. This is an issue when dealing with projections, since there is no way to guarantee
that the message broker has the correct information on our end, and we assume that the projection will trigger the
message broker to send messages to the message receiver or the message store. This ensures that the projection message
includes the necessary information. 

## Decision

We will use the Value projection.

We will support the case of a message broker that can only support a message receiver, and not a message store.
We will assume that the message received can update the database. For our initial assumption, we will still need to
have the ability to run the projection locally without a message broker; there are now [two ways](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Local_primary_key)
to support this requirement.
We will assume that the message broker and operation's executor can access the database.

## Consequences

Using projections will be the way we handle all events that change the value of the database. It will make sure
that the value has been updated correctly within the event. We will be able to provide two levels of security in our
application. The first is that if an event of type Value does not come, the projection will not trigger. The second
is that if an event of type Value comes and is processed and cannot update the database, it does not trigger the
projection.

If a projection cannot be handled due to lack of information, it will cause a processing error which can be debugged more easily.
However, if a projection is delayed due to a lack of time, it will lead to a transient failure which is harder to debug
as it must involve at least the message broker and the operation executor to be detectable.

Since we cannot assume that all events are of type Value, it will be needed for most exceptions to come via the
message broker to handle these exceptions as required (or handled elsewhere).

# 11 - Extract text from Cassandra

Date: 2020-Oct-25

## Status

Accepted

## Context

Cassandra has been storing data for key-value in a number of cells. We need to
be able to extract this data into a human-readable form for processing downstream.
Cassandra has been storing data by using a combination of a primary key, text and
a list of timestamps.

## Decision

We decided to extract the text from Cassandra to create the following:

- one text per entity storing its key
- one text per entity storing its timestamps
- one text per entity storing any list of associated IDs

## Consequences

As a consequence of using timestamps and lists, Cassandra holds multiple texts for
each entity, however it only holds one set of timestamps for each entity. This
allows data to be reconstructed using Cassandra time-to-text functions (e.g.
`time_diff` and `time_is_within_a_period`), but also ensures that data is stored
by time, rather than as a simple list of timestamps. By doing this, we allow
the possibility that different timestamps will be stored for the same entity, but
in the future we may be able to look up the timestamp-to-entity table to
retrieve the entities associated with that timestamp.

By storing IDs of entities in a list, Cassandra enables efficient query operations
to be performed in query time on the ID list, including querying specific ranges
of IDs, but this also ensures that all values associated with an ID list are
stored in Cassandra. This results in lists of IDs being stored in Cassandra, in
addition to the list of timestamps (which is associated with a specific entity).

A consequence of storing a list of timestamps is that data is stored as time
rather than as a simple list of timestamps. In the future we may want to store
the entity ID together with the timestamp for future processing (e.g. querying for
timestamps within a period), but currently it is simply stored as a timestamp. By
doing this, we are likely to be able to look up the entity ID together with the
timestamp using Cassandra time-to-text functions (e.g. `time_diff` and
`time_is_within_a_period`), but this will not work as long as the list of
timestamps contains an item other than the timestamps associated with the
entities.

To allow efficient queries to be performed on lists of timestamps, the data types
for timestamps must be defined in a text. Timestamps stored in a text are
constructed as text-timestamp pairs. This allows a timestamp-to-entity lookup table
to be looked up by text. This is the table that the timestamps that the entity
belongs to live under. In Cassandra, the timestamps are held within a `TimeUUID`
type. The UUID for that type is unique to the entity. When used in Cassandra,
timestamps are used when querying entity IDs. In Cassandra, timestamps cannot be
used to query entity IDs by type (`.entity`). This table also holds lists of
timestamps. This table allows the time-to-text functionality of Cassandra to be
used to be able to look up entities, by identifying a text based on
timestamp-to-entity lookup.

Timestamps are not stored as text in Cassandra. This ensures that the ID for the
entity that the timestamp comes from is also stored on the entity. By storing
IDs, which are text, alongside the text of a time, the ability to perform the
functions outlined in [ADR 0012](0012_use_node_id_as_id.md) is
enabled. However, if the ID of the entity is included in the list of timestamps,
then a new line will be created, since it's new. If the ID is not included, the

By storing timestamps in this way, a timestamp-to-entity lookup table can be
constructed, in which timestamps appear as the key for a list of associated

## Status

## Context

We're using Relay for our front end, and we've been experimenting with it.

I was concerned at first that we wouldn't have the tools we need to make Relay work well, like server-side rendering (SSR) or hot-reloading, but I'm happy to say Relay has come a long way and both are easy to enable.

One of my main concerns was that Relay can only fetch data once a route is visited. So we would have to re-fetch data on subsequent visits to the same page, if the data hadn't changed. Thankfully, by using GraphQL we're able to create input variables for every query we make, and every time we re-fetch data, we're able to pass a 'last-fetched' timestamp so the server can tell us if the data has changed. So if the data hasn't changed, the server should be able to return cached data, even if it is served multiple times in a row.

I'm also concerned about the Relay client-side tools, because they seem a lot less mature than the Relay server tools. To fix this, we could fork the Relay client-side tools and work on them independently, but I don't have enough time to do that right now.

I also learned a lot of Relay tricks over time, but I also had to spend a lot of time re-inventing things or looking up how other teams have implemented Relay features.

As a result, I was thinking we should switch from Relay to Apollo in our front-end. However, I felt like there were still many things I wanted to learn and work out about Relay, so I decided it was best to continue using Relay for the short term.

## Decision

Use Relay for our front end.

## Consequences

I can continue learning about Relay as I continue work on the app, and the community around Relay is pretty active, so finding help is easy. There's also a large Relay community which produce all sorts of tools and libraries that make Relay easier to work with, but also use it (eg: [Relay Tools](https://github.com/facebook/relay-tools)).

The front end of the project is still pretty new, and it's not as if we'd be taking up too much time with Relay features.

To mitigate the downsides of Relay, we can continue to enable SSR and hot-reloading, and we can continue to fetch data multiple times on a single route.

One potential downside of Relay is that it's less easy to add additional state, eg: 'is-authenticated', because the state will essentially be a bunch of variables on each page. However, we can achieve this in any case, without introducing variables or props passing around the entire tree - eg: using [Redux with Relay](https://github.com/facebook/redux-relay).

To find out more about Relay, have a read of the [Relay docs](https://www.relay.io/docs/react/).

As a result, I'm pretty happy with how things are going and want to continue to use Relay.

## Status

Accepted

## Context

Given that this server is an application server, we are faced with a need to setup PHP, the open source language for backend systems, in a user and accessible manner. This server will not only provide the application code, but will also provide an environment in which this code can run efficiently.
 
## Decision

Nginx, which stands for "engine x" in Russian, is an open source web server with an "engine-like" architecture. Unlike a traditional web server, where incoming requests land on the same server that serves the file out, Nginx uses a "front-engine" model where a separate engine uses the PHP interpreter to execute PHP code which has been written in a fashion compatible with the Nginx protocol. This means that the front-end of the server is stateless, and will always respond to the same incoming request with the same response, whereas the engine will be responsible for creating and maintaining the user's request/response session.
 
Each stack has a Nginx web-server which is responsible for receiving the incoming HTTP requests and forwarding them on to an Nginx "engine" which handles the PHP execution and keeps the sessions for each user alive. 

## Consequences

This architecture provides a very stable setup for processing PHP applications, with a separate frontend which accepts HTTP requests, forwards them to the Nginx engine and subsequently returns an HTTP response to the client.
