## Context

The eIDAS specification states that member states (MS) that export IDs shall run
an Identity Provider and a Matching Authority per ID type in order to verify the
legitimacy of the exported ID. If an ID is part of a cohort, multiple IDs
could be available in the eIDAS database for the same ID type and different
IDs within the same cohort have different keys. Hence the need for a
customisable way of routing traffic to the different IDs.

AWS ELBs do not currently support custom routing rules for HTTPS, including
the support of request-uri prefixes and custom headers.

The AWS Load Balancer Controller adds support for custom routing rules for HTTPS,
in order to achieve load balancing at network, instance and application levels
for EC2, ECS, ALB and ELB traffic using the internal HTTPS network between
ElBs and ECSs. See the internal-external HTTPS documentation for
[more information](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/elb/latest/internal-elbs/introduction-internal-external-https.html)
and [the Kubernetes documentation for how ELBs work for Ingress](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/services-networking/ingress/#alb-ingress).

## Decision

We are going to use the AWS Load Balancer Controller for the following:

- all ECS traffic routes
- all ALB traffic routes

This decision covers:

- HTTP ELB traffic for TLS
- HTTPS ELB traffic for TLS

We are going to use AWS Load Balancer Controller HTTP ElB routing rule to specify
that the traffic should be routed to each ECS service using the round robin method
for the configured ELB.

## Consequences

This removes the need for implementing manual configuration of the ELB's routing
rule to apply HTTP ELB to all ECS services for TLS. The end result is an
ELB in front of ECS that allows us to manage the configuration centrally in the
Cloud Foundry API.

When we are collecting measurements to create a model, we need to ensure that the measurements we collect include the right variables to allow us to estimate our model parameters and understand the underlying physical processes. For example, the measurements for a mixing model include the concentrations of the species involved, and the concentrations of the parent and daughter products for the decay series. It is possible to collect measurements of species concentrations and daughter product concentrations but not both. In this case, a daughter product decay series could be constructed but it would not be possible to identify the mixing ratio. There is only one way to collect data to enable us to measure everything. It is not possible to collect multiple measurements to separate the measurements by variable. A single measurement will measure one variable only. When multiple measurements are made, the measurements should measure more than one variable.

In this case, we can estimate the measurement we make for each measurement by comparing it to a reference measurement, and then a second measurement of the reference. As long as the measurement reference of the measurements contains the measurement of all variables or a subset of all variables, the measurement will be able to be made, and the value of the measurement will be the same as the reference value.

For an example, the measurement for the mixing model has a reference measurement of 10 g of an agent, which is made up of the mixing ratio agent/parent agent, which is 0.75%, and the mixing ratio parent agent/daughter product, which is 0.02. The measurement for the mixing ratio agent/parent agent is 0.75, and the measurement for the mixing ratio parent agent/daughter product is 0.02. A measurement of agent/parent agent is made from 0.75%, and a measurement of parent agent/daughter product is made from 0.02. These two measurements can be mixed together and can be used as the measurement for the mixing model.

We currently use a measurement collection class and it is up to the user to measure the measurements using appropriate measurements.

When we use measurements and an appropriate measurement set, we will use a measurement collection and the measurement will contain all variables or a subset of the variables required.

Measurements for different variables are stored in separate collections. This would ensure that only the right variables are stored within a given measurement.

For a mixing model, we collect measurements from different processes, which are different measurements, for different species. Measurements for different species can be measured without impacting each other. For example, the mixing model can measure the mixing of agent to agent/parent agent, and agent to daughter product, and collect the separate measurements.

The data storage has a separate structure which is composed of different collections which are the measurements of a process for a variable.

When collecting a measurement, we will retrieve the measurement using the measurement storage, either the measure or the collection of measures. The measure will include all the variables or a subset of the variables required.

In a measurement collection, the measurements are stored for different processes. They have a reference measure which contains the data for the variables.

## Status

Accepted

## Context

The way the government has designed the Covid-19 recovery and transition plan, with all its phases and transitions, is very specific. This makes it possible to make very clear, specific objectives for each phase.

There is a trade-off with this approach, however: If specific objectives are clearly defined, then any work that does not contribute to those objectives is seen as unnecessary. This is not a problem for phases of the plan that have a very specific, defined outcome. It can be a problem for phases that have broad, general outcomes that require a broad range of activities to achieve. 

An example of this is the "Improve mental health and wellbeing" phase, which has an outcome of "Reducing mental health problems and improving mental wellbeing for all". This requires a broad range of activities in order to achieve the outcome, but only a few of them will contribute directly to the outcome. Most of the work in this phase will be used for other purposes. For example, activities around data collection and analysis, which is not directly related to the outcome, but helps service managers monitor progress and make decisions.

As the plan is being implemented, we will need to review the specificity of the plan, and ensure that it does not impede us from being able to respond to changes in the future.

## Decision

We will ensure the specificity of the plan is at an appropriate level.

* For phases with specific outcomes, such as "Increase the uptake of Covid-19 vaccines" we will ensure that the activities we undertake are directly aligned with the specific outcome.
* For phases with broad outcomes, such as "Improve mental health and wellbeing", we will ensure that a wide range of activities are undertaken, but that the activities we choose do not preclude the option of doing other things later that contribute to the broad outcome.
* We will recognise that the outcomes of phases are often very difficult to measure at the start of the phase, and will revisit the specificity of the plan as the phase progresses and learn more about the likely outcome.

## Consequences

We will not be able to unilaterally make decisions that could change the plan entirely. We must propose changes to the plan to the infrastructure team. If it is an entirely different plan, it will need to go through the same process for approval.

We will be able to focus our activities on what is relevant for the phase we are working on. This will ensure our time is spent efficiently.

We will recognise that the plan is likely to change over time, and revisit its specificity as we learn more about the likely outcome.

### Context
Hpack is a method of encoding and serializing structured data. It's a way of describing how a schema is constructed. For example, let's say we have a simple object like this:
``` js
{
    "a": 1,
    "b": 2
}
```

Instead of serializing to JSON, Hpack describes the data structure and metadata with something like:
``` js
{
    "name": "test-schema",
    "type": "object",
    "description": "Test schema",
    "properties": [
      {
        "name": "a",
        "description": "test-a",
        "value": 1,
        "nullable": false
      },
      {
        "name": "b",
        "description": "test-b",
        "value": 2,
        "nullable": false
      }
    ],
    "minCount": 0,
    "maxCount": 1
}
```

The `properties` entry is an array of key-value pairs, and then each key has metadata like `value`, `description`, and `nullable`.

The metadata, specifically `value` and `nullable` is added in v0.5.

In Hpack, the value is a constant and part of the schema - it's a reflection of a certain value. This means that if you only add the properties key, you will get the schema for only a single object.

This is fine for simple objects, but what happens if you want to describe a compound object?  One example is an object like this:
``` js
{
    "a": 1,
    "b": {
      "c": 3,
      "d": 4
    }
}
```

An object like this will need to be defined with two properties - `"a"` and `"b"` - where `"b" is itself a schema, defined by `"c" and `"d"`. 

But in JSON Schema, this object could be encoded with the properties key only:
``` json
{
    "a": 1,
    "b": {
        "c": 3,
        "d": 4
    }
}
```

So if an object has nested objects, JSON Schema does not reflect that structure and metadata in any way beyond the properties key. 

For this reason, Hpack is considered the closest to JSON Schema available.

But JSON Schema defines the format itself, whereas Hpack is a way of encoding information about data structure.  This has a few consequences:

1. If you want to generate a schema for a data object using JSON Schema, then Hpack is a necessary and perhaps an auxiliary step.
2. If you want to validate an existing JSON Schema-encoded data object, then you have to somehow interpret the schema first to understand how to generate a new schema, and then generate a valid Hpack schema based on that. This is why JSON Schema is easier to process when it is already in its final, canonical format.
3. JSON Schema encoding assumes that there will only be one Schema for a data entity. With Hpack encoding, however, you can encode many schemas for a single data entity. For example, the above object, `"a" and "b" are different schemas, but they both refer to the same data entity.

#### Advantages of Hpack
* It's a close equivalent to JSON Schema
* It's fairly human-readable
* We can use a format that is closer to JSON than JSON Schema (as it's encoded directly)
* It's fairly easy to interpret and generate schemas based on it

#### Disadvantages of Hpack
* The way that the properties key is used makes it harder to serialize complex data structures into Hpack. 
* Schema generation and validation is still manual, since there's no schema generator. (I am aware that some tools exist that will do this for JSON, but not for Hpack, and there may be tools that will do Hpack-to-JSON conversion.)
* JSON Schema tools are not available.

### Decision
Although the disadvantages make our implementation harder, the advantages make our implementation worthwhile and provide a useful way to encode data structures.

To that end, we have decided to encode data using Hpack as a way to describe data structure, although the final serialized data will still be JSON.

### Consequences
As above, JSON Schema is assumed to have a strong relationship with Hpack and the Hpack schema is considered a good representation of the JSON Schema. 

The Hpack-encoded JSON data will be easy to read and debug and can

# 16. Use double array in memory for pixel data

Date: 2020-Nov-11

## Status

Accepted

## Context

* the image destination is currently implemented as a `sfCanvas`. A `sfCanvas` has two parts:

  * metadata about the image destination (resolution, color model, etc.)

Use a pixel data buffer consisting of a 2-dimensional array in memeory to store pixel data.

## Consequences

* pixel data will be stored in memeory, which will increase the memory consumption of `sfimage`

As we started to automate testing of the Verify Service Provider, it became apparent that the use of Selenium

The decision is to use [Playwright](https://playwright.dev) to manage automated tests of the Verify Service

for describing automated user interactions using plain English.

While Playwright's API is mainly focused around the management of browser instances, its support for awaiting
page loads (among other things) and its storage of the last page state makes it easier to write tests using
modern Javascript / CSS / DOM instead of relying on fragile Selenium-style selectors and CSS-in-DOM selectors.

[NightmareJS](https://github.com/LBHackney-IT/nightmarejs) library and our approach to creating our own

the use of Playwright implies the use of the [NightmareJS](https://github.com/LBHackney-IT/nightmarejs) library to
create the basis of our tests. The NightmareJS library was built to help with creating frontend-centric automated

use of page object models avoids the need to use fragile CSS selectors and reduces the amount of tests we

# 10 - Channel lifecycle

Date: 2020-Feb-20

## Status

Accepted

## Context

As part of our implementation for Cassandra-backed messaging we are going to look into how we can manage the lifecycle of channels.

To define a channel we need to define the name, version and whether or not it is ephemeral. For Cassandra-backed messaging we would also need to define whether the channel is persistent or not. This would determine whether or not the Cassandra table was created for a given channel.

For example, we might have 2 channels:

1. `order-channel-v1-ephemeral`
2. `order-channel-v1-persistent`

The first channel would be ephemeral, while the second would be persistent. This means that only the first message in `order-channel-v1-ephemeral` is written to the Cassandra table and the ephemeral channel is deleted when it is marked as `CLOSED`.

## Decision

To keep the implementation simple, we are going to use an idempotent key space identifier to identify a channel. This will be used in the `KEY SPACE` and `VERSION` metadata for channels.

### Cassandra tables

To add support to the channel lifecycle we will add 2 tables to the existing Cassandra table structure:

1. `channel_version` table:
   * `key`: the channel identifier
   * `version`: the channel version
   * `ephemeral`: whether the channel is ephemeral
2. `channel` table:
   * `key`: the channel identifier
   * `created`: the time the channel was first created
   * `closed`: the time the channel was last closed
   * `ephemeral`: whether the channel is ephemeral
   * `version`: the channel version
3. `message_version` table
   * `key`: the message identifier
   * `message version`: the message version
   * `channel`: the channel identifier
   * `ephemeral`: whether the channel is ephemeral
   * `version`: the channel version

### Cassandra schema

To add the new tables we will add the following SQL to the end of the existing `messages` schema:

``` sql
CREATE TABLE channel_version (
  key varchar(254) not null primary key,
  version varchar(254) not null,
  ephemeral boolean not null
)
;

CREATE TABLE channel (
  key varchar(254) not null primary key,
  created timestamp not null,
  closed timestamp not null,
  ephemeral boolean not null,
  version varchar(254) not null
)
;

CREATE TABLE message_version (
  key varchar(254) not null primary key,
  version varchar(254) not null,
  channel varchar(254) not null,
  ephemeral boolean not null,
  version varchar(254) not null
)
```

### Channel version

To create a channel version we will store it in the `channel_version` table using the channel identifier and version as the key. The table will be initialized with zero records and updated each time a new channel version is created. A channel will be written to the `channel` table only if there exists a channel version that has not been written to Cassandra.

### Channel lifecycle

To delete a channel we will delete the channel version associated with the channel identifier first, then delete the channel. If there is a message associated with the channel, then the message will also be deleted.

### Start/stop channels

To start a channel, we will write the channel version to Cassandra with an empty version. The channel will be started when the channel version has been written to Cassandra. We can ignore the messages with versions equal to 0 as they will be written to the channel after it has been started.

To stop a channel we will delete its channel version using the idempotent key space identifier. This will delete any queued messages as well.

## Consequences

In addition to the ability to manage channel lifecycles, the updated schema provides additional capabilities that are required for Cassandra-backed messaging.

## Status

Accepted

## Context

The code operates with various objects that should be protected from being altered in an unintended way.
An example of these objects are the state and the input/output objects, that are used in the various operations.
There is a need for mechanisms to ensure that these objects won't be changed in an unintended way to avoid bugs and to maintain the proper state of the system.
There are two possible approaches to protect these objects:
- Use of functional programming
- Use of exceptions

## Decision

In the context of protecting the state and input/output objects from being altered in an unintended way,
and facing the concern that any changes should be intentional and either desired or not done by a higher planning authority (that can be the user of the tool),
we have decided to use exceptions to protect these objects.
The need to protect these objects from being altered is fulfilled by the fact that the state and input/output objects cannot be changed in an accidental way.
However, the same cannot be said about the methods of the various classes.
There is a need for mechanisms to ensure that the methods cannot be misused and instead are only used as the intended functional unit.
This is fulfilled by the use of (optional) validation (or constraints) in the class.
As these constraints are usually not implemented within the class (using lambdas),
the class cannot change these constraints on its own (enabling integrity of the methods and the class).

## Consequences

### Advantages

* Easier to detect mistakes during the refactoring / development
* Easier to follow the possible ways a class can be used
* We don't have to learn and use a different language to write our business logic

### Disadvantages

* There is a risk that some constraints will be broken
* Testing is harder, as some constraints will be broken even when calling an internal method

## Context
Many existing images of the form "a LaTeX equation" are based on 
some `tex` image and the math mode of LaTeX.

When an "a LaTeX equation" image is made from an equation in LaTeX 
and "evaluated" to an image, a picture is printed.

Many "LaTeX equation" images have been made using a picture and 
evaluated as an image, not by LaTeX (i.e. the LaTeX mode).

Many LaTeX-based "LaTeX equation" images can only be "evaluated"
to produce an image; they cannot be "evaluated" and then used 
as LaTeX mode equations.

Some LaTeX users (e.g. in forums, user pages) can only evaluate

In order to have an "evaluation" of "LaTeX equation" images 
in various LaTeX users, all images should be self-contained, i.e.,
by "evaluating" the image, one gets an independent LaTeX
document that can be evaluated.

## Decision

No "evaluating" of images, but only producing an image.
These "images" will be called an image/image-with-tex-mode
(which is now quite long).

## Consequences

- Images and image/image-with-tex-mode are very easy to
  reproduce: a picture, a LaTeX document and some LaTeX
  (e.g. `\dots{}a{\tt{abc}})
- Images can be easily used by LaTeX editors.

## Context

The decision to use a service history system was motivated by the fact that as we build out our API in `HMPPS Digital`, we will likely find that our data model requires us to store a lot of information about the history of a service. For example, when we store information about a prison, we will need to know when each change happened, and what the change was:

- When did we start to store this data?
- How many people have worked on this prison
- How many staff have worked on this prison in total?
- What staff have worked on this prison?

Similarly, for all services there will be a need to know:

- When did this service start
- How many users have used this service
- How many users have used this service in total
- What users have used this service

There are two types of service history that we need to be able to track:

1. The history of the data model used for the service, i.e. the data structure used to store the service's information
2. The history of the service itself, i.e. the service's operational history

## Decision

We've decided to use the [Service history API](https://github.com/alphagov/service-history) and [service-version](https://github.com/alphagov/service-version) projects to track the service history for our services. This is a common pattern for projects at GDS.

We will also track the operational history of our services using [logit.io](https://logit.io) in order to track service performance and other metrics.

## Consequences

### General consequences

This choice has been made across multiple teams in GDS, so it's a common pattern of service history in GDS.

### Advantages

- Can track operational history, i.e. service performance and metrics
- Can see how long something has been active
- Can see what user has used something at what point in time, i.e. what the service has been used for in the past
- Can see what service has used something at what point in time, i.e. what services have worked on each other's services in the past
- We'll be able to make this choice for future services too

### Disadvantages

- This is a complex choice for teams to make, which takes a bit of time and thought

## Context

Kotlin offers significant productivity enhancements over Java for developers. The Java compiler is responsible for the vast majority of compilation time in a project. Kotlin’s compilation is significantly faster because the Kotlin compiler can be stopped and resumed mid-compilation and is less reliant on the JVM’s garbage collector. The JVM’s garbage collector is usually a source of project slowdown and causes developers to have to worry about how long certain operations take or how long the program will run before needing to be restarted.

Developers working on the backend of the Android platform can save valuable time on development, testing and debugging Android features with Kotlin. The Google team is actively pushing Kotlin and its usage in all Android projects in the Android platform for a long-term goal of migrating all back-end code to Kotlin.

While using Kotlin for projects helps the productivity of a project and provide significant long-term goals, some problems were encountered during the transition. The first was that Android 9.4 and prior still did not officially support Kotlin. Running a Kotlin program on those versions of Android still was possible but a developer had to be presented with a big list of options for how to allow Kotlin to run.

Android has officially supported Kotlin since version 9.5. For the most recent developments and features that Google is adding to Kotlin as well as Kotlin libraries such as Retrofit and Room, Kotlin is the best choice.

## Decision

In the context of maintaining the Android SDK and the various projects that it encompasses, we decided to use Kotlin as the primary programming language and main component language for all Java projects that will be considered Kotlin projects.

We will leave the Java language primarily to Java-specific functionality, such as writing custom View adapters and custom Android components. We will use the Java language when interacting with 3rd-party libraries that do not have a supported [Kotlin interface](https://developer.android.com/kotlin/docs/reference/to-kotlin/interoperability-with-java.html#_kotlin_interoperability_with_java).

To the extent possible, we will use [Kotlin on a JVM](https://developer.android.com/reference/jdk/play-java/kotlin). We will not use [Kotlin on the JVM](https://developer.android.com/kotlin/docs/reference/to-kotlin/interoperability-with-java.html#_kotlin_interoperability_with_java_not_on_vm) feature due to its drawbacks described by Google’s developer documentation.

We will allow the use of [Kotlin on a JVM feature](https://developer.android.com/kotlin/docs/reference/to-kotlin/interoperability-with-java.html#_kotlin_interoperability_with_java_not_on_vm) for minor features that do not contribute significantly to overall project development time.

## Status

Accepted

## Consequences

With the new programming language being Kotlin, the number of languages that Android developers know and must learn and become productive in is increasing. To alleviate this, Google has created the [JetBrains IntelliJ IDE](https://www.jetbrains.com/kotlin/kotlin-on-android) that allows Android developers to run Kotlin programs in the IntelliJ IDE and can be used to learn Kotlin’s features. With JetBrains providing the tools to learn Kotlin in the IDE, the long-term goal of migrating to Kotlin as a primary language is easily achievable.

_In Retrospect:_

The initial resistance to Kotlin, both due to its newness and the plethora of other languages Android developers have become familiar with over the years, was significant. It was a challenging and frustrating experience navigating JetBrains’ learning path in terms of creating Kotlin programs in the IntelliJ IDE. However, the learning path is now clearer, the tools are more accessible and a full listing of Kotlin features is available for review. A significant portion of the team did not have any prior knowledge of Kotlin and was required to learn the Kotlin language along with the other languages they are most familiar with, such as Java. This caused the initial learning curve of Kotlin to be steep, but after a period of increased familiarity with Kotlin and its usage, the productivity benefits and significant long-term benefits of Kotlin for Android applications are observable. With that in mind, it’s recommended that prior knowledge of Kotlin is helpful, but not required for understanding and writing Kotlin code, since a quick learning of Kotlin is possible once some understanding of the language and its usage is gained.

Date: 2021-05-04

## Status

Accepted

## Context

When choosing a CSS-in-JS library, we wanted a library that allowed us to scope components to individual modules and
prevent CSS from leaking into global scope. We found three main candidates:

- [CSS Modules](https://github.com/css-modules/css-modules)
- [Styled Components](https://github.com/vercel/styled-components)
- [Styletron](https://github.com/styletron/styletron)

## Decision

We have chosen Styletron as our CSS-in-JS library. It stands out from the other two libraries in a few key ways.

First, Styletron allows developers to write atomic CSS (a.k.a. utility classes), which means that CSS can be scoped
independently to each individual component. The developers no longer have to worry about accidentally writing
global class definitions and being unable to find the source of their CSS as the code grows in size and complexity.

Because developers can write atomic CSS, they can modify the utility class definitions without having to edit large
blocks of code. If a developer needed to add a new utility class, for example, to make the text in the content
section smaller, they would only need to add a new class definition. A developer would not have to add a new
class definition and then switch to the component section to add the utility class definition for the `h-small`
class.

By creating a single file for each component that only contains its own utility classes, Styletron reduces the
complexity of the code base. It prevents CSS from leaking into global scope, which can lead to accidental CSS
in leaks and maintainability problems.

## Consequences

- CSS leaks are prevented, which means that developers will not have to worry about accidentally leaking global
  class definitions when scaling their components.
- CSS can be scoped to a component or individual utility class, which means that code will be more readable and
  maintainable.
- The component code itself is less complex.
- Developers no longer have to create utility class definitions for the style they want to apply.
- Developers must add a utility class name for every style they want to apply. This can be a problem for more
  complex components.
- Developers can use atomic CSS for style that apply to multiple elements, such as margin and font size. This can
  make it difficult to understand what style is intended to apply to which element.
- Components can only apply utility classes to elements that are directly related to the component, which means
  that developers cannot use utility classes that could be used for styling elements that are not directly related
  to the component. For example, developers cannot use utility classes to apply margin to elements that are not
  directly related to the component. The developer needs to create a custom utility class for this purpose.

Despite these problems, we believe that the benefits of style outweigh the consequences.

Date: 2017-10-14

## Status

Accepted

## Context

Some records in the register have data that are considered personal information
or confidential by the authority. For example, the names and addresses of
members of staff, and their salaries.

In cases like these we cannot completely delete the record, but we need to
remove the offending data so that the rest of the record can be deleted.

## Decision

If a record contains data that are considered personal information or
confidential by the authority, it is not to be deleted in its entirety, but
only the data that are considered personal information or confidential will
be removed. These records will be marked as being "restored" so that they
will be included in the published index of records.

These records may still be used for statistical analyses, etc, but the
underlying data that make up those statistics will be treated as confidential.
For example, although a record may show that Mr. Smith received a salary
of £50,000 in 2016, that salary data will not be published.

The records that have been restored and have had their offending data removed
will be clearly marked in the published index of records as having been
restored.

## Consequences

This decision is necessary in order to make the published index of records
useful for researchers, analysts, and others who need to perform statistical
studies, but need to be careful with personal information and confidential
data.

People whose records have been restored and had their offending data removed
may expect their records to be deleted completely from the index. This may
be disappointing, but it is only marginally less disappointing than seeing
their records published in the index in their entirety.

Date: 2018-05-16

## Status

Accepted

## Context

We need an API to expose the data from this project.

### Existing

#### REST

REST was originally implemented to make it easy for a web browser to fetch data from the project.
This is accomplished by creating a number of endpoints that expose a set of data related to a single resource,
such as a specific user. These endpoints can be accessed via HTTP requests, and are typically responsible
for sending back data using JSON or XML formats.

While REST has been used in the project, it is not the most RESTful design pattern. Since REST assumes
many requests to the same endpoint result in the same data, this leads to the need to store each unique
request to the database within a database connection. This would be hard to do without caching as it would
result in many database calls per request, which could lead to significant performance degradation as the
number of requests to the database grows.

While caching has been used to mitigate the degradation of performance, it has only been used within
a single database, and has not been available across multiple instances of the same data source.

REST has been used in this project because of its ease of implementation and familiarity. However, due to its
inability to support high throughput, it is not well suited to the needs of this application.

#### GraphQL

The advent of modern client-side technologies, specifically APIs, has caused a number of different architectures
to emerge in the quest to deliver scalable and sustainable APIs. One of the most notable is Graph-like
RESTful APIs, or GraphQL. Unlike REST, which assumes the client wants data in a specific shape, GraphQL
assumes the client needs data in a variety of shapes. This means that rather than storing each unique set
of data separately, it is stored once, and can be shaped and retrieved as required by the user.

This ensures a number of benefits to high throughput API requirements, such as:
- the application storing each set of data once rather than multiple times;
- the application only ever sending the data required for the given request rather than a full set of
possible data for each request;
- all clients receiving the same data regardless of the number of clients.

## Decision

To meet the project's requirement of high throughput and scalability, and to make use of modern
client-side technologies, GraphQL has been chosen to be used to expose the data from this project.

## Consequences

Since the project adopted the GraphQL API, the method of delivering data to clients has been changed; instead of
using HTTP requests, the clients use a GraphQL query language to retrieve the data they need. Although not
intended for use in client-side applications, it can be used to meet the needs of our modern client-side
applications.

While the implementation of the GraphQL query language may be relatively simple in and of itself, the
implementation of our node-based server requires significant effort, for the purposes of caching, data
mutation, and data subscriptions.

In addition to the above, since the data of the project is in the form of a graph, the data must be stored
as a graph in order to be accessible via the GraphQL query language. This results in the use of a graph
database such as Neo4j.

Although this results in some of the benefits described by [GraphQL](https://graphql.org/learn/), it is also
important to recognize that some "benefits" of GraphQL are not applicable to the needs of this project, as
it is an application built specifically for a browser. For example, caching and the ability to scale to
millions of clients are difficult to accomplish using a graph database for client-side applications.

## Context

While we're focusing on implementing a better error message system in the repository, we can create a separate ADR to decide what users should get when fatal errors occur in the `kafka-repository`.

For now, our error message system is still being implemented, and we're planning to be able to customize the error message format while we're at it.

Currently, our error messages are formatted with multiple sections with an `!` in front of each section. Here's an example of a message we send out that looks like this:

```
ERROR(123) The configuration key 'foo' does not exist in 'config.json'.
```

This format is useful, but isn't very readable to someone who isn't familiar with `kafka-repository`.

## Decision

For fatal errors, we're going to change our message format to the following:

```
ERROR(123) [custom-error-message]
```

So for example, the error message `The configuration key 'foo' does not exist in 'config.json'` would be formatted as `ERROR(123) The configuration key 'foo' does not exist in 'config.json'`.

Note that we're keeping the error code in the message, which makes sense, because the error code is a primary key for the error. When an exception is thrown, the message is constructed with the error code and the exception message is inserted into the string between the error code and `()`.

## Consequences

We'll need to update the message formatting across all the errors in `kafka-repository`.

This will make it easier to debug issues when something goes silently bad. For example, in the past when a `getKills` operation failed and no exception was thrown, the message was formatted as `KILLS(0) The endpoint 'https://foo.bar:9090/kills' is not available.`. This makes no sense, because the message doesn't contain any information about what's wrong. Now, even though there's no exception (which means we can't get the exception message), the error code `Kills` tells us something is wrong and that we should debug the error.

## Context and Problem Statement

We have to create long living feature branches, therefore some long living branches have a problem with naming.
When we want to add an extra branch to it, the long living branch is still there.
While we rename the long living branch it is not clear, which of those long living branches we talk about.
We should have rules and guidelines for naming long living branches.

## Considered Options

* Use feature branches
* Use release branches
* Use long-living branches
* Use long-lasting branches

## Decision Outcome

We will use long-lasting branches.

While we use long-lasting branches, long-living branches must always include the following:

* release version: `feature-xxxx`
* branch number: `feature-xxxx-1`
* long-lasting branch number: `feature-xxxx-0`

* Long-living branches always contain a long-lasting branch number.
* Long-lasting branch numbers are increased for every long-living branch.
* Long-lasting branch number is always the last number.

Naming long-living branches follows the rules:

* All letters in the name are in one case.
* When using numbers in the name, there are always hyphens between numbers.
* All hyphens between numbers are replaced with slashes (`\`).
* All slashes in the name are replaced with hyphens (`-`).

### Example

```
feature-01-xyz
```

### Example with number containing hyphens in the name

```
feature-01-xyz
```

### Example with long-lasting branch number included

```
feature-01-xyz-1
```

### Example with release version included in the long-lasting branch number

```
feature-01-xyz-0
```

## Context

To be able to verify that a unit test code works and to be able to compare the output of the unit test with the previous version of the project, we need test suites. The test suite refers to a group of test methods which are to be executed together. Here, the test suite performs the unit tests.

There are two kinds of test suites in Java:

- Default test suite
- JUnit Test Suite

### Default Test Suite

A default test suite is used by executing the `test` Maven command. The target class is added to the default test suite using the `defaultTestSuites` attribute of the test classpath and the `test/src/test/java/` directory.

```java
test/src/test/java/
    test/src/test/java/myPackage/
        customTestClass.java
            ...
    test/src/test/java/myPackage/customTestClass$DefaultTestSuites.java
```

### JUnit Test Suite

There are many JUnit Test Suites available. `JUnit:runner-suite` is the JUnit Test Suite used to compile the project. The `testsuite` attribute of the test classpath and the `test/src/test/java/` directory and the `public` declaration of the test class are used to add to the JUnit Test Suite.

```java
test/src/test/java/
    test/src/test/java/myPackage/
        public class customTestClass$JUnitTestSuite {
        	...
            public static final String TESTSUIT_CLASS = "com.company.CustomTestSuite";
        }
```

The `public` declaration of the test class is used because JUnit Test Suite refers to the methods in public classes and within the test class the `public` declaration is used when testing multiple methods within the same class. Here, the `public` declaration is used when executing the default test suite and to get the `public` declaration of the test class for the JUnit Test Suite, the `inner` declaration of the test class is used. Here the `public` declaration of the test class is obtained as a result of the `public` declaration of the test class using the `inner` declaration of the test class.

## Decision

We will choose JUnit Test Suite when compiling the project with JUnit Test Suite. We will use the `customTestClass$JUnitTestSuite` declaration of the test class for the JUnit Test Suite and the `defaultTestSuites` attribute of the test classpath and the `test/src/test/java/` directory and the `public` declaration of the test class are used to add to the default test suite.

## Consequences

- To execute all test methods in the project, a test suite of JUnit Test Suite is used.
- To run the default test suite, Maven command `test` is used.
- When compiling the project with JUnit Test Suite, the test suite gets the custom test class as a result.
- When compiling the project without JUnit Test Suite, the test suite gets a default test class as a result.
- When compiling the project with the default test suite, the test suite gets a custom test class as a result.
- When compiling the project using a custom test suite, the test suite gets a custom test class as a result.

## References

- [JUnit Test Suite](https://www.junit.org/junit5/docs/current/user-guide/)
- [Maven CLI](https://www.maven.org/en/commandline/help/)

## Status

Pending

## Context

Data migrations can be done in a number of ways:

- a) apply an SQL script to the database
- b) use a tool (such as a database migration CLI) to generate the SQL
- c) use a tool to generate the appropriate datatypes automatically in the case of migrations

As far as I am aware (and I haven't done that much data migrating yet) all of these options result in code such as:

```sql
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS items;
CREATE TABLE items (
    id varchar(255),
    name varchar(255),
    price varchar(255),
    created timestamp,
    updated timestamp
);
```

Which contains multiple lines each containing up to 45 spaces.

There are a number of obvious problems with this kind of SQL:

- it is very difficult for someone reading the script to understand
- it is almost impossible for a tool to parse
- it uses hard-coded identifiers (like `items`)
- it has no tests (well, apart from unit tests)
- it does not use generic types (e.g. timestamps), which makes it hard to understand what is a string and what is a date

There are a number of tools that will handle these problems:

- flyway
- db-migrate
- golang-db

## Decision

We should use a database migration tool.

We should use whatever tools we choose as long as they are free, open-source and cross-platform.

We should keep the generated SQL script together with the code that generated it, in version control.

We should test the SQL scripts in unit tests.

We should use generic types (e.g. timestamps).

We should prefix all identifier columns with an `a_` prefix.

We should run the SQL scripts in the test database and integrate some of the results into the unit tests.

## Consequences

Data migration should be much easier in the future.

We will have to generate and keep the generation scripts.

We will have to integrate the generation scripts into our unit tests.

Testing the SQL scripts can catch issues earlier.

For 2020, we have a plan to rewrite indexing logic in Rust. This should be done gradually and we want to have the build up to the final rewrite happen within the current indexing process.

- content_items_published
- search_terms

- content
- translations
- versions
- thumbnails

Removing these indexes will make indexing more efficient and will allow us to continue to learn about the indexing process and better understand what data sources can be included within an index.

## Status

Accepted

## Context

We regularly have the requirement to create mocks for our testing.

There are some problems that have been identified around the current generation of these types of objects.

These problems can be split into a number of categories:

1. We have limited control over what options are available when it comes to creating the types of mock objects that we need. We currently cannot generate every combination of mock objects.

   For example, given the below stub, it is not possible to generate a mock that has a `callback` but NOT a `returns`.

   ```php
   public function stub(): self
   {
       return new self(false, "test: this is not a test: callback + return");
   }
   ```

2. It is not possible to configure (without using a different class) the way mocks are generated. For example, it is not possible to configure how many parameters a mock will accept.

3. There is a lack of ability to generate multiple test scenarios/patterns that utilise the different mock options (e.g. scenarios for all possible combinations of callback/return)

4. There is a lack of ability to generate all the different combinations to test multiple scenarios. For example, the ability to be able to test all the scenarios where either a callback or a return is used.

5. There is a need to be able to generate mocks for all of our different types. In some cases, this has involved creating a unique helper class, which is undesirable

6. Some of our existing mocks have specific properties that make them tricky to use or have made it difficult to write tests that utilise these mock objects. For example, the following (simplified) stub generates an object that has a property that is not public and is not documented.

   ```php
   private function stub(): self
   {
       return new self(0, new self(), new self());
   }
   ```

## Decision

We have decided to generate all mocks of the different types in a way that gives us the following capabilities:

* Use a method to retrieve each type of mock that can be used to satisfy our needs.
* Have the ability to generate the mock objects that we need.
* Have the ability to generate a test scenarios for all the different mock options.

This results in the following classes being created:

* [MocksFactoryInterface]: an interface that allows the creation of all the mock objects.
* [InterfacesFactoryInterface]: an interface that allows the generation of all the interfaces (which are mock classes with methods).
* [StructsFactoryInterface]: an interface that allows the generation of all the structs (which are mock classes without methods).

In order to make it easier to manage these interfaces, they are placed under the `/src/packages/core/interfaces/` and `/src/packages/core/structs/` folders respectively.

## Consequences

It is necessary to update our code so that it makes use of the new abilities. As a result, all classes that produce a mock are either already stored under `/src/packages/core/interfaces/` or `/src/packages/core/structs/` or are going to be moved there. Any existing use of mocks that are not currently stored under these folders must be migrated to use an existing method to retrieve the specific mock type for our tests (e.g. `test_doSomething_callback()`, `test_doSomething_return()` etc.)

The next step in this work is to implement the test scenarios for mocks.

## Status

## Context

The API endpoints used in this project comply with the REST paradigm and can be divided into two distinct groups:

* API clients
* API resources

### API Clients

These are client applications that make calls to the API and are used to access the server's functionality. In this project, the only client application is the application used to develop the API, that is, the API itself.

This group can be subdivided into two categories.

* API services (e.g. the UI or another API) which consume data from multiple endpoints, typically grouped by topic or namespace. For example, the user management API services which fetch user information from multiple endpoints.
* API consumers which access a single endpoint. For example, the "Who" endpoint which returns all the users.

### API Resources

These endpoints provide data within the framework of the REST architecture.

* API resources are the core of the API and are responsible for serving clients with information that is returned using REST principles when the request is fulfilled.
* API views provide API resources as XML or JSON format.
* The server returns the data when the client calls the API resource.
* API documents contains the metadata about API resource such as its type and the data model used to describe it.

### REST

The REST architecture is based on the following four constraints:

* **Uniform Interface**
* **Client-Server**
* **Cacheable**
* **Layered System**

Using API clients, API resources and API views in this project satisfies all the given constraints. For details see the respective [docs](https://github.com/sap-cloud-sdk/cloud-sdk-test-project-api/tree/master/docs/rest-constraints).

### More details

[REST](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/REST)
[Uniform interface](https://martinfowler.com/articles/microservices-uniforminterface/uniform-interface-rest.html)
[Client-Server](https://martinfowler.com/articles/microservices-uniforminterface/client-server-rest.html)
[Cacheable](https://martinfowler.com/articles/microservices-uniforminterface/cacheable-rest.html)
[Layered system](https://martinfowler.com/articles/microservices-uniforminterface/layered-system-rest.html)

## Decision

In this project API clients and API resources comply with REST architectural constraints.

## Consequences

REST compliance makes the following possibilities available.

* API clients are able to make calls to API resources without additional communication.
* When the API resource is not changed, the server can return an API resource exactly in the same state with every request. This is essential for caching to be effective.
* If the data from the API resources is replayed on another client, it can be used in future requests on the same client.
* The API resource may be used by API services and API consumers.
* API services can be reused as API resources.
* An API resource may be called several times with different queries. This supports caching.
* The API resource can be reloaded. For example, the "Who" endpoint can be called several times to get the same user information with the latest state.
* The server can retrieve API data from API client when a request gets its version identifier from client cache.
* Cacheable responses can be reused by the same client to API resource on the same client for the same time period.

Accepted

## Context

Previously the state was entirely managed by the ViewModel and exposed as a single stream of data. This was done so that data could be efficiently updated in real-time using the [RxJS](https://github.com/square/rxjs).

However as the application grew more complex to manage as a result of the following issues:
 - When the stream was updated, it always refreshed the whole stream even when only a single part of the UI was updated. This lead to a lot of unnecessary work (e.g. if only the user name was changed, the whole stream was re-updated).
 - When a property was updated multiple times in quick succession, there was a noticeable delay (e.g. on opening the chat window).
 - When a property was updated, there was no way to determine how many (if any) UI elements the property updated had affected. This was causing a range of issues, from the chat not being scrollable to the chat being partially hidden because of an updated property.
 - As the view model continued to hold the entire state, we continued to update the entire view instead of separate parts. The whole view started to suffer from the un-desired behaviour listed above.

## Decision

We decided to expose the entire state instead of individual streams. The reason for this was that it will enable a more direct relationship between the application state and the view. For example, now if we want to only update one of the elements bound to a data stream, we can be confident that it will work instead of causing some unexpected side-effect.

We will still use [RxJS](https://github.com/square/rxjs) but we will expose the entire state via observables and not be concerned about the side-effect of re-refreshing the entire stream because the entire view will be re-updated, instead of just one element on the view.

## Consequences

We are now able to more directly map the application state to the view and can be confident that updates to the application state only affect the view. We've also saved a lot of unnecessary work (e.g. the performance of opening chat is now a lot more efficient and the opening of chat no longer has noticeable delay).

## Status

Accepted

## Context

Since this repo uses makefiles primarily for dependency management, and the makefiles exist here already (for the build tasks).

## Decision

We will try to use makefiles to execute the build tasks, rather than a shell script with if/else statements.

* Easier to test makefiles in IDE
* Less error prone in CI, where the script is run by a shell
* Potentially (although unlikly) more portable across shells if makefiles can be read there
* Easier to debug, using a known build platform
* More portable outside of the shell
* Makefiles work by nature of *every* shell (even Windows has *something* like makefiles)
* Makefiles are standard part of the software

## Consequences

**Consequences of makefiles not working everywhere**

For example:

* If the makefile platform is Windows, Windows should still have a shell (cmd.exe) that can interpret makefiles
* If the makefile platform is Windows, the build tasks are likely not executed by the shell, and have to be set up to be executed by a shell


**Consequences of makefiles working everywhere**

* makefiles may be considered strange by software engineers that are unfamiliar with makefiles, e.g. students
* the shell may execute a bunch of irrelevant commands on Windows, because Windows includes `*.bat` files for executing the makefiles, but makefiles are only valid for a shell (though the Windows shell CMD.EXE can run every file)
* may ignore the build setup when used on Windows, to execute only the `make` files.
* makefiles may run the build setup (if we create an if/else statement for Windows)

## Context

We've sought to document the architectural decisions made on this project.
We’ve used a variety of methods for recording these decisions:
- [MADR](https://adr.github.io/madr/) style documents
- Spooked-style comments in the source
- README files

This proposal is to follow the decision records process, as proposed by Michael Nygard.
The approach has been well-documented at [www.thoughtworks.com/radar/techniques/lightweight-architecture-decision-records](http://www.thoughtworks.com/radar/techniques/lightweight-architecture-decision-records).
The approach should be familiar to people familiar with Agile and lean software development.

Following this approach will provide:
- An audit trail of architectural decisions for team and client stakeholders.
- A way of mitigating architectural risk.
- A process for discussing and learning about prior decisions.

## Decision

We will follow Michael Nygard's proposal to use lightweight architecture decision records (LADR).
We will maintain a directory of LADR documents in this repository.

We will follow the template in the original proposal.
There are further proposed templates which we can choose to use in the future:
- [Michael Nygard's template](http://thinkrelevance.com/blog/2011/11/15/documenting-architecture-decisions)
- [Jake Wharton's template](https://github.com/joelparkerhenderson/decision-record/blob/master/0000-template.md)
- [PEP 800](https://www.python.org/dev/peps/pep-0080/)

We will link the LADR documents to the [relevant GitHub PR](https://github.com/libero/community/pull/XXX) or [relevant branch](https://github.com/libero/community/branch/main) to make it easy to correlate the decision record with the change in code.
The filenames of the LADR documents will follow a naming scheme to help indicate the decision:
`XXX-decision-title.md`

We will use `XXX` as a unique identifier for each decision; the XXX will increment with each new decision.
There are various options for numbering decision records; we have chosen to follow the scheme `XXX-decision-title`, where XXX is a unique number.

## Status

Accepted.

## Consequences

### Positive

- We will have a documented audit trail of architectural decisions.
- We will have a process for discussing and learning about prior decisions.

### Negative

- We will have to write short documents describing architectural decisions.
- Some architectural decisions will not be made in the design phase; they will be made when we come to make changes to the code.

### Neutral

- Some LADR documents will follow a template that's not fully based on our current code conventions.

### Other considerations

- There is a possible exception when a decision is made at a meeting; there's no clear way to capture the decision record (this could be the subject of future research).
- It should be possible to write a tool to generate decision records; there's little in the way of research here and it is the subject of future work.
- While the template should be a good fit with our current development practice, it's possible that a different project may not benefit from the same template in the future.
- While our approach is based on the MADR style document, we are not formally following the [lightweight architecture decision record (LADR)](http://thinkrelevance.com/blog/2011/11/15/documenting-architecture-decisions) process; we will be recording decision records in the same file store.
- The term "architectural decision" is often used loosely in software; some people use it to describe a change to the code and not to a decision that affects the way the code is organized or written.
- Some people use the term "design decision" when referring to an architectural decision; they usually refer to a decision that affects the way the code is organized or written, not to a decision that affects how the system will be deployed or implemented.

## 0. Context

The Cloud Foundry (or Cloud Foundry for Private Cloud, aka CP) project defines a concept called a root tenant in an architecture in which a large number of tenants share the same compute (and storage) resources. The root tenant is the highest-level container (there's no other concept in CF for level of abstraction above the tenant), and all tenants inherit the capabilities of the root tenant, so the root tenant must offer high levels of abstraction in its support of tenancy.

## 1. Decision

The CF project's decision to include a synthetic root tenant means that in cases where a tenant can't or doesn't want to set up a regular root tenant (see ADR 003), we can instantiate a synthetic root tenant instead, for which the usual deployment and configuration have to happen in three places:

   - The root tenant instance (e.g., the instance of a cloud-init on a VM)
   - A storage system to persist configuration
   - A DNS system for the resolution of tenant domains

The cloud-init instance is the source of truth for a tenant, so the root tenant (even in the case of a synthetic one) is uniquely identified with it, because it knows about all the tenants that have been created. The root tenant config system (probably a DB or key-value store) is the source of truth for the root tenant itself; it stores configuration in a manner that allows tenants to add or change their root tenant configuration. Finally, the root tenant DNS entry system is used for resolving a tenant's domain name fully qualified as its root tenant domain plus its tenant name. So, for instance, if `tenant-a` on `test-cp.org` resolves to `test-cp.org`, then the root tenant DNS entry resolves to `test-cp.org`.

## 2. Status

Accepted

## 3. Consequences

If a tenant does not set up a regular root tenant, there must be a synthetic root tenant. This adds some complexity to the deployment of tenants (for which no single process or container is the source of truth). This complexity is increased because we must also monitor the root tenant configuration database (or key-value store) for updates to the root tenant itself. The DNS record system must also be updated whenever a tenant is deleted or renamed so that future tenants can resolve the root tenant name and all tenants can resolve an internal tenant name. A CF operator would need to be aware of these consequences when building a product.

However, the ability to provide synthetic root tenants eases the burden of deploying tenants because an operator no longer has to deploy the root tenant configuration and DNS system (or install, configure, and deploy them) for a tenant to be set up. The operator simply deploys a root tenant instance and creates the corresponding DNS entry. This eases the operational burden because the operator no longer has to update multiple configuration records for each tenant deployed, and tenants become more flexible because their root tenant configurations are owned and controlled by them, instead of having an operator update a tenant's root tenant configuration.

## Context

At this point, we can manage the Subject Viewer's configuration through the `subjects-cache` store or by building the configuration into the runtime JAR. The option to use the cache is usually picked by those managing an enterprise cluster deploying the Subject Viewer. However, the store/cache is not visible to users of the Subject Viewer.

Currently we have a requirement to support the ability to change the Subject Viewer configuration on the fly, and we cannot depend on Enterprise cluster admins to make this change. We had planned to build the `config.yml` and `config.json` files into the Subject Viewer JAR, so that users of the Subject Viewer could edit them on the fly. However, this presents a number of problems:

- The ability to edit the files is limited to the host from which the JAR was built (so it would only work in the same network/domain)
- The configuration files could only be edited in the same JVM
- The configuration files could only be edited in the same host JVM

There are a number of options that were considered that would meet the above requirements:

- Make the configuration files ephemeral and be written to a shared file system (e.g. NFS, SFTP) at runtime, and then read them from the cache at startup
- Use a shared (S3, etc.) file system to store the files, and ask for them to be present in the cache at startup. Have them written to the file system in real-time while the Subject Viewer is running
- Run an additional process that would write the configuration file to the cache at runtime and read it during the startup process

Each of these options have a number of pros/cons:

### Make the configuration files ephemeral and be written to a shared file system (e.g. NFS, SFTP) at runtime, and then read them from the cache at startup

- `+` Subject Viewer doesn't have to start/stop to wait for files to be cached
- `+` It's the same process that's doing the caching so it's the same process that's doing the access
- `-` It's another process, even if it is in the same JVM
- `-` Files cannot be edited in place while the Subject Viewer is running

### Use a shared (S3, etc.) file system to store the files, and ask for them to be present in the cache at startup

- `+` Subject Viewer doesn't have to start/stop to wait for files to be cached
- `+` It's the same process that's doing the caching so it's the same process that's doing the access
- `-` Files cannot be edited in place while the Subject Viewer is running
- `-` Another process to have to manage
- `-` Still another process even if it is in the same JVM
- `+` Files can still be edited locally
- `+` Files can still be edited in another process
- `+` Files can still be edited in the `config.yml` file

### Run an additional process that would write the configuration file to the cache at runtime and read it during the startup process

- `+` Subject Viewer doesn't have to start/stop to wait for files to be cached
- `+` Same process is doing the caching and the access
- `-` Another process to have to manage
- `-` Files cannot be edited in place while the Subject Viewer is running

## Decision

Based on the above pros/cons, we decided to run an additional process that would write the configuration file to the cache at runtime and read it during the startup process:

- This is what we have done in the existing Subject Viewer code
- The config file is built into the JAR so that we can deploy the Subject Viewer to multiple hosts or environments without having to upload the config file
- It's the same process that's doing the caching and the access, so it's the same process that's doing the access
- The process is invoked at startup in such a way that it's the first thing the JVM does, so it has the most control over what happens at startup
- It's an additional process to have to manage, but we are quite familiar with this process already

The decision for what the feedback should say at the end of a routing interaction was made using two primary sources of input: user interviews and user tests. User interviews conducted in 2019 fall on average 80% of users using Google Maps have been happy with Google Maps directions over the past three years, and over 70% of users will take a wrong turn while following Google Maps directions, which can be disappointing. However, after receiving feedback from our users about incorrect directions, we realized we needed more information to decide what our feedback should say. User tests conducted in 2020 with 140 participants showed that 25% of users have been on a "wrong turn" experience, with 10% of those being in a state of confusion and requiring feedback. This may appear to undermine the first source of input, but in reality the feedback should be used to help users understand what the directions were and why they might have ended up with a "wrong turn" outcome. This decision is based on:

- the user should be referred to as "you" and "your" instead of "you're" and "your's" because it feels less possessive and less "in charge"
- Google Maps users respond positively to feedback that acknowledges that an incorrect turn happened and acknowledges this should be a source of surprise but also helps with overall directionality going forward

## Decision

Users should always be shown the following feedback after an incorrect turn:

  - An offer to learn more about how Google Maps directions work

- The question and answer interaction happens asynchronously, so the message will appear before or after a click to "learn more"

## Status

Accepted

## Context

We need to choose a technical approach to start with and choose how we will create and maintain the content of this new website. There are several architectural styles that could work here; modular monolith is only one of them. All of them require ongoing work to keep up to date and change more difficult to implement later on.

We will probably need to work quickly to get the first version of this site online as soon as we are able to and accept many changes to the technical approach during development.

We have a very clear idea of what the final result should look like, but as we keep building the site, we may discover that our original vision doesn't work well in practice or would be easy to implement. During development we will likely have to change parts of this vision, either by changing our approach or changing our mind about certain parts of it.

For this reason, we want to choose an approach that:

* Is simple to implement and maintain
* Fits our current skill sets
* Allows for rapid iterations and changes in scope and vision

But also allows for this scope to expand into something larger later on.

## Decision

We have chosen modular monolith for the following reasons:

* We have experience creating modular monolith systems, such as the Content Management System, and so our team understands this approach and its benefits
* Our experience with modular monolith systems has mainly been positive, such as the CMS or Alfresco
* It seems simpler to start with a system that has a well-defined architecture rather than starting with a single "approach" like a microservices monolith

## Consequences

By starting with modular monolith, we take the risk that we may choose an approach that's difficult to maintain later on, but it seems the best option right now. This is also the approach we've used for most of our previous projects.

We will need to learn about all of the parts of modular monolith, which will add some time to our development cycle, and some of these parts are more nuanced than we might expect at first, such as how to separate the effects of changing different components of the system.

We can mitigate some of the issues of modular monolith by building some additional systems around it, such as a project management tool to help us with changes.

## Context
Currently, the API design is quite naive for most entities, thus the messages will grow out of hand.
We need to design a message structure upfront.

## Decisions
The message structure is defined using Protobuf, the serialized
representation of gRPC messages. This enables efficient data transfer between
remote systems since it is a language-neutral message serialization method and
can greatly reduce protocol buffer parsing time for local systems.

The core/API message types are defined inside the api.proto file. In this file, there are two top-level message types:
* ApiStatus
* GetDogmaRequest

ApiStatus is the root message type and its fields are used to send information
about the status of the calls to the Dogmatiq API. A message of type ApiStatus
contains the following fields:
* request_id: string
* return_code: enum: SUCCESS or FAILED
* description: string
* timestamp: timestamp

A message of type GetDogmaRequest contains the following fields:
* request_id: string
* selector: string

## Consequences
* It is easy to change messages later without breaking the client code.
* There is no possibility to add fields to messages as they grow in size.
* The size of serialized messages will be expected to increase by an order of
  magnitude.
* All server-side code is using a gRPC client generated by Protobuf.
* Every client uses a Protobuf library.

## Status

Accepted

## Context

Since we're creating a new tool, we need to keep a way to identify where an installation comes from, as well as keep the ability to change these installation ID's for release version purposes. It would also be handy to be able to identify which installation belongs to which GitHub repository, for troubleshooting purposes. Ideally the installation ID should be created in one step and have the ability to be updated again to avoid confusion.

## Decision

We have decided to use a GUID for the Installation ID and have the installation ID be available from the start. The ID will be generated at the start and cannot be updated. This decision was made primarily because we had the desire to keep a UUID type as the ID so that one could use the hexidecimal representation and treat it as an incremental number, which will allow for changes in repository layout, and not break other tooling that may be used for versioning in future releases. Additionally the byte representation of a GUID can be used as a hash and have a bitwise representation used as a version identifier. The version identifier bitwise representation will allow future versions of the tool to be identified with ease, and have all the bits representing the version of the tool be used as a hash.

## Consequences

Guids have a unique identifier built into them, which allows us to identify the ID and store it easily, and provides the ability to update the ID later if you need to. This will allow for situations where we change the layout of our repositories. While there are a number of tools that can identify GUIDS, we are limited in our choices of what software we use to store the ID locally in the tool, and version the ID in the long term. Since the ID will be the hash and version identifier, we must think of long term storage and access of the ID in the tool. It should be possible to use a database, where the ID can be stored and accessed through a query, as well as read the long-term identifier value from it. This does not take into account the possibility that long-term ID storage may become inconvenient to be changed in the future.

## Alternatives

While we initially considered using a GUID, after further research, we've now decided that a UUID should be used. The reason behind this is that the GUID will only have an incremental number that goes from 0 to 9999, rather than a true unique number for which there is no upper limit. If a tool is developed where we need to identify more than the ID for an installation, then the ability for these IDs to grow by millions or more over time, will need to be taken into account. Additionally, we wanted an ID that could have more than the number 9999 in its ID. While a GUID has 32 characters, a UUID has 33 characters. We felt that we needed an ID that could have a character as its 33rd, so a UUID was the only way we could see of doing this. While a UUID does not provide a unique number on its own, when combined with the timestamp for the creation of the ID, it can provide a unique identifier. In this way we would not need a second ID to identify an installation. We also do not have to update the ID for release versions in this manner. It should be used in a similar manner to a GUID so that it can be used to store the ID and used as the long-term identification for an installation.

## Status

Accepted

## Context

The first version of Content Manager used content models defined in Java classes. The idea was to build different instances
of content according to the different models and manage their storage in the database independently. Although this gave us a lot of flexibility,
it also led to confusion around which content model a particular content instance belongs to.

We had an "abstract" content class, called "Content", and from that we derived other classes, "AbstractArticle", "AbstractPage"
and so on. The common superclass has a "content ID" field, which has been overwritten in all subclasses to some random integer.
In practice this has meant different integers being generated as content IDs for different models of content.

To simplify things, we tried to get rid of the "abstract" property from our "Content" class, so that all instances of our
content hierarchy can manage their own content ID and make it unique. However, this approach has some serious drawbacks,
since we haven't got an easy way of referencing the parent or child content of an instance, and this makes it difficult
to create the links we need for navigation, for example.

## Decision

We went with a mix of our own classes, called "SiteElement" and "Content", for handling all aspects of content in
CMS. The "site element" is simply a node in a graph that holds "content". This means that the "content" graph 
contains the "site element" nodes. All the "site elements" are stored as separate instances of our "Content" class, 
each with a unique ID.

The "Content" graph contains our "content" nodes, which are stored as individual instances of "Content". The "ID"
field now represents the content ID for each "Content" node (rather than a random integer), and the "parentID"
field, which was set on the "abstract" classes, now also exists on "Content", and is set by its parent node. 

In this way, we've got a single instance of "Content" that stores all the individual pieces of content for the site.

## Consequences

This is a much simpler model, and it's easier for developers (and other users) to understand. It also provides a way of
referring to parent/child relationships, which is an important need for navigation. There's a slight downside in that
it can become difficult to store a hierarchy for more than a few levels in it, but even so, we've found this to
be a much more robust approach.

The call-back gets the results from the handler and forwards it to the core.
