## Status

Accepted

## Context

We need to pass data from the container into react components, to make it accessible within the component.

We could pass data to the component via props, or use React Context to access shared data within all child components.

Using props would require us to pass each required prop down the chain to the lower components. This would lead to tight coupling, where child components are dependent on high level container props, which is hard to reason about.

Using React Context would give children access to shared data. This data can be managed within the component. The problem with this is that we lose type safety at the container level, and the context is set up in a way that is likely to cause issues later.

## Decision

We will use React Context to store shared data.

## Consequences

It is easier to make mistakes when using context, such as unintentionally re-triggering data updates.

## Context and Problem Statement

When choosing a deployment platform, one of the main criteria is to be able to run all services as containers and then deploy those containers to a hosting platform like PaaS. While this has previously been possible using the Docker daemon, and then the PaaS docker-compose API, it is now that the Platform as a Service docker-compose API is available, which allows us to deploy containers with more ease. Now the question is, are we able to use docker-compose on PaaS to deploy services and environments from Cloudfoundry?

## Considered Options

1. Deploy using containers from Cloudfoundry
2. Use custom buildpacks to deploy services from Cloudfoundry

## Decision Outcome

Use custom buildpacks

## Pros and Cons of the Options

### 1. Deploy using containers from Cloudfoundry

Use the Cloudfoundry CLI to deploy services directly to the PaaS docker-compose stack.

Pros:

- PaaS can take care of provisioning the infrastructure as needed
- We do not have to think about the buildpack part of the service
- PaaS has a requirement for Docker containers to be used on platforms, it will need to be set up regardless
- PaaS has a container registry to be able to deploy services, it will need to be set up regardless

Cons:

- The buildpacks we were planning to use did not work on PaaS and it was unclear when they might work again
- It is unclear how to set up the buildpacks on PaaS, although the Terraform does include a `docker_buildpack` module
- When we were using containers to deploy to ECS, we deployed a Docker daemon (ECS ECS IAM role) as a container to make that possible. PaaS does not have a provision for creating a container-in-a-container setup to meet this requirement.

### 2. Use custom buildpacks to deploy services from Cloudfoundry

Use the buildpack to deploy from Cloudfoundry to PaaS docker-compose stack.

Pros:

- Cloudfoundry has a custom buildpack API that has proven itself on PaaS
- Can deploy the buildpack in Terraform to be included in the PaaS deployment
- Can set up custom buildpacks on PaaS without Docker
- If we can write our own `buildpack-apply` Terraform module, we can control how the buildpacks are used on PaaS

Cons:

- The custom buildpack will add more cloud-orchestration technology to the PaaS deployment.
- If we are adding a module, we will need to maintain the code on a long-term basis
- We will need to configure and maintain the custom buildpack

## References

- [PaaS docker-compose documentation](https://www.cloudfoundry.org/terraform-docs/#services-with-docker-compose)

## Status

Proposed

## Context

As part of the process of creating an automated code formatter, we have a need to read various text files, such as configuration.
This text files can contain arbitrary JSON, so for the purposes of automation it will be useful to be able to parse plain text
files into a JSON type.

For the purpose of this ADR, we will assume that the text files are encoded using UTF-8 encoding.
A parser is not needed for JSON decoding, since this is well-supported.

A full "deserialization" procedure requires a specification of the expected data types for each field,
however this would vary depending on whether the data is expected to be a file, or just text.
It would also be a requirement for a custom "deserialization" implementation to be loaded at runtime,
however this is unlikely to be a requirement for the purposes of this ADR.
For the purposes of this ADR, we will assume the "deserialization" procedure can accept plain text.
This will ensure that the current formatters can read any plain text configuration files for use.

## Decision

We have decided to make the "deserialization" procedure part of the core,
as plain text files will need to be read in almost all situations.
This will allow us to remove the "deserialization" procedures as and when needed, without having to import a large amount of procedures.

The core currently has the following procedure:

`get_raw()`

which returns plain text.

This procedure can be reused to read in plain text, and can be later be removed.
An alternative API can later be used, such as

`get_json()`

which returns JSON.

This is likely the same implementation as `get_raw()`, however it is a different "deserialization" procedure.
This implies that the previous deserialization procedure can be removed.

We have opted for this procedure for reasons that are covered in decision:0001.

## Consequences

It is expected that this will ease in the process of creating new formatters, which can be based upon existing json formatters.
It will also ensure that any future procedures designed are capable of parsing plain text files.

## Context

In [2019-08](https://github.com/guardian/dotcom-rendering/pull/1005) it was decided that
we should use a more model-centric approach to rendering elements in Dotcom Rendering. This
was due to:
- having trouble keeping different rendering models consistent
- wanting more flexibility to override or change default values
- finding it hard to know where the rules for combining different values lived
- wanting things like code splitting, lazy loading, lazy-for-hidden to be explicit instead
  of implicit

Here's a link to that decision: https://github.com/guardian/dotcom-rendering/pull/1005#issuecomment-594741356

So I decided to implement these models in dotcom-rendering-elements.

However, after going forward, it's become apparent that these models have:
- some bugs in them
- haven't been clear about what exactly is meant by `islands`, `shared`, and `host`
- aren't helpful as an overall architecture for a component
- it's been difficult to override them when needed (because they are static model instances)

I knew that I could amend the previous decision and decided to do so.

Now I'm proposing some changes to the docs and this repo.

First, the definition of these terms:

- `host`: it's the DOM element that contains all other elements (it's the root)
- `islands`: it's the root DOM element of a standalone component (it's the root of its own subtree)
- `shared`: it's the root DOM element of a (part of) library that is shared between different hosts/islands (it's the root of its own subtree).
- `application`: the set of all hosts/islands and shared in a single application, which includes the DOM of the main web app.

Second, the rendering model can be thought of as a tree of `application` nodes and `island` nodes, with `host` always being the root node at the top level.

Third, there's three types of element:
- `base`, which is just the element itself (it has no children, just attributes)
- `application`, which has children (because it's the root of an application, which contains the host)
- `island`, which has children (because it's the root of its own island)

Elements can have other qualities, such as `islands`, `shared`, and `host`, but they are all
base types. They can also be overridden, even though there are some rules around it.

The reason for having a base type is so that `application` and `island` can share behavior
such as code splitting, lazy loading, and so on.

So for example, we can define:
```js
const Box = ({
  type = 'base',
  id,
  host,
  shared = {},
  islands = [],
})
```

Then we can have different values for `type`:
- 'base' (like 'div' or 'span')
- 'application' (we define this in dotcom-rendering-elements)
- 'island' (we define this in dotcom-rendering-elements)

We can also change the meaning of `host`, `shared`, and `islands`:
- 'host' can be an actual DOM element
- 'host' can be the `id` of a DOM element
- 'host' can be a function that returns the DOM element
- 'host' can be the `id` of a function that returns the DOM element
- 'host' can be a function that returns the `id` of a DOM element
- 'host' can be an object
- 'host' can be an array
- 'host' can be a function that returns an object
- 'host' can be a function that returns an array

The main question then is what is to be done with `host` in dotcom-rendering-elements
and why does it appear to follow this model and why should we follow this model?

## Decision

- dotcom-rendering-elements should not be model-centric. It should have no model instances
  at all.
- instead, it should be a bunch of plain js functions, each representing a renderable type.
  Each will be implemented like `function box(props)` or `function text(props)`
- we shouldn't have these static classes because we don't need them
- we also shouldn't have these `const` definitions because we don't

## Status

## Context

The easiest way for now to get a project from our template is to download the project.json file directly and modify that there.

However, this has meant that if we want to make a change to a project, either we need to make the change to every project template, or we need to somehow allow project.json files in the project template repository.

If we allow project.json files in the repository, it will be difficult to make sure that any projects built in the repository have the same structure. At the very least, we'd need to have some kind of schema of the structure to validate that our projects are built in correctly.

And even without a schema, a file like project.json is usually quite long and specific, so it's likely someone would make some mistake when modifying it manually. We'd need some way of fixing these kinds of mistakes.

However, the easiest way to allow developers to build projects that meet our template is to add an option to the SDK to create a .sb3 file using the project.json file. After all, the creation of the .sb3 file is the process of importing the project.json and the dependencies into the platform (i.e. exporting the correct project structure).

## Decision

We will allow the project.json file directly to be imported into the template using the SDK.

## Consequences

This adds some complexity to the project creation process, and allows us to do things like automatically creating .sb3 files if the project.json files are in the repository.

However, this is still a reasonable approach to allow developers to import projects from our template and build them more easily. And, if we decide that we have different versions of template dependencies, we can still have a schema.

## Status

Accepted

## Context

In this project configuration are stored in environment variables.

For this reason configurations need to be stored in a versioned way and the ability to rollback to previous configurations need to be available.

The ability to view previous configurations is also needed for troubleshooting and other tasks.

The fact that most of the configurations are data related makes it important that they are stored in a reliable and secure manner.

Also since some projects do not have CI and deployment automation, it can be important that configurations can be stored in a central place as a reference.

## Decision

Configuration files of projects with build-time configuration will be stored in the main repository.

For example, the `settings.gradle`, `build.gradle` and `react-app-rewired.config.js` of the projects.

Other configuration files, like `package-lock.json` or `npm.json` will be stored in the `config/` folder.

An example folder structure:

```
projects/
    ProjectA/
        config/
            package-lock.json
            npm.json
            settings.gradle
            build.gradle
        tests/
            package-lock.json
            test.json
            ...
    ProjectB/
        config/
            package-lock.json
            npm.json
            settings.gradle
            build.gradle
        tests/
            package-lock.json
            test.json
            ...
    ...
config/
    package-lock.json
    npm.json
    readme.md
    LICENSE-2.3
    CODE_LICENSE
    ...
```

## Consequences

Configuration files can be easily viewed through the versioning system of the projects.

If any projects do not have CI and deployment automation, configurations can be used as reference and even deployed using scripts.

Using `settings.gradle` and `build.gradle` makes it easier to have configuration files that other tools can also read like `react-app-rewired.config.js`.

Using a folder for configuration files allows other tools like `eslint --config` to also set configuration.

Configuration files can easily be copied and pasted between projects.

Some developers will automatically have access to configuration files that other tools cannot read.

Some developers will access configuration files with tools that cannot read them.

An effort can be made to reduce the ability to access configuration files that other tools cannot read, by prefixing filenames when copied between projects.

Some developers may try to do things like setting environment variables during the test-run. This will be addressed by writing another layer of abstraction like `jest.config.js`.

We have ruled out Auth0 and AuthN.
Auth0 has been successfully used in the project before, and provides a quick setup

is now open for contributions from outside Mozilla, and to make the
Firefox Accounts Login Page feature
available to a wider audience.

We have decided to not use a client-side ID provider because we felt that the user
experience should be the same (or at least, not more degraded) than using

for the product. As such, we have opted to use Cognito to provide
authentication capabilities.

In general we felt that Cognito would allow us to build a backend-less API which

build out to support WAM should be able to provide a layer of abstraction over

As such we have opted to use Cognito as our authentication provider.

authentication state and associated data which could in the future be used to inform the
management and allocation of permissions. This functionality is not currently required, however
as we learn more about our users' needs for authentication (especially concerning SSO)
it may make sense to revisit this in the future.

# Context

File format programmatically means we can programmatically change file formats
from scratch, without using an intermediate representation.

It would be preferable to avoid this, as long as possible:
1) it’s difficult to know how the changes will affect downstream tooling (like
   code generation, for instance)
1) it’s difficult to understand the changes in code, as we re-work and refactor
   code to support new file formats
1) new implementations might be non-idiomatic, as we’re not using the file format
   to build the program as the compiler would

Because it’s difficult for downstream tooling to work with changes to file format
directly, we would prefer to write a translator between the new file format and
the old file format, i.e. we would produce a file in the old format as a
result, not a file that uses the new format.

However, it’s impossible to do this if the interpreter is capable of executing
the programs that use the new file format.

# Decision

Thus, file format programmatically will be used to convert a file that uses a
new file format to a file that uses an old file format, which we can then
programmatically create.

# Status

Accepted

# Consequences

An interpreter is capable of executing the programs that use the new file format.

We have a translator between the new file format and the old file format, i.e. we
will create files of the old file format as a result.

A translator will be easier to work with if we can do a number of things, e.g.
* run it on every platform that we can run our program on
* support new features (e.g. in the future, old programs would need to work with
  the new file format)
* test it thoroughly
* integrate it into the code-generation tool that we’re using to build the
  old file format (see `old-file-format`)

## Status

Accepted

## Context

**Problem/Questions:**

- Traces could be lost, creating an unpredictable, complex, and confusing environment, where users and clients could not debug an erroneous component.
- Creating a trace, when an erroneous component fails, results in loss of information about the operation it was doing at the moment of failure.

**Tracer**

A **trace** represents a particular user request and an **operation** represents a particular user request for a service, with all of the sub-operations required to complete that request.

**Trace identifier**

A **trace identifier** is a long randomly-generated string that allows users and clients to uniquely identify a particular request. The value must be long enough to not collide with other trace identifiers.

**Logging entry**

A **logging entry** contains all the information about a particular operation, including the time it started and when it finished. Logging entries are sent to a trace endpoint to form an **operation**.

**Trace endpoint**

A **trace endpoint** is a URL that stores information about traces in the request. Typically this information is sent as logging entries to a request, and is then forwarded to the trace endpoint.

**Trace request**

A **trace request** contains the trace identifier and all the data that has been generated about a trace.

## Decision

**Implement a trace request**

An API endpoint to be used when tracing requests and operations.

The API response should have a `trace-id` value.

## Consequences

**Benefits:**

- The endpoint will allow us to trace every request and operation and be debuggable on a user/client point of view.
- Logs can be aggregated and parsed in an automated way to analyze the data, for debugging, performance, etc.

**Risks/Costs:**

- Data is needed in the API.
- Request/operations can have traces more than one in the future.

[Trace Request](https://martinfowler.com/API/Trace/TraceRequest.html)

## Context

There are several different ways for parsing HTML in JavaScript.

### [JSDOM](https://www.npmjs.com/package/jsdom)

JSDOM can parse HTML into a DOM element, which can then be used for querying and modifying the DOM. This would be very useful to our unit test, so that we could have tests that were able to change the DOM. JSDOM does not implement accessibility monitoring, which is required for our unit tests. As such we could not use it without implementing accessibility monitoring ourselves, which would not be necessary for our unit tests to work.

### [Cheerio](https://www.npmjs.com/package/cheerio)

Cheerio can parse HTML and CSS into a DOM element, and has accessibility monitoring built in. As such we could use it to create tests that would have accessiblity monitoring built in.

### [PhantomJS](https://www.npmjs.com/package/phantomjs)

PhantomJS can parse HTML and CSS into a DOM element, and has accessibility monitoring built in. As such we could use it to create tests that would have accessiblity monitoring built in.

## Decision

Use Cheerio to parse the HTML for our unit test.

## Consequences

While using Cheerio we will have the accessibility monitoring built in to our tests. We will not have to implement this separately.

We would be unable to use JSDOM to parse the HTML in our unit test, and therefore the accessibility monitoring would not be accessible to our unit test.

Using PhantomJS would have provided us with accessibility monitoring in the browser the unit test is running in, which we would not be able to access from the unit test. However, this would have made it possible to use [this approach](https://www.w3.org/2001/wct/tester/access/getting-started.html#step-1) to run accessibility tests on our unit test.

## Context

[ADR020](ADR020-cell-capacity-assignment.md) assigned capacity to cells
across all towers in a region. This process was performed entirely in code,
with no automated tests, and this was an error in the code, as it doesn't work
correctly as expected for all the cells present in a region.

As a result, cells with a very low capacity are currently unallocatable and
cannot be allocated to a cell capacity group, while cells with a very high
capacity can be allocated as a result, which leads to incorrect capacity
assignments.

This ADR presents the proposed solution to make the capacity allocation
deterministic and automated.

## Decision

We propose to implement a new mechanism to assign capacity to cells,
namely:

1. Make all the capacity groups of a region have their own capacity ranges
1. For each cell, allocate it to a capacity group whose capacity range
includes the cell's capacity
1. For each cell, allocate it to a single capacity group per level of the
hierarchy

### Detailed mechanism

The hierarchy of levels will be:

1. Region
1. Tower
1. Cell

### Detailed algorithm

The algorithm of assigning cells to capacity groups will be the following:

1. For each cell, calculate its capacity range
1. For each cell, calculate its range multiplier
1. For each cell, calculate the number of levels at which it is the lowest
capacity group
1. For each cell, calculate the number of levels at which it is the highest
capacity group
1. For each cell, calculate the number of cells it is the lowest capacity group
1. For each cell, calculate the number of cells it is the highest capacity group

A cell is considered the lowest capacity group at a given level if its
capacity range is lower than the capacity range of all the cells above it
in the hierarchy. It is considered the highest capacity group at a given
level if its capacity range is higher than the capacity range of all the cells
below it in the hierarchy.

Given these calculations, we can now allocate cells to capacity groups:

- A cell is allocated to a capacity group if its range multiplier
multiplies the range of the capacity group and the result is greater than
or equal to the capacity of the cell
- A cell is allocated to a capacity group if its range multiplier
multiplies the range of the capacity group and the result is less than
or equal to the capacity of the cell, but only if the cell is the
highest capacity group at the given level

### Implementation notes

For cells that are at the lowest capacity group at a given level, their
allocation to the capacity group will be done using the cell's own
capacity range; for cells that are at the highest capacity group at a given
level, their allocation will be done using their range multiplier
multiplied by the range of the capacity group.

We have also decided to assign the value '1' as range multiplier to cells
that are at the lowest capacity group at a given level.

### Example

Consider a situation where 4 cells are allocated to 2 capacity groups.

| Capacity group | Capacity range | Cells that live in this group |
| :----------------- | :----------------- | :------------------------------ |
| A | 0-240 | 152 |
| B | 400-800 | 400 |

The following capacity groups are configured:

| Capacity group | Capacity range | Cells that live in this group |
| :----------------- | :----------------- | :------------------------------ |
| A | 0-240 | 152 |
| B | 0-10000 | 400 |

Due to this setup, the capacity groups will be auto-populated as the
capacity ranges are not mutually inclusive, and each range gets allocated to
the capacity group by using the range multiplier of the capacity group on the
capacity range of the cell.

In this example, the B capacity group has higher range multiplier (100)
compared to A (1), so the B capacity group will have higher capacity.

The following table shows the capacity groups with their capacity ranges.

| Capacity group | Capacity range | Cells that live in this group |
| :----------------- | :----------------- | :------------------------------ |
| A | 0-240 | 152 |
| B | 0-10000 | 400 |

Using this ADR, each cell in the hierarchy of cells will be allocated to
either capacity group A or capacity group B

## Context and Problem Statement

An address can either be invalid or missing. If the address can be invalid, then what exactly is wrong with it? Should we notify the user of something? Or if it's missing, what should the user do?

## Decision Drivers

Should the user be asked for permission?

## Considered Options

## Decision Outcome

Invalid address during the loading of the web should only be shown once an error happens, and not on initial connection (i.e. after the wallet is opened). If the user gets persistent connectivity issues, then we should notify the user to enable VPN and/or use a different network (e.g. 5G).
In cases where the user wants to disable address auto-fill, then we should notify the user instead.
When in an offline mode and the user wants to use the web. If the user uses the offline mode, then the wallet should be used instead.

When in an offline mode and the user does not want to use the web. If the user uses the wallet instead, then the wallet is used.

## Context

The way the world has changed in the past few years is amazing, like a lot of applications on my plate: 
1. the internet has changed, with 
    1. Web 3.0 being a thing, 
    2. all companies having their own social networks, 
    3. all companies having their own version of the truth, 
    4. web applications being the main form of accessing the internet
    5. mobile being the main form of accessing the application
    6. all companies hiring remote workers and being open to this trend

1. software development has changed, with:
    1. The trend of writing smaller, more focused services being more visible
    2. The trend of doing everything in one repository being more visible
    3. The trend of the tech talent pool being more diverse
    4. Companies having more technical skills available to them

This has led to a couple of tech trends being visible:

1. a big question regarding architecture: will we build monoliths, microservices, or a combination of both?
2. a big question regarding our code structure: will we adhere to the monorepo model, where we store all services in one big repository, or micro-service development, where each of our services has its own repository?

Since I believe I have good code writing and code review habits, I am ready to take the monorepo challenge head-on. Monolith systems are less flexible and therefore less sustainable in my view. I believe that we have some technical skills that are important for building a sustainable project. I believe that we are in a stage where we can afford the extra overhead of having a monolith, for the time being.  

What we do not have:

1. a good solution for knowing how we do things at our company
2. a good solution for knowing how we do things outside our company

We cannot afford to make those mistakes, as we have too much at stake to afford having them. The reason why I am in this project is to gain more knowledge about how we do things outside of my company's world. In this sense, I could not be in a project that does not make it possible for me to learn more about how we do things outside of my company's world.  

Since there is a trend of micro-service systems development, I must see how I can see my services having their own repository. Since it is a trend to see micro-service systems being developed, the idea behind the monorepo solution is quite compelling. Monorepo systems have the following advantages:

1. All dependencies are stored in the same repository.
2. A monolith or micro-service architecture is more difficult to achieve.
3. All developers use the same technology stack.
4. The monolith or micro-service architecture is less flexible, but this is not seen as an issue in a small project like this one.
5. The monolith or micro-service architecture is less sustainable, but I believe we can use our technical skills to address this concern.

There is one big risk for projects with a monorepo architecture, which is a big change to the organizational model for our company. We have some technical skills that make it possible for us to be able to mitigate that risk. The reason why I believe that we can mitigate that risk is that there is already a movement of developers being open to this trend, even among senior technical talent. To be in a project where there is already a movement like that in place makes it a lot more likely that we can implement our desired organizational model changes. 

## Decision

We will go with the monorepo model, as it is a way of gaining knowledge about other technical communities. It gives us the opportunity to learn about other organizations' way of doing things. Since our project has a technical community like the rest of the world, it is the right choice to be in a project that gains us that knowledge.

## Consequences

Since it is an architectural decision that has a large effect on our organizational model, it will be harder for us to work in an agile manner. But the agile movement happens and cannot be stopped, so we're on our way to gaining the skills to be able to achieve both.

# ADR022: web app language and framework selection

## Context

This service will be responsible for supporting the operation of the publishing API.

We will need to select a language in which to code this service.

There are various options available to us.

We will need to consider which front-end technologies to use for the user interface.

We should try to use a language with broad support across hosting platforms.

There are many frameworks available for creating a web API.

We should try to use a framework that we have experience using before.

We should try to use a framework that has a large developer community.

We should try to use a framework that is actively maintained.

## Decision

We will write our service in [Go](https://golang.org/).

We will use the [Standard](https://golang.org/pkg/stdlib/), [GORM](https://github.com/jmoiron/gorm), and [Neo4j Go driver](https://github.com/joelparkerhenderson/neogorm) packages.

We will use [Indents](https://github.com/scakac/indents) for code formatting.

We will use the [Testify][] package for assertion help.

We will use the [go-swagger][] package to generate API documentation.

We will use the [Prometheus][]-exposed API key-value store for caching to avoid a database load.

We will host our app in Google App Engine (GAE) Flexible environment.

We will use a [light-weight WSGI server][].

We will document our API endpoints with generated Swagger API documentation.

We will deploy our app to [Github][].

We will use [CircleCI][for Continuous Integration].

## Consequences

There are multiple dependency groups for our application. This may make it harder to get our application installed in Google App Engine. [This][stackoverflow-question] question addresses that problem by packaging all of our dependencies into a monorepo using [GOV.UK PaaS][govuk-paas]. This is out of scope for this decision record.

We may want to choose a database other than [Neo4j](https://www.neo4j.com/) because we have been put off it by the way it exposes keys. We may want to use [Elasticsearch](https://www.elastic.co/guide/en/elasticsearch/reference/7.9/index-aliases-field-keys.html) instead. We should check to see if we can use Neo4j's equivalent before we make this decision.

Go applications can be written to be deployed to Google App Engine (GAE) Flexible environment.

`Prometheus` supports a number of databases. It uses the [PostgreSQL][] database by default. If we use another database, we must add it in our [configuration][].

We have various continuous integration (CI) options from which to choose, including Travis and CircleCI. We can use Google App Engine's [Cloud Build][].

This architecture will allow us to monitor our application using Prometheus and test it using go tests.

## Context

We want our frontend application accessible from anywhere in the world, without a username or password login.

One technical approach to achieve this is to generate a magical link that can be shared between friends, family, colleagues and anyone who can access this link. This magic link can then be used by anyone to register, login and view the application. The magic link will be long and convoluted to avoid people from being able to guess it simply by luck. We can also add an expiry date and time to the magic link so that we can invalidate old or unused magic links.

## Decision

We have decided to implement passwordless magic link authentication on the front-end application. We use [Firebase Authentication](https://firebase.google.com/docs/auth/passwordless-auth) which is Firebase's authentication service. This supports generating short, random, obfuscated URLs that allow people to sign up and sign in to our services.

There are some limitations to what we can do with magic links. For example, we can't retrieve the user account detail from the magic link URL. We can only invalidate the link by changing the value in the database.

It's also important to understand that this type of service is suitable for our frontend, but we should use a more traditional authentication method for any backend APIs we build. This is especially relevant as our database is now managed in MongoDB.

We've included Firebase Authentication in our `README.md` file so that people can find it easily, and we can remind ourselves of what we're doing when we're feeling overwhelmed.

## Consequences

- People will be able to sign up and login to the application without a username or password
- We can invalidate old or unused magic links
- We can't retrieve the account detail of the user from the magic link URL
- We'll need to take steps to make sure that we store all our other data (e.g. the user account detail) in a database
- This service is supported by Google and Firebase, which makes it reliable and long-term sustainable
- Firebase Authentication doesn't work with Server-side code, so we'll need to make sure we pass the magic link details to the front-end client
- We're able to link other services (like our APIs) to Firebase Authentication using the 'customizable method' approach (mentioned in the Firebase documentation)
- We need to follow all the best practices listed in Firebase Authentication documentation for implementation and best usage

## Problem

URL's should be readable, when a user gives a link or enters a URL in
the browser.

Usually it's OK for an URL to be shortened, if it's very long and has
some characters like '&' or '&amp'.

Some people want to encode a special character '&' in the URL to make it
look like '&amp'.

### Problem 1

An openURL (like https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Main_Page) should use
encoded characters to make it easier to read and understand.

### Problem 2

Is it possible to write every (encoded) character into an openURL?

### Problem 3

Some URLs start with `http`:

```
http://www.xyz.abc/def.xyz
```

Should this be also encoded as:

```
http://www.xyz.abc/def.xyz?
```

### Problem 4

Some URLs end with a `#!`:

```
http://www.xyz.abc/def.xyz#!
```

Should this be also encoded as:

```
http://www.xyz.abc/def.xyz#!?
```

### Problem 5

Some URLs have a fragment:

```
http://www.xyz.abc/def.xyz/#ref
```

Should this be also encoded as:

```
http://www.xyz.abc/def.xyz/ref?
```

### Problem 6

Some URLs have a hash-fragment (like '#ref'):

```
http://www.xyz.abc/def.xyz/#ref
```

Should this be also encoded as:

```
http://www.xyz.abc/def.xyz/ref?
```

## Considered Alternatives

* no encoding

### Problem 1

* encoding


## Decision

* encoding
* the encoding scheme is UTF-8 (with only ASCII characters)
* URL-encoding is applied (it's basically a subset of UTF-8):
    * `!` becomes `%21`
    * `&` becomes `%26`
    * `#` becomes `%23`
    * `?` becomes `%3F`
    * `%21` becomes `!`
    * `%26` becomes `&`
    * `%23` becomes `#`
    * `%3F` becomes `?`
* a URL should not be encoded twice

### Problem 2

* it is not possible
* it's possible to have "magic chars" in the URL, like `!` or `&`
* it's possible to use encoded characters like `%21` in the URL (not `!`)

### Problem 3

* no
* a URL should be human-readable (even if it has encoded chars)

## Context

To make product pages more readable we have introduced a new layout and structure.
The new code was written using a mix of existing (public) code, and code we built for Q3, and is in [a
PR](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-service-team/pull/30250).

The main issue motivating this decision is that the new site is slower than the old, because:

* there is no CSS minification or compression
* we cannot use HTTP caching because we always generate a unique cookie for GOV.UK

This is not a good experience for our users, especially on low-cost devices, and we should work to resolve this.

## Decision

We will rewrite the new site using a [GOV.UK
template](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-elements-govuk-govuk).

## Consequences

By rewriting using a GOV.UK template we can benefit from all the work that has already been done to optimise the site for speed, usability and accessibility. Some examples of the things we can be sure that it achieves are:

* the content is written in plain language
* the structure is designed to reduce cognitive load on the user
* we can use clear, simple and descriptive class names in our code
* the markup is more than 95% parsable by a screen reader
* the site is designed to be used on mobile devices
* the markup conforms to GDS standards for tagging (class names)
* the markup is structured to make it less ambiguous about what is a component, and what is not
* code is written in ES5 (the lowest common denominator)
* we can add version number to the query string when using a public build (for development)
* the site is not automatically indexed by search engines
* all pages load in less than 500ms
* the HTML source is minified, and uses Gzipped compression (HTTP cacheable)

There are some potential downsides of this approach, such as:

* the layout will not exactly match the old layout
* the code will need to be maintained
* we will need to migrate the GOV.UK template to the next major version in 2018
* we need to migrate the GOV.UK template to work with [GOV.UK
header](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-header) and [GOV.UK footer](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-footer)

On balance, though, we think this is a good approach. The use of a GOV.UK template is the foundation for a fast, highly accessible site, and we can rewrite the code, and content, to match the needs of product pages, and then build on that as we continue to learn.

The [prerequisite work](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-service-team/pull/28418) to rewrite content as HTML is also valuable, because we then have consistent markup between versions of the content, and are able to use the same class names.

## Considered Alternatives

* Use Legacy Trackable Interface
* Use CoreTracker and CoreTrackable Interface

## Decision Outcome

* Chosen Alternative: Use CoreTracker and CoreTrackable Interface
* Allows flexibility to be tracked by both legacy and new tracking systems.
* More intuitive API for working with tracked items.
* Clear separation of concerns for legacy and new tracking implementations.

## Pros and Cons of the Alternatives

### Use Legacy Trackable Interface

* `+` Existing implementation already exists.
* `+` Works with legacy tracking systems.
* `-` Difficult to work with new tracking systems.
* `-` API is not intuitive for new code.
* `-` Uses old-style object orientation, which can make it hard to work with modern JavaScript.
* `-` API relies on `constructor` and `this`, which can lead to subtle bugs in long-running codebases.
* `-` Doesn't support modern JavaScript features like class fields and get/set accessor methods.
* `-` Can be confusing to work with because of lack of clearly-defined interfaces and type systems.
* `-` Often used to implement generic containers that need to track their own contents (e.g. file managers, project managers, etc.) which can make it confusing to work with.

### Use CoreTracker and CoreTrackable Interface

* `+` Allows new tracking systems to be tracked with new terminology and concepts (e.g. "core", "version").
* `+` Better API makes it easier to work with tracked items in new code.
* `+` Clearly defines the interface between the tracking system and the tracked item, which makes it easier for developers to understand what they have and how they can work with it.
* `+` Uses modern JavaScript features.
* `-` Requires rewriting all existing classes and code that uses CoreTracker/CoreTrackableInterface to use the new classes.
* `-` Requires writing documentation for all existing classes.

## Context

Content Performance Manager (CPM) and Audit Tool (AT) are two separate tools used by the same team to support content data warehousing and ongoing content audits. While they share a lot of commonalities, there are also a number of key differences between the two. This ADR is a post hoc justification for the decision to create these two separate tools, and is meant to be used primarily as a reference for onboarding new team members and others who are interested to learn more about the history and driving rationale behind the decision to create two separate tools.

The [AMP project](https://github.com/alphagov/AMP) provides a significant amount of context for this ADR, especially in the `docs/adr` folder and the `docs/AMP_technical_overview_draft.md` document (a copy of which is available in this repository).

In particular, this is a follow-up to the [ADR 002: Use Python and Django as core for Content Performance Manager](002-use-python-and-django-as-core-for-content-performance-manager.md).

In the original proposal for CPM, there was an emphasis on being able to load arbitrary data into it for use in search indexing or other uses. This original proposal did not include AT, instead proposing that we should create a separate tool for the purposes of performing automated content audits. Since then, we have determined that we wanted both to be able to perform data warehousing tasks, as well as perform automated content audits. This resulted in us postponing the decision of whether we should merge the functions of CPM and AT until we had more information and resources to address the proposed challenges.

In the interim, we learned more about the differing requirements of the two functions. We noted that while CPM is used by Content Editors to upload and manage data, AT is used by Content Managers and SEO Analysts to review data for content audits. This resulted in two assumptions being made by the project team in the interim:
1. We have sufficient resources to address the proposed challenges.
2. We have sufficient resources to address the proposed challenges for both CPM and AT.

It is the second assumption that bears the greatest relevance to this ADR.

The purpose of this ADR is to document the history and driving rationale behind the decision to create two separate tools, and to address the following questions:

The `homeassistant-api` and the `homeassistant-homeassistant-integration` repos are merged into one.
The `API`-client is moved from the frontend to the server-side, which means the following changes are required:

- Switch from API-first design to client-first design.
- Create a server-side API, which is then exposed to the frontend clients through an API-gateway.

To achieve this we implement several endpoints, which are divided into two categories:

- **entity-related endpoints:** fetch and set data related to entities with physical/digital nature (e.g. entities representing light switches, door/window sensors, etc.)
- **scene-related endpoints:** fetch and set data related to scenes (e.g. scene representing "Turn On TV")

The API-gateway provides a single access point for all these endpoints, which is managed via a stateful REST API. This is similar to the way the official Homeassistant API works.

The following endpoints are defined on the API-gateway:

### Entities

- **get entity by ID**
  - https://integration.homeassistant.io/api/entity/#entity/<id>
  - response: { id: <id>, object_id: <object_id>, ... }
- **set entity value**
  - https://integration.homeassistant.io/api/entity/#entity/<id>/set-value
  - response: { ... }
- **get entity by name**
  - https://integration.homeassistant.io/api/entity/#entity/<name>
  - response: { id: <id>, object_id: <object_id>, ... }

### Scenes

- **get scene by ID**
  - https://integration.homeassistant.io/api/scene/#scene/<id>
  - response: { id: <id>, object_id: <object_id>, ... }
- **set scene value**
  - https://integration.homeassistant.io/api/scene/#scene/<id>/set-value
  - response: { ... }

## Consequences

The following consequences are foreseen:

- the main codebase is significantly smaller
- there is a single interface to all the functionalities of the APIs
- clients only use one API-gateway for all API requests
- all API requests go through the API-gateway, which is aware of all the entities and scenes
- clients get direct access to the entity data, which might make sense
- since the API-gateway is stateless, client-side state (e.g. open-sessions) is implemented by side-store (e.g. cookie).

## Status

## Context

We use a custom metadata to track the state of applications (in the background) as well as which pages they affect from the front-end application. This metadata is loaded with every HTTP request to front-end and can be changed by webops.

During the page loading process it is assumed that if a page is affected by more than one application, a new application can be written to the index later to replace this old application and will become visible in front-end.

As the front-end application loads asynchronously, the page may still be affected by several applications. If a page is affected by more than one application this will still be recorded within the page-metadata for their lifetime and we may end up in a deadlock situation.

In a deadlock situation both front-end and server would be unable to perform further HTTP requests to each other. This would still be a deadlock situation for the front-end application and the server would be unable to perform requests for page-metadata. As a deadlock situation for front-end is a bug for the application it is assumed this will only happen temporarily and then re-loads the application once and resolves the deadlock.

## Decision

We use another metadata to track changes to `meta` tags and use these to determine application reloads during the application lifecycle in front-end.

## Consequences

The result is a temporary deadlock situation while reloading the front-end.

If the front-end application is able to be reset without any further processing on the page, then the front-end application can be reset when it is not used anymore.

## Status

Accepted

## Context

We are making a serverless app which will have a number of functions, most of which should be called as a unit.
For example, the same data validation rules should apply for the same inputs regardless of the endpoint.
This could be made easier to handle by using functions, but we want these to be treated as unit.
We should be able to test the same function unit whether it lives in the same endpoint or a different endpoint.
Our unit tests should be able to test the function independently from its containing endpoint and also the unit should be re-testable without the integration part.

## Decision

We separate types and functions in our serverless app.
Types are the different entity which can exist (for example, a User or a Service, but not a date).
Functions are actions which can be performed on types and create other types.
Each function can be treated as a unit and is either called by a user directly or by another function.
Types can be created by functions and can be validated and have validation rules, etc.
The functions which are used to validate can also be called as unit.

## Consequences

Using this approach:
- We can have separate unit tests for separate functions, which can be run separately, to avoid unnecessary integration part.
- It is easier to maintain our test code, which can be refactored without changing the implementation of each function.
- It is easier to refactor and simplify functions, for example to treat validations of different data types in the same way.
- We can use the types to create mock implementations in our unit tests.
- We can use the types in our integration tests.
- If a function is used in more than one endpoint, we can have only one unit test.

## Examples

`service-search` / `list-service-users` / `get-service-information` / `create-service-user`

`service-search` can either:
- be called directly by the user
- be called by the unit test `list-service-users`
- be called by the unit test `get-service-information`
- be called by the unit test `create-service-user`

`list-service-users` can either:
- be called directly by the user
- be called by the unit test `get-service-information`
- be called by the unit test `create-service-user`

`get-service-information` can either:
- be called directly by the user
- be called by the unit test `create-service-user`

`create-service-user` can either:
- be called directly by the user
- be called by the unit test `list-service-users`
- be called by the unit test `get-service-information`

## Status

## Context

We need to build our service to be usable by humans over time periods that are greater than the length of a single execution in AWS Lambda. A good way to design our service to be usable over long periods of time is to mimic real-world scenarios that are long in duration and evolve over time. Some of these scenarios have long cold start up times. We need to design our service so that it is more flexible.

The use case for this service is the scheduling of automated tests. Our service should be durable and should allow a set of tests to be scheduled to run on a specified, long timeframe.

## Decision

Our service will be designed with the following characteristics:

- The ability to perform as an event trigger from a log source
- Scheduling of a Lambda for a given date and time in the future
- A mechanism for triggering an event from the Lambda
- The ability to be triggered on a number of different data sources

The data source could be an S3 bucket if we wish to monitor for a change in content of an object, or it can be a database where a schedule is maintained. These are all valid use cases. The first scenario would be valid for use in scheduling tests after a change in an S3 bucket but they are two different scenarios. We will need to define our mechanism for triggering an event from a Lambda in a manner that has flexibility to accomodate scheduling.

The ability to be triggered by the Lambda from other sources means that we can use an AWS SQS queue or something that is configured on a Lambda or via another source such as a database. This will provide the ability to trigger a Lambda to a database on a schedule.

A DynamoDB table has been defined as a container for managing schedules and there is a persistent schedule record, with a corresponding schedule ID and date. This will allow for scheduling events on a particular date in the future. We can then schedule an event to trigger from a Lambda and from the event we can use a database to schedule a future event on a particular date.

This can then be triggered on a number of different use-cases.

## Consequences

The use of DynamoDB to mimic real world use cases will reduce the ability of the Lambda to execute when it is not triggered from the Lambda. The DynamoDB would need to be populated and refreshed every so often, which might have additional consequences to it.

DynamoDB events can be triggered to events, which will allow us to have events triggered from an AWS SQS queue such as Lambda. This will allow a set of data changes to be scheduled for a future date.

The schedule will have to be refreshed regularly by a Lambda.

### Problem statement

Currently, JSON messages are expected to be well-formed.
So we drop messages containing JSON elements which cannot be parsed into well-formed messages.
Do we make the same check if we are not expected to send metadata that includes those elements?

### Possible solutions

* make the same check, the well-formed message must contain a single JSON element
* relax the well-formed message, it may contain multiple JSON elements and the message must be well-formed without these elements

### Considered options

* do not make the check, the message is expected to contain a single JSON element in the future
* make the check if the message is not expected to contain a single JSON element
* make the check and check for all possible message contents
* relax the check, the message is expected to contain a single JSON element

### Positive consequences

* we accept the extra JSON elements
* we do not expect all JSONs
* we do not relax the message, the expected JSON element must be well-formed

### Negative consequences

* we do not check all possible messages, e.g. messages with multiple JSON elements
* we do not relax the message and validate it as before

# ADR034: Continuously deploy platform CF applications

## Context

Traditionally, we would have applications on one branch, deploy one version on master/main, then deploy all applications on release. This approach has some drawbacks:

  * Deployment will fail if we need to deploy two versions of our CF applications at once, or more. For example, during our release migration it was not clear which branch should be master/main and which should be release. As a consequence we had some applications deployed to release and others to master/main and we would have had to merge master/main and release and deploy again.
  * For applications deployed on release there would be nothing to test the application against in master/main which would require us to merge those applications to release again, which has the potential to cause some regression.

One of the benefits of using the platform is that there is a clearly defined release process and a branch that can be used as release. We have this in place for all applications.

## Decision

We will continue to deploy our applications using the release branch for release applications and master/main for all other applications.

## Status

Accepted.

## Consequences

Deploying on release using the release branch has some drawbacks:

  * If we deploy two versions of our CF application at once, or more, we would have to merge those to release and deploy all again.
  * Our applications do not get the benefit of all the upstream commits made in master/main.

On the flip side, deploying from master/main enables us to benefit from the commit history and changes made during the development of our applications.

## Status

accepted

## Context

### Why
We aim to make sure the most relevant and accurate data is published in the first place. We should choose a tool that offers support for multiple data sources. This would enable us to ingest data from more than one data source. We would like to be able to analyse this data too.

### Currently
Google Sheets is currently a data source. We use this for importing data in google sheets.

### Future
We could make this tool flexible enough to be used across all data sources. We could make it available as an API, either as a hosted API or self hosted API.

### Other tooling that might support this
- Excel (we can import data from this too)
- PowerBI
- AWS CloudWatch

### Other services that might provide data
- API Gateway (might enable us to collect data from multiple APIs)
- Web Scrapper

## Decision
We will use Excel 2021 as our data crunching tool.

## Consequences

### Data crunching
We will be unable to import data from more than one data source. This means we will need to collect all data in Google Sheets or Excel and create and import the files into the crunching tool. We also have to consider exporting the data from the crunching tool somewhere else in this process. 

### How does this play with Data Pipeline?
We import data in this pipeline (Google Sheets to Data Warehouse to Data Pipeline) then we need to export data out of the Data Pipeline. Which is what we already do, using the Export Template to do so.

### Data Management
Managing data governance with data stored in Excel (and other tools) can be difficult.

### Risks
Managing data import/export to/from other systems is a risk that needs to be mitigated.

We will be able to use a familiar tool in all our workflows. It will be easy for us to import data from the Data Warehouse, as this is data that we already export in the form of Excel. We will need to import data from Google Sheets to the Data Warehouse in batches. This allows for the incremental approach of the Data Pipeline.

### Use of data source
We do not export all data to Google Sheets, Google Sheets is only a source of data. It allows for analysis and publishing of the key takeaways from these analyses. This tool is therefore not a data pipeline.

### Future changes
We could modify the system to support more data sources at a later date.

### Other tooling
Since we can import data from Excel we can use that as a base for future tools that import or export data.

### Support
We are more self-service and able to fix issues ourselves since we are more hands-on with this technology.

## Status

## Context

The aim of the CDH ETL is to populate a data warehouse with metrics generated by the CDH. To achieve this, we need to extract the relevant information from the CDH as well as import and load this information into the data warehouse.

There are a number of possible options to achieve these aims:

### Extract

- Extract the data feed files directly from the CDH itself (by mounting the data feed file system directly onto the CDH API)
- Use the CDH's [ETL](https://www.cdh.io/dev/deploy-apps/etl/) functionality to pull out metrics
- Use the CDH [Metrics API](https://metrics.cdh.io/docs/get-started) to extract key-value pairs

### Import

- Use the data feed files to import into the data warehouse
- Import the data feed files using the CDH [ETL](https://www.cdh.io/dev/deploy-apps/etl/) functionality
- Import the data feed files using the CDH [Metrics API](https://metrics.cdh.io/docs/get-started)

### Load

- Load the data feed files using the CDH [ETL](https://www.cdh.io/dev/deploy-apps/etl/) functionality
- Load the data feed files using the CDH [Metrics API](https://metrics.cdh.io/docs/get-started)

## Decision

We have decided to use ETL functionality, specifically the data feed ETL, to pull key-value pairs from the CDH. The CDH ETL offers a means to extract data based on specific fields (based on the structure of data feed files), and also a means to transform data (for example to remove unused columns).

We have opted to use the CDH ETL because the team only have a single CDH instance, therefore sharing ETL functionality between different projects (by using the CDH ETL) is more likely to succeed. Using the CDH ETL makes our dependency on the CDH both more obvious and more brittle, which is also a risk. We've opted for this decision to reduce the possibility of inadvertently exporting the CDH instance into AWS/Azure.

We have opted to use the CDH ETL to extract the data feed file because we wanted a simple and known-tested methodology to ensure reliability.

We have opted to use the CDH ETL to import because CDH doesn't have a simple method to import data feed files. CDH has a [Data Feed Gateway](https://github.com/cloudfoundry/data-feed-gateway) service which is an ETL which we opted to not use in preference to the CDH ETL. The reason is because the Data Feed Gateway project isn't actively maintained anymore and there's a risk that future functionality we need wouldn't be supported in the future.

We have opted to use the CDH ETL to export because this is the method that CDH support. CDH doesn't support a method to import data feed files directly using the CDH Metrics API. It's not straightforward to import the data feed using the CDH Metrics API either.

## Consequences

We have a consistent methodology for ETL that has been used in various projects within the Cloud Foundry team. It makes our dependency on the CDH both more obvious and more brittle, but it is not considered too great a risk for the data warehouse team.

Using CDH [ETL](https://www.cdh.io/dev/deploy-apps/etl/) as a method for extracting data from CDH has resulted in an additional database requirement in the form of a CDH ETL cache in AWS.

## Context

In our quest to define aggregates which are able to control their own garbage collection, we can only use one time events to achieve this. The problem was identified in [ADR 0002](0002-aggregate-lifetime-control.md)
We are now moving to a 1.0 Release and need to ensure the long life of the aggregate. 

## Decision

To ensure long life of aggregates we will:

* Aggregate lifetime will be defined using one event which can be raised for every aggregate. This is a **"LongLife"** event. This means that the aggregate must call `AggregateRoot.SetLongLife()` to enable the long life
* If the aggregate has a "LongLife" event, the event will be raised every frame and will be listened by AggregateLifecycle. If the lifecycle is active, it will be passed.
* If the AggregateLifecycle is in an inactive state and no event is registered that listens to the LongLife event, it is not activated and the aggregate will be destroyed when its lifetime ends (as defined by the "End" event)

## Consequences

Without the "LongLife" event, the 1.0 release could not be executed due to the "lifetime" function not being able to be called for the "LongLife" event. However, this solution is not perfect since we are using a *generic* interface for the "Lifetime" function that cannot be called for every "Aggregate" because they are controlled differently (due to the "Lifecycle")

## Context

One of the standard releases of the Wikibase are the release notes of the respective version.
These were initially done manually, collected and published online.

Some releases include more information about the
[revisions or changelog] than the release notes.
The official release notes, published on the release notes page, are also not
maintained in a structured, machine-readable format.

Some of the first Wikibase releases include a changelog
as a file in the repository.
These changlogs are not public and are not easily accessible.

## Decision

There are three options for how Wikibase presents the release notes to the
world.

The first would be to collect the release notes from the Wikibase release
notes page and would be stored at the mediawiki repository.
This is a simple way to implement release notes for Wikibase.

The second would be to have the changelog section in the repository.
This is a simple way to implement release notes for Wikibase and allows
additional information (such as bug fixes, etc) to be recorded along with
revisions and changes to the code.

Finally, the third is to have the changelog section in the repository and
publish release notes online from those changlogs.
This way the public can read about changes to the code and is updated
automatically by publishing of new releases.

In order to decide between the first and second,
some pros were examined for both.
Here they are listed below, with the following structure:

### [Option 1] (e.g. collecting the release notes from the Wikibase release notes page)

#### Pros
- Simple to implement.
- Allows for additional updates (such as bug fixes) to be recorded along with
changes to the code.

#### Cons
- The public has no access to the changelog.
- The changelog is not easily accessible.
- Not updated automatically by publishing of new releases.

### [Option 2] (e.g. having the changelog section in the repository)

#### Pros
- The public can read about changes to the code.
- The changelog is easily accessible.
- Updated automatically by publishing of new releases.

#### Cons
- Information about releases is not easily discoverable.
- More complex to implement.

### [Option 3] (e.g. having the changelog section in the repository and publishing release notes online from those changlogs)

#### Pros
- The public can read about changes to the code.
- The changelog is easily accessible.
- Updated automatically by publishing of new releases.

#### Cons
- More complex to implement.

## Notes

While this version of Wikibase is mostly completed in December 2018,
its features and improvements will probably continue to grow
even after the release of the first version.
Some of those will be probably not even be released.
Some improvements will be needed on the code itself:
- The code is usually in a development branch (e.g. `master`) and when
a release is prepared, this branch should be cut to a release branch (e.g. `4.0-rc.5`).
- As the code of a Wikibase is very large,
the release notes should be stored in the repository for long term maintenance,
so some code for storing the release notes is needed
(e.g. the current code used for this task in the [Wikibase Release notes backlog extension],
but there's a need to improve this extension).
- When the changlogs are part of the Wikibase code,

There are different options to store the release notes for Wikibase and their
corresponding implementation.

### Choosing a tool to collect release notes
If we use the first option,
there is a need to choose a tool to collect the release notes.
This can be done either (a) using the [Wikibase Release notes backlog extension],

- If we chose (b),

## Context

Previously, we tracked metrics for a single Content Item by using the Content Item's ID as the key. This made sense while our initial content modeling was still relatively simple, where each content model had a single point-in-time content history associated with it.

However, as we began exporting content history for items that had multiple revisions (e.g. Guides, Travel Advice, Travel Advice Scotland) and also as we began using a shared "content repository" to keep content history data (not just the live content), this approach became unwieldy. If one content item had a history in either Content Item (e.g. Guides), then it was not possible to collect metrics for the entire content history.

## Decision

To address these concerns, we decided to use the basepath of a content item as its primary key for metrics. This approach has two benefits:

- We can collect the metrics associated with a content item's entire history by aggregating up the basepaths of all of the items under that content item. This is accomplished by using our "search" endpoint and the `withBasePath` and `orderBy` query parameters to collect search results by basepath.
- We can also do a "split by" analysis at the basepath level, allowing for an aggregation of data for the entire content history.

This approach does result in a loss of some individual-level metrics, such as the percentage of pageviews that come from a particular region and the last-viewed page on a particular basepath. However, these metrics are less important to our overall goals and we believe they can be re-instilled in future iterations of the project, if necessary.

## Consequence

By using the basepath of a content item as its primary key for metrics, it is possible to collect metrics for the entire content history. Furthermore, this approach allows us to collect data at the basepath level, allowing us to be able to perform aggregation at the basepath level.

This approach does result in a loss of some individual-level metrics. However, these metrics are likely not critical to the project's overall goals and can be re-instilled in future iterations.

## Status

Accepted

## Context

Whilst AWS VPC networking is well understood the best way to configure the networking within the VPC
is not necessarily clear.

## Decisions

AWS recommend splitting the network into 2 separate VPCs. These are:

- Public Subnet - Allows ingress from the outside world.
- Private Subnet - Allows ingress from within the VPC only.

Whilst there are several benefits from this recommendation it is not clear why separating the 2
networks should be undertaken. AWS do not mention a reason for this in their documentation
but it is possible to split 2 different networks based on the concept of a subnet mask.

In this example we can treat the 2 subnets as:

- Private Subnet: 10.0.0.0/18 (single network / subnet)
- Public Subnet: 10.0.255.0/16 (single network / subnet)

There are several benefits from this approach. The most important of these is to have
more flexibility to assign IP addresses without having to be concerned about potential
conflicts with the address ranges used for private networks.

There is a concern that the VPC would be less flexible if there was no single subnet (as the
concept of subnet is synonymous with a single IP address range) within the VPC. The VPC could
still allow more flexibility using CIDRs for assigning subnet ranges but it would not provide
the flexibility of subnet.

## Consequences

Whilst a VPC with multiple subnets can be simpler to understand as it is split into 2 separate 
networks it can also be harder to understand as we don't necessarily have a clear concept of how the 
subnets are related.

### 0. Record definitions

In [ADR-0002](0002-record-definitions.md) it was agreed that all data entities
will be separated into records.

Currently there are three types of records.

#### 1. System records

System records store system specific data, such as user, roles and the
corresponding permissions.

#### 2. Service records

Service records store service specific data, such as patients, families and
medical-services.

#### 3. Data records

Data records are the raw data which constitute services, such as blood
pressures, heart-beats and the corresponding users of these services.

### 1. Data model

Currently there are two concepts in our data model.

#### 1. Data container

A data container is a collection of records for one specific type of data, e.g. the patients
in the patient data container.

#### 2. Data instance

A data instance is a copy of a record and is created per data container. There are 
two options when creating a data instance:

- A. all instances of a particular record type are created using the same
  unique identifier (e.g. users of data containers can identify themselves via their
  unique identifier)
- B. each instance of a particular record type gets an unique identifier (e.g.
  each patient has a unique ID which is different from every other patient ID)

In the case of data containers we allow both A and B. If an instance is not created
using the unique identifier the first time it is created, this should have the consequence
that the data container must be created using a unique identifier.

With services and data there is a similar situation.

### 2. Database

Currently there are two services related to the data:

- 1. patient-db which can store each data instance (either patient or user)
- 2. medical-service-db which can store each data instance (either service or user)

### 3. Access

Currently only the services can access the data records.

Create a common records layer.

#### 1. Database

With this in mind we can remove the `patient-db` service from the stack. A new

#### 2. Logic

There should be a common records service for all services that store common
records. This should provide the following methods:

- create common record
- get common record by ID
- update common record

instance of a data record storing common records. This will ensure common
records will exist even if they have not been accessed.

Data containers can be accessed directly by the data records.

const data = context.data
```

It's not hard to update props, but it's hard to get data from props because it's nested and they use different APIs.

Using `context` means that the `props` API was only used for creating the data structure.
The state and data data structures were created using `state` and `data`, which API, respectively.
It's possible to change this code and use props to store state and data, but it has consequences for the way that the code is written and consumed.

For example, you can't use this code to store data outside of the component.
We have a variety of different use cases for storing data, and all of them can be implemented using the context API.
The use cases include:

- the data structure of the component
- the application data (e.g. in a UI)

In these cases, data must be stored outside of the component.
If a data structure is part of the component, then it's inside of the component.
The use of props means that some data must be stored outside of the component, which will make it harder to understand how the different data structures are stored.

We know that we don't need to store data as a data structure inside of the component, so we can just do something like this:

```
const props = context.props
const state = context.state
const data = context.data
```

And then we can use `props` to create the data structure, and use context to get that data structure from other data.

This data structure must be used for other data, e.g. in a UI.

Since this is a data structure outside of the component, then it should be stored like this:

```
const props = context.props
const state = context.state
const data = context.data
```

That will allow us to access that data in other data structures.

Then we can use a number of different methods to get data:

- `get_data`: the method that you use to get data from context, to get the data and context data
- `get_state`: the method that you use to get the state structure from the context
- `get_props`: the method that you use to get the props structure from context.
  It takes a state and returns a data structure

The method for getting data can change, but there would still be a method that gets the state data.

This means that you can't update the props data structure, but you can get that data from the context.

The reason why we do this is that the props API was created to allow us to make the data structure outside of the component.
So the method for getting data changes, but a method for getting the data is still available.

## Decision

We will do like this:

```
const props = context.props
const state = context.state
const data = context.data
```

## Status

Accepted

## Consequences

- The API is different than before.
- It will be harder for new developers to understand how the different data structures are stored.
- Props is a data structure that we access data from.
- We can't use the data structure from props for anything else
- It will be easier to understand how data is stored in the component
- Props data structures will be created using context APIs
- The API that stores the data structure is the `context` API
```
