# 8. Use npm to host HEE frontend framework

Date: 2020-04-05

## Status

Accepted

## Context

Previously to work on HEE Frontend we would start off from scratch, with a folder full of files for each folder of API. Once we finished the API there was no framework in place to generate the static front end, so we had to hand roll each of those folders from scratch for every service. This became laborious and error prone.

We came across [npm-react-boilerplate](https://github.com/prose/npm-react-boilerplate) which offers a way to package up a "vanilla" React project to allow us to publish it. We took this approach and built [HEE-frontend-boilerplate](https://github.com/NHS-digital/heef-frontend-boilerplate) which offers a set of conventions for HEE apps.

## Decision

In HEE-frontend-boilerplate we will define HEE frontend conventions, and use npm to package it up as a framework, the name of the package being `npm-react-boilerplate-ui`

The repository will continue to hold the template and example project for our "vanilla" React project.

When we work on the HEE frontend we will create a new branch and publish the framework under `npm-react-boilerplate-ui` publishing notes to describe how we will use the framework in our code

Once a decision has been made for how we will use the framework we will add a step to add the framework to HEE-frontend-boilerplate in the form of a folder structure change that copies 30 files from npm-react-boilerplate-ui and places them at the root `src/` folder.

Alternatively we could add the framework in the form of a plugin.

## Consequences

Once we have a consistent set of conventions and a framework in place, then we'll only need to develop a set of templates for each one of our services, and test and deploy the code from there.

We will need to use npm for this package, allowing people to depend on it and use it in their projects. We're not as comfortable with this as we are with the local npm that we use during the development process, however it is also the package that would be used by any team using this library in production.

We will be able to version the project, allowing us to version the code used for each version of the service.

Once we have agreed a methodology for using the framework and added it to HEE-frontend-boilerplate we will need to remember to remove the framework when we're done with it, once the example project exists and can be used to describe using the framework, and once the templates have been generated from the example project template.

There is a need to document how to use the framework, such as using the npm command to install it.

Accepted

## Context

The tool will be collecting time series data in form of measurements over time. We need to be able to analyze that data and perform real time analysis. Time series database will provide an efficient solution for storing and querying time series data.

## Decision

We will be using [InfluxDB](https://www.influxdb.com/) for storing time series data.

InfluxDB is one of the fastest and most scalable open source time series databases. It is easy to integrate with many tools like Node.js, Python, and Go.

## Consequences

InfluxDB will be the main storage for all time series data collected by the tool. Data will be organized under measurement category and time series data can be accessed efficiently through queries. The data model for InfluxDB is a series of time intervals, so timestamps need to be provided when storing data in InfluxDB.

In order to provide a more flexible solution for data retrieval, and to allow for more custom metrics, measurements can have a tags as additional attributes. Each measurement will have a unique ID and tags will be assigned to the measurement when they are created.
InfluxDB can ingest data from many sources, and we should aim to connect as many sources as possible. It is possible to insert data manually, or by importing it from a file. InfluxDB can be run in single-node or multi-node configuration to increase performance and provide failover solution. We should consider setting up a cluster if load increases.

## Status

## Context

## Decision

### Context

We previously went with an approach where we decided on a new migration version and started creating a new version and merge migration.
We decided on the oldest split for a new version and used it to create the new version.
The approach we decided upon [does not support testing of the new code](https://www.wellington.gov.uk/en/knowledge/how/business-process/using-scripts-for-work)

As part of this process, we decided to retire a split before merging it:

*https://github.com/Wellington-TA-Cloud/tech-ops/blob/79a7244d57f3c11f8dcb531c6b4d2c79e76e8c/Wellington.Services.Code/TechOps/Migrations/Delete.SplitMigration.gsp#L83*

That approach was decided upon:
*https://www.wellington.gov.uk/en/knowledge/how/business-process/using-scripts-for-work*

This approach has some drawbacks:
*https://www.wellington.gov.uk/en/knowledge/how/business-process/using-scripts-for-work#do-you-have-a-different-plan-in-store-if-you-don-t-actually-need-to-implement-a-new-version*

- In the event that we decide that we need to go back to the old migration plan, we will need to create a new version
- The only way to achieve this is to delete the old code and write the new version
- It will be difficult to decide which parts of the code belong to the old and new versions
- The only way to ensure that there is no overlap between the old and new code is to delete and recreate the code
- The only way to test the new code is to use our existing tests, but these tests are also run for the old version so we would have to make sure that the old tests do not interfere with the tests for the new version

We’ve previously decided that we should try to keep the tests for any new version as similar as possible to the old tests, but the tests will be out-of-date and run on old code, so there's some risk that if someone did use the new test code without being up-to-date with what had changed, they might not detect the bugs that would have been caught by the old test code.
There's also some risk that the bug might appear in some unexpected way without the feature being added. We will have to find some way to mitigate this, for example, by including a test note when we run the test to remind us that the feature did not appear where we expected it to.

### Decision

To delete old migrate version and make a new version, merge the new and old code together in a git merge.

### Status

Implemented

### Consequences

- We need to delete the old code
- We need to merge the new and old code together
- We need to remove the old version of the test plan before merging the code
- We need to make a new test plan for the new migration version and merge tests with the old tests in a git merge
- We need to delete the old tests before merging the code
- It will be easy to create a new feature and it will be easy for someone using the new version to implement it
- Feature code will be merge with the old migration code
- There's a risk that feature code is added to the old migration codebase instead of the new
- It will be easy to test feature code using the old test data
- There's some risk that feature code is used with a different feature scenario than intended
- The old feature code will be used in tests, but the new feature code will also be present in tests
- There's a risk that feature code is added to the old migration codebase instead of the new
- The feature code will be stored in the old migration repository as well as the new one

The application's user base should be restricted to a certain group (e.g. the Ministry of Justice staff or other government employees, depending on the project's scope).

Authentication and access control mechanisms ensure that the right people can access specific data and functionalities within the application.

In the UK, GOV.UK uses a bespoke authentication system called GOV.UK Sign In (G-Sign In). It is not expected that government projects should use this authentication system, instead, it is preferable to use one that is consistent across digital government services.

An alternative authentication scheme to GOV.UK Sign In is DfE's Single Sign In service, which supports authentication using existing logins (e.g. Google, Microsoft).

## Decision

The application will be provided with a single sign in service using DfE's Single Sign In service. This will support authentication using existing UK government service logins.

This decision will remove the need to develop and implement our own authentication scheme and make it easier to manage access control for the application.

## Consequences

The application will allow only a limited group of people (e.g. the Ministry of Justice staff or other government employees, depending on the project's scope) to access it. This will ensure that access to the application is controlled and restricted for the right people.

The authentication service should offer a mechanism for changing passwords should passwords need to be changed. The SSO service should also have a mechanism for account recovery in the case that passwords need to be forgotten.

Any data that the application processes or stores must be retained by the SSO service in line with its privacy and security policies.

The application will be capable of removing access to a particular user at any point in time.

Access to the application's data and functionalities will be controlled using the SSO service's access control model.

## Status

Accepted

## Context

We're making several changes related to cryptography:

* Switch from [cryptographically signed headers](https://github.com/tendermint/tendermint/blob/78fa44d599a27e44c9f7713e946f48e8e8f9578/config/genesis_block.toml#L10) to _un_signed headers (`genesis_block.toml`).
  The genesis block message and headers no longer need to be cryptographically signed by Tendermint itself.
  Tendermint still _proposes_ the headers, but the final validator set (aka final state) remains un-signed.
* Switch from [cryptographically signed tags](https://github.com/tendermint/tendermint/blob/78fa44d599a27e44c9f7713e946f48e8e8f9578/config/state_machine_genesis.toml#L3) to _unsigned_ tags, and allow users to add arbitrary information to tags, such as the order in which to apply them.
* Switch from [cryptographically signed checkpoints](https://github.com/tendermint/tendermint/blob/78fa44d599a27e44c9f7713e946f48e8e8f9578/config/state_machine_genesis.toml#L28) to _unsigned_ checkpoints, and allow users to add arbitrary information to them (e.g., a link to the corresponding finalized state).
* Switch from cryptographically signed messages to _unsigned_ messages.

### Why Switch?

We're switching back from cryptographically signed tags and messages for several reasons:

* This brings us closer to [following the [BFT consensus protocol](https://github.com/tendermint/tendermint/blob/58f8749e349080a8977d727e45278143627b55b/consensus/bft_consensus_parameters.toml).
* Tags and messages were originally cryptographically signed for the following reasons:
  * Tags: enforce sequential execution in the consensus layer.
  * Messages: ensure messages follow the execution of a block in the consensus layer.
* Tags and messages had other problems too (which we will also fix):
  * Tendermint cannot build tags and messages when it makes a new proposal in `BeginBlock`, even though it can propose the block in its entirety.
  * Tags and messages live alongside the headers, where they do not need to be; this makes it more confusing to users.
  * Users cannot specify custom tags and messages.

### What's _not_ Changing

* We're *not* changing how long it takes to reach consensus.
* We're *not* changing the commitment graph logic.
* We're *not* removing checkpoints entirely.

## Decisions

* Switch from cryptographically signed headers to _un_signed headers (`genesis_block.toml`)
* Switch from cryptographically signed tags to _unsigned_ tags, and allow users to add arbitrary information to tags, such as the order in which to apply them.
* Switch from cryptographically signed messages to _unsigned_ messages.
* Switch from cryptographically signed checkpoints to _unsigned_ checkpoints, and allow users to add arbitrary information to them (e.g., a link to the corresponding finalized state).

## Consequences

### Positive

* We're bringing our crypto practices in line with the BFT consensus protocol.
* We're simplifying our process for creating tags and messages.
* We're opening up the possibility for users to define custom tags and messages, which would allow, for example, the consensus layer to specify its own ordering of tags (in order of application).

### Negative

* Tags will now be applied in the consensus layer without cryptographic enforcement of their order.  There is some risk of inconsistent ordering, which would need to be addressed by other means (e.g., tags should follow a linear fashion).

### Neutral

* Checkpoints will now be made in the consensus layer without

Date: 2017-07-25

## Status

Accepted

## Context

A service life-cycle consists of several phases, beginning with deployment and ending with removal from service. Each phase can be represented as a state in the life-cycle model used by the service. The state transitions from a previous state only under certain conditions known as phase changes.

There are three types of life-cycle phase changes:

- Automatic phase changes
  These changes happen at a predetermined point or interval, based on state-defined events (e.g. reaching a deployment number).
  They are detected by a lifecycle manager.
- Deployable phase changes
  These changes happen when the user performs a specific action (e.g. applying a release label).
  The action is executed by a lifecycle manager.
- Incurable phase changes
  These changes happen when the user performs a specific action (e.g. changing a deployment number), however a deployable phase change
  has been performed previously.
  The action is executed by a lifecycle manager.

Phase changes are executed by lifecycle managers, which maintain state of the life-cycle in their memory and perform the lifecycle steps at the given point. There can be several lifecycle managers. 

Managing services life-cycle requires the lifecycle managers to track the life-cycle state in memory and to be able to decide which phases have been performed, by which lifecycle manager. The lifecycle state must be available to the clients as well in a distributed environment. 

## Decision

A *service-life-cycle-manager* class shall manage lifecycle of a service.

A *service-life-cycle* class shall represent service life-cycle.

A *service-life-cycle-state* class shall be the used state in the life-cycle.

A *deployment-number* class shall be the used phase change to increment deployment number. 

### *service-life-cycle-manager*

A *service-life-cycle-manager* provides a *ServiceLifeCycle* for the *Service* and manages the *ServiceLifeCycle*.

- It shall be executed on a lifecycle server.
- It shall store the entire history of the lifecycle in its memory, maintaining the information as long as the service (and the life-cycle) exists.
- It shall apply all phase changes to the service.
- It shall report state changes for each performed phase change.

### *service-life-cycle*

A *service-life-cycle* is the state on a lifecycle server at a particular time. A *Service* can have one active *ServiceLifeCycle* at a time.

The state of the lifecycle server can be used to retrieve the service's state.

### *service-life-cycle-state*

A *service-life-cycle-state* represents a single phase of a service's life-cycle. A single state can be applied by one instance.

A *Service* can have several states for different types of phase changes. 

### *deployment-number*

A *deployment-number* class shall represent a number of deployments (as used by the deployment number phase change) and be passed to the *release* class.

There might exist a *service-based-test-plan* with state changes based on deployment numbers (the release/service number of the phase change).

## Consequences

The deployment of lifecycle management services requires the ability to store information about all phase changes (and hence all *service-life-cycle-states*). 

This requires the ability to store both *automatic* and *deployable* phase changes.

The service's state at any time is updated to *service-life-cycle-state* on the next state change (this will be implemented by the *service-life-cycle-manager*).

If any *service-life-cycle-manager* is killed/is no longer functional, the stored information must be used to reconstruct the service life-cycle.

## Links

This ADR is related to the decision for a single lifecycle manager per service life-cycle in [ADR 0027](0027-single-lifecycle-manager.md).

Date: 2019-06-05

## Status

Accepted

## Context

As part of the Workday service we are building we will have 8 application containers and an API.

Currently we know how to deploy application containers to Kubernetes but we are unclear on how to manage and configure the APIs as we have some specific configuration requirements based on AWS credentials and Google Project ID.

In researching available Kubernetes solutions for managing APIs we came across the following candidates:

- [Helm](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/helm)
- [Terraform](https://www.terraform.io/)
- [Kustomize](https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/manage-kubernetes-objects/kustomization/)

Below is the notes from our investigation into these solutions.

### 1. Helm

As part of our investigation into serving Kubernetes managed containers we investigated using [Helm](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/helm) to provide a simple way to describe and install Kubernetes applications. Helm provides a [package manager](https://helm.sh/docs/getting_started/#package_manager) for Kubernetes applications.

Pros:

- It would allow us to create a repeatable process for installing our API based on the community standard.
- We could easily make API configuration available as part of the [chart definition](https://helm.sh/docs/helm_chart_repository/#chart-repository).

Cons:

- Since there are some complexities around the [installation of Helm chart dependencies](https://helm.sh/docs/helm_chart_repository/#dependencies) it could be difficult for us to manage Helm charts.
- Since Helm charts are essentially containers we would need to replicate or write a [Helm chart](https://helm.sh/docs/helm_chart_repository/#chart-repository) based on Terraform configuration.

### 2. Terraform

[Terraform](https://www.terraform.io/) is an infrastructure-as-a-service (IaaS) platform that enables provisioning and management of cloud-based infrastructure. It allows us to configure the underlying infrastructure required to build an application and can be used to build infrastructure based on cloud provider APIs.

Pros:

- Allows for a repeatable process for installing the APIs we are building.
- We can manage all dependencies for our API and application containers within Terraform.

Cons:

- Our API is not a standard application and it is [not possible to create a Terraform module](https://www.terraform.io/docs/modules/#module-modules-language-overview) based on it. We would therefore have to replicate our API for Terraform use.

### 3. Kustomize

[Kustomize](https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/manage-kubernetes-objects/kustomization/) provides an easy way to overlay and merge files for use in [the Templating Language](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/tasks/manage-kubernetes-objects/#the-templating-language). This is used in conjunction with [Helm](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/helm).

Pros:

- Allows for a repeatable process for installing the APIs we are building.
- Helm can be extended to use the Templating Language. We could create custom values that would be used in the Helm chart definition.

Cons:

- The Templating Language isn't clear or intuitive and the API that we are building is unlikely to use it.

## Decision

We will use Helm and Kustomize as we can provide a repeatable process for installing the APIs we are building and are the community standards for managing the APIs we are building.

## Consequences

We will need to learn more about how to create a Helm chart as well as how to configure it.

As we will need to store our Helm definition in [a repository](https://helm.sh/docs/helm_chart_repository/#charts-repository) we will need to manage this like we would manage source code in version control.

As mentioned by Helm in the community [they are working on implementing new versions of Helm for Linux distributions](https://lists.kubernetes.org/g/kubernetes-dev/topic/98527772#9376) that would allow us to define Helm charts using language.

about those actions to the player.

We would like to use the most uniform interface possible in managing the process.
Thus, we would like to use a similar interface to the UI, in managing actions,
that we use in managing the player characters.

This proposal is that we will use a command pattern for all actions and outcomes
of the game, so that those can be communicated from the game to the UI, in
the format 'command - outcome'.

## Considered Alternatives

* Give the player and creatures the same command/control infrastructure
* Use similar infrastructure to the UI, in managing actions and outcomes

## Decision Outcome

* Chosen Alternative: Use similar infrastructure to the UI, in managing actions
and outcomes, because we would like to develop the game using a similar approach
to the UI, in the area of the display and communication of the player.

### Positive Consequences

* We can reuse much of the infrastructure of the UI
* The UI and player controller have already been set up, so this can be implemented
relatively quickly

### Negative Consequences

* Actions and outcomes now have two 'contexts'
* We have to keep track of when we are using actions and when we are using outcomes

## Pros and Cons of the Alternatives

### Give the player and creatures the same command/control infrastructure

This would allow the player to call a `createCommandInterface` function and
receive a similar `commandInterface` as the UI.

This would allow the player to call a function that would result in a `gameAction`
being run by the game.

We already have a `createCommandInterface` function implemented in the `playerController`.
This is responsible for instantiating an `actionInterface`, which provides the
function `runCommand`, which can run a `gameAction`.

This does introduce two 'contexts' when we are implementing the actions.
One with the UI, and one with the player controller.
This would allow us to reuse the existing UI `actionInterface` object in the
`actionController`.

This does mean we have to keep track of which interface is responsible for giving
the game an action, or action outcome.
It would be easier to know that if we had 'contexts' for each action.

This would allow us to reuse large amounts of the UI infrastructure.

We would not have to reimplement anything.
Instead, we would just be adapting it to the context of the game.

### Use similar infrastructure to the UI, in managing actions and outcomes

We have already found that the controller of the UI uses a function `observeCommand`,
which subscribes to a list of `gameActions`.

We have already found that the player controller uses a function `runCommand`,
which is invoked for every `gameAction`.

This will allow us to reuse `runCommand` from the player controller in the
`actionController`, allowing for an easier implementation of the `command` interface.

We have to keep track of whether the action interface `runCommand` is sending an
action to the UI, or an outcome to the UI.
It's not very obvious when it's sending an action.

We do not get the benefit of being able to reuse the UI infrastructure.
Instead, we have to reimplement the UI infrastructure.

## Context

Choosing a dependency manager and build system is one of the first decisions you make when starting a new project.

### Option 1: gradle

**Pros**

- It's been on the market for quite some time, which means more plugins and documentation are available
- It's the default that other projects are using and the way people learn about the way the build system works
- Gradle scripts are easier to understand than groovy and can be run with maven and GAV

**Cons**

- Gradle is a long class with thousands of lines of code that must be maintained and updated
- It can be challenging to use the flexibility without also falling into the common pitfalls
- Gradle scripts are easy to write but difficult to debug and understand if not written in a specific, consistent style

### Option 2: Maven

**Pros**

- It's been used by the OSS community for quite some time
- Maven is the standard in the Java world that people might use to organize their projects
- Writing maven dependencies is the way people are familiar with in the Java world
- It can be easy to debug and understand the code if written in a specific, consistent style

**Cons**

- Writing maven dependencies is the way people are familiar with the Java world. It's a 3rd party dependency with plugins and is usually used in the OSS world.
- The build system is usually used for assembling the project into an artifact with a special build and version number.
- Writing Maven rules can be difficult to understand without the right knowledge and tools

### Option 3: Leiningen

**Pros**

- It's a fully 3rd party build system
- It's fast, easy to understand and have full build control and automation over the whole build process

**Cons**

- Leiningen has not been widely used by the OSS community
- The Java development team needs to learn another build system
- Leiningen relies on a different runtime, which will cause our users to have to install Leiningen Runtime
- There's not yet an official artifact layout of the Leiningen Runtime to be able to make statements about the stability of the build and dependencies

## Decision

We will use Maven as a build system and dependency manager since:

- It's widely used by other projects in this field
- It's easier to understand than Gradle due to its dependency organization and XML structure
- It is more stable since it's been used for a long time and is used in the OSS world by established corporations

The OSS Java team is comfortable using Maven already so no training is needed.

## Consequences

Using maven means we have to get used to writing maven dependencies, however, we have a lot of resources and examples and it's not hard to get used to it.

Writing in maven means that we have to write XML. This is not a problem because it's not hard to understand and debug if written in a specific, consistent style.

If we do everything in the best case scenario, we have to maintain every aspect of the build system ourselves.

## Context

An existing problem with the database was discovered during testing of
`create_task_list` which was to rename a column in the data tables. The
database was not in a transactional state at the time that the query was
running and the existing structure of the ID field was causing problems.

ID fields are already self-normalized because of the need for unique keys but
are not fully normalized either due to their long-term storage and inherent
behavior. This is evidenced by the fact that the ID field is a text field even
though its contents follow the numeric ID paradigm:
1. The field has no data-types associated with it
2. It can store arbitrary characters, which might include non-numeric
   characters
3. The numeric ID paradigm is represented by only the first n digits

As a result, long-term storage becomes a pain, because if there's a need to
rename or update an ID field, there's a need to add the new ID value to the
existing data records as well as all subsequent data records. This is because
a data record's long-term storage is not simply a collection of data
that's been saved in time; rather, it's an entire record that's been stored
continuously as a unit for a specific amount of time. If a data record is
updated, that record has multiple copies in storage.

In the original case, the ID field was set up as a `text` field in the MySQL
database. In this case, when the query to rename the column was run, it was
impossible to simply rename the column because an existing value was stored in
the text field. Although it was feasible to run a new query to generate the
unique list of IDs, a query that was run for a data record that had multiple
records in storage at the time that the query was run.

The issue was discovered that we didn't have a mechanism for determining
the ID of a data record in a transactional state. This is a key piece of
information that's needed to fix this issue, because once we have a way of
determining the ID of a data record in a transactional state, then we can
simply rename the ID field for the data table and the ID column will reflect
a data record ID that is no longer active.

So the goal is to find a mechanism that we can use to identify data record
IDs that are in a transactional state. There are some existing constraints for
this, since no database can be updated without state-saving.

## Decision

To decide how to accomplish the above goal, we first need to find some
way of storing the ID value on the data record that exists throughout its
life cycle. That way, we can determine the ID value based on that record's
ongoing storage.

Ideally, this will involve some kind of storage versioning system. A
database versioning system would have a series of points in time for a
particular record where a snapshot of the record's data was saved.

In this case, we will define an ongoing data record ID history in the
database with a number of snapshots (rows) associated with each record.
Each row will contain the ID value and the associated storage time and date
which is either the creation date of the data record or the last updated date
of the data record. This ensures that there's an ongoing record ID history for
every data record.

When the database is running in transaction mode, the table should be
updating its own version control record in time. If the data record's
record ID history is updated, the data record's ID value will reflect the
most recent ID value in the data record history.

Once we define the ongoing data record ID history, we will be able to determine
a data record ID in a transactional state by selecting a row from the
record history table where the data record ID is the same as the ID
value stored in the existing ID field of the data table.

## Consequences

It will be necessary to add a history table to all records that have
ongoing record ID histories. All data record ID histories that aren't
historical will have the same format, which will have the following structure:
1. The ID value
2. The storage date of the ID value
3. A binary field that stores the state of the ID value

The "state" binary field should be used to determine whether a data record ID
is historical or active. If the "state" field is an integer greater than 0,
then the ID value is active. If the "state" field is an integer less than 0

* Ease of use
* Flexibility

* Don't specify version in GET request

Example: `GET /people/v2.0.0/search`

* Good, because this matches pattern.

* Bad, because it's hard to change things without introducing backwards-incompatibility.

* Good, because it provides a pattern for service providers to implement.
* Bad, because it's inconsistent with other endpoints on the API.

## Context
The "Configuration" repo contains configuration settings for the entire infrastructure and deployment pipeline. It is normally
read-only, but in some circumstances it requires writing changes.

Most of the Configuration-related PR's are very small, and they are aimed at fixing some minor thing such as a typo
in one of the configuration keys. This is not the best way of having a long-term history of configuration changes.

Although not all Configuration repo changes are PR's (e.g., the release notes), all Configuration repo changes follow
the same format. With this in mind, it is not hard to imagine that some configuration changes need to be implemented
immediately in production rather than at the next release.

Configuration changes usually cover multiple directories in the configuration repo, and they also commonly require
reapplying the old values when updating other directories. This is commonly referred to as "cherry-picking" and
is typically applied in one or more places in the configuration repo. This makes it impossible to reliably
read the history of changes with the old values being replaced by new values when cherry-picking changes in
the configuration.

To enable fast and easy cherry-picking, the configuration repo should have a build artifact and a changelog history.

## Decision
The configuration repo will be enabled with build artifacts and changelog history.

## Consequences
To implement this ADR it will be necessary to do the following:
- Create the [changelog history](../0012-adding-the-changelog.md) for the configuration repo.
- Build artifacts ([GitHub Actions](https://github.com/devops-engineering-at-gov-uk/pipeline-lock/issues/156#issuecomment-760619220)).

## Related Decisions
### Creating a Changelog History
To ensure the configuration repo has a changelog history, [an Angular CLI plugin](https://github.com/drGrove/change-log)
has been developed. To add a changelog to the configuration repo, it should be available as a GitHub repository
and have build artifacts that are then pushed to the GitHub releases and npm artifacts.

### Building the Artifacts
To build artifacts from the configuration repo, [a CircleCI](https://circleci.com/) based job is available.

## Status

Accepted

## Context

When you make a change to a test, but that test fails the build because there is an assertion failure. Then you could choose to either make the test fail again, or accept the test failure and keep the build.

However, when you make a change to a test, but it doesn't fail the build. Then you could choose to either fix the test so it passes again, or add a new assert, like this:

```
Assert.True("Here be assertion that fails when the app runs, but passes when you test the code. See https://www.asp.net/topic/aspnet/understanding/testing/xunit?hl=en-us")
```

But when you make the test fail again and the build fails, then the assertion will fail as if it was always there:

```
// Here be assertion that always fails.
```

## Decision

Add a second assertion that always fails.

This allows you to have the code be executed during development. However, if something goes wrong and your code fails, your build will break, ensuring that you can find the bug.

If this becomes tedious, then you can add another assert, that always fails and add a `return` statement after that.

This is similar to how Xunit's [runnable tests](https://www.xunit.net/blog/2011/xunit-2-testing-runnable-tests) are
constructed.

## Consequences

Builds fail when the assertion fails.

Tests pass if they can execute without failure.

# Use a naming convention for git branches

Date: 2020-10-09

## Status

Accepted

## Context

We want to have a standard for naming our git branches, so that we can quickly identify branches in build logs, PRs, or documentation. The following rules apply to all new git branches that use naming scheme from the first bullet point of the accepted answer to the following <a href="https://stackoverflow.com/questions/42022291/standard-for-naming-git-branches/42029491#42029491">accepted answer on Stack Overflow (October 2020 edition). 

## Decision

We will use a modified version of the following naming scheme for branches in the Clojure repository:

* <`master`> - <`task` | `question` | <`task ID>`
* <`task` | `question` | <`task ID`> - <`feature`>
* <`feature`> - <`task` | `question` | <`task ID>`
* <`feature`> - <`task` | `question` | <`task ID`> - <`question ID`>

Note that `master` is no longer "master" as this designation was assigned to a feature. See <https://docs.google.com/document/d/1J9_5XwFhIcj_H64dK9Vmqx9gP0xJvmD_lNm8M-51E/edit#0F0F24F4026478753A3055AC5C6F677C77562700> for more details. 

### Naming rules

* Only lowercase and underscores are allowed in branch names

* Avoid spaces (except for underscores in task/question names)

* Use underscores in task/question names as they exist within the task/question name

## Consequences

A new naming scheme provides consistency and reduces the burden of mental work when deciding between using the `master` branch or a branch for feature work. The build logs will be easier to read, and documentation, such as READMEs, will be clearer and easier to read, especially for users unfamiliar with the project.

## Status

## Context

A component's state is the set of attributes that encapsulate its internal state for the purpose of rendering an entity. In most cases, the state can be inferred from the available attributes, if the component is stateless. A state can be explicitly defined or implicit. Components are usually either stateless or not stateless.

## Decision

We decide that:
  - components are stateless by default
  - state is explicit in the definition of the component
  - explicitly defined state is composed of entities and attributes
  - entities and attributes may be composed of further entities and attributes
  - the state is only defined once and used thereafter
  - states are encapsulated inside a component (i.e. they are private for that component)

## Consequences

The state of components can be explicitly defined. It is explicitly defined at the start of the component. It remains unchanged throughout the component's life-time, thus encapsulating a set of state variables.

State is used to store the entities and the attributes which are required for rendering the component. It does not follow the convention of creating temporary states. To avoid temporal dependency, prefer temporary states over using the component state in temporal logic.

Temporal dependency will be avoided using attributes and entities. This leads to a flat state tree, since attributes and entities are also states.

If the state is used for temporal operations (e.g. `timer`, `observer`), a change will be forced when used.

Temporal dependency can be achieved by wrapping all code to a single entity (to avoid temporal dependency).

## Decision

On the ADR, we decided to defer having examples ship until the 1.0 release of the library. The reasoning behind this decision is that it was initially thought that the examples could be used to bootstrap the library but the idea was dropped as it felt like it was making the assumption that the projects using the library already understand how to install a CLI. In hindsight, while the CLI installation documentation is very well written and the project ships with a `.gitignore` and `.npmignore` file, it felt awkward to ship examples that would have a dependency on these files for the first release of the library.

## Context

While working on the [modular-red](https://github.com/modular-red/modular-red) project, we found a need to ship CLI installation examples. The installation examples were made up of a `setup.js` and a `tests/generate-red.js` file. The `setup.js` file was supposed to be run when the library was installed and would modify the install file to add a `.gitignore` file to the projects using the library. However, the `tests/generate-red.js` file was shipped to serve as an example of what the "generated" install file would look like once it was installed with the library. However, since the `setup.js` file modifies the install file, it's not entirely clear when the example install file is "generated". We thought it was a good idea to ship the example as-is but it quickly became evident that people who wanted to install modular-red needed to run the `tests/generate-red.js` file in order for the example to be a useful example. However, the `setup.js` file must be installed in the `packages` repository in order to serve as an example to those who wish to install the library, which was problematic because it was not a `semver` package. We realized that it was not possible to have a `semver` package in the `packages` repository since the examples would need to be shipped along with the library, which would have been the main purpose of the `semver` package in the first place. Since the `setup.js` file was written in ES6, we realized that since the `semver` package was shipped along with the library, it would need to be ES5 to be consumed by the `tests/generate-red.js` file or the latter would throw exceptions when running it in a browser.

## Consequences

The lack of "install example" code for the 1.0 release is an "Anti-Pattern", as described by [Martin Fowler](https://martinfowler.com/refactoring/anti-pattern.html).

This should be revisited before the 1.0 release.

If this decision is revisited, we would need to decide between "having no install examples" or "having a barebones install example". In the original project, the package manager and the installation example are both shipped for free. Having the installation example and the `semver` package shipped together is a relatively simple and familiar pattern but can be easily broken in two ways. The first is by relying on the installation example to ship to NPM while the second is by relying on the `semver` package to ship to NPM while the third is by relying on the installation example to provide a CLI instead of the `semver` package. The choice will have a big impact on how the installation example is perceived and how the `semver` package is used when it is shipped to NPM. The `semver` package can be used to make a CLI, or a CLI-like tool that has a `--help` function with multiple steps, without the help of an installation example. In this case, it would still be a simple and familiar pattern but it is a much different pattern in and of itself, and one that we do not want.

## Context and Problem Statement

As the OpenID Pilot program grows, we will need to support an increasing number of authentication methods and sign-up flows. Google OAuth 2.0 already provides a sign-up flow and users can sign-up and sign-in to our tenant using their Google account. We needed to store a variety of additional fields about a user to support other authentication flows that we don't know about yet. Finally, Google Cloud's [Security Incident Response (SAR) team](https://docs.google.com/document/d/18HMFRI7-3-3iI6oJ2wJ7NlNmVAvAzVEm123Ue0I7O4/edit?usp=sharing) had previously [presented](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1B3a8VdArQ0e5z32hOqCzWbBMlIuN3e40L04z8O09qI/) their plans to introduce [Google Cloud Firestore](https://cloud.google.com/cloud-firestore/) as a storage solution for the OpenID Pilot program. The reason for this decision is to learn more about [Cloud Firestore](https://cloud.google.com/cloud-firestore/) and determine whether we can support our sign-up and sign-in flows using [Cloud Firestore](https://cloud.google.com/cloud-firestore/).

## Decision Drivers

* How easily can we store a variety of additional user data in Cloud Firestore?
* Is the system capable of handling a high number of documents?
* Is the system capable of supporting our sign-up and sign-in flows?

## Considered Options

1. Use MongoDB
2. Use Google Cloud Firestore
3. Use a combination of Google Cloud Firestore and MongoDB
4. Use a combination of Firebase Auth and Firestore
5. Use Firebase Auth alone

## Decision Outcome

Chosen option: "Use Firebase Auth alone", because Firebase Auth provides the sign-up and sign-in flows that we need to provide for our tenants, and we can store a variety of additional data in Firebase Auth as needed.

### Positive Consequences

* We can continue to make changes to our frontend code with minimal updates to our infrastructure.

### Negative Consequences

* The primary data fields for a user are email address, first name, and last name.
* We will still need to collect additional data in the future. It is possible that we will need to collect more data if we want to request Google APIs for the first time, since the OpenID Pilot program already accepts Google OAuth 2.0 sign-up credentials and doesn't require the user to confirm their email address.
* The user's Google account doesn't need to be set up and linked, but the OpenID Pilot tenant must be set up and linked.

## Pros and Cons of the Options

### 1. MongoDB

* Pro
  * Has been the basis for an existing tenant.
* Con
  * Doesn't provide sign-up and sign-in flows.

### 2. Google Cloud Firestore

* Pro
  * Provides sign-up and sign-in flows.
  * Provides the ability to store additional data.
* Con
  * Is a relatively new product (released in 2018).
  * Doesn't provide the ability to store additional data, but we can store additional data with [one-off migrations](https://developers.google.com/datastore/migrate-data-from-mongo-cloud-firestore#migrate-from-mongo).

### 3. Combination of Google Cloud Firestore and MongoDB

* Pro
  * Provides sign-up and sign-in flows.
  * Provides the ability to store additional data in MongoDB.
* Con
  * Complicates the infrastructure for our tenants.

### 4. Combination of Firebase Auth and Firestore

* Pro
  * Provides sign-up and sign-in flows.
  * Provides the ability to store additional data.
* Con
  * Doesn't provide the ability to store additional data if needed.

### 5. Firebase Auth alone

* Pro
  * Provides sign-up and sign-in flows.
  * Provides the ability to store additional data.
* Con
  * Can be written to as a single transaction.

## Context

By default, `\Shopware\Core\Framework\DataAbstractionLayer\Field\Flag\CacheAware` is enabled for `\Shopware\Core\Framework\DataAbstractionLayer\Field\Flag\ForceUpdate`.

The default implementation is very simple and uses a hardcoded TTL. This can be configurable on property level (in `\Shopware\Core\Framework\DataAbstractionLayer\Field\Flag\ForceUpdate` in `_after_save_callback`).
Given its simplicity, a more complex TTL can be implemented in it without a huge performance impact.

For the default implementation of `\Shopware\Core\Framework\DataAbstractionLayer\Field\Flag\ForceUpdate`, the `_after_save_callback` is invoked immediately after `save` is called.
With the implementation of this flag for `\Shopware\Core\Framework\DataAbstractionLayer\Field\Flag\CacheAware`, this is postponed to the configured (in `\Shopware\Core\Framework\DataAbstractionLayer\Field\Flag\CacheAware` in `_after_save_callback`) timeframe (in code: `cache->incrementable(CacheKeyFactory::create(string $entityId, string $propertyName));`).
Since in this case, we can implement the needed caching logic using a `CacheInterface`, the `_after_save_callback` can still be invoked immediately after `save`.

For the moment, this logic can only be implemented for single properties.
However, it would be a lot simpler to have different settings for different properties (for example, only `CacheAwarePropertyInfoStore` for `comment` and `description`?).
For this approach, a field specific configuration would be needed and the choice for the approach would have to be done already at the beginning.

### Options
1. Implement multiple `CacheAwarePropertyInfoStores` for different properties.
2. Do not implement `CacheAwarePropertyInfoStore` and make the default implementation more complex (to allow the TTL setting).
3. Implement new fields in `\Shopware\Core\Framework\DataAbstractionLayer\Field\Flag\CacheAware` for storing TTL of property groups.
4. Implement new fields in `\Shopware\Core\Framework\DataAbstractionLayer\Field\Flag\CacheAware` for storing TTL of single properties.

## Decision

We decided to implement multiple `CacheAwarePropertyInfoStores` for different properties, because it would be a lot of effort for us to introduce an additional field in `\Shopware\Core\Framework\DataAbstractionLayer\Field\Flag\CacheAware`.

## Consequences

### Pros
- can implement caching logic easily
- implementation is clear and transparent
- no field specific configuration would be needed

### Cons
- there will be multiple implementations, which makes the code a bit more complex

# 9. Support links between ADRs inside an ADR

Date: 2021-Jan-09

## Status

Accepted

## Context

The decision record template can mention other ADRs to show how this decision builds on prior work.
For example, the decision record for ADR 0004 might refer to ADR 0003 in its text by number alone,
rather than providing the full link with the title (e.g., "as discussed in [ADR 0003](https://github.com/se-dataman/docs/blob/main/adr/0003-build-decision-records.md).

## Decision

Support this link generation by using the following format for the ADR link:

```
https://github.com/se-dataman/docs/blob/main/adr/{decision-record-number}-{decision-record-title}.md
```

To replace `{decision-record-number}` and `{decision-record-title}` with the relevant ADR number and title,
the decision record template will be passed to a utility function, which returns the correct link.
Passing such a function to the template makes it possible for users of the template to rely on a standard format,
even though the template itself is not considered.

## Consequences

For users of the decision record template, it is possible for an incorrect link to have been provided (in case of a typo in the decision record title),
whereas the template still receives the correct value when used with other template types.

Users can reliably expect links to work when used with the template.

## Status

## Context

Part of the core infrastructure of the Digital Business Platform
is the Rails Event Store, built on top of the [Goose](https://github.com/joelparkerhenderson/go-seperate-services) framework. This ADR serves to
document a [proposed](https://github.com/OpenFairDB/open_fair_db_events) new way to track the
[list of events](https://docs.oasis-open.org/raml/raml-glossary/core-glossary#GlossaryEvent)
that occur
in the system.

Since in the context of the Digital Business Platform the most important
events are changes to the system state (e.g. creation/update/deletion of
services), their tracking requires the use of a (sub-)database tables.

However, the current tracking of events is not efficient (each lookup
causes the whole event list to be re-read) and also does not offer
the possibility to perform more query operations on the stored event list
beyond simple checking for events of a specific type.

In general, the data stored for an event contains:

- the event itself (an [Event](https://github.com/OpenFairDB/open_fair_db_events/blob/1d3ab0ea6d407b79f3e37e9c6ab764c7c9f6944/event.rb) class that
contains the event-related data);
- associated metadata (used when multiple events occur for the same underlying service entity,
a [ServiceEventStore](https://github.com/OpenFairDB/open_fair_db_events/blob/1d3ab0ea6d407b79f3e37e9c6ab764c7c9f6944/service_event_store.rb) class that
contains the event ID (a [UUID](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/9.5/DDL-UUID.html)) and the timestamp
at which the event occurred);
- associated data (in the form of a [map](https://github.com/OpenFairDB/open_fair_db_events/blob/1d3ab0ea6d407b79f3e37e9c6ab764c7c9f6944/service_event.rb) that contains additional
information specific to the type of the event that occurred);

However, if we want to have more complex queries (e.g. listing of events
that occurred within a specific period), we need to store these three
types of data efficiently.

- Events of a specific type can be listed with a simple query on the
type name;
- If we want to list the events that occurred between a certain period,
we need to store the timestamps (to enable sorting) and the event IDs
(to enable listing) for all events, which would also be necessary to do
a merge query for finding the events that occurred between two periods;
- It is not possible to fetch all events at once from the event store.

If we use the existing `events` table and the `service_events` table,
the number of operations that can be performed with the stored data is quite
limited.

We want to change this situation so that more complex queries can be executed
and the system can be debugged more easily (for instance, by logging
historical events).

## Decision

We propose to create a single table that can store all the events.
For each event, there will be a field for the event type, a list of
associated timestamps, and a list of event IDs.

In an ideal case, the following table will be used:

- `table_name`: `events`
- columns: `id` (UUID), `type`, `timestamps`, `event_ids`

Note that, even though the current "event list" can be constructed from
the set of event IDs that have already occurred, we will only be able to
read the timestamps and the list of event IDs from the event store as
a whole (but not only by querying the `events` table).

This way, any query for events that have occurred in the past can be done
within the store and the query can be executed in the same fashion as
with the existing data store.

## Status

Accepted

## Context

The TESS project uses JPEG2000 as the image format for the light curves. Light curves are a series of "points" linked together by a unique ID. While the points themselves can be represented by a single JPEG2000 file, the series of points are represented by an `mfdata` file which contains the unique ID for each point. We need to create these `mfdata` files, and to create them we need to ingest all the light curves into TESS data pipeline.

## Decision

We will ingesting the light curves from the JPEG2000 files into TESS data pipeline using the `ImportLightCurve` module available within the `TESSDataPipeline` package.

This module will import the light curves from the `mfdata` file, and convert the data within the `mfdata` file into an array within the `DataPointSet`. We then convert these data points into a list of features which can be used within the visualization modules.

We will also create a `StreamId` for each `mfdata` file we import in order to support streaming large data sets in TESS.

## Consequences

There will be a new stream id per `mfdata` file that we import into TESS data pipeline. This stream id will be a large string to accommodate the long names required to comply with the TESS standard and to be short enough to reduce the amount of data loss as we parse the names.

No errors will be generated if the data within the `mfdata` file cannot be converted to the correct data type for the data points. If an error is generated, this will raise an exception that is logged, but this process will not be terminated or interrupted.

No features will be created for light curves that have been imported using the `ImportLightCurve` module, and only features relating to the imported light curves will be created.

If you want to do anything that's dependent on the order of items within an import, these operations should happen between the `createStreamId` and `importFromMFDataFile` functions.

Having researched what is the best way to give authentication to our platform, we have discovered that there are many options including:

1.  A custom Auth0 implementation
2.  Using the Auth0 Free plan with email as the identity provider
3.  A custom SAML implementation
4.  Using GitHub as the identity provider

Having read the research material, it appears that the use of custom SAML implementation is not appropriate for the use case of a microservice architecture (see links below for reference) and is considered too complex to be considered feasible.

Auth0: https://auth0.com/blog/saml-in-microservices-architecture

https://github.com/auth0/saml-microservices-architecture-project#microservices-architecture

Auth0 has two options available for email and social logins:

1.  Using a custom implementation where you add to your users, and user attributes, in to your custom Auth0 instance (e.g. GOV.UK sign in)
2.  Using a custom implementation to authenticate via an email address to a custom Auth0 instance (e.g. GOV.UK sign in)

https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-sign-in/wiki/Email-and-social-sign-in-in-GOV.UK

The first option has a number of benefits over the second option:

-   provides a higher resilience, and therefore a better user experience - this comes from using OAuth as the authentication mechanism (see links below for reference). OAuth creates a trust relationship between the service and the identity provider, therefore if the service is offline or the identity provider is unreachable, the user can still authenticate the next time they login to the service using cached data and access tokens which are stored on the service and the identity provider respectively.
-   better alignment with GOV.UK's technical approach - GOV.UK prefers to use OAuth as authentication mechanism because it is lightweight, self-service, and portable.
-   easier to change identity provider if we wish to.
-   lower maintenance cost (for Auth0) - Auth0 states that the custom login implementation is less prone to bugs and therefore lower in the number of incidents they come across.

The downside of this approach is that we need to change our user email field to include a `_oauth` before the email address (e.g. `user-name_oauth.gov.uk`).

The Auth0 Free plan would only support login to our service using email address which would only work if the user is online at the moment of login (no caching of access tokens).

We would need to set up and manage our custom implementation to authentication. This would include the following:

1.  setting up the authentication gateway in your app - this allows you to make a call to the Auth0 server instead of your custom service when a user accesses a protected endpoint
2.  setting up a custom client ID and secret
3.  setting up a custom login endpoint where users will login
4.  setting up a custom sign in page
5.  setting up a custom sign out page

https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-sign-in/wiki/Managing-a-custom-GOV.UK-sign-in-service

Auth0 has an instance, GitHub, which allows you to use GitHub as your identity provider. You use a login service called `github-oauth` which is set up in your application where users can login. There is a built-in, custom client ID which allows you to authenticate with GitHub. This client ID needs to be stored in the GOV.UK Sign In Service configuration.

https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-sign-in/wiki/Using-GitHub-as-an-identity-provider

We would need to set up and manage the authentication gateway in your app - this allows you to make a call to the Auth0 server instead of your custom service when a user accesses a protected endpoint

Auth0 has a custom implementation which can be deployed on GitHub as an Auth0 gateway. This gateway can be deployed using AWS' Elastic Application Auto Scaling (ELSS) which will be able to manage the gateway (for instance in the case of high traffic) as well as provide uptime monitoring and performance analysis.

https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-sign-in/wiki/Using-Auth0-with-GitHub

This gateway could be deployed using AWS' Elastic Load Balancer (ELB) which will provide failover in the case of high traffic. This is not self-scaling.

## Status

Accepted

## Context

At the start of this project, we chose to use a simplified version of the
Rails MVC framework, which we call Rails-Lite. Rails-Lite has made it
possible to complete this project more quickly, but has a number of notable
weaknesses.

Firstly, our data model is flat (i.e. it's just arrays of hashes), rather than
nested. This has made working with data more difficult, and has resulted in many
of our data models needing to be explicitly copied over to the front-end.

Secondly, while we can support multiple environments, including production,
we cannot add data models as needed for different environments. This has resulted
in data-specific code being duplicated across multiple environments.

Lastly, our approach to code reuse is not ideal. There are many small,
isolated pieces, which makes the code harder to follow.

## Decision

Use a 3rd party Rails MVC framework, [Thin Rails](https://github.com/jeromee/thin_rails). This application was written in Ruby 6 and is maintained by its creator,
who uses it every day. We have not reviewed our code with the framework and, as such, take the 3rd party aspect of this decision.

## Consequences

All of the above weaknesses have been eliminated by moving to a different MVC
framework. Furthermore, our API layer and front-end can share a single data model,
which makes it easier to manage, document and support.

The change to another MVC framework is largely hidden from developers, so it does not seem to have had much impact on the team. Our developers can write API clients and front-end code using existing data models, which makes the front-end development and deployment process easier.

As a result of this decision, the application is better tested, more readable, more flexible and more reusable. Overall, it is worth the effort to learn another MVC framework, especially one which has a 6-year history.

## Further Reading

* [Thin Rails](https://github.com/jeromee/thin_rails)

## Links

* [A Beginner's Guide to the 6-S Framework](http://jeromee.net/a-starter-guide-to-ruby-on-rails-6/)

Date: 2020-01-22

## Status

Accepted

## Context

Previously, content that was not English was stored in two places. This could be in the main content store, but only if it was English, or it could be in Search. If content wasn't English, it was stored in Search, where it was exposed.

Google Search results had to make requests to Search in order to view the Search Results page, Search had to parse that page in order to return data to Google Search. Search was, therefore, a dependency of Google Search.

The ability to change language, either on a search or from the Search page, was facilitated through a Search bookmarklet which was loaded on page load. The ability to search in a specific language was maintained through this bookmarklet.

## Decision

Google Search will no longer require Search to be stored in this platform. Instead the search will get the list of search results through the main content store.

## Consequences

Search will be an independent module of Google Search. This will enable us to make more changes to Search without needing to change Google Search. This will also enable Search to be hosted on Google's own servers and for our customisable Search implementation to be changed to match the new Search implementation.

Google Search will no longer need to parse the Search Results page in order to return data to Google Search. However, Google Search will still need to be able to read data from the search results. This will be achieved by [reloading the search results page](https://github.com/Google/search-results-loader) at the start of each page view. This page will then be cached for 15 seconds (one-time cache) and all subsequent searches from that same IP address will receive the cached response for 30 minutes (inactivity-based cache).

Search will be the responsible party for providing language capabilities for Search and for ensuring that the search is constructed with the correct language.

Search results will be displayed on a page that is not maintained by the search (ie. the Google Search Results page).

Search bookmarks will no longer be required by Google Search.

Google Search will use their own language capability APIs (rather than the existing Search bookmarklet) in order to determine the language of the search.

## Status

Approved.

## Context

For years, we've made the mistake of supplying the public final static variable getters as the source of truth for a variable (e.g., a boolean).

The intention was good, but the implementation often was flawed, and led to:

- A number of confusing code locations that need to be changed when a variable is renamed.
- A long list of possible code locations that might need to be changed
- A long list of places the code was changed
- Long compile time
- Long compile time of the tests

Our use of long compile times is:
```
./manage test --testcase=100s+
```

When an immutble object, like a data class, exists, it's best to add a `get_value` or `get_value` method. The `private final` declaration is a guard to stop changing the value.

`public final` is the same as `private final`, but it has a wider spread.

When we use `private final`, we're signaling the design is immutable.

When we use `public final`, we're not signaling the design is immutable, but we're also not going to use it for data classes, where they would be more idiomatic `private final`.

Using `public final` with data classes seems wrong, because they are not immutable by design. They could easily change the data they're holding. We could make data classes immutable by serializing their value in the `fields`, but that's a bit ugly.

Using `private final` would have prevented us from needing to supply getters and setters, and it would have ensured we wouldn't have had so many places to change code in 2020.

### Examples

The existing `public final` and `private final` declarations were documented in a [JIRA ticket](https://github.com/transcom/mymove-service/issues/3539) around 2020.

Here are some examples to illustrate:

#### No public final

```ruby
class Example
  def initialize(a: :int, b: :boolean)
    @a = a
    @b = b
  end

  def show
    "a=:#{a}, b=:#{b}"
  end
end

# Using private final would make show not to display.
```

#### With public final

```ruby
class Example
  def initialize(a: :int, b: :boolean)
    @a = a
    @b = b
  end

  def show
    # In order to access a variable defined by public final, we need to use the getter.
    # If we want to use a getter that needs a new instance, then it's not a final variable.
    # Here, the show method will get an immutable instance, which is final.
  end
end

# It's not the most idiomatic in ruby, but it allows for more flexible methods, like show.
```

### Alternatives

#### Use constructors

Using a constructor is the best option to create immutable objects. Here's an example using constructors

```ruby
class ImmutableString
  def initialize(s: :string)
    @s = s
  end

  def show
    @s
  end
end

# In this way, all methods need to include a @s in their code, and all methods should be prefixed with @s.
```

Here, we create the object and give it value at the time of creation. We can then use the getters for all the objects of type `ImmutableString`.

## Decision

We'll start using `public final` for declarations that will no longer change.

## Consequences

### Positive

- It's consistent with the other teams in the organization.
- It's more idiomatic for the public API.

### Negative

- You might accidentally use it with data classes.

### Neutral

- You can always override getter methods in data classes.

### Further work

Add documentation that clarifies when we should and should not use `public final`.

## Status

Accepted

## Context

Pottery originally specified that its text files were JSON, with each
document representing a page on a pottery site.  A recent update to
Pottery allows pages to be composed of multiple text files, so a single page
will have multiple text files associated with it.

Because pages can now be made up of multiple text files, and the text files
are no longer the root file for a page, it's no longer valid to describe the
text files as "the shards" of a page's text, since the shards are not
the root file for a page.

## Decision

We will treat each text file on a page as a "shard" of the page's text.

Pottery-derived text files will be markdown files, described by [markdown-to-markdown
engine](https://github.com/jschneier/markdown-to-markdown), since their syntax
should be treated as a subset of standard markdown, with support for
markdown-to-markdown.  As such, a text editor will be able to display
these files in a rich text format and provide syntax highlighting.

## Consequences

It will be possible for tools that consume pottery text to easily extract an
individual text file, in case they wish to display individual pages (rather than
multiple pages in one).

## Status

Accepted

## Context

As the job scheduler in the Cluster has been tasked to be distributed for multiple worker nodes to process, the wait mechanism needs to be implemented.

The only option for the wait mechanism is to wait inside the job manager.

If you run out of space in worker's memory, it will kill the job manager and job container that you are running in the cluster, instead of throwing an error. The job manager cannot report this to the UI and users can't understand what's happening.

## Decision

Decided that instead of throwing an error when you wait for a task and it's being delayed, we use the broadcast mechanism to notify all the services other services to be aware of that it's delayed. The UI can be sent an error instead to tell them about the error, so the user can decide what they want to do next, but the wait mechanism still persists as before.

In terms of code, we need to create a separate api endpoint that has all the messages related to job's progress. This will be broadcasted to all the other apis and services. This will cause UI, and all the other apis to receive the messages that some jobs are waiting for. The broadcast api will receive the messages and will send them to all the apis and services registered in the system.

We could reuse the pub/sub system in Kubernetes to broadcast the messages instead, since this is what our system is designed to do. So UI, and all the apis and services will receive those messages.

In this way, the job manager will keep being the wait mechanism for the queued jobs.

We decided this because we can't afford to wait inside the job manager. We have so many functions and processes running in the job manager. We needed to have a simpler wait mechanism. Also, we will be expanding the system and there's a possiblity that we might need to distribute the job manager, so we should decide on a simpler wait mechanism.

## Consequences

The queue manager will be able to broadcast those messages for you to notify the other apis and services that job is waiting and it was not deleted.

If the queue manager is not able to broadcast those messages to other apis and services because we are not on the same network, then the queue manager has to be distributed to be able to broadcast those messages in this case. The queue manager in this case is serving multiple worker nodes, and it is broadcasting all the events to the worker node from which it is being distributed.

So there's a new possibility that the queue manager has to be distributed because there are queues. This will make it difficult to deploy a single queue manager to multiple worker nodes.

This makes the code harder to test, because the api has to be exposed to the client, and then we have to send those messages to the API which is running on the other worker node, or we can call a localhost.

In this way, the queue manager and all the services will be able to be notified. Also, the job manager's code is much simpler. The job manager has just a listener to broadcast those messages. So the job manager can be distributed just like the rest of the job manager.

## Context

Currently in the monolith we are only processing concurrent requests from a single server which creates the following types of risks and impacts on performance

* A failure to process one message can stop a batch of messages from being processed creating a bottleneck

* The system is susceptible to race conditions that can be used to trigger infinite loads on the system 

* We can become unaware of bottlenecks until it's late in the discovery process

* We have limited visibility of what messages are processed concurrently and how this is impacting the overall flow of discovery

## Decision

Implement a queue which can handle requests concurrent to each other, without causing failure to process messages

This queue should be shared across all services responsible for processing messages

For example a Discovery Queue, a Content Data Queue and a Trackservice Data Queue

This queue should be implemented as an observable data stream which allows consumers to discover the messages on the queue by their time in the queue and their message Id

All consumers of this queue should be added to the singleton object and should be responsible for handling queue messages

All services which consume messages should also implement retry mechanisms as should the consumers 

This should mitigate against the effects of processing concurrent requests.

The following will occur:

1 When the queue is empty, the consumers will pause and return the latest known state

2 When the queue is not empty, the consumers will grab the first 10 messages from the queue and process them, if available

3 When the queue is empty and the consumers are waiting, the consumer will return the latest known state

4 When a consumer fails during the consumption process it should be retried

## Status

Accepted

## Context

We use two different approaches to manage and version our code:

- in GitHub repositories for long-term storage and versioning of code;
- in GitLab for short-term development and versioning of code.

These projects should be closely linked to facilitate:

1. Easy retrieval of long-term historical data for use in external reports and presentations;
2. Easy linking of code commits to documented changes in reports and presentations;
3. Easy synchronization of code between repositories.

There are currently four active projects:

1. Datalabs;
2. Open FIDO;
3. Community Edition;
4. Open FIDO Platform.

The Open FIDO project uses two repositories, which makes linking code to commits difficult:

1. Main code repository for source code;
2. Open-FIDO-Docs repository for documentation.

These problems can be addressed by using a common organizational pattern for projects, which creates a directory structure that makes it easy to identify links between code and documentation changes.

The Open FIDO Platform project does not have its own repository, but instead gets its code from Open FIDO. This project makes the most of the Open FIDO project code by providing a common view of the code and by making it easy to retrieve the latest code changes.

## Decision

For the purpose of this ADR, we will follow two steps:

1. We will review the organizational pattern used for Datalabs projects (in GitHub), in Open FIDO, and in Community Edition;
2. We will use the Datalabs organizational pattern as a foundation for the projects Open FIDO, Community Edition, and Open FIDO Platform. This will also include the existing organizational pattern for the existing Open FIDO project.

The organizational pattern should:

- be common to all Datalabs projects;
- be easily understood to all new developers;
- provide a straightforward mapping between commits and documentation changes.

The organizational pattern should be defined in terms of directories and files, and also as a series of Git commands and file names so that it can be easily implemented and maintained by developers.

## Consequences

A common organizational pattern for all Datalabs projects facilitates code synchronization and links the code to its documentation changes. The pattern provides developers with a clear indication of the historical sources of the code, which is necessary for producing accurate reports.

Having the Open FIDO code organized in the manner described allows us to use a common code base, which streamlines development activities.

This ADR does not address the problem of having to access long-term data for use in reports. The existing Open FIDO project already does this by making its history available in the `code-as-code` database. This database also provides easy access to the latest code changes for use in other documents. This pattern does not change this.

## Status

Accepted

## Context

The plan is to store data in an API of this project.

One of the goals of this project is to be used by many users.

Each user should be identified by a unique identifier, and should be able to modify this data.

Data should be accessible only to a specific user (or group of users), and not be visible to other users.

Identity Provider (IDP) is the service that manages authentication of users.

Examples: Google, Facebook, Microsoft, Cognito.

User data is usually stored in a database to avoid repeatedly asking the IDP for account details. This data is also used to send emails and other communication from IDP.

Services that provide IDP can be either public (or general-purpose) or private (or enterprise).
Examples: https://auth.google.com/ (public) vs. https://login.microsoftonline.com/ (private)

## Decision

We will use [Cognito](https://aws.amazon.com/cognito/) as IDP.

Cognito is the public-facing part of [Amazon Cognito
Services](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cognito/latest/developerguide/what-is-amazon-cognito.html) in AWS.

## Consequences

Cognito supports both public and private settings, and is primarily a backend (server-side) service for authentication.

In most of cases we will have access only to API and it's data, so we do not need a separate database for storing user data.

Cognito supports social sign-on (Google, Facebook, ...) and federated identity (login with my organization's email and Microsoft Office 365). We will need to use these capabilities in future iterations of this project to make it more user-friendly.

Cognito supports [SSO_OFF_THIRD_PARTY](https://github.com/openid-client-libraries/openid-client-lib/blob/master/spec/protocol_utilities.rb#L35-L38). This supports [OpenID
Connect as a losey data format](https://openid.net/specs/openid-connect-data-format/).

We can use a single "instance" of Cognito to serve all users of all APIs we develop in AWS.

We can allow/disallow users to self-serve and create new accounts or sign in.

AWS recommends using Cognito as IDP for applications such as this one.

Using Cognito will make it easier to change IDP in future iterations of the project, or to provide authentication via other services.

## Context

Since we decided to store records using colour to indicate their status, we need to consider how to display records that have been superseded. 

Since records may be archived, we must decide if a superseded record should retain its original colour, or be displayed in a different colour when being viewed in archive.

We need to decide if records which have been superseded and archived should be treated as a discrete sub-group, and displayed using a different colour when being viewed in archive, or if they should be displayed with the same colour as other records being viewed in archive.

## Decision

We will use two colours when displaying records in archive.

A lightgreen will be used to indicate that a record has been superseded, and the original red will be used to indicate that it is still current.

In order to aid readers of records, a text description will be given for superseded records.

## Consequences

This decision provides some indication to readers of records that the record is no longer current. 

It is possible for readers to become confused as to what colour to apply when viewing a record in archive, or in the active time line.

We will have to change the format of records that have been archived.

Since it is not possible to change the colour of records once they have been archived, we will need to keep an eye on records to ensure that they are not forgotten and treated as current.
