## Status

Accepted

## Context

Since the prototype of the tool lives in beta.ons.gov.uk, it is accessible to anyone who can access the ONS website.

It is important that only a limited number of people can access the prototype to ensure that the team can easily make changes to it and continue to work with users and other stakeholders without security problems.

Given this context, we should ensure the prototype has a basic authentication strategy in place that protects it from being accessible to the public.

## Decision

Given that most prototypes live on the beta.ons.gov.uk website, it is preferable to use the basic-auth strategy that is provided by GOV.UK PaaS to access them. Basic authentication uses a string to identify an authenticated user and is the easiest form of authentication to implement.

## Consequences

This strategy has some limitations:

- the authenticated user is identified by a string not a user identity
- no password is required to authenticate
- the string is visible in the url
- it is not possible to set an expiry date on a session

However, these are limitations that we consider acceptable for this project since:

- our prototypes are publically accessible by default and it is the domain of the project that they are securely stored

Furthermore, beta.ons.gov.uk uses the nginx web server, which implements [client IP authentication](https://www.nginx.org/en/download/index.html) for logged-in users.

In other words, since our IP address has been published, we can securely identify and manage who is able to access the prototype with a number of limitations. The limitations are acceptable for this tool's purpose and domain.

## Status

Accepted

## Context

The project has a need to fetch data from the UK Data Lab API to build datasets during the ETL process. The only client side code is for the ETL itself, and there is no other front end code. [Citerus](https://citerus.com/) was made to handle the generation of these sorts of client side requests.

### Options

#### 1. Install and use [Citerus](https://citerus.com/) as is
- This does not require the installation of any node packages beyond npm, and requires only a URL and authentication credentials from the UK Data Lab API
- Adds complexity to the installation of the application as the choice of the dependency needs to be documented within the README.md file
- Removes a degree of separation from the team and the client
- Adds an additional dependency that the team are not familiar with
- Adds an additional dependency that the client are not familiar with
- Can be customised for the use case

#### 2. Install and use [Citerus](https://citerus.com/) as a node package
- This would require a node package repository (npm/GitHub), and would require the client side code to be hosted under version control (GitHub)
- Requires the installation of additional node packages
- Removes a degree of separation from the team and the client
- Adds complexity to the installation of the application as a separate repository would need to be created, and the build step would need to be written using npm scripts
- Adds an additional dependency that the team are not familiar with
- Adds an additional dependency that the client are not familiar with
- Can be customised for the use case

## Decision

Use Citerus as a git submodule. This removes the need to install any additional node packages.

## Consequences

We have maintained a degree of separation from the client side development work.

We have limited the installation process to a series of commands on the command line.

This prevents the package becoming publicly available.

We have added an additional dependency that the team have no previous experience with.

The client is able to easily install Citerus as the dependency will be maintained by the team.

The client side code will still need to be hosted under version control (GitHub).

We have limited the use of dependency package manager to the installation process, and removed the need to use it during the build process.

It may prove to be more challenging to find out about new features Citerus have implemented before using them.

We have not added the process for publishing Citerus as a node package as Citerus will not be made available to clients without the installation of additional node packages. It is also [likely that its use case will no longer exist at the time of release](https://citerus.com/docs/dev/citerus-data-api/#/resources-and-services/data-api).

A package manager may still be required in order to deploy the application to an environment that has only the client side code, and a server side environment that has Citerus available. This is not seen to be an issue when using GitHub Pages or Heroku.

Citerus has not been updated for a long time. There is no active support.

If the team decide to stop maintaining Citerus and a new one is chosen, there will be a period of overlap between the old Citerus and the new one before the code is migrated from the old one to the new one.

## Status

Accepted

## Context

The current cloudformation template we have is quite convoluted. The intention was to have a single template which could create all the AWS resources necessary to deploy the TIS. This approach was taken because it easier to manage a single template compared to multiple templates. When a template needs a change, the update will either occur across all AWS accounts associated with the TIS deployment, or it won't occur at all. With this approach it's easy to keep things consistent across all accounts.

While this approach has been beneficial in the short term, I have noticed that as our template gets more and more complex, it's getting harder to make sense of the template, and to spot what the current version of the template is. This has led to the creation of multiple versions of the template, and confusion around which is the latest version, and which should be used for a TIS deploy.

Another problem with keeping things consistent across all accounts is that it's easy to make mistakes in these configurations. For instance, a mis-spelled property value in one cloudformation template would be replicated in every other TIS-deploying AWS account, rather than AWS accounts where the developer has access to the TIS deploy. I would also like to think that the cloudformation template we have should be reusable, but it can't be without maintaining a template history. We can't rely on cloudformation's history to manage old versions of the template as a consequence of this approach.

In short, I have noticed that managing these multiple templates is leading to more problems than we would save from having a single template.

## Decision

Rebuild our current template from scratch. We will use some of the knowledge we've gained from working with the existing template to make this easier.

## Consequences

Because our existing template is quite convoluted and is not easy to understand or easy to maintain, we'll need to spend some time actually rebuilding the template. Fortunately, as noted above, the template is largely a collection of simple cloudformation stacks and stacks resources. This should make rebuilding the template from scratch relatively simple. With our experience managing the existing template, we should also be able to spot a lot of the patterns that exist within the template from previous iterations and continue to use them. This should keep costs low, because there should be less rework involved in this process than a more direct, path-less rewrite of the template.

While this should have the happy side effect of reducing confusion around the template, we should always be aware that we have to make sure to do the right thing when we're making such a significant change. In theory, we might want to consider whether we should have the template be reusable. At this time, I'm not so sure. In the future, we may decide that it's good for a template to be reusable, but until then, I'll continue to think of the template as a way for managing the deployment of the TIS.

## Context and problem statement

How should we handle data that is no longer accurate, stale (usually meaning >=5 years old) and maybe unreachable?

## Decision drivers

* Must work on fridges and pub-sub systems
* How accurate (and current) are the data we're trying to achieve?
* Are users willing to pay for new data?

## Considered options

1. Fix everything stale data that is present in the fridge system that could have a different fridge location or system
2. Ignore stale data, add a daily "clean up" and send mail or collect feedback
3. Start publishing API that allows consumers to fetch and pay for the latest data

## Decision outcome

The option chosen is 2, because at the moment the existing data is stale, but it's not a problem for the fridge system.


### Positive consequences

* Reduce time and cost for producing new data
* Less data in the fridge
* It's not worth updating the 15K records, but we can collect feedback and fix it when it comes up
* We use the fridge data, so we'd be able to use the fridge data for future analytics
* We can move the issue from Pomegranate to Fridge

### Negative consequences

* We'll continue to collect stale data, but it's ok since we can clean it out during routine fridge maintenance

## Pros and cons of the options

### Fix everything stale data that is present in the fridge system that could have a different fridge location or system

* Good, because we will have better data for the future
* Good, because it would take less time to update all the data
* Bad, because it's a lot of work
* Bad, because we'll need to make sure we don't update multiple records (like multiple fridge locations)


### Ignore stale data, add a daily "clean up" and send mail or collect feedback

* Good, because it's less work
* Good, because less time to update stale data
* Bad, because we may make mistakes (especially with older records) and let stale records stay
* Bad, because there's a chance some stale records stay while updates fail
* Bad, because we'll have to remember to collect the stale record data

### Start publishing API that allows consumers to fetch and pay for the latest data

* Good, because we would make the best data possible
* Good, because it'd be easier to keep the fridge data updated
* Bad, because it's hard to write
* Bad, because it's hard to maintain

## Status

> Accepted

> May 1, 2020

## Context

There is a number of options when defining a `Model` within the skypy framework.
The options available are a `Function`, `Parameter`, and `Variable`.

The function will return an output within a set number of executions.
For example a `lambda` function with 3 outputs would be `lambda x, y, z: [result1, result2, result3]`.
A function doesn't change and doesn't get passed as a parameter or as a global variable.
The use of functions means that the same function would be called throughout the `Model`.

A parameter is a variable that gets passed to the function for each evaluation.
An example would be `x, y, z` as the parameters for a function, `f(x, y, z)`.
You'll have a variable (as an independent variable) that changes the function parameters.

A variable is a variable that changes and is accessible throughout the model.
A variable is assigned to a variable (as a dependent variable) at some point in the model.
The variable can then be changed later, for example a log that is kept within the model.

An independent variable is a parameter which is used to adjust the variables through a function.

The different types of variables can be thought of as the space and time coordinates of a particular calculation.
There is also the concept of a dependent variable which can be used as the `y` value in a function where it is changed.

The current implementation uses the variable type, `Variable`, and this was determined as the most flexible option when the project was first started.
The variables are assigned to `Variable` and the function gets assigned to `Function`.

Some types of `Variables` get stored as `Dataset` objects within the model, this enables time based calculation to be performed.
This is done using a `Vector` to store the variables, as the independent variable for a parameter is a function based on time.

The function type allows us to use standard mathematical functions that we can use with other frameworks.

#### Pros

> A function allows you to re-use the function and keep the model lightweight as all variables are re-used with function calls.

> A function allows us to re-use the function and perform calculations based on the user inputs, which was not possible with a variable or a parameter.

> A function can be implemented as a lambda which is light weight and can be stored within a single memory space.

> A function allows us to re-use the function and store all required values in the function to reduce the model size.

#### Cons

> The Model was originally thought to be used solely for functions.
> A function does not get passed and the Model can be written to handle both variables and functions.
> A function needs to be re-called each time.
> Some users may want to be able to store the variable used as the `y` value within the `M`.
> All information required to re-create the function needs to be stored in the model.

## Decisions

- all of the functions defined in the model will be stored in the model using a `Function` class.

- the variables that are used for functions will be stored in the model using a `Parameter` class.

- the variables that are used by the model and are not changing on each evaluation and are global will be stored in the model using a `Variable` class.

- all of the calculation methods must return a `Dataset` that is stored as a dependent variable.

- all calculations will be performed using a `Function` class which will be stored in the model.

## Consequences

- The use of the `Parameter` class provides some limitations to the type of calculations that can be performed.
- The use of the `Variable` class allows more flexibility.
- It allows a wider variety of calculations to be performed.
- It's [relatively difficult](https://github.com/stefanmaric/skypy/pull/66) to support a dependent variable.
- The main aim is to perform calculations that change the dependent variable over time, or for some model parameter.
- By storing all the other variables as parameters in the model, we can make these more flexible (if the user changes their value) for later evaluations.

Date: 2017-09-07

## Status

Accepted

## Context

The API endpoint(s) needs to be accessible from outside of the client network.

There are a number of options to access the API endpoint(s) from outside the client network.

### Options:

1. Public API Endpoint
2. VPN
3. Bastion
4. NAT

#### 1. Public API Endpoint
This is a server with a public IP address that can be accessed over the Internet by clients.

* Pro
* Consistent Configuration
* Easy to Implement

#### 2. VPN
This creates a private network across a potentially long distance. It creates a series of points of presence (clients) that are backed by a central server (server). All traffic from client to server is routed through the server (server). This is a form of client-to-server or peer-to-server (P2P) networking.

* Pro
* Established Standard
* Easily Scalable
* Well Known Implementation Examples (e.g. VMWare, OpenShift)

#### 3. Bastion
A bastion server is a security appliance or virtual machine that provides access to a network that is isolated from the Internet. It provides a secure gateway for network services, enabling clients to access internal network services without direct access to the Internet.

* Pro
* Provides a Layer Between Client and Server

#### 4. NAT
Network Address Translation, often just called NAT. NAT is a protocol that allows a client to access a server by assigning a NAT in the client IP address. When a client's IP address is NATed, NAT will translate the client IP address to the NAT IP address for every request to the server. If there is a NAT service in the server IP address, and it has the ability to NAT it to the client IP address.

* Pro
* Client is Typically Configured with NAT Service

## Decision

The client will use a Virtual Private Network (VPN) to connect to the API endpoint(s).

The client will be configured with a NAT service, if available.

## Consequences

If configured correctly, the client and server will have a secure connection to each other and be accessible to clients without being directly on the Internet. The server will be behind an existing network infrastructure (e.g. client network, OpenShift, VMWare, etc.).

There will need to be a router (NAT) in front of the API endpoint.

It will not be possible for non-client to initiate a connection to an API endpoint.

# Validation

## Status

proposed

## Context

Currently, the API allows users to specify multiple searches and processes requests to the API. This is necessary to cater for different use cases of different users.

We do not have an agreed implementation to cater for those different use cases, as the different search processes are not necessarily dependent on the different request processes and, as the search processes are not necessarily related to each other, the API server does not have a reliable mechanism to relate those different processes to the different searches.

This creates uncertainty and complexity around the ways in which different search and request processes can be used to trigger a request and perform validation.

## Decisions

- Add an argument to each `GET` request that specifies the "group" or "scope" for a particular operation. This provides a mechanism through which we can build "processes" from multiple searches.
- Accept searches in requests with a specified group.
- Specify the order of validation. 
- Specify the order of request processing.
- Provide mechanisms for implementing validation.

## Examples

### Fetching searches from a particular organisation

```
/organisations/organisations?scope=0
```

returns the searches for the organisation with the ID `0`.

### Fetching searches from a particular organisation for a given date range

```
/organisations/organisations?scope=0&dateRange=0-15
```

returns the searches for the organisation with the ID `0`, for the first 15 days of the 21st century (1-15 Jan 2001).

### Running searches from a particular organisation, and returning all searches

```
/organisations/organisations/0?scope=0
```

returns all searches for the organisation with the ID `0`.

### Running a search to gather records

```
/organisations/organisations/0?scope=0&recordType=2&searchType=3
```

searches for 2 types of records for the organisation with the ID `0`, based on search type 3.

## Consequences

### Advantages

- Provides reliability
- Provides a mechanism for defining processes for multiple searches.
- Allows us to specify a preferred way to validate.

### Disadvantages

- Involves adding new options and APIs to the client.
- Adds new complexity to the client.
- Requires implementation.
- Reduces ability to make arbitrary searches and requests to the API.

### Neutral

- May allow us to implement some validation mechanisms.
- May remove the need to implement some validation mechanisms.
- Could be implemented with an extra argument.

**User Story:** _[As a User, I want to be able to update the APP by using the [Beta Channel](https://github.com/dev-beta/app-channel) or [Stable Channel](https://dev.flutter.com/stable). _

* _[Using Beta Channel as App Channel and Updating Apps in AppChannel]_
* _[Using Stable Channel as App Channel]_
* _[Using Stable Channel as App Channel and Updating Apps in AppChannel]_
* _[Use the App Preview Channel]_

## Decision Outcome

* Chosen Alternative: _[Using Beta Channel as App Channel]_
* _This is the best alternative since the Channel is stable and supports beta in AppStore.

## Pros and Cons of the Alternatives

### _[Using Beta Channel as App Channel]_

* `+` [Flutter recommends the Beta channel](https://dev.flutter.com/channel-documentation#channels-recommended-by-flutter)
* `+` Apps released from the Beta channel will be promoted to the [App Store as App Preview](https://developers.google.com/play/android/docs/app-publish/beta-release) in app channel, which has better app store description and is designed to have more info for beta users
* `-` Some apps using app preview may not appear in the playStore as App Preview

### _[Using Beta Channel as App Channel and Updating Apps in AppChannel]_

* `-` Apps released from the beta channel will have different versions of google play store
* `-` A possible app update to 6.0 in App Store may not apply to beta

### _[Using Stable Channel as App Channel]_

* `+` Apps released from the stable channel will have a single version of Google Play Store (App Store version)
* `-` The Beta Channel will not be supported
* `-` Apps using app preview will not have previews of apps in playStore

### _[Using Stable Channel as App Channel and Updating Apps in AppChannel]_

* `+` apps released from the stable channel will have single google play store versions
* `-` a possible app update to 6.0 in App Store will not apply to beta

# ADR003: Container Orchestration

## Context

TTA Smart Hub will be using containers for a number of different functions including:

* Deployment of the API and CLI
* Deployment of the TTA Smart Hub
* Provisioning a PaaS Platform

As such we need to have a container orchestration platform to provide high availability, continuous integration and deployment, and ease of release.

## Decision

TTA Smart Hub will use Kubernetes as the container orchestration platform for a number of reasons:

* Kubernetes is an emerging industry favourite and has been used extensively in production for the last few years.
* Kubernetes is open source and free to use.
* Kubernetes has been the subject of much research and engineering and a large amount of documentation is available.
* Kubernetes provides a large amount of out of the box functionality including rolling out/rolling back updates and blue-green deployments.
* Kubernetes provides several implementation platforms for hosting including AWS ECS and AKS.
* Kubernetes provides a large amount of community and vendor support (e.g. AWS ECS provides managed Kubernetes clusters).
* Kubernetes has been the subject of some government research and recommendation.

## Status

Accepted

## Consequences

The use of Kubernetes provides the following consequences:

* the team should be able to make better use of community support and resources to mitigate risk
* we will require access to AWS ECS and AKS
* the team should have a base level of Kubernetes expertise to manage and maintain the infrastructure
* there are a number of implementations of Kubernetes to choose from
* Kubernetes has been designed around a declarative API rather than imperative API which makes it somewhat difficult to learn and iterate
* Google recommends Kubernetes for modern cloud-native applications
* There are [no hard and fast rules] for best practice within the Kubernetes community. Many decisions are made based on consensus between users and vendors. This in part makes it difficult to understand what best practice is or is not within the community at any given time. This risk is mitigated through time and documentation.

## Problem

-   Keys and leaf values may contain holes in them
-   This may cause problems in searching and displaying those keys
-   In case of multiple keys, the values for keys containing holes might be replaced
-   In case of multiple keys, only the first key with a hole might be considered.
-   Non-leaf keys may also contain holes

## Constraints

-   In cases of multiple keys, only the first encountered hole should be used

## Assumptions

## Considered Alternatives

## Decision

-   Holes in keys do not impact searching
-   Non-leaf keys do not have holes
-   Non-leaf keys start at 0
-   For every non-leaf key, the value of the key is increased by 1 if there is a hole in the key.
  For keys containing the character 'f', this value is increased by 2.
  Keys containing 'fl', 'fm', 'ff' are considered to have a hole.
  Their values are increased by 3 in that case.
  For keys containing the character 'l', the value of the key is increased by 4 if there is a hole in the key.
  For keys containing the character 'm', this value is increased by 5 if there is a hole in the key.
  For keys containing the character 'r', this value is increased by 6 if there is a hole in the key.
  Keys containing 'rl', 'rm', 'rf' are considered to have a hole.
  Their values are increased by 7 in that case.
-   If there is a hole in a key, and the key is inserted after other keys, its value is increased by (number of inserted keys) * 8.
-   This allows every key to have the same value if there is a hole in the key.
-   It ensures that the key values will not be replaced by other keys in case multiple keys are inserted in one iteration.
-   This ensures every key will be correctly considered, even if inserted after other keys with holes.
-   By using the inserted keys to calculate the value increase, the insert operation correctly takes the inserted keys into account, in case more than one key is inserted at once.
-   This ensures that if there is a hole in a key inserted after other keys, the values of the keys are not replaced by the new key's value, because 8 is not equal to 7.
-   This ensures the new key's value is not replaced by another key's value if a key with a hole is inserted after a key without a hole.
-   If a key with a hole is inserted before other keys, there is no increase in the value of the key.
-   Keys with a hole can be inserted before other keys with a hole.
-   There is no need to decrease the value of a key when it is inserted before another key with a hole, because we use the inserted keys to calculate the value increase in the next iteration.
-   If multiple keys are inserted, the order in which they are inserted should not impact the final results.
-   This ensures a list containing a key with a hole and followed by a key without a hole has a value that correctly represents the number of keys with a hole.
-   The number of inserted keys is taken into account to calculate the increase.
-   Keys with a hole could also be inserted before a key that does not have a hole, which would be incorrect for some of these keys.

## Rationale

Non-leaf keys do not contain holes, which would cause confusion.

## Status

Accepted

## Context

We need a strategy for communicating domain events to consumers that are not closely related to each other.

### Use a "bus" for publishing/consuming events

We already have a "bus" for publishing/consuming events which is the fanout mechanism which broadcast events to all interested consumers in a distributed application environment.

The concept of a "bus" is inspired by the notion of a message broker which is often used in distributed systems to enable loosely coupled application units to communicate. While the goal is to provide a loosely coupled system, it is up to the implementation of the bus to enable the various features. An event bus is a message broker which can store events and publish these to interested consumers.

From an architectural point of view, the existence of a message broker is a high pattern in many architectural domains.

For this reason we want to use a message broker to manage event distribution in a distributed manner.

#### Choosing a message broker

There are many options for a message broker but we wanted a lightweight open source option.

* Redis (Memory Store)
* RabbitMQ
* ZeroMQ

We choose *ZeroMQ* due to its low footprint and use at the project's start.

It is quite useful in a development environment.

It is important to understand though that there are some limitations to using ZeroMQ for production, especially when it comes to scalability and reliability.

While the author did use Redis in his previous projects, this approach is really well-known for many years.

## Decision

We will use [ZeroMQ](http://zeromq.org/) (as mentioned in the context section) to distribute events in a distributed manner.

## Consequences

By using a zero-MQ queue we will be able to broadcast events to interested consumers while maintaining a lightweight footprint and a quick development environment.

We will be using a new system so it is not easy to understand and maintain.

Our use of ZeroMQ also has a negative impact on the reliability of the underlying system.

The "bus" can be used in a variety of scenarios for things other than the event bus.
* We can publish other events from the application bus
* We can consume events from the external "bus" (in the case of the event store)
* We can emit events that are used for synchronization purposes.

For full context and details please check the `zeromq-bus` GitHub repository.

Date: 2018-11-04

## Status

Accepted

## Context

The redis cluster is used for both caching and publishing actions.

- Caching will happen in front of the application, in a reverse proxy mode, e.g. Varnish.
- The state and actions table store will be held in the cluster.

The actions table is queried by the admin API for daily actions, which in turn queries the db and fetches all the actions for a specific day (the id is the date).

While the API seems to accept this query, there is no particular caching level.

As a consequence:

- the actions table is queried for every call to the admin API.
- As the table is queried for every call to the admin API, and each call to the admin API fetches all the actions for a specific day, which in turn queries the db (using the id), there are two different ways to get data from the db and that might be a performance blocker for some calls to the admin API.
- As the database is queried for every call to the admin API, it is likely to become a bottleneck.

An alternative solution would have been to leverage the write operations as a caching mechanism (instead of using the table queries to fetch the data), which could have been used to mitigate this problem. However such a solution cannot be done in this case as the actions table is queried by the application for every call to the admin API.

## Decision

Change the architecture so that the cache is behind the application. Redis is used only to write actions to the db.

## Consequences

- The use of redis in the caching layer is redundant.
- The `v1` API uses the actions table to fetch the list of actions, and the caching layer will be queried for this list of actions.
- Some API calls to the `v1` API will not be routed to the cache, so the caching layer is effectively bypassed for those calls, e.g. `list-actions /next-day`.

## Status

## Context

We want to be confident that our code works as advertised and avoid writing tests manually. There are many unit testing frameworks for Haskell but there are fewer UI testing frameworks. We also want to be able to run tests across multiple platforms. We consider testing of components on multiple platforms to be essential for a UI testing framework.

### Approaches to testing in Haskell

1. **Unit testing**: This tests small portions of Haskell code, such as functions. It is also known as low-level testing.
2. **Integration testing**: This tests how multiple units of Haskell code work together. It is also known as mid-level testing.
3. **System testing**: This tests the whole Haskell program. It is also known as high-level testing.
4. **UI testing**: This tests the graphical user interface.

We intend to do all of these. However, Haskell UI testing frameworks are quite new. Haskell has been working on developing these frameworks since it was used in [Mirantis]. However, there is little in our application that utilizes this toolkit outside of the initial proof-of-concept.

As such, the main reason we have decided to use a UI testing framework is that it will enable us to be confident that all components, including front-end components, work as designed.

UI testing is also a form of integration testing and so it supports and verifies the integration tests.

### Common UI testing frameworks for Haskell

- [Mirantis UI testing](https://www.mirantis.com/blog/mirantis-ui-testing-framework) (not fully supported by the community)
- [Widget tests](https://www.widge.framework)
- [Lwt-ui](https://dankogai.github.io/lwt-ui/)

## Decision

We will use Widget tests as our UI testing framework.

This framework seems to fulfill our requirements. It is fully supported by the community and helps with providing good UI test documentation. The framework was specifically created for use with the rest of the [Wix.js](https://wixjs.com/) framework but has been generalized enough to support various other types of Haskell UI frameworks. However, since most of our application will be built using the Wix.js framework, we don't think it will be an issue.

## Consequences

We will need to provide a data interface to enable automatic acceptance tests to be written using this framework.

**Pros**:

- We'll have a UI testing framework that has been fully adopted by the community
- Widget tests support the creation of tests that verify more than just the rendered HTML

**Cons**:

- Tests might be complicated to write and might become harder to read and maintain over time

## Status

Accepted

## Context

In a previous ADR we decided that the use of custom Exception for application errors, and 
the use of methods that must have validation for the payload in the case of a POST to 
`/bookables/search`, in particular the `search` method. The following is a code snippet from the 
code implementing this method: 
```
search = new search(searchType, searchType);
search.setSearch(search, search)
``` 
As well as setting the value of a class that exists in the memory, this also is done to the 
persistence layer so that the search is persisted as a result of the call to a search type. This 
persistence has become a source of problems as it seems that the search method is not able to create 
persistence without the persistence being overwritten, which leads to an un-created state.

### Proposed solutions

* Use a dedicated method that is able to create the searches. This could either be a static class with 
    a dedicated search creation method (e.g. `createBookingSearch()`), or a method in an object that is tied to 
    persistence
* Use a dedicated class that is able to create the searches and persist them, if required

## Decision

In order to avoid creating a new class that ties to persistent storage, it was decided to use the 
`datashield4j` library instead, which creates a method for executing queries that are used to get 
persistence stored objects.

There are now two methods required to be used by the `search` object. The first is to register a search with 
the underlying search method, which creates a `searchType` object based on the searchType passed to the 
constructor and sets the value of this as a static class that will be used as a search in the underlying 
search method. The other method is to register a search with the `searchType` based on a `searchQuery`
object, which creates a `searchType` object based on the searchType passed to the constructor and 
creates a `search` object that uses the underlying searchType to create a search for the query passed
to the constructor.

## Consequences

### Advantages

* Search methods that are independent to persistent storage, are now possible
* It is possible to use a single instance of the search class, rather than creating a new search object
    each time a search is made

### Disadvantages

* It is not straightforward to implement persistent queries to obtain searches
    * The way it has been implemented is a temporary workaround, that is not likely to be sustainable 
    * Will have to update other code that uses this class
* In a future iteration, we could look at the way that queries to get searches are implemented, and take 
    advantage of some of the methods used to get the searches. We think that this method is very 
    straightforward to implement, but there is some complexity in that the queries can be created 
    dynamically as searches are made
* We must take advantage of the database structure for storing searches, which is a way of storing 
    searches
* We must acknowledge that, in an initial iteration of the search type, search type is persisted without 
    the `createSearchQuery` method (search type) 
* We must acknowledge that, in an initial iteration of the search type, search type is persisted without 
    a `createSearchType` method (search type)

## Status

Accepted

## Context

Terraform supports several different ways of organizing resources. This decision record serves to document our choices and provide some guidance to those who wish to learn more about Terraform resources.

### Directory Structure

Terraform resources can be organized in the following ways:

* Directory structure in terraform/resources
* Terraform modules
* Terraform projects

Each of these methods are explored in detail below.

### Directory Structure

Organizing resources as directories in the terraform/resources directory allows for easy management and tracking of multiple groups of resources. For example, a single terraform module might organize its state, logs, and terraform projects into multiple directories. 

We follow the general rule that directories should be nested. This is supported by Terraform itself. For example, the following Terraform module:

```
module "aws/aws-auth" {
  source       = "../../"
  aws_auth     = "{ aws_auth_aws_account_id }"
  read_policy = "{ aws_auth_aws_account_id }"
}
```

creates three directories: 

* *logs*
* *projects*
* *state*

All of the terraform/resources for AWS are grouped into this module. 

In this example, the directories are created by the Terraform provider itself and the *source* input attribute is used to provide the directories. The directories can be identified using the `./--directory-to-terraform` CLI command.

## Decision

We will organize resources that should be kept together as directories within a terraform/resources directory. 

## Consequences

If we make this choice, we have a consistent pattern for managing resources. There are multiple terraform projects but also multiple directories that will be created. All directories contain all of the terraform modules.

### Other Resources

In addition to the pattern for managing resources as directories within a terraform/resources directory, we also have several modules that we do not group together. These are generally kept in an AWS/Modules folder.

There is also an AWS project that does not group the other terraform projects. This is also kept in the AWS/Modules folder.

These projects may be organized further by using a Directory. This is a less flexible approach and it is generally better to choose a pattern. 

## Links

* [GitHub](https://github.com/terraform/docs/blob/master/modules.md)
* [The Terraform Provider](https://github.com/hashicorp/terraform/blob/master/modules/directory_resource/examples/directory_resource.go)

# Use document database as a repository for aggregates

**User Story:** 

The `klokwrk-backoffice` has a requirement for storing data related to orders, users and products. 
Users have a need for easy access to their ordering history and data and so do customers and so do support teams.
We need to store a lot of data associated with orders and so do we for customers and products.

We are aware that orders and customers are always needed, but not so much about users.
Users will get their information from the dashboard and so we think we can get away with storing the minimum of user information here.

We have considered using [Elasticsearch](https://www.elastic.co/products/elasticsearch), but it seemed too expensive and there was no obvious way for us to get started with it.

We have considered using [MongoDB](https://www.mongodb.com/), which is the database we use for the existing parts of `klokwrk-backoffice`.
We have several advantages of doing this here.
Firstly it allows us to leverage our existing knowledge, and so there's less learning.
Secondly it fits in with our architectural principle of horizontal scaling.
Finally it's cheaper.

We believe we can support vertical scaling if we need it in the future, without much difficulty.

**Assumptions:**

1. We will have the capacity to support horizontal scaling

**Risks:**

1. Users will not have the ability to view their own data

## Considered Alternatives

### Elasticsearch

We have looked at Elasticsearch, and there were several pros and cons.
Pros:
- It's proven, and we have used it before
- It's scalable
- It's fast
Cons:
- It's expensive
- It's hard to configure
- It's complex
- It's hard to get started with

### MongoDB

We have looked at MongoDB, and there were several pros and cons.
Pros:
- It's proven
- We use it for other parts of `klokwrk-backoffice`
- It's scalable
- It's fast
- It's cheaper
- We can use our existing knowledge
- We can set a limit on the size of documents
Cons:
- It's harder to configure than a traditional database
- It's a bit complex

### MySQL

We have looked at MySQL, and there were several pros and cons.
Pros:
- It's proven
- We use it for other parts of `klokwrk-backoffice`
- It's scalable
- It's fast
- It's cheaper
- We can set a limit on the size of documents
- We can use a ORM to reduce boilerplate code
Cons:
- It's more complex than storing our documents in MongoDB
- It's slower to scale

### Text Search

We have looked at ElasticSearch and MongoDB in the context of [searching](https://www.elastic.co/guide/en/elasticsearch/reference/6.3/text-search.html) for orders, users and products.

Using Elasticsearch would give us the ability to do full-text searching across orders, users and products, which will be useful later on.
It would also give us the ability to search across multiple orders for a particular user.
The downside of this is though that we will have to store a lot of redundant information.
It will effectively double the amount of data we store, since we will need to store the text for each set of data we store.
We would also have to be careful about caching to avoid inadvertently flooding the search index with data in the event that some data is duplicated across records.

**Reasoning:**

The reason behind using MongoDB is because it will give us a lot of flexibility over how we build our APIs, and because it's cheaper than Elasticsearch and MySQL.
The downside of MongoDB is that it's harder to set up than MySQL, although I think this is less an issue now that we're using Docker and other tools of modern application infrastructure.
The biggest reason behind using MongoDB is that it will allow us to scale.
If and when we decide to add products to `klokwrk-backoffice`, we can continue to support and scale the entire stack.

**Questioning**

We should have discussed the impact that a text-search capability would have on the data structure, and the extent of the data duplication that would be introduced.

## Decision Outcome

Use MongoDB

## Pros and Cons of the Options

### Elasticsearch

* `+` Offers full text search across orders, users and products
* `+` Supports fetching multiple orders for a user
* `+`

Date: 2020-07-09

## Status

Accepted

## Context

Historically the V8 code base has been versioned. This versioning has served two main purposes:

- To make it clear which of the many changes to the codebase belong to which of the numerous V8 teams (e.g. V8, V6, V3).

- To allow us to run on the various V8 engines that exist (e.g. V8.1, V8.2, V9.0).

With the upcoming V8 rewrite we have an opportunity to make this simpler. We can achieve this by 

- Having all of the new V8 features run inside a single version of V8.

- Having all of the engine implementations (based on V8) run inside a single version of V8.

We can achieve this by only doing this with the V8 JavaScript engine, not the engine implementations that run V8, such as 

- node
- chrome
- electron

## Decision

Make a clear versioning scheme, with the following meanings:

**The patch version will be a single number.**

For example, `V8.34.0`, where `34` is a patch version.

**The major version will be a two digit number.**

For example, `V8.34.0`, where `34` is a major version.

The major version number will only be used for versioning the JS engine, but not the engine implementation which runs this JS engine.

For example, the node engine implementation will be `V8.34.0`, because it runs the V8.34.0 JS engine.

The electron engine implementation will be `V8.34.0`, because it runs the V8.34.0 JS engine.

The chrome engine implementation will be `V8.34.0`, because it runs the V8.34.0 JS engine.

We will use the patch version to make engine versioning and upgrading simpler. For example, an electron engine upgraded to `V8.35.0` will have to patch the V8 JavaScript engine to `V8.35.0`, instead of the previous version `V8.34.0`.

We will use the patch version to make sure that only one type of feature is released with a new V8 release. For example, when we make a breaking change to V8 that fixes a security vulnerability, and release a new major version, the minor version increment will be `1` (e.g. V8.34.1), instead of `2` (e.g. V8.34.0). This versioning scheme has some drawbacks, however, e.g. we can’t update the minor version for non-security patches, but we need this for keeping track of other types of changes, such as non-security bug fixes, as well as making sure that major version changes don't get cherry-picked.

We will use the patch version to ensure that only non-security bug fixes are released on the V8 JS engine, and will not use the patch version for making a major version change to the JS engine. This has the effect of protecting us from accidentally cherry-picking major changes to the JS engine while keeping the stability of the major version relatively high.

## Consequences

An additional change in versioning is needed in all of our engines to ensure that they use the new numbering scheme. There are additional drawbacks to this scheme, because, as mentioned above, we can't update the minor version of the JS engine for non-security bug fixes, and we have to make sure that the patch version isn't used to make major version changes to the JS engine.

## Context

GOV.UK Finance is moving to Workday for finance and accounting operations.
This presents a change for suppliers who have been using Coda (or MISO) for finance operations.

To ensure a smooth migration, and make sure CCS can obtain accurate data for reporting and future audits, we have outlined the integration and submission principles below for use throughout the integration process.

## Decision

The principle of the data integrations is to always submit data in the same format that it is received from the supplier (Coda or MISO).
This ensures that data can be reliably processed from suppliers to Workday.

We have also outlined some additional principles which apply to particular submissions:

### 1. Maintain data integrity

The data that we receive from suppliers should never be submitted in a form that could alter or corrupt it.
This includes not adding or removing information (i.e. white space at the start or end of a string).

### 2. Workday does not replace Coda

Coda remains the platform for managing Coda supplier data such as contact details and finance staff names, but it does not replace MISO or Workday for receiving and managing Coda invoices and accounts management respectively.

### 3. Data can be duplicated

Data that CCS receives from suppliers is a duplicate of data that is already being stored in Coda/MISO, so the value of this data is primarily the *format* rather than the *value*.
For example, a row may represent the "Customer", and the cell value is their "Address", and this value does not need to be the same for each row.

### 4. Data can be truncated

Data that CCS receives from suppliers will be truncated to the maximum allowable length in Workday, so suppliers should use a consistent level of detail when submitting data in a text format.
For example, a name no longer than 30 characters, an address not more than 100 characters, etc.

### 5. Only submit what is essential

Although suppliers are now required to submit data daily, CCS should only submit data that is essential to the operation of Workday.
For example, while maintaining Coda supplier data, submitting the account and contact details are the only data that CCS needs from the supplier.

Many of the fields that suppliers submit to Coda have variations, for example there are different types of VAT rate.
Where a field has variations, the value should be submitted as the `primary` value when submitting to Workday.

# ADR012: Haproxy healthcheck

## Context

The HAProxy application that sits behind the load balancer is configured with a healthcheck script (`haproxy-healthcheck`). This script does not exist as part of the deployment, but it is included in the repository via the terraform `rule-by-rule` example set up. This has been done since it was believed the healthcheck was a deployment artifact rather than a mechanism for dynamically determining the health of HAProxy, but it has persisted despite us trying to clean it up for a while.

## Decision

The healthcheck does not need to be in the repository as HAProxy healthchecks happen by the application of the healthcheck config to the instance from HAProxy itself, including it as part of the deployment would make HAProxy vulnerable to healthcheck failures during the terraform `terraform apply` process. The HAProxy example set up via terraform needs to be removed from the terraform deployment template.

## Status

Accepted.

## Consequences

The HAProxy instance starts and closes the healthcheck via [haproxy/haproxy#141](https://github.com/haproxy/haproxy/pull/141), which the healthcheck doesn't check for in any way, but we accept the risk.

## Context

Hackney have several projects written in Python, and it is a common language between projects. This allows us to easily shift developers between projects and share code. We want to ensure all developers are using a common Python environment so they can share code and best practices.

Hackney have used containers to deploy their applications in AWS. Since containers install software via the docker repositories, this presents the need for developers to ensure that any libraries or development dependencies they install are still available within the production environment in their AWS account.

Hackney have historically used either Vagrant + VirtualBox or Virtualbox + Vagrant to manage a development environment. This approach involves creating a VM in Docker for each Python application we want to develop and deploying that to a personal machine or local machine. This method is slow to set up but means that developers can replicate the exact AWS environment in local development environments.

## Decision

We will set up a Python development environment using:

- the Docker for Applications project to provide the infrastructure to deploy our Python applications
- poetry, a Python dependency manager to manage our code dependencies
- pytest, a de facto standard for unit testing
- pre-commit hooks to enforce coding best practices (e.g. always use a hyphen when referring to a file name)
- pre-commit to ensure that our applications can be run from the local machine
- gofmt to enforce a consistent style for each application

## Consequences

- If a developer uses more than one Docker installation, they will need to move their application development from one Docker container to the other as part of the deployment process.
- Our Docker containers will install python libraries, so our applications can be run with the same dependencies that are used in production AWS accounts.
- Using containers as our main development environments means that any external dependencies we have (e.g. GitHub Actions) must also be accessible from the machine on which we run the containers.
- Developers will have fast feedback cycles and can more easily switch between applications.

The EASi developers required a process and set of guidelines for workflow to ensure

[as described in 
https://www.easi.team/wiki/EASi-Process-Model](https://www.easi.team/wiki/EASI-Process-Model).

The EASi Process Model is based on a [version-based Agile

In addition, the team agreed to set forth a process and set of guidelines for writing
code that will be used throughout the EASi project. This process and set of
guidelines are collectively referred to as the EASi coding guidelines. The
EASI coding guidelines are a collection of guidelines for a variety of areas
including, but not limited to, the use of programming practices, programming
languages, code structure, documentation and testing. These guidelines can be
found in
[https://www.easi.team/wiki/EASI-coding-guidelines](https://www.easi.team/wiki/EASI-coding-guidelines).

The EASi project will be run using the EASi Process Model and the EASi coding
guidelines.

The implementation of the EASi Process Model and the EASi coding guidelines will
result in more stable and sustainable EASi code and increase the quality of
the EASi code.

The process for EASi development will be more stable and sustainable and produce
consistently coded code.

The team will be able to better understand the nature of the EASi code as it
progresses from a development state to production state.

https://www.easi.team/wiki/EASI-Process-Model](https://www.easi.team/wiki/EASI-Process-Model)

## Decision

Layer code, either frontend or backend, should be deployed in one of two ways:

* **Layer is independent** e.g. frontend, backend
* **Layer is integrated** e.g. data layer

The choice depends on how complex the deployment of the layer is. Our current frontend or backend code is deployed at a lower level than an ETL, and the deployment of the data layer is an easy process within our existing setup. For simplicity, we are going to deploy all our code that has no dependencies to external systems (that is the frontend, backend and all code in the data loader) as layers, and deploy them to our main servers.

* Our deployment process should be simpler and easier to run
* Our data layer should be able to handle changes to our server configuration without significant work

As we continue to expand the capabilities of the TTA Smart Hub, it is important to continue to define our API contract and specifications to ensure that we are building our API for longevity and discoverability.

## Decisions

### API Structure

The TTA Smart Hub will provide the following API endpoints:
- https://api.ttahub.com/clients
  - GET: Returns all active clients
  - POST: Creates a new client
  - GET: Returns a specific client by client id
- https://api.ttahub.com/projects
  - GET: Returns all active projects
  - POST: Creates a new project
  - GET: Returns a specific project by project id
- https://api.ttahub.com/users
  - GET: Returns all active users
  - POST: Creates a new user
  - GET: Returns a specific user by user id
- https://api.ttahub.com/permissions
  - GET: Returns all available permissions
  - POST: Creates a new permission
  - GET: Returns a specific permission by permission id
- https://api.ttahub.com/clients/{client}/projects
  - GET: Returns all projects for a specific client
- https://api.ttahub.com/projects/{project}/clients
  - GET: Returns all clients for a specific project
- https://api.ttahub.com/projects/{project}/users
  - GET: Returns all users for a specific project
- https://api.ttahub.com/projects/{project}/permissions
  - GET: Returns all permissions for a specific project

### API Authentication

API authentication will be accomplished by using OAuth 2.0 API keys. All endpoints besides `/users` will require API keys for authentication. API keys are not shared among users and will be revoked if they are found to be compromised.

### API Roles

TTA Smart Hub API roles will be:
- Owner
- Organization Owner
- Administrator
- Analyst

### API Authentication Response

API authentication response includes the following fields:
- `api_key`: API key used for authentication
- `expiration`: When API key expires
- `scope`: List of APIs that key has access to

### API Authentication Request/Response

API authentication request/response includes the following fields:
- `api_key`: API key used for authentication
- `expiration`: When API key expires
- `scope`: List of APIs that key has access to
- `level`: Authentication level

### API Data Request/Response Format

* `{schema}_items`: [schema_name].[item_name].[item_key]
  * Examples:
    * clients.[number].[field]
    * users.[number].[field]
    * projects.[number].[field]
    * permissions.[number].[field]
* [schema]: List of properties required in responses
* `total`: Total number of items in the list
* `next`: Link to the next page of results
* `current`: Number of items currently being reviewed
* `offset`: Number of items skipped so far
* `number`: Number of the item being returned (1-based)
* `fields`: List of fields being returned in the response
* `sort`: The field by which items are being sorted (1-based)
* `as_of`: Timestamp of the last data update (ISO 8601 format)

### API Data Response Type

All API data responses will be JSON and conform to the above format. Some fields may be null when they do not have a defined value.

### API data request

API data requests include the following fields:
- `field`: Field by which to sort
- `sort`: Sort order (ASC or DESC)
- `as_of`: Timestamp from which to calculate the response
- `current`: Number of items to be skipped so far
- `offset`: Number of items skipped so far
- `number`: Number of the item being returned (1-based)

## Consequences

In following these guidelines, we will ensure our API is discoverable and maintainable in the long term.

# Context

The API endpoints will read and write to the database. This will present some security and data integrity concerns, especially as the API will be open to the public. The main concern is that the API will not enforce the same data integrity that the client applications do. This means that if a client application fails to validate data before passing it to the API, it may not be caught either. For example, this could result in an incorrect date format being submitted, which would be difficult to detect.

A second concern is that the API will be open to the public. While a majority of requests will come from mobile clients, this does not completely preclude attackers from targeting the API directly. For example, attackers could be attempting to exhaust database resources, or send massive amounts of traffic to the API.

# Decision

We have decided to prevent attackers from directly accessing the database by way of the API. Instead, the API will forward requests to a dedicated database in an isolated environment. This prevents attackers from being able to bypass the API and access the database directly, and from being able to exhaust our database resources.

# Status

Accepted

# Consequences

We will have to provision a database for use by the API. We will also have to provision a cache to prevent excessive calls to the database. If attackers were able to launch DDoS attacks on the API, this would potentially still overwhelm the cache and database. While not as likely to be successful as directly attacking the database itself, it is still possible to imagine scenarios in which a DDoS attack on the API would overwhelm both our cache and database. It would be also possible to envision scenarios in which attackers were able to exhaust our database resources by submitting a large number of requests in quick succession, despite the use of a cache. We think this is unlikely but possible. We will have to accept this risk and hopefully it will be minimal.

## Status

Accepted

## Context

The preservation of a digital object’s long-term stability and accessibility requires a multi-part, risk-mitigating strategy. Digital preservation involves two key areas: 1) the preservation of the object’s file format and metadata, and 2) the preservation of digital copies of the object in multiple repositories.

A risk-mitigating strategy has three key components: 1) redundancy, 2) error detection and correction, and 3) authenticity verification. The last component is most critical to the long-term preservation of a digital object, and the subject of this ADR. Authenticity verification ensures that digital copies of an object created through digital preservation processes accurately represent the original, and that any modifications made are attributable to intentional design rather than to degradation of the file format over time.

## Decision

The authenticity of digital objects is the subject of continued research, and there is no single widely-adopted method for achieving this goal. At this point in time, the application team decided that the best approach to ensure authenticity is to apply checksum algorithms, as implemented in the file format. In addition, any application layer(s) that may create copies of digital objects should implement their own checksum algorithms for additional verification.

## Consequences

### Advantages

The application team will use checksum algorithms to ensure the authenticity of digital objects for both internal and public consumption.

### Disadvantages

There is no single method for achieving the goal of authentic digital copies. The application team will need to research and evaluate emerging best practices for assuring authenticity.

### Neutral

Researchers and application users will have the option of using checksum algorithms to verify the authenticity of digital objects.

## Status

Accepted

## Context

Historically the `Verify Service Provider` (VSP) has been made up of a number of different independent projects with distinct responsibilities and audiences.

A number of these projects were started out as "spike" projects to address a specific problem or capability that the JASMIN team wanted to see implemented as soon as possible, rather than following the typical project planning, design, and review processes.

One of the consequences of this spike-based approach has been that these projects have had to "jump to production" rather quickly, before the team has had a chance to review their architecture, design, or implementation.

This has sometimes led to the "jump to production" spikes having changed direction or scope from the original vision due to a perceived need to address something more immediate.

The team have had limited resources to devote to maintaining the projects as they've been developed.

Historically, the projects have tended to be quite small, with the team having focused on completing a specific task or piece of functionality at a time, rather than setting a long-term goal and working towards it.

All of the projects have been written in the JavaScript language.

All of the projects have been hosted on Github.

Some projects have been hosted on Cloud Foundry (CF).

Some projects have been hosted on Heroku.

## Decision

We have decided to move the different projects that the VSP makes up into a single repository and single deployment.

We have decided to change all of the projects to be written in the same programming language - javascript.

We have decided that we will make a single deployment into Heroku.

## Consequences

Having many projects in one repository will reduce friction as the team starts working on features across all the parts of the VSP. However, it will need careful management to avoid the codebase becoming too bloated to understand and maintain.

Moving all projects to JavaScript removes a risk factor: having parts of the code be written in different languages.

Hosting the projects all on Heroku gives the team greater flexibility when it comes to choosing monitoring and deployment tools, such as Heroku logging and Heroku deployment CLI. For the service team it's an opportunity to learn more about those tools and their capabilities.

Having all projects hosted on Heroku means that we cannot use Github as an audit tool for the projects' code. The best place to check this will be on a project-level.

Having all projects hosted on Heroku means that all projects need to be migrated to the same Heroku account.

Having all projects hosted on Heroku means that our Heroku account does not meet our licensing requirements for certain types of information security. As such, we have sought advice from the relevant team and will be moving all projects to AWS S3 at a later date.

The old, single `rotate()` function was too inflexible; with different results depending on the number of axis rotations applied, there were restrictions on how many degrees could be rotated at a time. This prevented users from implementing complex data visualization features, such as data tracks.

Since this was a long-running side project, we decided that we should only implement the rotating rectangle tools if we had not already implemented the temporal rotating rectangle tool. If the temporal rotating rectangle tool was not implemented, we could not easily store or query data relating to rotated rectangles.

Thus, we decided that the rotation should only apply to a single axis, and that only one axis should be used for rotating the rectangles when they are selected. For example, if the user selects two neighboring top-right aligned rectangles with a single mouse click, these should be rotated about the horizontal axis. If instead they were to click on the same rectangle with a single mouse click, they should be rotated about the vertical axis.

[Temporal rotating rectangle tool](https://github.com/zooniverse/front-end-monorepo/blob/120e80e5c37b05e48122247b8b77053574757056/packages/lib-classifier/src/components/data-visualization/tools/rotating-rectangle-tool/TemporalRotatingRectangleTool/TemporalRotatingRectangleTool.js)

## Decision

We decided to implement this feature using a `rotate()` function which would be stored in the `data-visualization` utility folder. The `rotate()` function would take a number of axis rotations to apply to a single rectangle. Each axis rotation would be equivalent to 90 degrees, measured in the direction which makes the rectangle's side length grow largest.

We also considered implementing a `rotateAxis()` function, which would only apply a single axis of rotation to the rectangle. Such a function would only make sense if the axis of rotation were guaranteed to be the same between rotations. For this reason, we decided that this function would not be implemented. The `rotate()` function is therefore the more general solution, and we decided that it would be used.

With such a function implemented, a `rotateOverlappingRectangles()` function was implemented, which would take the number of axis rotations to apply to a set of overlapping rectangles. These rectangles could be the same.

## Consequences

Using this feature, data tracks can now be easily implemented in data visualizations. This was not easy to implement without it. When a data track is created, a rotated rectangle is typically used to represent it, although this is not a strict requirement. In either case, data tracks can now be implemented simply using the `rotateOverlappingRectangles()` function.

As this feature is relatively new, we decided that it should be available as a preset option in the `DataTrackCreator` tool. This would make it easier for users to select and rotate rectangles for their data tracks. Data tracks that are rotated are still easily queryable using the `getTrack()` function, despite the rotation taking place after the track was created.

## Context

- eIDAS specification requires to manage identities on the EU and EU member state level.
- Identities on the EU level are managed by the European Commission and identities on the EU member state level are managed by the member state itself.
- Since the European Commission is the IDP the only way how to manage identities on the EU level is through the IDP.
- Therefore, all member states need to be able to get their IDs for EU entities from the IDP.
- IDs for non-EU entities need to be shared between the member states.
- Therefore there is a need for a mechanism for sharing IDs for EU entities and non-EU entities between member states.

## Decision

- A mechanism for sharing IDs for EU entities and non-EU entities between member states is implemented via a sync request.
- A special endpoint, e.g., `https://idp.opg-datamanager.eu/entities/sync` is exposed for this purpose, which accepts and responds to the requests in JSON format.
- The endpoint is secured via token authentication, e.g., JWT.
- `POST` request can be sent to the endpoint only for entities, which are stored in the `entities` table of the IDP.

### Request

The request has following format

```json
{
    "sessionId": "...",
    "query": {
        "IDP": "idp_name_for_the_request",
        "scope": "read | write",
        "entityIds": "...",
        "attributeFilter": "{...}"
    },
    "requestType": "eu | memberState"
}
```

### Response

The response has following format

```json
{
    "status": "SUCCESS | FAILED",
    "errorMessage": "...",
    "result": {
        "IDP": "idp_name_for_the_request",
        "euEntityIds": "...",
        "memberStateEntityIds": "...",
        "attributeIds": "...",
        "attributeValues": {
            "attributeId": "...",
            "attributeValue": "...",
            "attributeDescription": "...",
            "value": "...",
            "valueDescription": "...",
            "language": "...",
            "isEu": true | false
        }
    }
}
```

## Consequences

### Risks

- In the case of the `scope` being "write", the IDP gets full write access on entity's data.
- In the case of the `scope` being "read", the IDP gets read access only.

### Benefits

- Sync mechanism is implemented in a way that it does not put any burden on the IDP.
- Data transfer is [protected from unauthorized access](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc3274).

## Status

Accepted

## Context

In the context of the Data Platform team, 

* We have been looking at how the Data Platform should manage and retain data, 
* While working on the new data platform team's first major deliverable 
* We had to address many decisions around data management 

As part of our initial discovery of the Data Platform, we needed to understand which decision would best suit our Data Platform's purpose. 
When trying to understand which decision would be best, we came across a Data Platform project that was in an early phase. In that phase the project was still in discovery and understanding phase. We wanted to know if this Data Platform defined data retention on the data component level or the system level.

Based on our discovery we felt that it was important that Data Platform users could be consistent, which meant that data retention rules needed to be defined on the data component level.

## Decision

We decided that all our data components would define their own data retention rules. In this way we can allow for flexibility as we continue to learn about our data components, data retention rules, and the most appropriate rules for each data component. 

Defining retention rules on the data component level means that we don't need to update the system-wide data retention rules whenever we need to make a change to a data component's data retention rules. This allows for easier communication, collaboration, and iteration on these components. 

It also allows for different versions of data to be retained and published over time to the Data Catalog's content store.

## Consequences

With our data retention defined on the data component level, we have flexibility to do whatever we believe is appropriate for each data component data retention needs. This allows us to iterate quickly on each data component, or set of data components.

This approach also means that each data component should contain data retention rules that address a range of time periods and scenarios.

# 11 - Annotation aware lifecycle

Date: 2020-May-18

## Status

Accepted

## Context

We need to be able to specify if a component should be run from an annotation
attached to a lifecycle resource for use in testing or continuous delivery
environments.

For example:

```ts
class MyLifecycleClass implements ILifecycle {
    run(annotation?: RunAnnotation): Promise<MyResult> {
      // get the annotation if provided, otherwise get the default annotation
      const localAnnotation = new RunAnnotation();
      if (annotation) {
        // merge local with annotation
      }
      // perform the run action
      return this.runWithAnnotation(localAnnotation);
    }
  }
```

The above example shows a lifecycle class implementing ILifecycle. The
interface `ILifecycle` is:

```ts
interface ILifecycle {
    run(annotation?: RunAnnotation): Promise<TResult>;
}
```

Since we have `annotation?: RunAnnotation` in the above interface, we can
write in type script:

```ts
this.runWithAnnotation(annotation);
```

which is a local call to the run method with the annotation attached to it.

We have to be able to tell the compiler that this will only occur in some
use-cases and not always. We can do this by adding `?` to the end of the
method signature. This is an optional method:

```ts
run(annotation?: RunAnnotation)?
```

Since this is optional, any of the above cases are valid and the compiler
will not generate any errors.

## Decision

We will add a `annotation` field to every instance of `ILifecycle`.

If `this.run()` is called without an annotation, the `annotation` field will be
initialized with the default annotation `defaultAnnotation` which is defined
as a variable `const defaultAnnotation = new RunAnnotation();` in the
lifecycle class.

This approach will simplify adding optional annotation-aware methods to lifecycle
resources without generating compiler errors.

We will add a `AnnotationAware()` method to the `ILifecycle` interface and
in the process of adding a new lifecycle resource, we can implement a new
`AnnotationAware()` method.

## Consequences

### Advantages

- Adding a new optional method to a lifecycle class is no longer an error.
- The default annotation behavior works without the need of adding an additional
  property to the lifecycle interface.

### Disadvantages

- Not all methods will work if the annotation hasn't been explicitly
  specified. The default run behavior is defined in the lifecycle resource
  for use in non-annotated runs.
- We can only implement this for new lifecycle resources. If any existing
  lifecycle classes need to be annotated, we need to implement a new lifecycle
  resource which uses the new lifecycle class.

Date: 2018-09-11

## Status

Accepted

## Context

The upcoming alpha will support both Ledger and Trust Wallet as options for user wallets.

This ADR aims to establish the rule for what the app will do with wallets that are either not Ledger or Trust Wallet (in terms of feature support) and with regards to the interface provided for users.

### Choices Considered

There are a few choices that were considered when thinking about how the app should respond to wallet requests that fall outside the scope of our supported wallets:

- Leave the feature unsupported (in terms of code) and the interface undefined. This means that it will be possible to create a generic interface to access the wallet functionality later on if it proves necessary.
- Add wallet support for all other wallet types by creating a generic interface to the functionality. This means that it will be possible to create a generic interface to access the wallet functionality later on if it proves necessary.
- Provide a basic interface to wallet functionality that is tied specifically to that functionality. This means that if we have a different wallet supported by the app, the user can access wallet features via the interface but the interface is not generic and may not be reusable in the future for other wallets.

### Decision Outcome

The decision was made to add wallet support to all other wallet types by creating a generic interface to the functionality.

The reason for this choice is that we want to be as flexible as possible regarding wallet support. By providing a generic interface, we allow us to easily integrate future wallet types into the platform if it so happens that we want to support another wallet in addition to Trust and Ledger. This means that the functionality provided by the interface will be reusable in the future.

The decision was made to provide a basic interface to the wallet functionality that is tied specifically to that functionality. This means that if we have a different wallet supported by the app, the user can access wallet features via the interface but the interface is not generic and may not be reused in the future for other wallets. The reason for this choice is that we don't intend to use the interface to access the functionality for a wallet that is not Trust or Ledger. Providing an interface specifically to the wallet functionality means that if we have an interface to other wallet functionality in the future, it will be generic and may be used to access the functionality for any wallet. We would prefer that the interface would be generic in this case since the functionality would likely be the same, but this was not possible using the existing interface.

The decision was made to leave the functionality (i.e. the code) that is not wallet-related feature support independent.

The reason for this choice is that we want to add features which are specific to the Trust and Ledger ecosystems such as the option to import from/to Trust and the option to import/export from/to Ledger. While these features seem necessary at this point in time, we should keep open the possibility that we may want to remove these features in the future. It is preferable to add features that are ecosystem specific and can be modified or removed without requiring significant refactoring.

## Consequences

- The generic interface will be implemented.
- The generic interface will have methods to perform the basic wallet features such as withdraw, deposit, transfer, and query balance.
- The generic interface will not have methods to perform Trust or Ledger specific functionality.
