## Context and Problem Statement

Metatags are used to add information about a web page, such as its title, description, and keywords, for display in a search engine results page. They can also be used to track the performance of the web page, and to identify the author of the web page.

Since this information is visible to search engine crawlers and bots, it is extremely important that it is accurate and up to date. Even a single missing or misspelled character can have dramatic effects on search engine rankings.

## Considered Options

### Option 1: The metatags in the header are read and displayed
* If the metatags in the header cannot be read then the information is visible to robots but search engines will ignore the page.
* If the metatags in the header are read, then the information is visible in search engines.
* This is done for consistency and to make sure that search engines can read the webpage easily.

### Option 2: The metatags in the body are read and displayed
* If the metatags in the body cannot be read then the information is visible to search engines but search engines will ignore the page.
* If the metatags in the body are read, then the information is visible in search engines.
* This is done to increase search engine indexability.

### Option 3: The metatags are hidden from search engines
* Search engines won't display the information, but the information is still read and stored by bots that use robots.txt. This means robots could use the information to identify their source, location, etc.
* Search engines will display the information and bots will consume it.
* This is done to increase search engine indexability while decreasing search engine spam.

## Decision Outcome

Chosen option: "Option 3", because we want to keep this site free of unnecessary spam. Option 1 would decrease the usability of the site by not showing the relevant data, but could be implemented later. Option 2 is needed for future development of the site if we want to collect and display information about web page views.

### Positive Consequences

* A more accurate site description and title.

### Negative Consequences

* Not displaying site information could lead to a poor search engine indexation.

## Context and Problem Statement

Snb-project provides the possibility for the registration of complex metadata. 
The registration of all possible metadata can be easily done with only one class, by using a simple JSON data format.
The current registration data model was designed to register simple values.
In a registration such as `registration: [data]`, the data must be either a JSON object (a map, a dictionary) or a JSON array.
The attribute value must be a JSON object for attributes that have a "complex" value.
For example, if the complex value attribute type is a list, then the attribute value must be a list of JSON objects, which themselves can be simple or complex.

This is difficult to define formally and to implement, and even so that only applies to certain types of metadata (e.g. data, persons, organizations) and not others (e.g. location).

## Decision Drivers

* Easy to implement
* Good fit with [ADR-0007](https://github.com/UST-DATS/snb-project/blob/master/src/adr/0007-use-json-format-to-store-metadata.md)
* Support for the complex metadata attribute should be straightforward

## Considered Options

* Do not provide a complex metadata attribute
* Provide all complex metadata attributes
* Provide the current complex metadata attribute along with additional code and metadata attribute for more complex cases
* Provide the current complex metadata attribute only
* Provide a simple version of the complex metadata attribute

## Decision Outcome

Chosen option: "Provide additional code and metadata for more complex cases", since this fulfils all three of the decision drivers.

### Positive Consequences

* Complex metadata can be supported, e.g. multiple values for a property with complex value type (attribute)
* Registration of data with complex metadata is straightforward
* Can support the storage of simple and complex metadata values
* Can still store simple metadata

### Negative Consequences

* More complex metadata will be hard to support
* There is a hard boundary between "simple" and "complex" metadata
* This might be a short-term solution until a decision is made about the overall structure of the registration data model.
* Registration of data with simple metadata will be easy to support.
* This solution can be implemented as it is now, without further planning

* [ADR-0007](https://github.com/UST-DATS/snb-project/blob/master/src/adr/0007-use-json-format-to-store-metadata.md)

## Context

Traditionally, authentication and access control have been separate concerns. Authentication is usually implemented as a thin layer on top of a database, and grants permissions based on user-supplied credentials. Access control, in contrast, is usually implemented as a more complex system that grants permissions based on more nuanced factors such as organizational roles, location, and time of day.

Often, there are no clear guidelines for designing access control systems, and the result is often a complicated, convoluted mess of code and configuration that is difficult to understand and even more to change. As such, most systems built today use some form of RBAC to make adding new permissions and roles simpler and easier to reason about.

This ADR defines the approach that will be used to approach RBAC in this project. It also defines a number of key principles that will guide implementation.

## Decision

Based on the existing best practices and the proposed [Django-RBAC](https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/stable/rubs/), this project will adopt the following RBAC principles:

-   The system will be built around the concept of a **primary group**. This group will store all of the user's permissions and roles in database tables associated with that group.
-   All other user permissions and roles will be granted through **additional groups** (e.g. `create_superuser`), which are given to users by the primary group.
-   Only one of each additional group will be allowed to be added to a user.
-   The system will store all permissions as **domain-specific classes**. This would be an attribute of each group (e.g. `manage_emails`), and would have different meanings for different users based on their group membership.
-   Permissions will have a **primary domain**, which will be the core domain of the permission (e.g. `manage_emails`).
-   For every permission, there will be at least one **associated domain**, which can be more specific than the primary domain. A permission with multiple associated domains is not valid.
-   The permission manager should handle the following:
    -   Managing permissions and associated domains
    -   Adding/removing permissions/associated domains to/from users
-   The Django Admin will be able to display all permissions and associated domains for each user.

Note that this ADR does not define what permissions the primary group has. This will be left up to the group itself. For example, the primary group could have permissions such as `manage_emails`, `manage_projects`, and `manage_users`.

## Consequences

Using a strong RBAC approach will allow us to:

-   Implement granular access control without having to re-invent the wheel
-   Grant fine-grained permissions to users
-   Avoid having to constantly re-invent ourselves to solve access-related problems
-   Decouple authentication and access control
-   Allow users to take on a variety of roles

Implementing strong RBAC will also:

-   Increase the complexity of the project
-   Increase the complexity of the code

Due to RBAC being a widely-understood and well-researched solution, and to the fact that this project is intended for use by an organization with sophisticated users, these consequences are viewed as positive.

## References

-   [Django-RBAC](https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/stable/rubs/), retrieved 28 October 2018
-   [Python 3 - Objects oriented permissions](https://www.digitalocean.com/community/tutorials/python-3-objects-oriented-permissions), retrieved 28 October 2018
-   [Security - A primer on permission and authentication in Django](https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/stable/intro/)
-   [Permission and Authentication in Django](http://docs.getdjangopackages.org/en/latest/permissions/), retrieved 28 October 2018
-   [Django-security](https://github.com/django-security/django-security), retrieved 28 October 2018

## Status

Accepted

## Context

We want to be able to debug connectivity issues and understand why a tenant's applications have restricted access to other tenants' applications. In Cloud foundry, applications have a default security group that controls the ingress traffic. You can grant more fine-grained permissions to applications using security group rules.

A key issue is whether the default security group used by applications, which comes with the network, is a tenant-wide security group and can accept ingress traffic from any tenant's applications (which would be acceptable) or whether it's an individual application's security group, in which case it will not be accessible to any tenant's applications. A tenant's security group does not default to a wide range of IPs.

We wanted to be sure whether our VPC flow logs were being collected by the AWS VPC flow logging service and whether any ingress traffic was being denied for security reasons.

The flow logs do not show ingress traffic for applications that cannot establish a connection (the connection could have failed or the application may have been stopped), but they do show egress traffic and the source and destination IPs of the applications.

## Decision

We believed this to be the default in case a tenant did not have an application-level security group in place. This default security group was the source of the issue.

Using the flow logs, we were able to discern that all egress traffic from the tenancy-monitoring application and the tenant-application services was successfully transmitted; the only traffic that was not transmitted was ingress traffic. In particular, there was no inbound SSH traffic for the two containers. The reason for this is that their default security group (mentioned above) did not allow SSH traffic (which uses port 22) for traffic from anywhere in the tenant VPC, even though it allowed traffic for other protocols like TLS.

The [issue](https://github.com/alphagov/cloud-foundry-tenancy-monitoring/issues/12) in the tenancy-monitoring service does not currently allow configuration of the default security group, but it does provide a way for a container to establish a security group rule as its default security group (see this commit: https://github.com/alphagov/cloud-foundry-tenancy-monitoring/commit/af87f1c42ae96a437795273a27ad4178648adfc). There was an additional issue that was the subject of this conversation in the [tenant-application](https://github.com/alphagov/cloud-foundry-tenancy-monitoring). There was no ingress security group rule for ingress traffic from anywhere in the tenant VPC, because it can accept all traffic from the tenant VPC. Because the default security group is a tenant-wide security group for all services in this instance, it would be less efficient to allow the ingress traffic from every tenant's VPC.

## Context
We want to start our apps with a 'first run' experience that is familiar to
users of the system in general, and to include some experimental/
feature/bug-fix work that would be separate to the main app version. We
should aim that this first run is similar to the original system but with
some new and improved features to maximise ease of use and future-proofing.

The use of `first run` is defined as the first time a user executes the
system apps after a system restore. This usually means a system rebuild,
but as long as all of the apps for the system are re-installed at a
specific point, `first run` can be represented as a date of a year, month,
and day as a timestamp. 

We should decide whether `first run` is a data point that is captured and
stored during a `first run` or if it is an action that is performed.

To perform a `first run` system restore, we should update and use a version
that is not published to the app store for the use of experimental/
feature/bug-fix data. This version should be marked as such by the version
number to the system apps and the data should be published to the experiment
protocol service.

## Decision
We will use `first run` as a date of a year, month, and day as a timestamp to
represent the date and time of a user first executing the system apps after a
system restore.

We will only store timestamps for the `first run` date in the app-store
version. We will store timestamps in the experiment protocol service (in the
logs) for the `first run` date at the time of experiment data submission.

## Consequences

To use experimental/feature/bug-fix data, we should publish a version for the
system apps that is not published to the app store.

We should publish experimental/feature/bug-fix data, and the `first run` date
to the experiment protocol service (as part of the experimental/feature/bug-fix
data submission).

We should take care in selecting the experimental/feature/bug-fix data to be
recorded. It should be relevant and capable of supporting the experiment.

To decide whether experimental/feature/bug-fix data is recorded for a `first
run` or whether this is an action that is performed, we should analyse the

## Context and Problem Statement

Applications run by the Government of Justice and all its partner organizations must be both 
operable and auditable. As an added constraint, the operating system of these applications will likely be
hybrid (a mix of cloud and local servers).

In this context, we define two distinct operational and auditing requirements that we can address
separately, which can be accomplished through CQRS and Event Sourcing (ES). CQRS and ES serve different purposes
to address these distinct requirements.

## Decision Drivers

* The need to fulfill operational and auditing requirements
* We're assuming that we operate in a low-trust environment
* We're assuming that we operate at a high autonomy/governance level

## Considered Options

* Use CQRS and ES together to be both auditable and operative
* Use only CQRS to be both auditable and operative
* Use only ES to be auditable

## Decision Outcome

Chosen option: "Use only CQRS to be both auditable and operative", because this will allow for flexibility
to choose which part of the application to use and thus support fast iteration on our clients' operational
and auditing requirements. Additionally, the use of CQRS and ES will allow our clients to have direct access
to all their data and thus support faster iteration on our clients' operational requirements.

The use of ES will support the operational requirements, and the use of CQRS will support the auditing 
requirements. Since ES and CQRS have different purposes and can be used to address different 
operational requirements (even within the same application), ES and CQRS may be used independently
to allow for flexibility for our clients.

A final key argument is that we would like all applications to support a high level of autonomy, which ES and
CQRS help to enable. Both ES and CQRS support flexible and fine-grained access to data, which will allow our
clients to support fine-grain isolation of data access and thus allow our clients to support a high level 
of autonomy. To support this level of autonomy, clients should also be able to modify data and to track what
data they've modified. This flexibility is key to supporting high autonomy.

### Negative Consequences

* We'd have to support both CQRS and ES.
* While most of our clients' applications have relatively stable data requirements (i.e., the data
that they store doesn't change rapidly), our operations may have dynamic data requirements.

## Pros and Cons of the Options

### Use ES and CQRS together

CQRS and ES together would enable the fastest iteration on our clients' operational requirements. This is because
ES will be used to write to the data store and CQRS will be used to send requests to the operating 
system (i.e., our applications' clients), which operate as separate services.

Since ES and CQRS serve different purposes to support different operational requirements, our clients
can use one of either ES or CQRS to address our client's requirements. For example, our client's 
application's ES could be used to send emails on behalf of the client, while the client's CQRS
could be used to send emails when we develop our own email client.

This kind of CQRS and ES deployment will enable our client to keep fast iteration on our client's 
operational requirements while maintaining full audit capabilities (i.e., the ability to track what data is stored
where and who has changed which data).

CQRS and ES together would likely require the CQRS module to be built in a different way than the ES module
(to a new version of the CQRS module) to expose all required functionality. Since all our clients' 
applications have the capability to store persistent data, this CQRS module has to be implemented somewhere
in our CQRS architecture. We'd have to implement both ES and CQRS modules. We would add ES and CQRS modules
to the set of modules in our open-source project.

Since the two modules would serve different purposes and be implemented in a different way and stored in 
separate directories in our open-source repository, they would be easier to find and easier to remove when
necessary. While it's possible that there's a different reason to separate these modules, I don't see the
need to use separate modules here.

_Our users need a way to send notifications and emails to users. We have
chosen to follow the [publish-subscribe pattern](https://martinfowler.com/eaa_patterns/publish-subscribe.html) as documented by
Martin Fowler in his book, _Release It!_ The first version of this pattern uses
the _EventBus_ API to observe which methods in _BasePack_ will be registered as
observers to the published events. We have a number of [open-source
projects](https://github.com/orgs/james-project/projects/4083) that implement this kind of 
middleware which we can use to achieve the goal.

In the current release, we use a simple CQRS-inspired approach where we
handle all events in the `BasePack` in the `BasePackSubscriber` class and publish
all those events to a RabbitMQ broker, which will handle any registered
notifications. A consumer registers to any event by adding their address to
the group on the broker.

As of version 1.x, `BasePackSubscriber` monitors all the subscriptions and will
execute their `handle` methods in the correct sequence for each event. It would
be nice to decouple the notification execution from the subscription registration
in order to make it simple. 

This could be achieved via a message broker with a registry. If we choose
this approach, then our `BasePackSubscriber` will expose a port and receive
registry/unregister requests and then forward those to the message broker for
distribution.

In a real-world, we will have consumers that do not have access to the broker
or are a different system completely. We need to be able to distribute these
types of notifications to anyone as the broker could have bugs, or be in
maintenance and not be updated anymore. Alternatively, we can build an event
queue based on some technology that has a database and keep the records on
the Broker.

We have used the [JSMQ](https://github.com/jmq/jsmq) library to facilitate
these methods. JSMQ is using [redis](https://redis.io/) for the data store and
has a port that can be configured and registered to the broker.

## Considered Alternatives

* Using plain rabbitMQ without the registration feature; this is to follow
the standard approach for subscribing to events.
* Using a registry for the brokers with JSMQ library and distribute the
notifications to a consumer
* Using a registry for the brokers with the JSMQ library and register all
notifications to the broker as consumers 

## Decision Outcome

* Chosen Alternative: Using a registry for the brokers with JSMQ library and
register all notifications to the broker as consumers

Since this implements the publish-subscribe and the registration feature to
the broker is very important to help us maintain the platform.

## Pros and Cons of the Alternatives

### Using plain rabbitMQ without the registration feature

We had an alternative here but decided not to take it anymore since we're
trying to simplify things and we're making consumers consume notifications. This
is done for the same reason as we're not using a queue for handling notifications. 

* `+` simpler code, since all methods that receive notifications are added to
`BasePackSubscriber`, which manages the message broker, which publishes the event
* `+` we can add a port for registering notifications to the broker.
* `+` we can add a port for publishing the events to a different broker.
* `-` the Broker is not in our control
* `-` we'd have to manually distribute the event registration and the notification
registry
* `-` if we decide to add notifications to the consumers, it'd be a non-atomic 
operation
* `-` we'd have to do a lot of things ourselves (get the configuration for 
brokers and how to communicate with them)

### Using a registry for the brokers with JSMQ library and distribute the notifications to a consumer

* `+` we can have a registry, which means all brokers will be registered
* `+` we can add a port for registering the notifications to the broker.
* `+` we can add a port for publishing the events to a different broker
* `-` the Broker is not in our control
* `-` we have to manually distribute the event registration and the notification 
registry
* `-` we'd have to do a lot of things ourselves (get the configuration for 
brokers and how to communicate with them)

## Context

One of the main goals of this project is to have an easy way to create pages
for the OpenFIDO project. One of the many questions to solve for that goal
is how the project will handle text content. This will include page text,
tool tip text, and any other text content used in the OpenFIDO service.

Using a CMS allows developers to have a user interface to modify and test
content, something that is useful when working on development. Having an external
CMS is something that was done in the work for the
[GOV.UK prototype](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-prototype-kit) project. This
project provides an easy way to create content pages, but with some drawbacks.
One of the main issues with this CMS is that it is only usable during development
for the prototype kit project.

Since this project will be another tool for GOV.UK (as stated in the
[project brief](https://github.com/alphagov/open-fido/blob/master/Project_Brief.docx)),
it will most likely receive use from an external audience (i.e. not just
developers). Given this, it is prudent to choose a CMS that is accessible
to people other than those working on the project.

## Decision

While it may be technically feasible to create a CMS using the
[govuk-prototype-kit project's CMS](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-prototype-kit),
this project should not be used for the OpenFIDO CMS. Instead, the CMS
should be an outside service that is accessible to anyone.

There are a number of options in this category and each have their own pros
and cons. Examples of these are, Ghost, CMS Liberator, and/or MediaWiki. For
the purpose of this document, we will assume that the CMS is one of the more
popular, general-purpose systems.

Based on experience of using the existing CMS for the prototype kit project and
a little research, Ghost is the most promising candidate. Ghost is fast and
has been proven in production use to meet a number of requirements. For the
purpose of this document, we will assume that all of these qualities exist
for the OpenFIDO CMS as well.

## Status

Accepted.

## Consequences

Choosing an external CMS will add another component to the OpenFIDO service
to be maintained. The system should be chosen such that it will be easy to
learn and maintain over time.

A CMS service should meet a number of basic requirements to be acceptable.
These include, having a consistent hosting environment, storing content in
a format that is easy to import and export, and providing a user interface
that is easy to use.

A CMS service should meet some or all of the following requirements to be
considered good enough for use in this project:

- being able to receive email content
- being open-source
- being hosted in Europe
- being hosted by a government entity

## Context

Using AB Testing to determine whether one feature or change is more successful than another is a common method to make decisions on improvements to our application.

AB testing works by randomly assigning users to groups in an AB test, and then by tracking which of those groups perform better based on specified metrics. A common example of this is the 1% AB test, where we randomly select 1% of users to be in the experimental group, and the remaining 99% form the control group. In this scenario, the experimental group does not get the new feature or change, while the control group does. This enables us to compare how well each group performs against the other.

We have conducted AB tests on our applications before, but have not used AB testing infrastructure to support AB testing for a long time. Since AB testing has a long history, there are a lot of different implementations out there. This makes a simple decision more complicated, as we'd have to decide which to use.

In order to help understand which of these implementations would work best, and to reduce the amount of time to spend researching, we have chosen a hosted solution to use for AB testing. This solution is called AB Test Kit and is a [custom Rails tool](https://github.com/markbates/ab_test_kit) that has been developed by Shopify to be used with Rails applications.

It has been used by several Shopify customers and has proved its effectiveness. The host is highly recommended by Shopify.

## Decision

We will use AB Test Kit to perform AB testing on our applications.

## Consequences

We've found a simple and effective AB testing infrastructure which has been developed in collaboration with Shopify, and as a result has been used by their customers for quite some time. We will have more information and confidence when deciding the merits of using AB tests when testing improvements to our application, as well as being able to communicate the results to users of our applications.

## Context

An instance will receive the `circrequests` entry for every transaction with a source/dest IP address that has been routed through the cache.
After a transaction has been added to the cache there are now a number of entry types to handle:
- Cache hits
- Cache misses (a number of which are now `circrequests`)
- New entries that have been added to the cache due to `circrequests`

To avoid ambiguity the cache will now have an additional entry to identify its source in terms of `circrequests`.

This presents some problems:
1. We are only able to query the cache using one entry type (the existing `entrytype`) to identify the request for an entry
2. It is very difficult to track how many times a single entry is created
3. There are two different ways of storing information in the cache for requests that can be identified as `circrequests`

## Decision

Instead of maintaining a separate `circrequests` entry for every transaction we will instead use one entry for
all requests that can be identified as `circrequests`.

## Consequences

The cache will have two separate types of entry:
- Cache hits
- Circrequests

This will:
- Provide a single point of access for requests that have been routed through the cache
- Allow for queries into the cache to be scoped to a single type of entry
- Reduce the number of steps involved in identifying the source of a request in the cache
- Be easy to implement using existing functions
- Provide some form of uniqueness ID to requests that use the cache. This would be useful to identify
a transaction that uses the cache in the event of a duplicate transaction (see https://stackoverflow.com/questions/52467436/cache-keys-are-the-transaction-IDs-and-are-dupes-in-the-redis-stores-in-case-of-a-duplicate-transaction-are-all-the-events-re-written-to-cache)

The cache will still provide both of the following methods:
- The entrytype `entrytype`
- The original transaction ID from the transaction (via `hash/get(entrytype, "transactionID")`)

For the time being we will also preserve the 6-byte `source/dest IP` for the purpose of `circrequests` data
and this will be stored in its own entry (e.g. `entrytype: "source/dest IP: x.x.x.x,y.y.y.y")`

`hash/set()` and `hash/get()` are both fast which allows for fast lookup for entries. Fast lookup is critical to the 
expected performance of 50k-100k transactions/sec.

## Context

There are several package managers available for Node. Jest itself runs without a package manager, but will require one when we start using dependencies.

While I was using the Node Package Manager in my previous project, I had encountered problems with the way it can organize a package's code into folders and subfolders. Specifically, I had run into problems with the `node_modules` folder when attempting to organize files across multiple directories within a single package. See these [examples](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/6806643/how-to-manage-packages-installed-with-npm-without-the-node_modules-folder) and [article](https://github.com/joelparkerhenderson/the-node-pkg-distributor) for inspiration.

For my current project, I was drawn to the idea of using Yarn. Yarn seems to provide a much more intuitive experience in its code organization, specifically by allowing the `node_modules` folder to remain a singular folder containing npm-managed dependencies, and then providing subfolders for the project's code. The article I'm referencing, by Michael Nygard, specifically states, "Yarn's internal storage mechanism is conceptually quite simple: it's just plain old JavaScript (with no new syntax added), that lives in a folder in your hard drive, and is updated to reflect your state of dependency." I was particularly interested in the `yarn.json` file, which seems to serve as a single point of entry for the package's code.

However, when I installed the CLI in an attempt to use Yarn, I ran into a problem that hasn't been reported as an issue in this article. The CLI will not install, but will return the following error:

```
> site@0.1.0 lint /home/mchelen-govuk.dsdmoj.uk
> yarn lint

use of 'yarn' is not possible, must use 'yarn' to start the CLI

Referenced from: ./lib/lint/rules.js
```

After investigation, I came to the following conclusions:

- The error message indicates a problem in the local installation, rather than an issue in the upstream Yarn project.
- The `yarn` command appears to be broken in my environment.
- I was able to get the code running by using `yarn workspaces`, but this seemed to be a temporary fix, as it doesn't actually provide a simple user experience when switching between projects.
- The only workaround I could find was to run `yarn --frozen-lockfile` when running `yarn workspace`, but this prevents us from using `yarn test` and so on.

## Decision

In order to use a package manager, the Node Package Manager was chosen.

## Consequences

Because of the way npm organizes code into folders and subfolders, it was necessary to follow the examples from [Joel Parker Henderson's article](https://github.com/joelparkerhenderson/the-node-pkg-distributor), in order to avoid problems arising from the way npm deals with multiple directories under a single package name. This will make it difficult for others to read the code from the `node_modules` folder, but they should be able to re-create the directory structure locally by following the instructions in the article.

## Context

Since we are supporting multiple game modes, we're going to need to define the dimensions and position of objects based on the mode. We already have the general game area, but we need to define how the gameplay will be affected by the different modes.

For example, in the _One Life_ mode, there's a huge area with multiple generators to spawn enemies, so we can create a single entity to spawn those enemies. In _VS_ mode, we can only create a single entity to spawn enemies, so we'll need to use two entities in the same layer for different entity types in the same layer. This is going to get hairy fast, so we'll need to find a way to describe those layer types.

We were going to use custom JSON to describe those entity types but it's not going to work with the game engine, so we'll need to find another solution.

## Decision

We're going to use the _Schema.org/SDL_1_0_Specification_ to define those entity types. SDL is designed to support multiple entity types without creating multiple entity types on your server and the game. There are only three specific entities defined for each layer:
* _Entity_: Is a root type for all entities, you can think of it like the container of your other entities, you can think of it like a JS object, it is a schema_specific_entity type.

In order to define those entity types, we're going to define a top-level object. Each group corresponds to one of our entity types. Here's an example of what an _Entity_ would look like:

## Status

Accepted

## Context

Background task allows users to run programs on data from the program data source.
At this time we only support the `db` and `table` in the data source. `db` will store the background task ID and `table` will contain the data for the task. It should be an independent process from the `server`. This process must be:
- atomic
- fault-tolerant

## Decision

After trying several approaches, we found that using a [redis](https://redis.io) is a good approach to manage the data for the background task. In particular since we want to be able to interrupt the background task in case of a network failure. The `redis` server should have been installed on the `server`. At this time, we only support the `redis` type of data source in the `server`. We decided to use the existing `redis` database instead of investing additional effort in creating a `redis` server on the `server` and using it via redis client (e.g. [node](https://github.com/NodeRedis/node-redis)).

The `server` will save the data for the background task on its own database.

The `server` will provide an HTTP interface for the background task so that it can retrieve the data once it was available.

The `redis` and `server` should be both owned by the same username.

## Consequences

- `redis` is already an open source software and it is a community project.
- `redis` can be installed on many platform:
  - Linux
  - macOS
  - Windows
  - MacOS X
- `redis` has a mature and stable release for many years
- `redis` has active community to help solve any problem

While it is mature and stable, `redis` still has the release plan for next year: [2021-redis-roadmap](https://github.com/redis-store/redis-roadmap/blob/main/docs/index.md).

As a `redis` client, `node` should be used by `node` runtime.

### Background tasks
The background tasks can be stored in the `redis` database and will be available for all time.

### Network failures
In case of the failure to `redis`, the `table` will be removed.

### Concurrent users
Using `redis` requires to cache the keys. If we have concurrent users, it is an issue.

If concurrent users want to run the background tasks, one of the `table` will be deleted. In terms of a table that it should be an idempotent task. This could be solved by removing the `table` while we have still enough memory in the `redis` server.

## Status

Accepted

## Context

Need to compare two WhaleObservation objects to discern differences.

`compareByDate` implements a `Comparator<WhaleObservation>` using an inner `compareByDate` object, which in turn uses an inner `compareByDate` object to do the actual comparing (see `compareByDate` method documentation).

If we use the existing `compareByDate` and reverse its `compareByDate` method, it will sort in reverse date order, which is likely not what we want.
If we use a different `compareByDate` object, we'd need to implement a `Comparator<WhaleObservation>` using a class that is not `compareByDate` (see `compareTo` method documentation).
If we use `compareByDate`, it will sort by date.

## Decision

We will add a second `Comparator<WhaleObservation>` which implements a `compareByDate` using a class that is not `compareByDate`. This new `comparator` will sort in the reverse order from the original `compareByDate`.
We will then use the `compareByDate` and the `reverse` `comparator` in the `compareTo` method to determine the order of the objects.

This implements a stable-stable comparison.

## Consequences

WhaleObservation objects will be compared by date in reverse order (most recent last).

WhaleObservation objects with the same date will be sorted by time of day (all-or-nothing comparison).

## Status

Accepted

## Context

There are a number of tools which can be used to manage workflow and
manage branches, including git checkout / git push; pull requests; GitHub
labels; and possibly others. The main way to do this is via:
  - [git](https://www.git.wiki.kernel.org/index.php)
  - [git-flow](https://datasift.github.io/git-flow/IntroducingGitFlow.html)
  - [GitHub](https://github.com/): Pull requests, labels, milestones
  - [labels](https://github.com/labels)
  - [milestones](https://github.com/milestones)

We need to decide how to make pull requests via Git to merge code between
branches.

We need to decide on our Git workflow and practice.

We need to decide on a way to merge branches into master.

We need to decide on a way to merge the current master branch into
develop.

We need to decide on a way to manage code organization on GitHub.

## Decision

1. Use pull requests as the primary development tool. This is done via
  [GitHub pull requests](https://github.com/features/pull-requests). This
  is done for several reasons:
  - Pull requests are an accepted standard for collaborating on code.
  - They provide a basic form of code review (using comments on pull
    requests).
  - They provide a mechanism for branching and merging branches.
  - They are the preferred way for GitHub to determine a change which needs
    to be made, i.e. a new release (based on milestones).

2. Use git-flow as our Git workflow and practice. This is done because it
  provides a method for managing branches, based on the concept of release
  branches. The methodology is documented at [datasift.github.io/git-flow
  (Introducing GitFlow.html)](https://datasift.github.io/git-flow/IntroducingGitFlow.html).

3. Use labels to manage code organization on GitHub, including milestones.

## Consequences

Since this is an emerging pattern, it is likely that people will re-use
patterns as we make the decision to use pull requests as the primary
development tool.

There are likely to be issues with the workflow. There are some issues,
for example, with merge conflicts, where we'd prefer to have a more linear
process. This is likely to be the same issues that all new projects in
their early stages have. It's likely that in practice a more linear process
is preferable. Pull requests are an effective mechanism for collaborating on
code, but the pull requests process is likely a more linear workflow.

Using labels to organize GitHub is an effective way to do this, allowing
us to group changes to code together.

Using labels to track milestones is an effective way to manage the release
branches.

In Dec 2019 we decided to create [Forwarders](https://github.com/Alfresco/Alfresco-Data-Model/blob/master/release/specification/forwarders.html)
so that external users can publish Alfresco metadata to external Alfresco Instances, for e.g. content delivery network.

1. We can not get the search metadata in our Alfresco Search GUI.

### Why is the solution different than previous solutions?

This decision is different from the previous one because the solution uses an abstraction layer (Elastic Search) over Alfresco Search.
Elastic Search and Alfresco Search both are capable to perform the required operations but from a different perspective.

**Here are the positive consequences of abstraction**
- The abstraction layer helps us to split the tasks.
- The abstraction layer serves the internal logic of Alfresco Search and can be implemented using Elastic Search features.

**Here are the negative consequences of abstraction**
- More complexity will be added because we must implement more abstraction.

### Decision Outcome

**We decided to implement the Forwarders using Elastic Search for the following reasons:**

- It is more flexible than Alfresco Search.
- It is easier to perform advanced searches like text searches and text term counts.

With the proposed architecture the following tasks would be done:

1. We will implement a Java code that will be able to send the data to Elastic Search and will store all required search metadata
1. We will create an UI component to expose the Elastic Search service.
1. We will implement a REST API to manage all operations in the service.

**Pros and Cons**

#### Pros

- More control over the search metadata we use in Alfresco Search
- It is easier to implement advanced search, like text searches, text term counts, and text term frequency counts.
- It is easier to implement the search in the Alfresco GUI.

#### Cons

- We add more complexity to the architecture of the software.
- We must store more metadata to Elastic Search.

### Creating Forwarders using Alfresco Search

#### Pros

- We use the same tool we use to implement Alfresco Search.

#### Cons

- We can not perform advanced searches.
- We must store all metadata in Alfresco Storage
- The forwarding capability is still not as good as Elastic Search in terms of performance and reliability.
- We can not perform advanced searches like text searches and text term counts.

## Status

Accepted

## Context

The intention is to be able to use this library (named lib-classifier)
for multiple projects, not just `panoptes-javascript`. We want to
make it easier for users to create their own instances of
`lib-classifier` that would work for multiple projects.

We need a mechanism that would allow us to specify the options that
get passed into the library (e.g. the defaults). We want them to be
easily updated without generating a new version of the library.

Ideally, this mechanism would allow other developers to easily override
the configuration.

## Decision

We will add a `default.js` file to the package. This would be used to
provide a default configuration when starting a new lib-classifier
instance (defaults will only apply to `panoptes-javascript`
by the version of this library.) The default.js is a json
object and the keys are the names of the options. The value of the
options defaults to the value specified in the `options.js` file, or
the value that will be passed in when starting a lib-classifier
instance.

The `options.js` file contains two keys: `defaults` and
`overrides`. The `defaults` value is an array of objects, each
representing an option (e.g. label: 'option key', default: 'option value').
The `overrides` value is an array of objects that override the defaults.
For example:

```
overrides: [
  {
    key: 'key',
    value: 'value'
  },
  {
    key: 'key',
    value: 'value'
  }
]
```

To specify the overrides, an option key and value must be provided
in a single entry. The overrides value (if present) is treated as a list
of entries, rather than a single entry.

To specify a custom start command, a `start.js` file should be added
to the `lib-classifier` package. The file would be named
`start.<command>.<file>.js`, e.g. `start.server.js` for a server
start command, or `start.client.js` for a client start command,
and the command would be a string, e.g. `server` or `client`.

The start file would be a json object representing the configuration.
It would have a `defaults` key, which contains an array of objects
each representing an option. For example:

```
defaults: {
  label: 'option key',
  default: 'option value',
  overrides: []
}
```

This start file would be used when executing `lib-classifier --help`
to specify the help text, or when running a local instance to create
a start file, which would be used when running a `panoptes-javascript
--help`.

## Consequences

This method provides a mechanism for creating a new library that
can be shared across multiple projects, and provides a way for
other developers to easily override the configuration.

This approach does not completely specify how to build the
`default.js` file, which should be a simple json file that
can be created by other developers easily, and used in the same
way as the `options.js` file.

For example, the `default.js` file could include the
`options.js` file, to derive the values, but should be written
using a single json object.

## Status

Accepted

Implements [47. DDD defines ubiquitous language](0047-ddd-defines-ubiquitous-language.md)

## Context

The runtime dependencies of a process are its dependencies on other AWS services.

These dependencies can be identified at several levels of abstraction:

* Within a component/process
* Within a service
* Within a service group

Within a component, we define a runtime dependency as a dependency on GCP services. These dependencies may be identified at a high level (e.g., “Google Cloud Storage”) or at a low level (e.g., “Google Cloud Pub/Sub”).

Within a service, we can identify runtime dependencies as dependencies on GCP services, or dependencies on other services within GCP (e.g., GSP).

In the real world, the terms “runtime” and “cloud” are often used interchangeably, but within the architectural scope, the distinction between “runtime” and “cloud” is necessary for a complete description of the process’s dependencies. The runtime refers to the operating conditions (e.g., a process that runs during the lifetime of a container), while the cloud refers to infrastructure configuration (e.g., the configuration of the VMs that run the processes).

The combination of a cloud and a runtime environment is responsible for maintaining continuous deployment and testing of a service during development, as well as continuous integration and deployment of a service for production.

### Alternative approaches

Based on the knowledge gained while building the [Cloud Storage](0048-cloud-storage.md) and [Dataflow Diagram](0022-dataflow-diagram.md), we considered following alternative approaches for modeling runtime dependencies:

* Using “hosted” environments
* Using “cloud native” environments

The GCP services included in the [Dataflow Diagram](0022-dataflow-diagram.md) serve both as runtime and cloud environments. By using the concept of runtime and cloud environments, we can realize our vision by using the right environment for the right job.

## Decision

The runtime environment is the GCP configuration required to run the application in Google Cloud Platform, based on the GCP services.

In addition to the runtime environment, a cloud environment exists, since the GCP services are also the means by which the process is deployed and operated.

There is a clear distinction between a cloud environment, which is permanent, and a runtime environment, which is only active during the operation of the process.

## Consequences

- This concept is necessary for understanding the process of delivering and maintaining services.
- Dependencies on GCP services and/or other GCP-based services can be identified.
- It is possible to use a dependency injection library to identify dependencies of processes on GCP services.

## References

- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cloud_environment, retrieved 31 August 2021
- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Runtime_environment, retrieved 31 August 2021

Date: 05/04/2016

## Status

Accepted

## Context

We like to use an environment variable to configure our applications.  For example, the project manager uses an environment variable to determine the root directory for the project.

This was done because environment variables are easy to change and can be loaded in at startup, and are easy to read for developers.  For example the `README.md` in the `bin/` directory in VS Code shows the environment variables loaded by an application.

Configuration variables set in the app as static fields do not change and cannot be changed after deployment, making development easier, since we have fast-changing development environments.

## Decision

Avoid setting configuration variables in the `config/*.config.js` files, especially at compile time.

## Consequences

The static fields that store the configuration variables (e.g. `the-project-manager.config.js`) should be renamed to `config.js` (without the `.config.js`).  The `config.js` files should be merged into other files, or a separate file can be loaded in using `require`.

## Reason

We like to maintain a simple and readable and writable codebase, and in our current way of doing it the `config.js` file is both readable and writable. However, we want to enable easier development and deployment.

If the `config.js` file is compiled and deployed and its static properties are accessed, the code will fail to run. Because the `config.js` file is a script, it can be included in other files, and it can be loaded using require, then we can access its static properties without the file being compiled.

## Other options

- We could store the configuration variables in `package.json`, and use `process.env` to get them at runtime.
- We could add a `.js` file as `config.js` that is required inside our applications.

Date: 2019-10-01

## Status

Accepted

## Context

We need to decide if we want to be able to run the front-end part of the Koshvani platform locally, to enable developers to work on the code, do rapid iterations and also debug it, or if we should assume that it will be deployed to the Koshvani Platform (aka the hosting platform), where it is currently being developed.

### Options

#### Option 1: Build the front-end as a component

If the front-end is a component, it means it can be built to be runnable in the local environment. It can be executed using a command-line execution.

#### Option 2: Treat the front-end as an application

If the front-end is treated as an application, it means it cannot be built to be runnable locally, and instead must be deployed to the Koshvani Platform.

#### Option 3: Hybrid

If the front-end is considered as a hybrid between a component and an application, it can be deployed to the hosting platform, but can also be run locally using a local runner, which will be responsible for everything that cannot be run on the hosting platform (authentication, authorization, database).

## Decision

We decided that we will build the front-end as a component, because this allows us to reduce the front-end components, as well as adding more functionalities to it, and also debug it during its development, as well as being able to have a locally available application. We don't want to have to deploy every front-end component for testing, and instead have the hosting platform be responsible for deploying the full application. Also, if we build it as a hybrid with a local runner, it means that the hosting platform only has the front-end portion of the application, and the runner would handle everything that cannot be run on the hosting platform. This makes it difficult to reason about the application, and we would have to add more runner services in different layers of the application, which increases cost of ownership and increases deployment/maintenance.

## Consequences

### Positive

A number of positives include:

- Can debug the front-end during its development
- Can deploy the front-end locally for rapid iterations
- Front-end can evolve without waiting on the hosting platform to make changes
- Developers can use existing testing mechanisms, such as Jest, Redux Jest, Cypress, etc.

### Negative

A number of negatives include:

- Front-end is not directly executed on the hosting platform
- Need to write front-end code in a way that can be run locally, such as using Node, Typescript, Redux, etc.
- May have to write adapters for the front-end components, so that the backend can run the front-end locally
- Increases cost of ownership, as more layers of the application need to be maintained
- Increases complexity of the application, as it has a local runner and a deployment package
- More services need to be maintained
- More deployments need to be done

Date: 2020-10-20

## Status

Accepted

## Context

The decision record for [ADR 8](./0008-using-enzymes-to-model-degradation-in-biogeochemical-cycles.md) stated that we were going to use enzymes to model degradation. Since then we implemented the initial prototype of the ODE system for biogeochemical cycles, which works with a linear mass action model. Therefore, we needed to decide on a scheme for representing enzyme concentrations as continuous, not discrete variables.

## Decision

We decided to implement our enzyme model by using a linear mass action model. Therefore, we decided to treat enzyme concentrations as if they were continuous variables which could be measured in real time. We also considered the use of functional (rather than discrete) data to specify the concentrations, so that we could specify enzyme concentrations with any degree of precision at the level of enzymes.

The reasons behind this decision were:
- to reduce the number of ODE and enzymes,
- to handle any future need to model enzyme concentrations with a greater degree of precision, and
- to allow future modelers to specify enzyme concentrations for the purpose of modeling and simulation.

Some of the reasons behind this decision are specific to our enzyme model, which is built around the assumption of linear mass action kinetics. These are the same as those listed in the initial decision record for that purpose.

## Consequences

We will use a linear mass action model as we have done in our initial prototype.

We can specify the concentrations of enzymes with any degree of precision which can be measured within the scope of the model.

The linear mass action model will allow us to use enzymes to model degradation of C and N. This will provide us with a method for implementing enzyme concentrations for the purpose of modeling and simulation.

# Use VRS Type in the Parser

* Status: accepted
* Deciders: Vijay Budhram, Lauren Zugai, Aaron Collier
* Date: 2019-04-03

## Context and Problem Statement

`VRSQuery` is a parser that generates a list of the required events for a
VRS based on a query string. The question is what is the best way to parse
those query strings.

## Considered Options

* Use a custom data structure (VRSType) to parse the query string.
* Use existing java data structure (String) to parse the query string.

## Decision Outcome

Chosen option: "Use a custom data structure", because it was important for the
parser to be able to do more than use split and regex. We had to be able to
process a wide variety of query strings for VRS. For example, the query
string "CVC" could generate a VRS that doesn't contain any events (i.e.
"CVC: 0"). Another example is querying for a specific type: "CVC: 1001",
which indicates that there are only 1001 events for that type.

### Positive Consequences

* Allows for more flexible queries, i.e. queries with sub-strings like "CVC"
and ranges like "CVC: 10-20"

### Negative Consequences

* A new class was added, but the changes to existing code were minimal.
* A new class was added that doesn't have a wide-range of examples.
* A new class was added, but the code uses existing classes and data structures
  (String, Arrays) extensively.

3. Deprecate Dynamics Service Locator
==================================

Date: 2018-12-04

Status
------

Accepted

Context
-------
We are seeking to improve how the platform identifies and uses registered services.

Issues:

1. The existing implementation of a service locator uses a fully-loaded service locator server as a cache so that we can
   avoid the time necessary to lookup all registered services. This introduces some complexity around how we manage
   which services are in the cache, and which services are not. This is exacerbated by the fact that the service locator
   server is an additional application.

2. The service locator server is also used as a service registration point as well as a service discovery point.
   * The cache is used as a registration point when services are created.
   * A fully-updated cache is used as a discovery point to provide service lookup abilities.

3. We have now moved away from using a service registry and towards using a direct service lookup from within the
   hosting platform.

Decision
--------

We are going to deprecate the Dynamics Service Locator.

Consequences
------------

This means we will stop registering and supplying a service locator to Dynamics. As we migrate to a usage based
service locator, this means that services will be available to Dynamics without us having to populate a service
registry.
